They came in a mist.

The Tuatha de Danaan, the people of the gods of Dana — some called them the Men of Dea — came through the air and the high air to Ireland, and nobody saw them come.

They came from the north. In the place they had left behind there had been four cities, and in those cities they had fought their long battle for learning: great Falias, and shining Gorias, and Finias, and rich Murias that lay to the south. Each city had a wise man to teach the young men skill and knowledge and perfect wisdom. Senias taught in Murias. Arias, the fair-haired poet, taught in Finias. Urias of the noble nature taught in Gorias. And Morias taught in Falias itself.

From those four cities they brought four treasures, and you should remember them, because treasures in stories like this are never only treasures.

From Falias they brought a Stone of Virtue, the Lia Fail, the Stone of Destiny.

From Gorias they brought a Sword.

From Finias they brought a Spear of Victory.

And from Murias they brought the Cauldron. No company ever went away from that Cauldron unsatisfied. Not one.

Nuada was king of the Tuatha de Danaan in those days. But Manannan, son of Lir, was greater than the king, and everybody knew it, and Nuada knew it too.

There were others who stood high among them. There was Ogma, the king's brother, who taught them writing. There was Diancecht, who understood healing. There was Neit, a god of battle. There was Credenus the Craftsman, and Goibniu the Smith.

And the women. The greatest among their women were Badb, a battle goddess; and Macha, whose mast-feeding — the acorns she fattened on, as a pig fattens in an oak wood — was the heads of men killed in battle; and the Morrigu, the Crow of Battle. There were Eire and Fodla and Banba, the three daughters of the Dagda, and each of the three would give her name to Ireland in the time to come. There was Eadon, the nurse of poets.

And there was Brigit.

Brigit was a woman of poetry, and the poets worshipped her, for her sway was very great and very noble. She was a woman of healing too, and a woman of smith's work, and it was Brigit who first made the whistle for calling from one person to another through the night. One side of her face was ugly. The other side was very comely. Her name meant Breo-saighit, a fiery arrow.

There were many others among the women, shadow-forms and great queens. But beyond them all was Dana, who was called the Mother of the Gods.

Three things they held above all others: the plough, and the sun, and the hazel-tree. So it was said, long after, that Ireland was divided between those three — Coll the hazel, and Cecht the plough, and Grian the sun.

Below the sea they had a well. Nine hazels of wisdom grew over it — the hazels of inspiration, of the knowledge of poetry. Their leaves and their blossoms broke out in the same hour, and fell together on the well in a shower that raised a purple wave. Five salmon waited in that water. They ate the nuts as they fell, and the colour of the nuts came out in the red spots of their skin, and anyone who ate one of those salmon would know all wisdom and all poetry. Seven streams of wisdom sprang from that well and turned back into it again, and the people of many arts have all drunk from it, whether they knew it or not.

It was on the first day of Beltaine, that we call May Day now, that the Tuatha de Danaan came, and they landed in the north-west of Connacht.

The Firbolgs were in Ireland before them. The Men of the Bag, they were called, and they had come up from the South. When the Tuatha de Danaan landed, the Firbolgs saw nothing at all. Only a mist, lying on the hills.

Eochaid, son of Erc, was king of the Firbolgs, and messengers came to him at Teamhair. A new race of people had come into Ireland, they said, and whether they had come out of the earth, or down from the skies, or in on the wind, nobody could say. They had settled themselves at Magh Rein.

The messengers expected Eochaid to be astonished.

He was not. A dream had come to him in the night, and when he asked his Druids what it meant, they told him that it would not be long until a strong enemy came against him. So he had been waiting.

Eochaid took counsel with his chief advisers, and they agreed to send a good champion of their own to look at the strangers and to speak with them. They chose Sreng, a great fighting man. Sreng rose up and took his strong red-brown shield, and his two thick-handled spears, and his sword, and his head-covering, and his thick iron club, and he set out from Teamhair towards the place where the strangers were, at Magh Rein.

The watchers of the Tuatha de Danaan saw him before he got there. They sent out a champion of their own to meet him and talk with him. His name was Bres, and he carried his shield and his sword and his two spears.

The two champions walked towards each other slowly. Each kept a careful watch on the other, and each wondered at the other's weapons. When they were close enough to talk, they stopped, and each put his shield in front of his body and struck it hard into the ground, and they looked at one another over the rims.

Bres spoke first.

When Sreng heard that it was Irish he was speaking — his own tongue — he was less uneasy. They drew closer, and asked each other about family and race, as men do.

After a while they put their shields away. Sreng admitted he had raised his in dread of the thin, sharp spears Bres was holding. Bres said he had been in dread of the thick-handled spears Sreng carried, and asked whether all the Firbolgs were armed like that. Sreng undid the tyings of his spears to show them better, and Bres marvelled at them: so strong, so heavy, and sharp along the sides even though they had no points.

"These are called Craisech," said Sreng. "They break through shields. They crush flesh and bone. A thrust from one is death, or a wound that never heals."

Then he looked at the spears Bres carried — sharp, thin, hard-pointed.

In the end they exchanged spears, so that the fighters on each side could see what weapons the others were used to.

And Bres gave Sreng a message to take back. If the Firbolgs would give up half of Ireland, his people would take that half and be content, and there would be peace. If they would not give up that much, there would be a battle.

Before they parted, the two men said to one another that whatever happened afterwards, they themselves would be friends.

Sreng went back to Teamhair. He gave the message, and he showed them the spear, and he told his people what he thought: share the country, and do not go into battle against a people whose weapons were so much better than their own.

Eochaid and his chief men talked it over. And in the end they said, "We will not give up half the country to these strangers. If we do, they will soon take the whole of it."

It is not clear they were wrong.

As for the Men of Dea: when Bres came back and showed them the heavy spear, and told them about the strong, fierce man he had got it from, how sturdy he was and how well armed, they thought it likely there would soon be a battle. So they moved from where they were to a better place, farther west in Connacht. They settled themselves on the plain of Magh Nia, and built walls and dug ditches, with the great mountain Belgata at their backs.

And while they were moving and building, three of their queens went to Teamhair, where the Firbolgs were making their plans. Badb and Macha and the Morrigu. By the power of their enchantments they brought mists and clouds of darkness over the whole place, and sent down showers of fire and showers of blood upon the people, so that for three days nobody could see anybody else, or speak to them.

At the end of the three days the three Druids of the Firbolgs broke the enchantment. Their names were Cesarn and Gnathach and Ingnathach.

The Firbolgs gathered their men. They came with eleven battalions and took their stand at the eastern end of the plain of Magh Nia.

Nuada, king of the Men of Dea, sent his poets to make the same offer as before: give up half the country, and he would be content with it. King Eochaid told the poets to put the question to his chief men, who were gathered there, and when they heard it they would not consent.

"When will you begin the battle, then?" asked the messengers.

"We need a delay," they said. "We want time to put our spears and our armour in order, to brighten our helmets and sharpen our swords, and to have spears made like the ones you carry. And as for you," they said, "you'll be wanting spears like our Craisechs made for yourselves."

So they agreed on a delay of a quarter of a year, for preparation. That is how battles were fought, then. Everybody was to be ready.

It was on a Midsummer day that the battle began.

Three times nine hurlers of the Tuatha de Danaan went out against three times nine hurlers of the Firbolgs. The Tuatha de Danaan lost, and every one of them was killed.

Eochaid sent a messenger to ask whether they would fight every day or every second day. Nuada answered that they would fight every day, but that there should always be exactly the same number of men fighting on each side. Eochaid agreed, but he was not pleased, for the Firbolgs had more men than the Men of Dea, and he had been counting on that.

The battle went on for four days. Great feats were done on each side, and a great many champions came to their deaths. And every evening, for those who were still alive, the physicians of each side made a bath of healing, with every healing plant and herb in it, so that the men would rise whole and strong for the next day's fighting.

On the fourth day the Men of Dea got the upper hand, and the Firbolgs were driven back.

In the middle of the fighting a great thirst came on Eochaid, their king. He went off the field to look for a drink, with three fifties of his men to guard him. Three fifties of the Tuatha de Danaan followed them, all the way to the strand called Traigh Eothaile. There was a fierce fight on that strand, and at the end of it King Eochaid fell. They buried him there, and raised a great heap of stones over his grave.

He had only wanted a drink of water.

When there were no more than three hundred men left out of the eleven battalions of the Firbolgs, with Sreng at the head of them, Nuada offered them peace, and their choice of any one of the five provinces of Ireland. Sreng said they would take Connacht. He and his people lived there after, and their children after them. Ferdiad came of that people in the time to come, who made so good a fight against Cuchulain; and so did Erc, son of Cairbre, who gave Cuchulain his death.

That battle, the first the Men of Dea fought in Ireland, is called by some the first battle of Magh Tuireadh.

The Tuatha de Danaan took Teamhair for themselves.

It had other names. Druim Cain, the Beautiful Ridge. Liathdruim, the Grey Ridge. Druim na Descan, the Ridge of the Outlook. All of those were Teamhair. And from that time on it stood above every other place, for the king who held it was the High King over all Ireland.

The king's rath lay to the north. The Hill of the Hostages lay to the north-east of the High Seat, and the Green of Teamhair lay west of the Hill of the Hostages. North-east, in the Hill of the Sidhe, was a well called Nemnach, and out of it flowed a stream called Nith, and on that stream the first mill in Ireland was built.

North of the Hill of the Hostages stood the stone, the Lia Fail. It roared under the feet of every king who would take possession of Ireland. It still knew what it was for.

Near the House of the Women was the Wall of the Three Whispers. The House of the Women had seven doors to the east and seven doors to the west, and the feasts of Teamhair were held there. There was the Great House of a Thousand Soldiers, too, and near it, to the south, the little Hill of the Woman Soldiers.

That was Teamhair. The gods had it now.

But a king who has won a country must still keep it, and there was a thing about Nuada that nobody had spoken of yet.

Nuada won the battle. But he lost his arm in it. Sreng struck it off, and from that loss came trouble and vexation on all his people.

This was the law of the Tuatha de Danaan: no man who was not perfect in his shape could be king. It did not matter that Nuada had won. It did not matter that he had lost the arm winning. The law was the law, and they put him out of the kingship.

The king they chose in his place was Bres.

Bres was the most beautiful of all their young men. He was so beautiful that when people wanted to praise anything beautiful — a plain, a dun, ale, a flame, a woman, a man, a horse — what they said was, "It is as beautiful as Bres." His mother was a woman of the Tuatha de Danaan. Who his father was, nobody knew but her.

Beauty is not the same as luck, and it is not the same as goodness. Bres's reign brought no good fortune to his people.

The Fomor lived beyond the sea — or below the sea, to the west, some say — and in the days of Bres they began to put tribute on the Men of Dea, so as to bring them under their own rule.

The Fomor had first come to Ireland long before. They were dreadful to look at, and maimed: they had only one foot, or only one hand, and they were led by a giant and his mother. No army more horrible or more dreadful than that army of the Fomor ever came to Ireland. They had been friendly enough with the Firbolgs, and content to leave Ireland to them. But between the Fomor and the Men of Dea there was jealousy.

The tax they put on them was hard. A third part of their corn. A third part of their milk. A third part of their children. There was no smoke rising from any roof in Ireland that was not under tribute to the Fomor.

And Bres made no stand against them. He let them have their way.

Bres had his own tax, too. On every house in Ireland he put a demand for the milk of hornless dun cows, or of cows of some other single colour — enough milk for a hundred men.

Once, to deceive him, Nechtan singed every cow in Ireland in a fire of fern, and smeared them with the ashes of flax seed, so that they were all dark brown. He did that on the advice of the Druid Findgoll, son of Findemas.

Another time they made three hundred cows out of wood, with dark brown pails where their udders should have been, and filled the pails with black bog stuff. Bres came to look at the cows and to watch them being milked, and Cian, the father of Lugh, was there. When the cows were milked it was the bog stuff that squeezed out. Bres drank it, thinking it was milk, and he was not the better of it for a long time.

There was another thing against Bres. He was not open-handed.

The chief men of the Tuatha de Danaan grumbled. Their knives were never greased with meat in his house. However often they visited him, they went home with no smell of ale on their breath. There was no pleasure in his house and no merriment, and there was no call for poets, or singers, or harpers, or pipers, or horn-blowers, or jugglers, or fools. They had been used to watch their champions in trials of strength. Now the only use anybody's strength was put to was working for the king.

Ogma himself, the shining poet, was ordered to bring firewood to the palace every day, for the whole army, from the Islands of Mod. He was so weak for want of food that every day the sea swept away two-thirds of his bundle.

The Dagda was put to building raths, for he was a good builder, and he dug a trench round Rath Brese. The work tired him often. Once he nearly gave out altogether for want of food, and this is how that happened.

There was an idle blind man in the house, Cridenbel by name, with a sharp tongue, and he coveted the Dagda's share of food, for he thought his own was small beside it. He said to the Dagda, "For the sake of your good name, let the three best bits of your share be given to me."

The Dagda gave in to that, every night. And he suffered for it, because what the blind man called a bit was the size of a good pig, and with his three bits he took a full third of everything.

One day, when the Dagda was down in the trench, he saw his son, Angus Og, coming towards him.

"That's a good meeting," said Angus. "But what's wrong with you? You don't look well today."

"There's a reason for that," said the Dagda. "Every evening Cridenbel the blind man demands the three best bits of my share of food, and takes them from me."

"I'll give you some advice," said Angus. He put his hand into his bag and took out three pieces of gold and gave them to his father.

"Put these into the three bits you give Cridenbel this evening," he said. "Then they'll be the best bits in the dish. And the gold will turn inside him, and he'll die."

That evening the Dagda did it. No sooner had Cridenbel swallowed the gold than he died.

Some of the people went to the king. "The Dagda has killed Cridenbel," they said. "He gave him some deadly herb."

The king believed it. He was angry with the Dagda, and gave orders that he should be put to death.

"That is not the right judgment of a prince," said the Dagda. And he told them everything: how Cridenbel used to say, "Give me the three best bits in front of you, for my own share isn't good tonight." "And tonight," said the Dagda, "the three best things in front of me were three pieces of gold. So I gave them to him. And he died."

The king ordered the body to be cut open. They found the gold inside, and they knew the Dagda had told the truth.

The next day Angus came to him again. "Your work will soon be done," he said. "When they come to pay you your wages, take nothing they offer until the cattle of Ireland are brought before you. Then choose a heifer, black and black-maned. I'll tell you how to know her."

So when the Dagda had finished his work, and they asked him what reward he wanted, he did what Angus had told him. Bres thought that was foolishness. He had expected the Dagda to ask for far more than one heifer.

Then, at last, a poet came to the king's house looking for hospitality. He was Corpre, son of Etain, a poet of the Tuatha de Danaan.

This is how he was treated. They put him in a little, dark, narrow house, with no fire in it, no furniture, no bed. For his feast they brought him three small cakes, dry ones, on a little dish.

When he rose up in the morning he was not thankful. As he crossed the green, this is what he said:

"Without food ready on a dish; without milk enough for a calf to grow on; without shelter; without light in the darkness of night; without enough to pay a story-teller: may that be the prosperity of Bres."

From that day there was no good luck with Bres. He went downhill from then on, and he never stopped going.

That was the first satire ever made in Ireland. It will not be the last. Words, in Ireland, are weapons, and poets know it, and so, eventually, do kings.

Now, as for Nuada. After his arm was struck off he lay sick for a while. Then Diancecht the healer made him an arm of silver, with movement in every finger of it, and fitted it on him. From that day he was called Nuada Argat-lamh, Nuada of the Silver Hand.

But Miach, son of Diancecht, was a better healer than his father, and had done many things.

He met a young man at Teamhair once who had only one eye. "If you're a good physician," said the young man, "you'll put an eye in the place of the one I lost."

"I could put the eye of that cat in your lap in its place," said Miach.

"I'd like that well," said the young man.

So Miach put the cat's eye in his head. And the young man would as soon have been without it afterwards. When he wanted to sleep, that was when the eye would start open at the squeaking of the mice, or the flight of birds, or the movement of the rushes. And when he wanted to watch an army or a gathering, that was when the eye was sure to be fast asleep.

Miach was not satisfied with what his father had done for the king. He took Nuada's own hand, the one that had been struck off, and brought it to him and set it in its place.

"Joint to joint," he said, "and sinew to sinew."

Three days and three nights he stayed with the king. On the first day he held the hand against Nuada's side. On the second day he held it against his breast, until it was covered with skin. On the third day he laid bulrushes on it that had been blackened in the fire. And at the end of that time the king was healed.

Diancecht was vexed to see his son do a better cure than he had done himself.

He threw his sword at Miach's head. It cut the flesh, but the boy healed the wound with his skill. Diancecht threw it again. This time it reached the bone, and the boy was able to heal that too. Then Diancecht struck him a third time, and a fourth, until he cut out the brain, because he knew there was no physician who could cure that.

Miach died, and his father buried him.

Herbs grew up out of his grave, one for every joint and sinew in his body: three hundred and sixty-five of them. Airmed, his sister, came and spread out her cloak, and laid the herbs out on it in order, according to their virtues.

Diancecht saw her doing it. He came and mixed up the herbs.

That is why nobody knows all their right powers, even to this day.

When the Tuatha de Danaan saw Nuada as whole as he had been before, they gathered at Teamhair, where Bres was, and told him to give up the kingship, for he had held it long enough. He had to give it up, though he was not willing, and Nuada was king again.

Bres was sick with anger. He searched his mind for a way to be revenged on those who had put him out, and for a way to gather an army against them. And he went to his mother, Eri, daughter of Delbaith, and asked her to tell him what his race was.

"I know that well," she said.

She told him then that his father was a king of the Fomor, Elathan, son of Dalbaech. He had come to her once over a level sea, in some great vessel that seemed to be made of silver — she could never see its shape. He looked like a young man with yellow hair, and his clothes were sewn with gold, and he wore five rings of gold about his neck. She had refused the love of all the young men of her own people. She gave her love to him. And when he left her, she cried.

He had given her a ring from his hand, and told her to give it only to the man whose finger it would fit. Then he went away the same way he had come.

She brought out the ring for Bres. He put it on his middle finger, and it fitted him well.

They went together to the hill where she had stood when she saw the silver vessel coming, and down to the strand, and she and Bres and his people set out for the country of the Fomor.

When they came to that country they found a great plain, with many gatherings of people on it. They went to the gathering that looked the best, and the people there asked where they came from, and they said they came from Ireland.

"Have you hounds with you?" the people asked. It was the custom then, when strangers came to a gathering, to offer them some friendly challenge.

"We have hounds," said Bres.

The hounds were matched against each other, and the hounds of the Tuatha de Danaan were better than the hounds of the Fomor.

"Have you horses for a race?"

"We have," said Bres. And the horses of the Tuatha de Danaan beat the horses of the Fomor.

Then they asked whether anyone among them was good with a sword, and they said Bres was the best of them. But when Bres put his hand to his sword, Elathan his father, who was there in the gathering, knew the ring on it.

"Who is this young man?" he asked.

Then Bres's mother answered, and told him the whole story, and that Bres was his own son.

His father was sorrowful at that. "What drove you out of the country you were king over?" he asked.

And Bres, to his credit, told the truth. "Nothing drove me out but my own injustice and my own hardness. I took their treasures from the people, and their jewels, and their very food. There were never taxes on them before I was their king."

"That is bad," said his father. "It was their prosperity you should have thought of, more than your own kingship. Their good-will would have been better to you than their curses. And what have you come here looking for?"

"I've come looking for fighting men," said Bres, "so that I can take Ireland by force."

"You have no right to get it by injustice," said his father, "when you could not keep it by justice."

"What advice have you for me, then?" said Bres.

Elathan told him to go to the chief king of the Fomor, to see what advice and what help that king would give him.

The chief king of the Fomor was Balor of the Evil Eye.

After Nuada of the Silver Hand was back in the kingship, he held a great feast at Teamhair.

There were two door-keepers at Teamhair: Gamal, son of Figal, and Camel, son of Riagall. A young man came to the door where one of them stood, and asked to be brought in to the king.

"Who are you?" said the door-keeper.

"I am Lugh," said the young man. "Son of Cian of the Tuatha de Danaan, and of Ethlinn, daughter of Balor, King of the Fomor. I am foster-son of Taillte, daughter of the King of the Great Plain, and of Echaid the Rough, son of Duach."

"And what are you skilled in?" said the door-keeper. "Nobody without an art comes into Teamhair."

"Question me," said Lugh. "I am a carpenter."

"We don't want you. We have a carpenter already: Luchtar, son of Luachaid."

"Then I am a smith."

"We have a smith already: Colum Cuaillemech of the Three New Ways."

"Then I am a champion."

"No use to us. We have a champion: Ogma, the king's brother."

"Question me again," said Lugh. "I am a harper."

"No use to us. We have a harper: Abhean, son of Bicelmos, that the Men of the Three Gods brought out of the hills."

"I am a poet," said Lugh, "and a teller of tales."

"No use. We have a teller of tales: Ere, son of Ethaman."

"And I am a magician."

"No use. We have plenty of magicians, and people of power."

"I am a physician."

"No use. We have Diancecht for our physician."

"Let me be a cup-bearer."

"We don't want you. We have nine cup-bearers."

"I am a good worker in brass."

"We have a worker in brass already: Credne Cerd."

Then Lugh said, "Go and ask the king whether he has any one man who can do all of these things. If he has, I won't ask to come into Teamhair."

The door-keeper went in to the king and told him all of it. "There's a young man at the door," he said, "and his name ought to be the Ildánach, the Master of All Arts. Every single thing the people of your house can do, he can do all of them."

"Try him at the chess-boards," said Nuada.

The chess-boards were brought out. Every game that was played, Lugh won.

When Nuada was told that, he said, "Let him in. The like of him never came into Teamhair before."

So the door-keeper let him pass, and Lugh came into the king's house and sat down in the seat of knowledge.

There was a great flagstone in that house that four times twenty yoke of oxen could hardly have moved. Ogma picked it up and hurled it out through the house, so that it landed outside Teamhair. It was a challenge. Lugh hurled it back, and it landed in the middle of the king's house.

Then he played the harp for them. He had them laughing, and then he had them crying, and at the end he put them all to sleep with a sleepy tune.

When Nuada had seen all the things Lugh could do, he began to think that with this young man's help the country might get free of the taxes and the tyranny the Fomor had put on it. And this is what he did: he came down from his throne, and he put Lugh on it in his place for thirteen days, so that they could all listen to the advice he would give.

A king who will step down from his own throne for the sake of his people is rarer than a king with a silver hand.

This is the story of the birth of Lugh.

In the days when the Fomor used to come to Ireland, Balor of the Strong Blows — or, as some called him, Balor of the Evil Eye — lived on the Island of the Tower of Glass. It was dangerous for ships to go near that island, for the Fomor would come out and take them.

Some say that the sons of Nemed, in the old time before the Firbolgs came to Ireland, passed close to it in their ships. What they saw was a tower of glass in the middle of the sea, and on the tower something that looked like men. They went against it with Druid spells, and the Fomor worked against them with Druid spells of their own. The sons of Nemed attacked the tower, and it vanished, and they thought they had destroyed it. Then a great wave rose over them, and all their ships went down, and everybody in them.

And the tower was there as it had always been, and Balor living in it.

This is why he was called Balor of the Evil Eye. There was a power of death in one of his eyes, so that nobody could look into it and live. It got that power like this: once, when he was young, he passed a house where his father's Druids were making spells of death. The window was open and he looked in, and the smoke of the poisonous spells was rising, and it went into his eye. From that day on he had to keep that eye closed, unless he wanted to be the death of some enemy. Then the men who were with him would lift the eyelid with a ring of ivory.

A Druid once foretold that Balor would get his death from his own grandson.

At that time Balor had only one child, a daughter named Ethlinn. When he heard what the Druid said, he shut her up in the tower on the island. He put twelve women with her to take charge of her and guard her, and he told them never to let her see a man, or hear the name of a man.

So Ethlinn grew up in the tower, and she grew very beautiful. Sometimes she saw men passing in their currachs. Sometimes she saw a man in her dreams. But when she spoke about it to the women, they would give her no answer.

You can lock a girl in a tower. You cannot lock up what she dreams.

So Balor had no fear. He went on with war and robbery the way he always had, seizing every ship that passed, and sometimes crossing over to Ireland to do destruction there.

Now it happened that at that time three brothers of the Tuatha de Danaan lived together in a place called Druim na Teine, the Ridge of the Fire. They were Goibniu, and Samthainn, and Cian. Cian was a lord of land. Goibniu was the smith with the great name.

Cian had a wonderful cow, the Glas Gaibhnenn, and her milk never failed. Everyone who heard of her coveted her, and many had tried to steal her, so she had to be watched night and day.

Once Cian wanted some swords made, and he went to Goibniu's forge, leading the Glas Gaibhnenn by a halter. When he got to the forge both his brothers were there, for Samthainn had brought some steel to have weapons made for himself. Cian asked Samthainn to hold the halter while he went in to speak with Goibniu.

Balor had set his mind on the Glas Gaibhnenn a long time before, but he had never been able to get near her. Now he was watching, not far away. When he saw Samthainn holding the cow he put on the appearance of a little red-haired boy, and came up to him, and told him he had heard the two brothers in the forge saying to each other that they would use all of Samthainn's steel for their own swords, and make his out of iron.

"By my word," said Samthainn, "they won't cheat me so easily. You hold the cow, little lad, and I'll go in to them."

He rushed into the forge in a great rage. And the moment Balor had the halter in his hand he set off, dragging the Glas behind him, down to the strand and across the sea to his own island.

When Cian saw his brother come in, he rushed out. There were Balor and the Glas, out on the sea.

There was nothing he could do then but reproach his brother, and wander about as if his wits had left him, not knowing any way to get his cow back from Balor. At last he went to a Druid for advice. The Druid told him that while Balor lived the cow would never be brought back, for nobody would go within reach of his Evil Eye.

Then Cian went to a woman-Druid, Birog of the Mountain, for her help.

She dressed him in a woman's clothes and carried him across the sea on a blast of wind, to the tower where Ethlinn was. She called up to the women in the tower and asked them for shelter for a high queen she had just saved from some hardship. The women did not like to refuse a woman of the Tuatha de Danaan, and they let her in, and her companion with her. Then Birog put them all into a deep sleep with her enchantments, and Cian went to speak with Ethlinn.

When Ethlinn saw him, she said that was the face she had seen in her dreams.

She gave him her love. After a while he was taken away again, on a blast of wind.

When her time came, Ethlinn gave birth to a son. When Balor knew of it he ordered his people to wrap the child in a cloth, fasten it with a pin, and throw him into a current of the sea. As they were carrying the child across an arm of the sea, the pin dropped out, and the child slipped out of the cloth into the water, and they thought he had drowned.

But Birog of the Mountain took him away and brought him to his father, Cian. And Cian gave him to be fostered by Taillte, daughter of the King of the Great Plain.

That is how Lugh was born and reared.

Some say Balor came afterwards and struck the head off Cian on a white stone, and that the stone has the marks of blood on it to this day. It is more likely that it was some other man whose head he struck off, for it was the sons of Tuireann who brought Cian to his death. That is a different story, and a worse one.

After Lugh had come to Teamhair and made up his mind to join his father's people against the Fomor, he set himself to the work. He went to a quiet place in Grellach Dollaid, with Nuada and the Dagda and Ogma, and Goibniu and Diancecht were sent for to join them there. A full year they stayed there, making their plans in secret, so that the Fomor would not know they meant to rise against them until everything was ready, and until they knew their own strength. From that council the place got its name afterwards: the Whisper of the Men of Dea.

They broke up the council and agreed to meet again on that same day three years later. Each of them went his own way, and Lugh went back to his own friends, the sons of Manannan.

A good while after that, Nuada was holding a great assembly of the people on the Hill of Uisnech, to the west of Teamhair. They had not been there long when they saw an armed troop coming towards them from the east, across the plain. There was a young man at the front of the troop, commanding the rest, and the brightness of his face was like the setting sun, so that they could not look at him for the brightness of it.

When he came nearer they knew him. It was Lugh Lamh-Fada, Lugh of the Long Hand, come back to them.

With him were the Riders of the Sidhe from the Land of Promise, and his own foster-brothers, the sons of Manannan: Sgoith Gleigeil, the White Flower; and Goitne Gorm-Shuileach, the Blue-eyed Spear; and Sine Sindearg, of the Red Ring; and Donall Donn-Ruadh, of the Red-brown Hair.

This is how Lugh came.

Under him was Manannan's horse, the Aonbharr, of the One Mane. She was as swift as the naked cold wind of spring. The sea was the same as dry land to her. And nobody riding her was ever killed on her back.

On him was Manannan's breastplate, which kept whoever wore it from wounds.

On his head was a helmet with two beautiful precious stones set in the front and one at the back. When he took it off, his forehead was like the sun on a dry summer's day.

And at his side was Manannan's sword, the Freagarthach, the Answerer. Nobody wounded by it ever got away alive. And when that sword was bared in a battle, any man who saw it coming against him had no more strength left in him than a woman in childbirth.

The troop came up to where the King of Ireland was with the Tuatha de Danaan, and they welcomed each other.

They had not been there long before they saw another troop coming, a surly, slovenly one. It was nine times nine of the messengers of the Fomor, coming to collect rent and taxes from the men of Ireland. The four hardest and cruellest of them were Eine and Eathfaigh and Coron and Compar. The Tuatha de Danaan were in such dread of those four that not one of them would so much as punish his own son or his foster-son without their leave.

The Fomor came up to where the King of Ireland was with the Riders of the Sidhe, and the king and all the Tuatha de Danaan stood up for them.

"Why do you stand up for that surly, slovenly troop," said Lugh of the Long Hand, "when you didn't stand up for us?"

"We have to," said the king. "If there were only a child of ours sitting in front of them, they wouldn't think that too small a reason to kill him."

"By my word," said Lugh, "there's a great desire coming on me to kill them."

"That would bring harm on us," said the king. "We'd meet our own death and destruction through it."

"You have been under this oppression too long," said Lugh.

And with that he started up and went at the Fomor, killing and wounding, until he had made an end of eight nines of them. The last nine he let go, under the protection of Nuada the king.

"I would kill you along with the others," he told them, "but I'd sooner you carried the news to your own country than any of my people, in case they got some ill-treatment there."

So the nine went back until they came to Lochlann, where the men of the Fomor were, and told the story from beginning to end: how a young, well-featured lad had come into Ireland and killed all the tax-gatherers but themselves. "And the reason he let us go," they said, "was so that we could tell you the story ourselves."

"Do you know who this young man is?" said Balor of the Evil Eye.

"I know well," said Ceithlenn, his wife. "He is the son of your daughter and mine. And it was foretold that from the day he came into Ireland, we would never have power there again, for ever."

Then the chief men of the Fomor went into council. There was Eab, son of Neid, and Seanchab, grandson of Neid, and Sital Salmhor, and Liath, son of Lobais; and the nine poets of the Fomor, who had learning and the gift of foreknowledge; and Lobais the Druid; and Balor himself, and his twelve white-mouthed sons; and Ceithlenn of the Crooked Teeth, his queen.

It was just then that Bres and his father Elathan had come to ask the Fomor for help.

"I'll go to Ireland myself," said Bres, "with seven great battalions of the Riders of the Fomor, and I'll give battle to this Ildánach, this master of all arts. I'll strike his head off and bring it back here to you, to the green of Berbhe."

"That would be a fitting thing for you to do," they all said.

"Then let my ships be made ready," said Bres, "and let food and provisions be put in them."

They made no delay. They readied the ships and filled them with food and drink, and the two swift Luaths were sent out to gather the army to Bres. When they were all gathered they made ready their armour and their weapons, and they set out for Ireland.

Balor the king followed them down to the harbour.

"Give battle to that Ildánach," he said, "and strike his head off. Then tie that island they call Ireland to the backs of your ships, and let the destroying water take its place. Put it on the north side of Lochlann. Not one of the Men of Dea will follow it there, to the end of life and time."

Then they pushed out their ships and raised their painted sails, and went out of the harbour onto the untilled country, the ridges of the wide-lying sea. They never turned from their course until they came to the harbour of Eas Dara. From there they sent an army through West Connacht, and destroyed it altogether, through and through.

The King of Connacht at that time was Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda.

Lugh of the Long Hand was at Teamhair with the King of Ireland when it was shown to him that the Fomor had landed at Eas Dara.

He made ready Manannan's horse, the Aonbharr, in the hour between day and night, and he went to Nuada the king. He told him that the Fomor had landed at Eas Dara and had spoiled Bodb Dearg's country. "And what I want," he said, "is your help to give battle to them."

But Nuada was not minded to avenge a destruction that had been done to Bodb Dearg and not to himself.

Lugh did not like that answer. He rode out of Teamhair, westward.

Presently he saw three armed men coming towards him. They were his own father Cian, and Cian's brothers Cu and Ceithen: the three sons of Cainte. They greeted him.

"What has you up so early?" they said.

"I have good cause," said Lugh. "The Fomor have come into Ireland and robbed Bodb Dearg. What help will you give me against them?"

"Each one of us will keep a hundred off you in the battle," they said.

"That's a good help," said Lugh. "But there's a help I'd sooner have from you than that. Gather the Riders of the Sidhe to me, from every place where they are."

So Cu and Ceithen went south, and Cian went north, and Cian did not stop until he reached the Plain of Muirthemne. As he was crossing the plain he saw three armed men ahead of him. They were the three sons of Tuireann, son of Ogma.

Here is what you need to know. Between the three sons of Tuireann and the three sons of Cainte there was hatred and enmity, and whenever they met there was sure to be fighting.

"If my two brothers were here," Cian said to himself, "we'd make a brave fight of it. Since they're not, it's best for me to fall back."

There was a great herd of pigs near him. He struck himself with a Druid rod, and it put on him the shape of one of the pigs of the herd, and he began rooting up the ground like the rest of them.

"Did you see that armed man walking the plain a while ago?" said Brian, one of the sons of Tuireann, to his brothers.

"We saw him," they said.

"Do you know what took him away?"

"We don't."

"It's a pity you don't keep a better watch over the open country in a time of war," said Brian. "I know well what happened to him. He struck himself with his Druid rod into the shape of one of these pigs, and he's rooting up the ground now like any of them. And whoever he is, he's no friend of ours."

"That's bad for us," said the other two. "The pigs belong to one of the Tuatha de Danaan. Even if we kill every one of them, the Druid pig might still get away from us in the end."

"You got your learning badly in the city of learning," said Brian, "if you can't tell an enchanted beast from a natural one."

And as he said it he struck his two brothers with his own Druid rod, and turned them into two thin, fast hounds, and they began to yelp sharply on the track of the enchanted pig.

It was not long before the pig broke out from among the others. Not one of the others ran, only that one. It made for a wood, and at the edge of the wood Brian threw his spear, and the spear went through its body.

The pig cried out. "That was a bad thing you did, throwing at me when you knew who I was."

"It seems to me you talk like a man," said Brian.

"I was a man indeed," said the pig. "I am Cian, son of Cainte. Give me your protection now."

"I swear by the gods of the air," said Brian, "that if the life came back into you seven times, I would take it from you every time."

"If that's how it is," said Cian, "give me one request. Let me go back into my own shape."

"We'll do that," said Brian. "It's easier for me to kill a man than a pig."

So Cian took his own shape again. "Give me mercy now," he said.

"We will not," said Brian.

"Well, I've got the better of you all the same," said Cian. "If you had killed me in the shape of a pig, there'd only be the blood-price of a pig on me. But since you'll kill me in my own shape, there never was and never will be anyone killed for whose sake a heavier fine will be paid than for me. And the weapons I'm killed with, they will tell the deed to my son."

"Then it's not with weapons you'll be killed," said Brian, "but with the stones lying on the ground."

And they pelted him with stones, fiercely and roughly, until all that was left of him was a poor, miserable, broken heap. They buried him the depth of a man's body in the earth.

The earth would not take that murder from them. It cast the body up again.

Brian said it should go back into the earth, and they put it in a second time, and a second time the earth would not take it. Six times the sons of Tuireann buried the body, and six times it was cast up. The seventh time they put it underground, the earth kept it.

Then they went on to join Lugh of the Long Hand for the battle.

As for Lugh: after he parted from his father he went on from Teamhair, westward. He went to the hills that were called afterwards Gairech and Ilgairech, and to the ford of the Shannon that is called Athluain now, and to Bearna nah-Eadargana, the Gap of Separation, and over Magh Luirg, the Plain of Following, and to Corr Slieve na Seaghsa, the Round Mountain of the Poet's Spring, and to the head of Sean-Slieve, and through the place of the bright-faced Corann, and from there to Magh Mor an Aonaigh, the Great Plain of the Fair. That was where the Fomor were, and the spoils of Connacht with them.

Bres, son of Elathan, stood up and said, "It's a wonder to me that the sun is rising in the west today, when every other day it rises in the east."

"It would be better for us if it were the sun," said the Druids.

"What else is it?"

"It is the shining of the face of Lugh, son of Ethlinn."

Lugh came up to them and greeted them.

"Why do you come to us like a friend?" they said.

"There's good cause for that," he said. "Only half of me is of the Tuatha de Danaan. The other half is yours. Now give me back the milch cows of the men of Ireland."

"May early good luck never come to you," said one of them, angrily, "until you get either a dry cow or a milch cow here."

Lugh stayed near them three days and three nights, and at the end of that time the Riders of the Sidhe came to him. Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, came with twenty-nine hundred men.

"Why are you so slow to give battle?" he said.

"I was waiting for you," said Lugh.

Then the kings and chief men of the men of Ireland put on their armour, and raised the points of their spears over their heads, and made close fences of their shields. They attacked their enemies on Magh Mor an Aonaigh, and their enemies answered them. They threw their whining spears at each other, and when the spears were broken they drew their swords from their blue-bordered sheaths and struck at each other, and thickets of brown flame rose above them from the bitterness of their many-edged weapons.

Lugh saw the battle-pen where Bres, son of Elathan, was. He made a fierce attack on him and on the men guarding him, until he had made an end of two hundred of them.

When Bres saw that, he gave himself up to Lugh's protection. "Give me my life this time," he said, "and I'll bring the whole race of the Fomor to fight it out with you in a great battle. I bind myself to that by the sun and the moon, the sea and the land."

So Lugh gave him his life. Then the Druids who were with Bres asked for his protection too.

"By my word," said Lugh, "if the whole race of the Fomor put itself under my protection, I would not destroy them."

So Bres and the Druids set out for their own country.

Now, Lugh and the sons of Tuireann.

After the battle of Magh Mor an Aonaigh, Lugh met two of his kinsmen and asked them whether they had seen his father in the fight.

"We did not," they said.

"Then I'm sure he's not living," said Lugh. "And I give my word that no food or drink will go into my mouth until I know by what death my father died."

He set out, with the Riders of the Sidhe behind him, and came to the place where he and his father had parted, and from there to the place where his father had gone into the shape of a pig when he saw the sons of Tuireann.

When Lugh came to that place, the earth spoke to him.

"Your father was in great danger here, Lugh," it said, "when he saw the sons of Tuireann in front of him. It was into the shape of a pig he had to go. But it was in his own shape they killed him."

Lugh told that to his people. He found the place where his father was buried and told them to dig, so that he would know by what death the sons of Tuireann had made an end of him.

They raised the body out of the grave and looked at it. It was all one bed of wounds.

"It was the death of an enemy the sons of Tuireann gave my dear father," said Lugh.

He kissed him three times.

"I am in a bad way after this death," he said. "I can hear nothing with my ears. I can see nothing with my eyes. There is no living pulse in my heart, for grief after my father. You gods I worship — it's a pity I wasn't here when this was done. And it is a great thing that has been done here: that the people of the gods of Dana have done treachery on one another. They will be at a loss by it for a long time, and weakened by it. And from this out, Ireland will never be free of trouble, east or west."

They put Cian under the earth again. There was keening over his grave, and a stone was raised on it, and his name was written on it in Ogham.

"This hill will take its name from Cian," said Lugh, "though he himself is stripped and broken. It was the sons of Tuireann did this thing, and grief and anguish will fall on them from it, and on their children after them. It's no lying story I'm telling you. And it's a pity the way I am, and my heart is broken in my breast, since Cian, the brave man, is not living."

Then he told his people to go on ahead of him to Teamhair. "But don't tell the story," he said, "until I tell it myself."

When Lugh came to Teamhair he sat in the high seat of the king, and he looked about him, and he saw the three sons of Tuireann.

Those three were beyond everyone else at Teamhair in those days for quickness and skill, for a good hand in battle, for beauty, and for an honourable name.

Lugh told his people to shake the chain of silence. They shook it, and everyone listened.

"What are your minds fixed on at this moment, Men of Dea?" said Lugh.

"On yourself, indeed," they said.

"I have a question for you. What vengeance would each of you take on the man who killed your father?"

They were astonished to hear it. One of the chief men said, "Tell us — was it your own father who was killed?"

"It was indeed," said Lugh. "And I see in this house now the men who killed him, and they know better than I do what way they killed him."

"It's not the death of a single day I'd give the man who killed my father, if I had him in my power," said the king. "I'd cut off one of his limbs from day to day until I'd made an end of him."

All the chief men said the same. So did the sons of Tuireann, with the rest.

"The three men who killed my father are among those making that answer," said Lugh. "Let them pay the fine for him now, since you're all together in the one place. And if they won't, I will not break the protection of the king's house — but they must make no attempt to leave this house until they have settled with me."

"If it were I who had killed your father," said the king, "I'd be well content for you to take a fine from me for him."

"It's at us Lugh is saying all this," said the sons of Tuireann among themselves.

"Let's admit the killing of his father to him," said Iuchar and Iucharba.

"I'm afraid," said Brian, "that he wants us to admit it in front of everyone, and then he won't let us off with a fine afterwards."

"It's best to admit it," said the others. "And you speak it, since you're the eldest."

So Brian, son of Tuireann, said: "It's at us you're speaking, Lugh, because you think we've gone against the sons of Cainte before now. We didn't kill your father. But we'll pay the fine for him the same as if we had."

Notice what Brian did there. He denied it and paid for it in the same breath.

"I'll take a fine from you that you don't expect," said Lugh. "I'll say here what it is, and if it's too much for you, I'll let you off part of it."

"Let's hear it," they said.

"Here it is," said Lugh. "Three apples. And the skin of a pig. And a spear. And two horses, and a chariot. And seven pigs. And a dog's whelp. And a cooking-spit. And three shouts on a hill. That is the fine I'm asking. If it's too much for you, part of it will be taken off you presently. If you don't think it too much, pay it."

"It isn't too much," said Brian. "A hundred times as much wouldn't be too much. And because it's so small, we think it likely you have some treachery hidden behind it."

"I don't think it too little a fine," said Lugh. "And I give you the guarantee of the Tuatha de Danaan that I'll ask nothing else, and that I'll be faithful to you. Now give me the same pledge."

"It's a pity for you to ask that," said Brian. "Our own pledge is as good as any pledge in the world."

"Your own pledge isn't enough," said Lugh. "It's often the like of you promised to pay a fine this way, and tried to back out of it afterwards."

So the sons of Tuireann bound themselves by the King of Ireland, and by Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, and by the chief men of the Tuatha de Danaan, that they would pay that fine to Lugh.

"It would be as well now," said Lugh, "to give you a better knowledge of the fine."

"It would indeed," they said.

"This is how it is, then," said Lugh.

"The three apples I asked of you are the three apples from the Garden in the East of the World. No other apples will do. They are the most beautiful apples in the whole world, and there is the most virtue in them. They are the colour of burnt gold, and the size of the head of a child a month old, and they taste of honey. Whoever eats them is left with no pain of wounds and no vexation of sickness. And they never grow less for being eaten.

"The skin I asked of you is the pig-skin of Tuis, King of Greece. It heals all the wounds and all the sickness of the world. Whatever danger a man is in, if the skin can only reach him while there's life in him, it will cure him. This is how it was with that pig: every stream it went through was turned into wine for nine days after, and every wound it touched was healed. The Druids of Greece said the virtue wasn't in the pig but in the skin, so they skinned it, and the skin has been there ever since. And I don't think it will be easy for you to get it, with leave or without."

"And do you know what spear I'm asking for?"

"We don't."

"It is a very deadly spear that belongs to the King of Persia. The Luin, it's called. Every choice deed is done with it. Its head is kept steeped in a vessel of water, so that it won't burn down the place where it is. It will be hard to get.

"And do you know what two horses and what chariot I'm asking for? They are the chariot and the two wonderful horses of Dobar, King of Siogair. The sea is the same as land to them. There are no faster horses, and there's no chariot to equal that one in shape or in strength.

"And do you know what the seven pigs are? They are the pigs of Easal, King of the Golden Pillars. Though they are killed every night, they are found alive again the next day. And no disease and no sickness will come on anyone who eats a share of them.

"The whelp I asked of you is Fail-Inis, the whelp that belongs to the King of Ioruaidh, the Cold Country. All the wild beasts of the world fall down at the sight of her. She is more beautiful than the sun in his fiery wheels. It will be hard to get her.

"The cooking-spit I asked of you is one of the spits of the women of Inis Cenn-fhinne, the Island of Caer of the Fair Hair.

"And the three shouts you're to give on a hill must be given on the Hill of Miochaoin, in the north of Lochlann. Miochaoin and his sons are under bonds not to allow any shout to be given on that hill. It was with them my father got his learning. Even if I forgave you his death, they would not. If you get through all your other voyages before you reach them, it's my opinion they'll avenge him on you themselves.

"That is the fine I have asked of you," said Lugh.

Silence and darkness came down on the sons of Tuireann when they heard that.

They went to their father and told him the fine that had been put on them.

"That's bad news," said Tuireann. "It's to your death and destruction you'll be going, looking for those things. But even so — if Lugh himself had a mind to help you, you could work out the fine. All the men in the world couldn't do it, except by the power of Manannan, or of Lugh. So go and ask Lugh for the loan of Manannan's horse, the Aonbharr. If he wants the fine, he'll give it to you. If he doesn't, he'll say the horse isn't his, and he won't give the loan of a loan. Then ask him for the loan of Manannan's curragh, the Scuabtuinne, the Sweeper of the Waves. He'll give you that, because he's under bonds not to refuse a second request. And the curragh is better for you than the horse."

So the sons of Tuireann went to Lugh and greeted him, and told him they couldn't bring him the fine without his help, and so it would be well for them to have the loan of the Aonbharr.

"I have that horse only on loan myself," said Lugh. "I won't give the loan of a loan."

"Then give us the loan of Manannan's curragh," said Brian.

"I'll give that," said Lugh.

"Where is it?"

"At Brugh na Boinn."

They went back to Tuireann. Ethne, their sister, was with him. They told him they had got the curragh.

"You won't be much the better for it," said Tuireann. "Lugh would like well to have every piece of this fine that he can use before the battle with the Fomor. But he would like you to come to your deaths looking for it."

They went away, and left Tuireann sorrowing and lamenting. Ethne went with them to where the curragh was.

Brian got into it. "There's only room for one other person with me here," he said, and began to find fault with how narrow it was.

"You shouldn't be faulting the curragh," said Ethne. "And oh, my dear brother, it was a bad thing you did, killing the father of Lugh of the Long Hand. Whatever harm comes to you from it, it's only just."

"Don't say that, Ethne," they said. "We're in good heart, and we'll do brave deeds. We'd sooner be killed a hundred times over than die the death of cowards."

"My grief," said Ethne. "There's nothing more sorrowful than this: to see you driven out of your own country."

The three of them pushed their curragh out from the beautiful clear-bayed shore of Ireland.

"Which way first?" they said.

"We'll go for the apples," said Brian, "since they were the first thing we were told to bring. So we ask you, curragh of Manannan that is under us, to sail to the Garden in the East of the World."

The curragh did not neglect that order. It sailed on over the green-sided waves and the deep places until it came to its harbour in the east of the world.

"How do you want to get into the garden?" Brian asked his brothers. "I think the king's champions and the fighting men of the country are always guarding it, and the king himself is chief over them."

"What else should we do," said his brothers, "but make straight at them and attack them, and bring away the apples or fall ourselves? We can't get out of the dangers ahead of us without meeting our death somewhere."

"It would be better," said Brian, "for the story of our bravery and our craftiness to be told and live after us, than a story of folly and cowardice. Here's what's best. We'll go into the garden in the shape of swift hawks. The watchers have only light spears to throw at us. Take good care to keep out of their reach. When they've thrown them all, make a quick dive at the apples, and each of you bring one away in your claws, and I'll bring the third."

They said that was good advice. Brian struck himself and the others with his Druid rod and changed them into beautiful hawks, and they flew towards the garden.

The watchers saw them. They shouted on every side, and threw showers of spears and darts. But the hawks kept out of reach, as Brian had told them, until all the spears were spent. Then they swept down bravely on the apples and carried them away, without so much as a wound.

The news went through the city and the whole district.

The king had three wise, crafty daughters. They put themselves into the shape of three ospreys and followed the hawks out to sea, and sent flashes of lightning before them and after them, and the lightning scorched them badly.

"We're in a bad way now," said the sons of Tuireann. "We'll be burned through and through with this lightning if we don't get some relief."

"If I can give you relief I will," said Brian.

He struck himself and his brothers with the Druid rod, and they became three swans, and went down quickly into the sea. The ospreys left them then, and the sons of Tuireann got back into their boat.

After that they talked it over and agreed to go to Greece and bring away the skin of the pig, with leave or without it. So they went on until they came near the court of the King of Greece.

"What shape should we put on to go in here?" said Brian.

"What shape but our own?" said the others.

"That's not what I think best," said Brian. "We'll go in looking like poets from Ireland. Then the high people of Greece will hold us in respect and honour."

"That will be hard," they said, "when we have no poem, and we know very little about how to make one."

All the same, they tied their hair in the poet's tie and knocked at the door of the court. The door-keeper asked who was there.

"We are poets of Ireland," said Brian, "and we've come with a poem for the king."

The door-keeper went in and told the king there were poets from Ireland at the door.

"Let them in," said the king. "It was in search of a good man they came so far from their own country." And he ordered everything in the court to be well laid out, so that they would say they had seen no place so grand in all their travels.

So the sons of Tuireann were let in, looking like poets, and they fell to drinking and pleasure without delay. They thought they had never seen, and there was not in the world, a court as good as that one, or so large a household, or a place where they had been better treated.

Then the king's poets got up to give out their poems and songs. Brian, son of Tuireann, told his brothers to say a poem for the king.

"We have no poem," they said. "Don't ask any poem of us except the one we know already, and that's to take what we want by the strength of our hands if we're the strongest, or to fall by those against us if they're the strongest."

"That's not a good way to make a poem," said Brian.

He stood up himself and asked for a hearing. They all listened, and this is what he said:

"O Tuis, we do not hide your fame; we praise you as the oak among kings. The skin of a pig, bounty without hardness — that is the reward I ask for it.

"The war of a neighbour against an ear; the fair ear of his neighbour will be against him. He who gives us what he owns, his court will not be the scarcer for it.

"A raging army and a sudden sea are a danger to whoever goes against them. The skin of a pig, bounty without hardness — that is the reward I ask, O Tuis."

"That's a good poem," said the king. "But I don't understand a word of it."

"I'll tell you what it means," said Brian. "'O Tuis, we do not hide your fame; we praise you as the oak above the kings.' That is: as the oak is beyond the kingly trees of the wood, so you are beyond the kings of the world, for open-handedness and grandeur.

"'The skin of a pig, bounty without hardness.' That is: the pig-skin you own is what I'd like to get from you as a reward for my poem.

"'The war of a neighbour against an ear; the fair ear of his neighbour will be against him.' That is: you and I will be at each other's ears over the skin, unless I get it with your consent.

"That's the meaning of the poem," said Brian.

"I'd praise your poem," said the king, "if there weren't so much about my pig-skin in it. You have no good sense, man of poetry, to be asking me for that. I wouldn't give it to all the poets and the learned men and the great men of the world, since they couldn't take it without my consent. But I'll give you three times the full of the skin in gold, as the price of your poem."

"Good be with you, king," said Brian. "I knew well it was no easy thing I was asking, but I knew I'd get a good ransom for it. And I'm so covetous that I won't be satisfied without seeing the gold measured into the skin myself."

The king sent his servants with them to the treasure-house to measure out the gold.

"Measure out the full of it to my brothers first," said Brian, "and then give good measure to me, since it was I who made the poem."

When the skin was brought out, Brian made a quick, sudden snatch at it with his left hand. He drew his sword and struck at the man nearest him, and made two halves of him. He kept hold of the skin and wrapped it round himself, and the three of them rushed out of the court, cutting down every armed man in front of them, so that not one escaped death or wounding.

Then Brian went to where the king himself was. The king made no delay in attacking him. They made a hard fight of it, and at the end the King of Greece fell by the hand of Brian, son of Tuireann.

The brothers rested a while after that, and then they said they would go and look for another part of the fine.

"We'll go to Pisear, King of Persia," said Brian, "and ask him for the spear."

So they got into their boat and left the blue streams of the coast of Greece. "We're well off," they said, "now we have the apples and the skin." They stopped nowhere until they reached the borders of Persia.

"Let's go into the court looking like poets," said Brian, "the same as we did with the King of Greece."

"We're content to," said the others, "since everything turned out so well the last time we took to poetry. Not that it's easy to take up a calling that doesn't belong to us."

So they tied their hair in the poet's tie, and they were as well treated as they had been at the other court. When the time came for poems, Brian stood up, and this is what he said:

"It is little any spear looks to Pisear; the battles of enemies are broken; it is not too much for Pisear to wound every one of them.

"A yew, the most beautiful of the wood, it is called a king; it is not bulky. May the spear drive the whole crowd on to their wounds of death."

"That's a good poem," said the king. "But I don't understand why my own spear is brought into it, O Man of Poetry from Ireland."

"Because it's that spear of yours I'd like to get as the reward for my poem," said Brian.

"You have little sense to be asking me that," said the king. "The people of my court never showed more respect for poetry than they're showing now, by not putting you to death on the spot."

When Brian heard the king talk like that, he thought of the apple in his hand. He made a straight cast and hit the king in the forehead, so that his brains were put out through the back of his head. Then he bared his sword and attacked the people around him, and the other two did the same, and gave him brave help, until they had made an end of everyone of the court they met. Then they found the spear, with its head in a cauldron of water so that it would not set fire to the place.

After a while they said it was time to go and look for the rest of the great fine, and asked each other which way they should go.

"We'll go to the King of the Island of Siogair," said Brian. "It's he who has the two horses and the chariot the Ildánach asked for."

They went on, bringing the spear with them, and the three champions were proud after all they had done. They went on until they came to the court of the King of Siogair.

"Here's what we'll do this time," said Brian. "We'll go in looking like paid soldiers from Ireland, and make friends with the king, so we'll find out where the horses and the chariot are kept."

With that settled, they went on to the lawn in front of the king's house.

The king and his chief men got up and came through the fair that was going on there. The brothers greeted the king, and he asked who they were.

"We're trained fighting men from Ireland," they said, "and we earn our wages from the kings of the world."

"Do you want to stay with me for a while?" said the king.

"That's what we want," they said. So they made an agreement and took service with him.

They stayed in that court a fortnight and a month, and in all that time they never saw the horses.

"This is a bad way to be in," said Brian, "with no more news of the horses now than the first day we came."

"What's best to do now?" said his brothers.

"Let's do this," said Brian. "We'll take our arms and gather our things together and go to the king and tell him we're leaving the country and this part of the world, unless he shows us those horses."

They went to the king that same day. He asked them what they meant by getting ready for a journey.

"You'll hear that, high king," said Brian. "Trained fighting men from Ireland like ourselves always have trust put in them by the kings they guard. We're used to being told the secrets and the whispers of whoever we're with. And that is not how you've treated us since we came to you. You have two horses and a chariot that are the best in the world, so we're told, and we haven't been given a sight of them yet."

"It would be a pity for you to go on that account," said the king, "when I'd have shown them to you the first day if I'd known you wanted to see them. If you want to see them now, you may. I don't think any soldiers ever came here from Ireland that were thought more of, by me and my people, than you."

He sent for the horses, and they were yoked to the chariot. They went as fast as the cold spring wind, and the sea was the same as land to them.

Brian was watching the horses closely. Suddenly he took hold of the chariot, pulled the chariot-driver out and dashed him against the nearest rock, and leapt into his place himself. He threw the Persian spear at the king, and it went through his heart. Then he and his brothers scattered the people in front of them, and brought the chariot away.

"Now we'll go to Easal, the King of the Golden Pillars," said Brian, "for the seven pigs the Ildánach told us to bring him."

They sailed on without delay or drawback to that high country.

The people of that country were watching their harbours for fear of the sons of Tuireann. The story of them had been told everywhere by then: how they had been sent out of Ireland by force, and how they were carrying away all the gifted treasures of the world.

Easal came down to the edge of the harbour to meet them. He asked whether it was true, what he had heard: that the king of every country they had been to had fallen by them.

Brian said it was true, whatever Easal might want to do to them for it.

"What made you do that?" said Easal.

Brian told him it was the oppression and the hard sentence of another that had driven them to it. He told him everything that had happened, and how they had put down everyone who stood against them so far.

"What have you come to this country for now?" said the king.

"For your pigs," said Brian. "Bringing them away is part of the fine."

"And how do you think you'll get them?"

"If we get them with good-will," said Brian, "we're ready to take them thankfully. If we don't, we're ready to do battle with you and your people for them, so that you'll fall by us, and we'll bring away the pigs in spite of you."

"If that's to be the end of it," said the king, "it would be a pity to bring my people into a battle."

"It would be a pity indeed," said Brian.

The king whispered with his people and took their advice, and they agreed to give up the pigs of their own free will to the sons of Tuireann, since they could see that nobody had been able to stand against them up to then.

The sons of Tuireann thanked Easal, and they wondered to have got the pigs like that, when they had had to fight for every other part of the fine. More than that — they had left some of their own blood in every other place.

Easal brought them to his own house that night, and they were given food and drink and good beds and everything they could wish for. In the morning they came before the king, and the pigs were given to them.

"You've done well by us, giving us these pigs," said Brian. "They are the only part of the fine we've got without fighting." And he made a poem for the king, praising him and putting a great name on him for what he had done. It was the only honest poem he made on that whole journey.

"Where are you going next, sons of Tuireann?" said Easal.

"To the country of Ioruaidh," they said, "for a whelp that's there."

"Grant me one request," said Easal. "Bring me with you to the King of Ioruaidh. A daughter of mine is his wife, and I'd like to persuade him to give you the whelp without a battle."

"That will please us well," they said.

So the king's ship was made ready. We have no knowledge of what happened until they came to the delightful, wonderful coast of Ioruaidh. The people and the armies were watching the harbours and landing-places for them, and they knew them at once and shouted at them.

Easal went ashore peaceably, and went to his son-in-law the king, and told him the story of the sons of Tuireann from beginning to end.

"What's brought them to this country?" said the King of Ioruaidh.

"They've come to ask for the hound you have," said Easal.

"You had a bad thought, coming with them to ask it," said the king. "The gods haven't given that much luck to any three champions in the world, that they'd get my hound by force or by good-will."

"It would be better for you to let them have the hound," said Easal, "since they've put down so many of the kings of the world."

But everything he said was idleness to the king. So he went back to the sons of Tuireann and told them the whole of it.

When they heard the king's answer they made no delay. They put quick hands on their weapons, and offered battle to the army of Ioruaidh.

When the armies met there was a brave battle fought on both sides. The sons of Tuireann began to kill and strike at the men of Ioruaidh until they were separated from one another in the fight, so that Iuchar and Iucharba happened to be on one side, and Brian alone on the other. There was a gap of danger and a breaking of ranks in front of Brian on every path he took, until he came to the King of Ioruaidh in his battle-pen. Then those two brave champions began a fierce fight together, and neither of them spared the other.

In the end Brian overcame the king and bound him, and brought him through the middle of the army to the place where Easal was.

"There's your son-in-law for you," he said. "And I swear by my hand of valour, I'd think it easier to kill him three times than to bring him to you once like this."

So the whelp was given to the sons of Tuireann, and the king was unbound, and peace was made between them. And when they had brought all that to an end, they said goodbye to Easal and to all the rest.

Now as to Lugh of the Long Hand.

It was shown to him that the sons of Tuireann had got every one of the things he needed against the battle with the Fomor. So he sent a Druid spell after them, to put forgetfulness on them of the rest of the fine they had not yet got. And he put a great desire and longing on them to go home to Ireland. So they forgot that any part of the fine was still missing, and they turned back towards home.

Lugh was at a gathering of the people, a fair on the green outside Teamhair, and the King of Ireland with him, when it was made known to him that the sons of Tuireann had landed at Brugh na Boinn.

He went into the city of Teamhair and shut the gate behind him. He put on Manannan's smooth armour, and the cloak of the daughters of Flidais, and he took his own weapons in his hand.

The sons of Tuireann came to where the king was, and the king and the Tuatha de Danaan made them welcome. The king asked whether they had got the fine.

"We have," they said. "Where's Lugh, so we can give it to him?"

"He was here a while ago," said the king. The whole fair was searched for him, but he was not found.

"I know where he is," said Brian. "It's been made known to him that we've come to Ireland with these deadly weapons, and he's gone into Teamhair to avoid us."

Messengers were sent to him. His answer was that he would not come, but that the fine should be given to the king.

So the sons of Tuireann gave it to the king. When the king had taken it, they all went to the palace in Teamhair, and Lugh came out onto the lawn, and the fine was given to him.

"There is good payment here," said Lugh, "for anyone that was ever killed, or ever will be. But there's something missing from it yet that it isn't lawful to leave out. Where is the cooking-spit? And where are the three shouts on the hill that you haven't given yet?"

When the sons of Tuireann heard that, clouds of weakness came down on them.

They left that place and went to their father's house that night, and they told him everything they had done, and how Lugh had treated them. Grief and darkness came on Tuireann, and they spent the night together.

In the morning they went to their ship, and Ethne their sister went with them, crying and lamenting. This is what she said:

"It is a pity, Brian of my life, that it is not to Teamhair you are going, after all the troubles you have had before this — even if I could not follow you.

"O Salmon of the dumb Boinn, O Salmon of the Lifé River, since I cannot keep you here I am loath to part from you.

"O Rider of the Wave of Tuaidh, the man who stands best in the fight: if you come back again, I think it will not please your enemy.

"Is there pity with you for the sons of Tuireann, leaning now on their green shields? Their going is a cause for pity; my mind is filled up with it.

"That you should be tonight at Beinn Edair until the heavy coming of the morning — you who have taken forfeits from brave men — it is you have increased our grief.

"It is a pity your journey is away from Teamhair, and from the pleasant plains, and from great Uisnech of Midhe. There is nothing so pitiful as this."

After that lament they went out on the rough waves of the green sea. They were a quarter of a year on the sea without any news of the island.

Then Brian put on his water-dress and leapt over the side. He was a long time walking in the sea looking for the Island of the Fair-Haired Women, and in the end he found it. He went looking for the court, and when he came to it all he found was a troop of women doing needlework and embroidering borders. And among all the other things they had with them was the cooking-spit.

When Brian saw it, he picked it up and started to carry it to the door.

All the women began to laugh when they saw him doing that.

"That's a brave deed you've put your hand to," they said. "Even if your brothers were with you, the least of the three times fifty women of us wouldn't let the spit go with you or with them. But all the same, take a spit of the spits with you, since you had the daring to try and take it in spite of us."

It is the only part of the fine that was ever given out of pity.

Brian said goodbye to them and went to look for the boat. His brothers thought he had been away too long. They were just about to leave the place when they saw him coming towards them, and their courage rose greatly.

He got into the boat, and they went on to look for the Hill of Miochaoin.

When they got there, Miochaoin, the guardian of the hill, came towards them. Brian attacked him the moment he saw him, and the fight of those two champions was like the fight of two lions, until at last Miochaoin fell.

Then Miochaoin's three sons came out to fight the three sons of Tuireann.
