If anyone ever came from the east of the world to look at a fight, it was to see the fight of these champions he should have come, for the greatness of their blows and the courage of their minds. The sons of Miochaoin were Core and Conn and Aedh. They drove their three spears through the bodies of the sons of Tuireann. That did not discourage the sons of Tuireann at all. They put their own three spears through the bodies of the sons of Miochaoin, so that they fell into the clouds and the faintness of death.

"How are you now, my dear brothers?" said Brian.

"We're near our death," they said.

"Let's get up," he said, "and give three shouts on the hill. I see the signs of death coming on us."

"We can't," they said.

So Brian stood up, and lifted each of them with one hand, bleeding heavily all the while, until they had given the three shouts.

The fine was paid.

Brian brought them with him to the boat, and they were travelling the sea a long time. At last Brian said, "I see Beinn Edair, and our father's dun, and Teamhair of the Kings."

"We'd have our fill of health if we could see that," said the others. "For the love of your good name, brother, raise our heads on your breast until we see Ireland again, and life or death will be the same to us after. And O Brian, Flame of Valour without treachery, we'd sooner death took us than see you with wounds on your body and no physician to heal you."

They came to Beinn Edair, and from there to their father's house.

"Go, dear father, to Teamhair," Brian said to Tuireann, "and give this spit to Lugh, and bring back the skin that has healing in it, to save us. Ask it of him for friendship's sake, for we are of the one blood. Let him not give hardness for hardness. And oh, dear father, don't be long on your journey, or you won't find us alive."

Tuireann went to Teamhair and found Lugh of the Long Hand there. He gave him the spit, and asked him for the skin to heal his children.

Lugh said he would not give it.

Tuireann came back and told them he had not got the skin.

"Bring me with you to Lugh," said Brian, "to see if I can get it from him."

So they went to Lugh, and Brian asked him for the skin. Lugh said he would not give it. He said that if they gave him the breadth of the earth in gold for it, he would not take it from them — unless he was sure their death would come on them in satisfaction for the deed they had done.

When Brian heard that, he went back to where his two brothers were, and lay down between them. His life went out of him, and out of the other two at the same moment.

Their father cried and lamented over his three beautiful sons, who had the making of a king of Ireland in each of them. His strength left him, and he died.

They were buried together in the one grave.

Lugh had his fine. He had every weapon he needed for the war against the Fomor. And he had seen, standing on the lawn at Teamhair, exactly what the people of the gods of Dana were capable of doing to each other.

It was not long after Lugh got the fine from the sons of Tuireann that the Fomor came, and landed at Scetne.

This time the whole host of the Fomor came. Their king came with them, Balor of the Strong Blows and of the Evil Eye. And Bres came, and Indech, son of De Domnann, a king of the Fomor, and Elathan, son of Lobos, and Goll and Ingol, and Octriallach, son of Indech, and Elathan, son of Delbaeth.

Lugh sent the Dagda to spy out the Fomor, and to delay them until the men of Ireland could come to the battle.

So the Dagda went to their camp and asked them for a delay, and they said he could have it.

Then, to make sport of him, the Fomor made him porridge-broth, because he had a great love for broth. They filled the king's cauldron with four times twenty gallons of new milk, and the same of meal and fat. They put in goats and sheep and pigs as well, and boiled it all together. Then they poured the whole of it into a great hole in the ground.

They called him over to it and told him to eat his fill, so that nobody could reproach the Fomor for want of hospitality the way Bres had been reproached.

"And we'll make an end of you," said Indech, son of De Domnann, "if you leave any of it behind."

The Dagda took the ladle. It was big enough for a man and a woman to lie together in the bowl of it. He took up bits with it — half a salted pig to a bit, and a quarter of lard.

"If the broth tastes as good as the bits," he said, "this is good food."

He went on putting the full of the ladle into his mouth until the hole was empty. And when it was all gone he put his hand down and scraped up what was left, among the earth and the gravel.

Sleep came on him then, after the broth, and the Fomor laughed at him, for his belly was the size of the cauldron of a great house.

But after a while he got up, and heavy as he was, he made his way home. His clothes were no way handsome: a cape that came only to the hollow of his elbows, and a brown coat, long in front and short behind, and on his feet brogues of horse-hide with the hair on the outside. In his hand was a wheeled fork that it would take eight men to carry, and the track it left behind him was deep enough to be the boundary ditch of a province.

That is the Dagda. People laughed at him. People always laughed at him. It never did them any good.

On his way he saw the Battle-Crow, the Morrigu, washing herself in the river Unius of Connacht. One of her feet was at Ullad Echne, to the south of the water, and the other at Loscuinn, to the north of the water, and her hair hung down in nine loosened locks.

She told the Dagda that she would bring the heart's blood of Indech, son of De Domnann — who had threatened him — to the men of Ireland.

While he was away, Lugh had called together the Druids and the smiths and the physicians and the law-makers and the chariot-drivers of Ireland, to make their plans for the battle.

He asked the great magician Mathgen what he could do to help them.

"This is what I can do," said Mathgen. "By my power I can throw down all the mountains of Ireland on the Fomor, until their tops are rolling on the ground. And the twelve chief mountains of Ireland will bring you their help, and will fight for you: Slieve Leag, and Denda Ulad, and Bennai Boirche, and Bri Ruri, and Slieve Bladma, and Slieve Snechtae, and Slieve Mis, and Blai-Slieve, and Nemthann, and Slieve Macca Belgodon, and Segois, and Cruachan Aigle."

Then he asked the cup-bearers what help they could give.

"We'll put a strong thirst on the Fomor," they said, "and then we'll bring the twelve chief lochs of Ireland in front of them, and however great their thirst, they'll find no water in them: Derc-Loch, Loch Luimnech, Loch Orbsen, Loch Righ, Loch Mescdhae, Loch Cuan, Loch Laeig, Loch Echach, Loch Febail, Loch Decket, Loch Riach, Mor-Loch. And we'll go to the twelve chief rivers of Ireland: the Buas, the Boinn, the Banna, the Nem, the Laoi, the Sionnan, the Muaid, the Sligech, the Samair, the Fionn, the Ruirtech, the Siuir. They'll all be hidden from the Fomor, so they won't find a drop in them. But as for the men of Ireland, there'll be drink for them if they're in the battle to the end of seven years."

Figol, son of Mamos, the Druid, was asked what he would do.

"This is what I'll do," he said. "I'll make three showers of fire pour down on the faces of the army of the Fomor. I'll take from them two-thirds of their bravery and their strength, and I'll put sickness on their bodies and on the bodies of their horses. But for the men of Ireland, every breath they draw will be an increase of strength and bravery to them. If they're seven years in the battle, they'll never tire."

Then Lugh asked his two witches, Bechulle and Dianan, "What power can you bring to the battle?"

"That's easy to say," they said. "We'll put enchantment on the trees and the stones and the sods of the earth, until they become an armed host against the Fomor, and put terror on them, and put them to rout."

Then Lugh asked Carpre the poet, son of Etain, what he could do.

"That's not hard to say," said Carpre. "I'll make a satire on them at sunrise, with the wind from the north, and me on a hilltop with my back to a thorn-tree, and a stone and a thorn in my hand. And with that satire I'll put shame on them, and enchantment, so they won't be able to stand against fighting men."

Remember, this was the poet who had brought down Bres with a few lines about dry cakes. Nobody laughed.

Then Lugh asked Goibniu the Smith what he would be able to do.

"This," said Goibniu. "If the men of Ireland stay in the battle to the end of seven years, for every sword that's broken and every spear that's lost from its shaft, I'll put a new one in its place. No spear-point made by my hand will ever miss its mark. And no man it touches will ever taste life again. That's more than Dolb, the smith of the Fomor, can do."

"And you, Credne," Lugh said to his worker in brass, "what help can you give our men in the battle?"

"That's not hard to tell," said Credne. "Rivets for their spears, and hilts for their swords, and bosses and rims for their shields. I'll supply them all."

"And you, Luchta," he said to his carpenter, "what will you do?"

"I'll give them all they want of shields and spear-shafts," said Luchta.

Then he asked Diancecht, the physician, what he would do.

"Every man who's wounded there," said Diancecht, "unless his head is struck off, or his brain or his marrow is cut through, I'll make whole and sound again for the battle of the next day."

Then the Dagda spoke. "All those great things you're boasting you'll do," he said, "I'll do every one of them by myself."

"It's you are the good god!" they said, and they all gave a great shout of laughter.

That is where his name comes from. The Good God. They meant it as a joke. It stuck anyway, the way the true ones do.

Then Lugh spoke to the whole army, and put strength into them, so that each of them had in him the spirit of a king or a great lord.

When the delay was over, the Fomor and the men of Ireland came on towards each other until they reached the plain of Magh Tuireadh. This was not the same Magh Tuireadh where the first battle was fought. It was to the north, near Ess Dara.

Then the two armies threatened each other.

"The men of Ireland are daring enough to offer battle to us," said Bres to Indech, son of De Domnann.

"I give my word," said Indech, "their bones will be in small pieces if they don't give in to us and pay their tribute."

The Men of Dea had decided not to let Lugh go into the battle, because of how great a loss his death would be to them. They left nine of their men to keep watch on him.

On the first day none of the kings or princes went into the battle. Only the common fighting men fought, and they were fierce enough and proud enough.

The battle went on like that from day to day, and neither side had much advantage. But there was one thing the Fomor wondered at.

When their own weapons were broken or blunted in the fight, they lay where they were. When their own men were killed, they showed no sign of life the next day. It was not like that with the Tuatha de Danaan. If their men were killed today, or their weapons broken, they were as good as before tomorrow.

This is how that happened.

The well of Slaine lay west of Magh Tuireadh and east of Loch Arboch. Diancecht, and his son Octruil, and his daughter Airmed, used to sing spells over that well and put herbs into it. Men who had been wounded to death in the battle were brought to the well and put into it, dead men. And they came out of it whole and sound, by the power of the spells. And not only healed: there was such fire put into them that they were quicker in the fight than they had been before.

As for the weapons, this is how they were made new every day.

Goibniu the Smith stayed in the forge making swords and spears. He made a spear-head in three turns. Then Luchta the Carpenter made the shaft in three cuts, and the third cut was the finish, and set it in the ring of the spear. When the spear-heads were stuck in the side of the forge, he threw the shafts and the rings so that they went straight into the spear-heads and needed no more setting. Then Credne the Brazier made the rivets in three turns and cast the rings of the spears to them. And with that they were ready, and set together.

Three turns. Three cuts. Three turns. A spear.

All this went against the Fomor, and they sent one of their young men to spy about the camp and see if he could find out how these things were done. They sent Ruadan, son of Bres and of Brigit, daughter of the Dagda, because he was a son and a grandson of the Tuatha de Danaan. So he went and saw everything that was done, and came back to the Fomor.

When they heard his story, they decided that it was Goibniu the Smith who hindered them most. They sent Ruadan back and told him to make an end of him.

So Ruadan went back to the forge and asked Goibniu whether he would give him a spear-head. Then he asked Credne for rivets, and the carpenter for a shaft, and everything was given to him as he asked. There was a woman there, Cron, mother of Fianlug, grinding the spears.

When the spear was given to Ruadan, he turned and threw it at Goibniu, and wounded him.

Goibniu pulled it out and threw it back at Ruadan. It went through him, and he died. His father Bres and the army of the Fomor saw him die.

Then Brigit came and keened her son, shrieking and crying.

That was the first keening ever heard in Ireland. The whistle for calling through the night was Brigit's, and so was this.

As for Goibniu, he went into the well and was healed.

But after that Octriallach, son of Indech, called to the Fomor and told every man of them to take a stone from the stones of Drinnes and throw it into the well of Slane. They did that until the well was dried up, and there was a cairn raised over it. It is called Octriallach's Cairn.

It was while Goibniu was making spear-heads for the battle of Magh Tuireadh that a charge was brought against his wife. Everyone could see that it was heavy news to him, and that jealousy came on him. There was a spear-shaft in his hand when he heard the story — Nes was its name — and he sang spells over it, so that anyone struck with that spear afterwards would be burned up by it as if by fire.

At last the day of the great battle came.

The Fomor came out of their camp and stood in strong ranks. There was not a leader or a fighting man among them without good armour to his skin, and a helmet on his head, a broad spear in his right hand, a heavy sword in his belt, and a strong shield on his shoulder. To attack the army of the Fomor that day was to beat your head against a rock, or to go up fighting against a fire.

The Men of Dea rose up. They left Lugh with the nine comrades who were guarding him, and went on to the battle. Midhir was with them, and Bodb Dearg, and Diancecht. And Badb and Macha and the Morrigu called out that they would go along with them.

It was a hard battle, and for a while it went against the Tuatha de Danaan.

Nuada of the Silver Hand, their king, fell by Balor, King of the Fomor. So did Macha, daughter of Emmass. Cass-mail fell by Octriallach. And the Dagda got a dreadful wound from a casting spear thrown by Ceithlenn, the wife of Balor.

But while the battle was going on, Lugh broke away from those who were keeping him, and rushed out to the front of the Men of Dea.

Then there was a fierce battle fought. Lugh was heartening the men of Ireland to fight well, so that they would not be in bonds any longer. It was better for them, he said, to die protecting their own country than to live any longer under bonds and under tribute. He sang them a song of courage, and the hosts gave a great shout as they went into battle, and then they met, and each began to attack the other.

There was great slaughter, and laying low in graves, and many comely men fell there in the stall of death. Pride and shame were there side by side, and hardness, and red anger, and there was red blood on the white skin of young fighting men. The dashing of spear against shield and sword against sword, and the shouting of the fighters, and the whistling of casting-spears, and the rattling of scabbards, went through the battle like harsh thunder. Many slipped in the blood underfoot and fell, striking their heads against one another. And the river carried away the bodies of friends and enemies together.

Then Lugh and Balor met in the battle.

Lugh called out insults to him. Balor grew angry, and said to the men beside him, "Lift up my eyelid, so I can see this chatterer who's talking to me."

They raised Balor's eyelid.

But Lugh threw his red spear at him, and it drove the eye out through the back of Balor's head, so that the eye fell facing his own army. Three times nine of the Fomor died when they looked at it. If Lugh had not put out that eye when he did, the whole of Ireland would have been burned up in one flash.

After that Lugh struck his head off.

So the Druid's prophecy came true, the way prophecies do. Balor had locked his daughter in a tower of glass, and thrown her baby into the sea, and it had not made the smallest difference.

As for Indech, son of De Domnann, he fell and was crushed in the battle, and blood burst from his mouth. He called out for Leat Glas, his poet, as he lay there, but Leat Glas could not help him. Then the Morrigu came into the battle, heartening the Tuatha de Danaan to fight well. As she had promised the Dagda, she took the full of her two hands of Indech's blood and gave it to the armies waiting at the ford of Unius. It was called the Ford of Destruction from that day.

After that it was not a battle any more, but a rout, and the Fomor were beaten back to the sea.

Lugh and his comrades followed them, and they came up with Bres, son of Elathan, and no guard with him.

"It's better for you to spare my life than to kill me," said Bres. "If you spare me now, the cows of Ireland will never go dry."

"I'll ask advice about that from our wise men," said Lugh.

He told Maeltine Mor-Brethach, Maeltine of the Great Judgments, what Bres had said.

"Don't spare him for that," said Maeltine. "He has no power over their calves, though he has power over the cows while they're living."

"If you spare me," said Bres, "the men of Ireland will reap a harvest of corn every quarter."

"The spring is for ploughing and sowing," said Maeltine, "and the beginning of summer for the strength of the corn, and the beginning of autumn for its ripeness, and the winter for using it."

"That doesn't save you," said Lugh to Bres.

But then, to have an excuse for sparing him, Lugh said: "Tell us the best way for the men of Ireland to plough, and to sow, and to reap."

"Let their ploughing be on a Tuesday," said Bres, "and their casting of seed into the field on a Tuesday, and their reaping on a Tuesday."

Lugh said that would do, and let him go free.

It was in this battle that Ogma found Orna, the sword of Tethra, a king of the Fomor. He took it out of its sheath and cleaned it. When the sword was out of its sheath it told all the deeds that had been done by it. There used to be that power in swords. There may be still. We have stopped asking.

Lugh and the Dagda and Ogma went after the Fomor, because the Fomor had carried off the Dagda's harp, that was called Uaitne. They came to a feasting-house, and inside it they found Bres and his father Elathan, and there was the harp hanging on the wall.

The Dagda had bound the music into that harp, so that it would not sound until he called to it. Sometimes it was called Dur-da-Bla, the Oak of Two Blossoms, and sometimes Coir-cethar-chuin, the Four-Angled Music.

When he saw it hanging on the wall, this is what he said: "Come summer, come winter, from the mouth of harps and bags and pipes."

The harp sprang off the wall and came to the Dagda. It killed nine men on its way.

Then he played for them the three things harpers understand: the sleepy tune, and the laughing tune, and the crying tune. When he played the crying tune their women cried tears. Then he played the laughing tune, until their women and children laughed. And then he played the sleepy tune, and all the hosts fell asleep. And through that sleep the three of them walked away, through the Fomor who would have been glad to harm them.

When it was all over, the Dagda brought out the heifer he had taken as his wages from Bres, the time he was building his dun. She called to her calf. And at the sound of her call all the cattle of Ireland that the Fomor had carried off as tribute were back in their own fields again.

Cé, the Druid of Nuada of the Silver Hand, was wounded in the battle. He went south until he came to Carn Corrslebe, and there he sat down to rest, tired with his wounds, and with the fear that was on him, and with the journey. He saw a smooth plain in front of him, full of flowers, and a great desire came on him to reach that plain. He went on until he came to it, and there he died. When his grave was made there, a lake burst out over it and over the whole plain, and it was given the name of Loch Cé.

There were only four men of the Fomor left in Ireland after the battle. They went about the country spoiling corn and milk and fruit, and whatever came out of the sea, until they were driven out one Samhain night by the Morrigu and by Angus Og, so that the Fomor might never be over Ireland again.

When the battle was won and the bodies were cleared away, the Morrigu gave out the news of the great victory to the hosts, and to the royal heights of Ireland, and to its chief rivers and its river-mouths. This is what she said:

"Peace up to the skies, the skies down to earth, the earth under the skies; strength to every one."

As for the number of men who fell in that battle, it will not be known until we have numbered the stars of the sky, or the flakes of snow, or the dew on the grass, or the grass under the feet of cattle, or the horses of the Son of Lir in a stormy sea.

Lugh was made king over the Men of Dea, and he held his court at Nas.

While he was king, his foster-mother Taillte, daughter of Magh Mor, the Great Plain, died. Before her death she asked her husband Duach the Dark — he who built the Fort of the Hostages in Teamhair — to clear away the wood of Cuan, so that there could be a gathering of the people around her grave. So he called on the men of Ireland to cut down the wood with their wide-bladed knives and bill-hooks and hatchets, and within a month the whole wood was down.

Lugh buried her in the plain of Midhe, and raised a mound over her that can be seen to this day. He ordered fires to be kindled, and keening to be made, and games and sports to be held in the summer of every year out of respect for her. The place where they were held took its name from her. It is Taillten.

And as for Lugh's own mother, tall, beautiful Ethlinn — she who had grown up in a tower of glass and never been told the name of a man — she came to Teamhair after the battle of Magh Tuireadh, and Lugh gave her in marriage to Tadg, son of Nuada.

The children born to them were Muirne, who would be the mother of Finn, the Head of the Fianna of Ireland; and Tuiren, who would be the mother of Bran.

But that was a long way off yet. First the gods would have to lose Ireland.

Lugh held the kingship for a long time. Then the Dagda was made king in his place.

Lugh went away out of Ireland.

Some said he died at Uisnech, the place where the five provinces meet. Uisnech was where the first fire was ever kindled in Ireland. Mide, son of Brath, kindled it for the sons of Nemed, and it burned for six years, and every chief fire in Ireland was lit from that fire.

But gods do not die as easily as people say they do. Lugh was seen again in Ireland, at the time when Conchubar and the Men of the Red Branch went following white birds southward to the Boinn, at the time of Cuchulain's birth. And it was Lugh who came and kept watch over Cuchulain in his three days' sleep, at the time of the War for the Bull of Cuailgne.

And after that, he was seen again, by Conn of the Hundred Battles. This is how that happened.

Conn was at Teamhair, and he went up in the early morning to the Rath of the Kings at the rising of the sun. His three Druids were with him, Maol and Bloc and Bhuice, and his three poets, Ethain and Corb and Cesarn. He went up there with them every day, to look out on every side, so that if any men of the Sidhe came into Ireland, they would not come without his knowing it.

On this day he happened to stand on a stone that was in the rath. The stone screamed under his feet. It was heard all over Teamhair, and as far away as Bregia.

Conn asked his chief Druid how the stone came to be there, and what it screamed for. The Druid said he would not answer that until fifty-three days had passed. At the end of that time Conn asked him again, and this is what the Druid said:

"The Lia Fail is the name of that stone. It was brought out of Falias, and it was set up in Teamhair, and in Teamhair it will stay for ever. As long as there's a king in Teamhair, this will be the gathering-place for games; and if no king comes to the last day of the gathering, there will be hardship in that year. And when the stone screamed under your feet, the number of screams it gave was a foretelling of the number of kings of your race that will come after you. But it is not I who will name them for you."

While they were standing there, a great mist came down around them, and a darkness, so that they could not tell which way they were going. They heard the sound of a rider coming towards them.

"It would be a great grief to us," said Conn, "to be carried off into a strange country."

The rider threw three spears at them, and each came faster than the one before.

"It is the wounding of a king indeed," said the Druids, "for anyone to throw at Conn of Teamhair."

At that the rider stopped throwing his spears. He came up to them and bade Conn welcome, and asked him to come to his house.

They went on until they came to a beautiful plain, and there they saw a king's rath, with a golden tree at its door. Inside the rath was a grand house with a roof of white bronze. They went into the house, and the rider who had come to meet them was there before them, sitting in his royal seat. There had never been a man seen in Teamhair like him for comeliness, or for beauty, or for the wonder of his face.

There was a young woman in the house, with a band of gold on her head. Beside her was a silver vessel with hoops of gold, full of red ale, with a golden bowl on its edge and a golden cup at its mouth.

"Who am I to serve drink to?" she said to the master of the house.

"Serve it to Conn of the Hundred Battles," he said, "for he will win a hundred battles before he dies."

Then he told her to pour out the ale for Art of the Three Shouts, the son of Conn. And after that he went through the names of all the kings of Ireland who would come after Conn, and told the length of each one's life.

The young woman left the vessel with Conn, and the cup and the bowl. And she gave him, along with them, the rib of an ox and the rib of a hog. The ox-rib was twenty-four feet long.

The master of the house told them that the young woman was the Kingship of Ireland, for ever.

"And as for me," he said, "I am Lugh of the Long Hand, son of Ethlinn."

Then the mist lifted, and they were standing on the Rath of the Kings again, in the morning, with a vessel and a cup and a bowl, and nobody to tell them what any of it had cost.

Nobody knows now how long the Tuatha de Danaan ruled over Ireland. It was probably a long time. But in the end they were put out of it.

This is how it happened.

The sons of Gaedhal of the Shining Armour, the Very Gentle — the ones who were called afterwards the Sons of the Gael — made their first attempt to land in Ireland at Inver Slane, to the north of Leinster. They came to avenge Ith, one of their own race, who had come to Ireland once before and met his death there.

The sons of Miled led them, and they came from the south. Their Druids had told them there was no country for them to settle in until they came to that island in the west. "And if you don't get possession of it yourselves," the Druids said, "your children will."

When the Tuatha de Danaan saw the ships coming, they flocked down to the shore. By their enchantments they threw such a cloud over the whole island that the sons of Miled were confused, and all they could see was some large thing that looked like a pig.

Ireland, from the sea, looked like a pig. That is the kind of magic the gods had then.

Since the enchantments kept them from landing there, they sailed along the coast until at last they managed to land at Inver Sceine, in the west of Munster.

From there they marched in good order as far as Slieve Mis. There they were met by a queen of the Tuatha de Danaan, with a train of beautiful women attending her, and her Druids and wise men following behind. Amergin, one of the sons of Miled, spoke to her and asked her name. She said it was Banba, wife of Mac Cuill, Son of the Hazel.

They went on until they came to Slieve Eibhline, and there another queen of the Tuatha de Danaan met them, with her women and her Druids behind her. They asked her name, and she said it was Fodhla, wife of Mac Cecht, Son of the Plough.

They went on until they came to the hill of Uisnech, and there they saw another woman coming towards them, and they wondered as they watched her. One moment she was a wide-eyed and most beautiful queen. The next she was a sharp-beaked, grey-white crow. She came up to where Eremon, one of the sons of Miled, was standing, and sat down in front of him. He asked her who she was.

"I am Eriu," she said, "wife of Mac Greine, Son of the Sun."

The names of those three queens were often given to Ireland in the time that came after. They still are. Every time someone says Eire, they are saying her name.

After that the Sons of the Gael went on to Teamhair. The three sons of Cermait Honey-Mouth, son of the Dagda, held the kingship between them at that time and kept their court there. And the three were quarrelling with each other over the division of the treasures their father had left, and the quarrel was so hot that it looked as if it would come to a battle in the end.

The Sons of the Gael wondered to see them quarrelling over such things, when they had so fruitful an island — where the air was so wholesome, and the sun not too strong, and the cold not too bitter, and where there was such plenty of honey and acorns, and milk, and fish, and corn, and room enough for everybody.

They lived in great grandeur at the palace of Teamhair, with their Druids around them. Amergin went to them and told them they must give up the kingship there and then, or else leave it to the chance of a battle. He said he asked it in revenge for the death of Ith, of the race of the Gael, who had come to their court before and had been killed by treachery.

When the sons of Cermait Honey-Mouth heard Amergin say such fierce words they were astonished. They said they were not willing to fight just then, for their army was not ready.

"But you make us an offer," they said, "for we can see you have good judgment and knowledge. Only, if you make us an offer that isn't fair, we'll destroy you with our enchantments."

So Amergin told the men with him to go back to Inver Sceine, and to hurry into their ships again with the rest of the Sons of the Gael, and to go out from the shore the length of nine waves.

Then he made his offer to the Tuatha de Danaan. If they could stop his men from landing on their island, he and all his ships would go home to their own country and never try to come again. But if the Sons of the Gael could land on the coast in spite of them, the Tuatha de Danaan must give up the kingship and be under their rule.

The Tuatha de Danaan were well pleased with that offer. They thought that with their enchantments over the winds and the sea, and all their arts, they would easily keep them from ever setting foot in the country again.

So the Sons of the Gael did what Amergin told them. They went back to their ships and drew up their anchors and moved out the length of nine waves from the shore.

The moment the Men of Dea saw they had left the land, they took to their enchantments and their spells. They raised a great wind that scattered the ships of the Gael and drove them apart.

Amergin knew it was not a natural storm. Arranan, son of Miled, knew it too, and he climbed the mast of his ship to look about him. A great blast of wind came at him, and he fell back into the ship and died that moment.

There was great confusion among the Gael. The ships were tossed to and fro and came close to being lost. The ship that Donn, son of Miled, commanded was torn away from the others by the force of the storm and broken to pieces, and he and everyone with him were drowned: four-and-twenty men and women in all. Ir, son of Miled, died the same way. His body was thrown up on the shore, and it was buried on a small island that is called Sceilg Michill now. Ir was a brave man. He led the Sons of the Gael to the front of every battle, and he was their help and their shelter in battle, and his enemies were in dread of his name.

Heremon, another of the sons of Miled, was driven with his share of the ships to the left of the island, and he barely got safe to land. The place where he landed was called Inver Colpa, because Colpa of the Sword, another son of Miled, drowned there trying to get ashore.

Five of the sons of Miled in all were destroyed by the storm and the winds the Men of Dea had raised with their enchantments. Only three were left: Heber, and Heremon, and Amergin.

Before he was swept into the sea, Donn had shouted out: "It's treachery our learned men are doing on us, not putting down this wind!"

"There's no treachery," said Amergin, his brother.

And he stood up in front of them, and whatever enchantment he worked on the winds and the sea, these are the words he said with it:

"That they who are tossing on the great, wide, food-giving sea may reach the land now.

"That they may find a place upon its plains, its mountains, and its valleys; in its forests full of nuts and of all fruits; on its rivers and its streams, on its lakes and its great waters.

"That we may have our gatherings and our races in this land; that there may be a king of our own in Teamhair; that it may be the possession of our many kings.

"That the sons of Miled may be seen in this land, and their ships and their boats find a place there.

"This land that is now under darkness, it is for it we are asking. Let our chief men, let their learned wives, ask that we may come to the noble woman, great Eriu."

When he had said it, the wind dropped, and the sea was quiet again that same moment.

He had not fought the storm. He had asked the land. And the land had answered.

So those who were left of the sons of Miled and of the Sons of the Gael landed at Inver Sceine.

Amergin was the first to put his foot on the land. And when he stood on the shore of Ireland, this is what he said:

"I am the wind on the sea;
I am the wave of the sea;
I am the bull of seven battles;
I am the eagle on the rock;
I am a flash from the sun;
I am the most beautiful of plants;
I am a strong wild boar;
I am a salmon in the water;
I am a lake in the plain;
I am the word of knowledge;
I am the head of the spear in battle;
I am the god that puts fire in the head.
Who spreads light in the gathering on the hills?
Who can tell the ages of the moon?
Who can tell the place where the sun rests?"

The gods of Dana heard it. And they understood, perhaps before the Gael did, that a man had come to Ireland who could speak to it the way they spoke to it. That had never happened before.

Three days after the Gael landed, they were attacked by Eriu, wife of Mac Greine, Son of the Sun. She had a good share of men with her. They fought a hard battle, and many were killed on both sides. This was the first battle fought between the Sons of the Gael and the Men of Dea for the kingship of Ireland.

Fais, wife of Un, was killed in that battle, in a valley at the foot of the mountain, and the valley was named after her: the Valley of Fais. And Scota, wife of Miled, got her death in the battle, and she was buried in a valley on the north side of the mountain, near the sea.

But the Sons of the Gael lost no more than three hundred men, and they beat back the Men of Dea and killed a thousand of them.

Eriu was driven back to Tailltin, with as many of her men as she could hold together. When she got there she told the people how she had been worsted in the battle, and how the best of her men had got their death.

The Gael stayed on the battlefield and buried their dead. They gave a great burial to two of their Druids, Aer and Eithis, who had been killed in the fight.

When they had rested a while they went on to Inver Colpa in Leinster, and Heremon and his men joined them there. Then they sent messengers to the three kings of Ireland, the three sons of Cermait Honey-Mouth, and told them to come out and fight a battle that would settle the ownership of the country once and for all.

So they came out to Tailltin, and the best fighters of the Tuatha de Danaan with them.

There the two sides fell on each other. The Sons of the Gael remembered the death of Ith, and a great anger came on them, and they went at the Men of Dea to avenge him, and a fierce battle was fought. For a while neither side got the better of the other. But at last the Gael broke through the army of the Men of Dea and put them to rout, with great slaughter, and drove them out of that place.

Their three kings were killed in the rout. And the three queens of Ireland were killed: Eriu, and Fodhla, and Banba.

When the Tuatha de Danaan saw their leaders dead, they fell back in great disorder, and the Sons of the Gael came after them. In the pursuit the Gael lost two of their best leaders: Cuailgne, son of Breagan, at Slieve Cuailgne, and Fuad, his brother, at Slieve Fuad. They were not daunted by that. They followed the Men of Dea so hard that the Men of Dea were never able to bring their army together again, and had to own themselves beaten, and give up the country to the Gael.

Consider what that means. The gods lost. Not to other gods. To people.

The leaders, the sons of Miled, divided the provinces of Ireland between them. Heber took the two provinces of Munster, and gave a share of it to Amergin. Heremon took Leinster and Connacht for his share. Ulster was divided between Eimhir, son of Ir, son of Miled, and some others of their chief men.

It was from the sons of Eimhir — who were called the Children of Rudraighe, and who lived in Emain Macha for nine hundred years — that some of the best men of Ireland came. Fergus, son of Rogh, was one of them, and Conall Cearnach of the Red Branch of Ulster.

And from the sons of Ith, the first of the Gael to get his death in Ireland, there came in later times Fathadh Canaan, who got the sway over the whole world from the rising to the setting of the sun, and who took hostages of the streams, and of the birds, and of the languages.

This is what the poets of Ireland used to say. Every brave man good at fighting, every man who could do great deeds and not make much talk about them, was of the Sons of the Gael. Every skilled man who had music, and who did enchantments in secret, was of the Tuatha de Danaan.

But they gave a bad name to the Firbolgs, and to the men of Domnand, and to the Gaileoin, for lying and big talk and injustice. For all that, there were good fighters among them. Ferdiad, who made such a good stand against Cuchulain in the war for the Bull of Cuailgne, was one of them. The Gaileoin fought well in that same war. But the men of Ireland had no great liking for them, and their Druids drove them out of the country afterwards.

As for the Men of Dea, they were beaten, and they had given up the country.

They did not leave it.

After they were beaten, the Tuatha de Danaan would not go under the rule of the sons of Miled. They went away by themselves.

Manannan, son of Lir, understood all enchantments, so they left it to him to find places for them where they would be safe from their enemies. He chose the most beautiful of the hills and valleys of Ireland for them to settle in. And he put hidden walls around them, walls no man could see through — though they themselves could see through them, and pass through them.

That is where they went. Into the hills. Behind the walls you cannot see. They are there still.

Manannan made the Feast of Age for them. What they drank at it was the ale of Goibniu the Smith, and whoever tasted it was kept from age, and from sickness, and from death. For food at the feast he gave them his own swine, which, though they were killed and eaten one day, would be alive and fit for eating again the next, and would go on like that for ever.

After a while they said, "It would be better for us to have one king over us, than to be scattered the way we are through the whole of Ireland."

The ones with the best chance of the kingship at that time were Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda; and Ilbrech of Ess Ruadh; and Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh, the Hill of the White Field, on Slieve Fuad; and Midhir the Proud of Bri Leith; and Angus Og, son of the Dagda — though Angus did not want the kingship at all, and would sooner have been left as he was.

All the chief men except those five went into council together. They agreed to give the kingship to Bodb Dearg, for his father's sake, and for his own sake, and because he was the eldest of the children of the Dagda.

Bodb Dearg had his house in Sidhe Femen, and he put great enchantments about it.

Cliach, the Harper of the King of the Three Rosses in Connacht, went there once to ask for one of Bodb's daughters in marriage. He stayed outside the place for the whole length of a year, playing his harp, and he could get no nearer to Bodb or to his daughter. He went on playing until a lake burst up under his feet: the lake on the top of a mountain, Loch Bel Sead.

It was Bodb's swineherd who went to Da Derga's Inn, with his squealing pig along with him, on the night that Conaire, the High King of Ireland, met his death. It was said that whatever feast that swineherd went to, blood would be shed before it was over.

Bodb had three sons: Angus, and Artrach, and Aedh. In the time of the Fianna, later, they often lived among men.

Artrach had a house with seven doors, and a free welcome for everyone who came. The king's son of Ireland and the king's son of Alban used to come to Angus to learn the throwing of spears and darts. And troops of poets from Alban and from Ireland stayed with Aedh, who was the comeliest of Bodb's sons, so that his place was called the Rath of Aedh of the Poets. It was a beautiful rath in those days, with golden-yellow apples in it, and the crimson-pointed nuts of the wood.

But after the passing of the Fianna, the three brothers went back to the Tuatha de Danaan.

Bodb Dearg was not always in his own place. Sometimes he was with Angus at Brugh na Boinn.

Three sons of Lugaidh Menn, King of Ireland, went there once: Eochaid, and Fiacha, and Ruide. Their father had refused them any land until they won it for themselves. When he said that, they rose up together, like one man rising, and went and sat down on the green of Brugh na Boinn, and fasted there against the Tuatha de Danaan, to see whether they could win some good thing from them.

That is a thing you could do, then. You could sit down outside the hill of the gods and refuse to eat until they noticed you. It sometimes worked.

They had not been there long when they saw a young man coming towards them, quiet and pleasant-looking. He wished them good health, and they answered the same way.

"Where have you come from?" they asked him.

"From the rath over there, with the many lights," he said. "I am Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda. Come in with me now to the rath."

So they went in, and supper was made ready for them, but they did not touch it. Bodb Dearg asked them why they would take nothing.

"Because our father has refused us land," they said. "There are only two races in Ireland, the Sons of the Gael and the Men of Dea. When the one failed us, we came to the other."

The Men of Dea took counsel together. The chief among them was Midhir of the Yellow Hair, and this is what he said: "Let us give a wife to each of these three men. It's from a wife that good or bad fortune comes."

They agreed to that, and Midhir's three daughters, Doirenn and Aife and Aillbhe, were given to them.

Then Midhir asked Bodb to say what marriage portion should go with them.

"I'll tell you," said Bodb. "We are three times fifty sons of kings in this hill. Let every king's son give three times fifty ounces of red gold. And I myself will give them, along with that, three times fifty suits of clothing of all colours."

"I'll give them a gift," said a young man of the Tuatha de Danaan from Rachlainn in the sea. "A horn, and a vat. You have only to fill the vat with pure water and it will turn into mead, fit to drink and strong enough to make you drunk. And you have only to put salt water from the sea into the horn, and it will turn into wine that moment."

"A gift from me," said Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh. "Three times fifty swords, and three times fifty well-riveted long spears."

"A gift from me," said Angus Og, son of the Dagda. "A rath, and a good town with high walls, and bright sunny houses, and wide houses, in whatever place they please between Rath Chobtaige and Teamhair."

"A gift from me," said Aine, daughter of Modharn. "A woman-cook I have. There is a geis on her never to refuse food to anyone, and as she serves it out, her store fills itself up again."

"Another gift from me," said Bodb Dearg. "A good musician I have, Fertuinne, son of Trogain. If there were women in the sharpest pains of childbirth, and brave men wounded early in the day, in a place where saws were going through wood, they would all sleep at the sweetness of the music he makes. And whatever house he's in, the people of the whole country round will hear him."

They stayed at Brugh na Boinne three days and three nights. When they left, Angus told them to bring three apple-trees with them from the oak-wood: one in full bloom, one shedding its blossom, and the third covered with ripe fruit.

Then they went to their own dun that had been given to them, and it was a good place. They had a troop of young men there, and great troops of horses and of greyhounds. They had the three kinds of music that comely kings like to listen to: the music of harps, and of lutes, and the chanting of Trogain's son. They had three great sounds: the tramping on the green, and the uproar of racing, and the lowing of cattle. And three other sounds: the grunting of good pigs with the fat thick on them, and the voices of the crowd on the green lawn, and the noise of men drinking inside the house.

It was said of Eochaid that he never took a step backwards in flight, and that his house was never without music or the drinking of ale. It was said of Fiacha that there was no man of his time braver, and that he never said one word too many. And as for Ruide, he never refused anybody anything, and he never asked anything of any man.

When their lifetime was over, they went back to the Tuatha de Danaan, for they belonged to them through their wives. And they have stayed there ever since.

Bodb Dearg had a daughter, Scathniamh, the Flower of Brightness. In the time of the Fianna she gave her love to Caoilte. They were forced apart, and they never met again until Caoilte was old and withered, and one of the last of the Fianna left alive.

She came to him then, out of the cave of Cruachan, and asked him for the bride-price he had promised her, and that she had never been able to come and ask for until then.

Caoilte went to a cairn near by that was filled up with gold. It was wages that Conan Maol had earned and hidden there. And Caoilte gave the gold to Bodb Dearg's daughter.

The people who were there wondered to see the girl so young and comely, and Caoilte so grey and bent and withered.

"There's no wonder in that," said Caoilte. "I am of the sons of Miled, who wither and fade away. She is of the Tuatha de Danaan, who never change, and who never die."

That is the difference between them and us. It is not a difference in power. It is a difference in what time does to you.

The Dagda, the Red Man of All Knowledge, had his house at Brugh na Boinne.

The things most worth seeing in it were the Hall of the Morrigu, and the Bed of the Dagda, and the Birthplace of Cermait Honey-Mouth, and the Prison of the Grey of Macha, the horse that would afterwards be Cuchulain's. There was a little hill by the house called the Comb and the Casket of the Dagda's Wife, and another called the Hill of Dabilla, after the little hound that belonged to Boann. And the Valley of the Mata was there — the Mata was a sea-turtle, and it could suck down a man in armour.

It is likely that the Dagda set up his cooking-oven there, the one Druimne, son of Luchair, made for him at Teamhair. This is how it was made. The axle and the wheel were wood, and the body was iron, and there were twice nine wheels on its axle so that it would turn the faster. It turned as quick as a stream runs. There were three times nine spits off it, and three times nine pots. It would lie down low with the cinders, and rise up to the height of the roof with the flame.

The Dagda himself once made a great vat for Ainge, his daughter. She was not well satisfied with it. It would not stop dripping while the sea was in flood, though it never lost a drop during the ebb. So she gathered a bundle of twigs to make a new vat for herself. But Gaible, son of Nuada of the Silver Hand, stole the bundle from her and hurled it away. Where it fell, a beautiful wood grew up, and it was called Gaible's Wood.

The Dagda kept his household at Brugh na Boinne. His steward was Dichu. The smith of the Brugh was Len Linfiaclach. Len lived in the lake, making the bright vessels of Fand, daughter of Flidhais. Every evening when he stopped work he would throw his anvil eastward to Indeoin na Dese, the Anvil of the Dese, as far as the Grave End. It cast three showers as it went: a shower of fire, and a shower of water, and a shower of precious stones of pure purple.

But Tuirbe, father of Goibniu the Smith, could throw better still. He would throw his axe from Tulach na Bela, the Hill of the Axe, into the face of the incoming tide, and put his order on the sea, and the sea would not come past the axe.

Corann was the best of the harpers of the household. He was harper to the Dagda's son, Diancecht. Once he called with his harp to Cailcheir, one of the swine of Debrann. The pig ran northward with all the strength of its legs, and the champions of Connacht ran after it with all their strength, and their hounds with them, until they got as far as Ceis Corain. There they gave it up — all except Niall, who kept on the pig's track until he found it in the oak-wood of Tarba. Then it made away across the plain of Ai, and through a lake, and Niall and his hound were drowned following it through the lake.

The Dagda gave Corann a great tract of land for harping so well.

However great a house the Dagda had, Angus got it away from him in the end, with the help of Manannan, son of Lir.

Manannan told Angus to ask his father for the Brugh for the length of a day and a night, and said that he would use his art to take away the Dagda's power of refusing. So Angus asked for the Brugh, and his father gave it to him for a day and a night.

When the Dagda asked for it back, Angus said it had been given to him for ever. For the whole of life and time, he said, is made up of a day and a night, one following the other.

It was a trick. It was also true. The best tricks usually are.

When the Dagda heard that, he went away, and his people and his household with him, for Manannan had put an enchantment on them all.

But Dichu the Steward was away at the time, and his wife and his son, gone to get provisions for a feast for Manannan and his friends. When he came back and found his master gone, he took service with Angus.

Angus stayed in Brugh na Boinne. Some say he is there still, behind the hidden walls, drinking Goibniu's ale and eating the pigs that never fail.

As for the Dagda, he took no revenge, though he had the name of being revengeful and quick-tempered. Some say it was at Teamhair he made his home after that. Wherever it was, a great misfortune came on him there.

Corrgenn, a great man of Connacht, came to visit him once, and brought his wife with him. While they were there, Corrgenn got it into his head that something was going on that was not right between his wife and Aedh, one of the sons of the Dagda. A great jealousy and anger came on him, and he struck at the young man and killed him in front of his father's face.

Everyone thought the Dagda would take Corrgenn's life then and there, in revenge for his son. He would not. He said that if his son was guilty, there was no blame on Corrgenn for doing what he did.

So he spared his life for that time. But Corrgenn did not gain much by it.

The punishment the Dagda put on him was this. He must take the dead body of the young man on his back and never lay it down until he found a stone that was its exact fit in length and in breadth, a stone that would make a gravestone for him. When he found it, he could bury him in the nearest hill.

Corrgenn had no choice but to go. He set out with his load, and he had a long way to travel before he found a stone that would fit. He found it at last on the shore of Loch Feabhail. He left the body up on the nearest hill, and went down and raised the stone and brought it up, and dug a grave, and buried the Dagda's son.

Many an Ochone he gave while he was putting the stone over him. And when he had done it, he was spent, and he dropped dead there and then.

The Dagda brought his two builders, Garbhan and Imheall, to the place, and told them to build a rath around the grave. Garbhan cut the stones and shaped them, and Imheall set them all round the house until the work was finished, and then closed the top of the house with a slab.

The place was called the Hill of Aileac, that is, the Hill of Sighs and of a Stone. For it was tears of blood the Dagda shed for the death of his son.

The gods do not die. It turns out their children can.

As for Angus Og, son of the Dagda, sometimes he would come out of Brugh na Boinn and let himself be seen upon the earth.

A long time after the coming of the Gael, he was seen by Cormac, King of Teamhair. This is the account Cormac gave of him.

Cormac was alone one day in his Hall of Judgment. He often sat there reading the laws and thinking how best to carry them out. Suddenly he saw a stranger at the end of the hall, a very comely young man. He knew at once that it was Angus Og. He had often heard his people talk of him — though he himself used to say he did not believe there was any such person at all.

When his people came back into the hall he told them that he had seen Angus himself and talked with him, and that Angus had told him his name, and had foretold what would happen to him.

"He was a beautiful young man," Cormac said, "with high looks, and his appearance was more beautiful than all beauty. There were ornaments of gold on his clothes. In his hand he held a silver harp with strings of red gold, and the sound of its strings was sweeter than all the music under the sky. Over the harp were two birds that seemed to be playing on it. He sat beside me pleasantly and played his sweet music to me. And at the end he foretold things that put drunkenness on my wits."

That is how it goes with gods. You say you do not believe in them. And then one day you look up from your law books.

The birds that went about with Angus were four of his kisses, which had turned into birds. They used to fly about the young men of Ireland, crying after them. "Come, come," two of them would say. "I go, I go," the other two would say. It was hard to get free of them.

Even in his earliest youth Angus was called the Frightener, or the Disturber. The plough-teams of the world, and every kind of beast that men use, would run in terror before him.

Once he appeared in the shape of a landholder to two men, Ribh and Eocho, who were looking for a place to settle. The first place they chose was near Bregia, on a plain that belonged to Angus. He came to them then, leading his horse by the hand, and told them they should not stay there. They said they could not carry their goods away without horses. So he gave them his horse, and told them to load everything they wanted onto it, and the horse would carry it. And it did.

But the next place they chose was Magh Find, the Fine Plain, and that was the playing-ground of Angus and of Midhir. That time Midhir came to them in the same way and gave them a horse to put their goods on, and went on with them as far as Magh Dairbthenn.

Many women loved Angus.

There was one, Enghi, daughter of Elcmair, who loved him though she had never seen him. She went looking for him once, to the gathering for games between Cletech and the Sidhe in Broga. The bright troops of the Sidhe came to that gathering every Samhain evening, bringing a moderate share of food with them — that is, a nut.

The sons of Derc came from the north, out of Sidhe Findabrach, and went round among the young men and women without their knowing it, and carried away Elcmair's daughter. There was great lamenting then, and the place got the name Cnoguba, the Nut Lamentation, from the crying there was at that gathering.

She had gone looking for love. She got taken instead. It happens.

Derbrenn, the daughter of Eochaid Fedlech, was another whom Angus loved. She had six fosterlings, three boys and three girls. But the mother of the boys, Dalb Garb, Dalb the Rough, put a spell on them that she made from a gathering of the nuts of Caill Ochuid, and it turned them into swine.

Angus gave them into the care of Buichet, the Hospitaller of Leinster, and they stayed a year with him. At the end of that year a longing came on Buichet's wife to eat a bit of the flesh of one of them. So she gathered a hundred armed men and a hundred hounds to take them.

The pigs ran. They went to Brugh na Boinn, to Angus, and he made them welcome, and they asked for his help.

He said he could not give it until they had shaken the Tree of Tarbga, and eaten the salmon of Inver Umaill.

So they went to Glascarn and hid there a year with Derbrenn. Then they shook the Tree of Tarbga, and went on towards Inver Umaill.

But Maeve gathered the men of Connacht to hunt them. They all fell but one. Their heads were put in a mound, and the mound got the name of Duma Selga, the Mound of the Hunting.

And it was in the time of Maeve of Cruachan that Angus set his love on Caer Ormaith, of the Province of Connacht, and brought her away to Brugh na Boinn.

Angus loved often. Once, at least, it ended well.

The Morrigu. The Great Queen. The Crow of Battle.

Nobody knows where she lived after the coming of the Gael. Before that, she lived at Teamhair.

She had a great cooking-spit there that held three kinds of food on it at the one time: a piece of raw meat, and a piece of cooked meat, and a piece of butter. The raw meat cooked, and the cooked meat did not burn, and the butter did not melt, all three of them together on the spit.

Nine outlaws went to her once and asked her to make a spit for them. They carried it away with them. It had nine ribs, and each of the outlaws carried a rib in his hand wherever he went, until they all met again at the close of day. If they wanted the spit to be high, it could be raised to a man's height; at another time it would be no more than a fist's height over the fire. It never broke and it never grew less.

The Morrigu had a son, Mechi, and he was killed by Mac Cecht on Magh Mechi, which until then had been called Magh Fertaige.

Mechi had three hearts, and this is how they were: they had the shapes of three serpents through them. If Mechi had not died, those serpents would have grown, and whatever they left alive in Ireland would have wasted away. Mac Cecht burned the three hearts on Magh Luathad, the Plain of Ashes, and threw the ashes into the stream. The rushing water of the stream stopped, and boiled up, and every creature in it died.

The story does not tell us what the Morrigu said about that. It does not need to. She was the Crow of Battle, and she had lost a son, and she went on.

She was always meddling in Ireland in Cuchulain's time, stirring up wars and quarrels.

It was she who came and roused Cuchulain once, when he was only a boy, and was close to giving in to some enchantment worked against him.

"There's not the making of a hero in you," she said to him, "lying there under the feet of shadows."

With that Cuchulain got up and struck the head off a shadow that was standing over him, with his hurling-stick.

And when Conchubar sent Finched out to rouse the men of Ulster at the time of the war for the Bull of Cuailgne, he told him to go to that terrible fury, the Morrigu, and get help for Cuchulain.

She quarrelled with Cuchulain once, when he met her bringing a cow away from the Hill of Cruachan. Another time she helped Talchinem, a Druid of the household of Conaire Mor, to carry off a bull his wife had set her heart on.

She was much given to meddling with cattle. Once she took a cow from Odras, a woman of the household of the cow-chief of Cormac Hua Cuined, who was following her husband with cattle. The Morrigu brought the cow away with her to the Cave of Cruachan and the Hill of the Sidhe. Odras followed her there, until sleep fell on her in the oak-wood of Falga. The Morrigu woke her, and sang spells over her, and made her into a pool of water, which ran into the river that flows to the west of Slieve Buane.

It is not a good idea to follow the Morrigu home.

In the battle of Magh Rath she fluttered over Congal Claen in the shape of a bird, until he could not tell friend from foe. And again, at the battle of Cluantarbh, she was flying over the head of Murchadh, son of Brian. She had many shapes, and it was often in the shape of a crow that she fought her battles.

If it was not the Morrigu, it was Badb who showed herself in the battle of Dunbolg, where the men of Ireland fought under Aedh, son of Niall. And Brigit was seen in that same battle, on the side of the men of Leinster.

The gods had given up Ireland. They had never given up its wars.

Some said Aine was a daughter of Manannan. Some said she was the Morrigu herself. Either way, there was a stone that belonged to her, and it was called Cathair Aine.

If you sat on that stone, you were in danger of losing your wits. If you sat on it three times, you lost them for ever.

People whose wits had gone astray would find their way to it. Mad dogs would come from all over the country and gather round it, and then go down into the sea, to Aine's place there.

But those who did cures with herbs said she had power over the whole body. She gave gifts of poetry and of music. She often gave her love to men. They called her the Leanan Sidhe, the Sweetheart of the Sidhe.

It was not safe to offend Aine. She was very revengeful.

Oilioll Oluim, a king of Ireland, killed her brother once. This is what she did about it.

She made a great yew-tree by enchantment beside the river Maigh in Luimnech, and she put a little man in it, playing sweet music on a harp.

Oilioll's son was crossing the river with his step-brother, and they saw the tree and heard the sweet music coming out of it. First they quarrelled over which of them should have the little harper. Then they quarrelled over the tree. They asked Oilioll to judge between them, and he gave judgment for his own son.

The bad feeling over that judgment led to the battle of Magh Mucruimhe. Oilioll and his seven sons were killed there.

So Aine got her revenge. She had not raised a hand. She had only planted a tree, and put music in it, and waited for people to be people.

Aoibhell was another woman of the Sidhe. She made her home in Craig Liath.

At the time of the battle of Cluantarbh she set her love on a young man of Munster, Dubhlaing ua Artigan. The King of Ireland had sent him away in disgrace. But before the battle he came back, to join Murchadh, the king's son, and to fight for the Gael.

Aoibhell came to stop him. When he would not stay with her, she put a Druid covering around him, so that nobody could see him.

He went to where Murchadh was fighting and made a great attack on the enemies of Ireland, striking them down on every side.

Murchadh looked around. "It seems to me I hear the sound of the blows of Dubhlaing ua Artigan," he said, "but I don't see him."

Then Dubhlaing threw off the Druid covering. "I won't keep this on me," he said, "if you can't see me through it. And come with me now across the plain to where Aoibhell is. She can give us news of the battle."

So they went to her, and she told them both to leave the battle, for they would lose their lives in it.

"I'll tell you a little true story," Murchadh said to her. "Fear for my own body will never make me change my face. If we fall, the strangers will fall with us. Many a man will fall by my own hand, and the Gael will be sharing out their strong places."

"Stay with me, Dubhlaing," she said then, "and you'll have two hundred years of happy life with me."

"I won't give up Murchadh," he said, "or my own good name, for silver or gold."

Two hundred years. Think about that for a moment. That is what he turned down, and he knew exactly what he was turning down.

Anger came on Aoibhell when he said it. "Murchadh will fall," she said, "and you will fall yourself, and your proud blood will be on the plain tomorrow."

They went back into the battle, and got their death there.

It was Aoibhell who gave a golden harp to the son of Meardha, when he was getting his learning at the school of the Sidhe in Connacht and heard that his father had got his death at the hands of the King of Lochlann. Whoever heard that harp played did not live long after. Meardha's son went to where the three sons of the King of Lochlann were, and played his harp for them, and they died.

It was that harp Cuchulain heard when his enemies were gathering against him at Muirthemne. And he knew by it that his life was near its end.

Midhir took a hill for himself. His wife Fuamach lived there with him, and his daughter, Bri.

Leith, son of Celtchar of Cualu, was the most beautiful of the young men of the Sidhe of Ireland in those days, and he loved Bri, Midhir's daughter.

Once Bri went out with her young girls to meet him at the Grave of the Daughters, beside Teamhair. Leith came, and his young men with him, as far as the Hill of the After Repentance. They could come no closer to one another than that, because of the slingers on Midhir's hill, who answered one another until their spears were as thick as a swarm of bees on a fine day. Cochlan, Leith's servant, got a sharp wound from them, and died.

Then the girl turned back to Midhir's hill, and her heart broke inside her, and she died.

"Though I'm not let come to this girl," said Leith, "I'll leave my name with her."

And the hill was called Bri Leith from that day.

After a while Midhir took Etain Echraide to be his wife.

Fuamach, the wife he already had, was bitterly jealous when she saw the love Midhir gave to Etain. She called on the Druid Bresal Etarlaim to help her, and he put spells on Etain so that Fuamach was able to drive her away.

When she was driven out of Bri Leith, Angus Og, son of the Dagda, took her into his keeping. When Midhir asked for her back, Angus would not give her up, but carried her with him everywhere he went. Wherever they rested, he made a sunny house for her and filled it with sweet-smelling flowers, and put invisible walls around it, walls no one could see through, and that could not be seen.

When news came to Fuamach of how well Angus was caring for Etain, anger and jealousy came on her again, and she searched her mind for a way to destroy Etain altogether.

This is what she did. She persuaded Midhir and Angus to go out and meet each other and make peace, for there had been a quarrel between them since Etain was sent away. And while Angus was away from Brugh na Boinn, Fuamach went and found Etain there in her sunny house. She turned her with Druid spells into a fly. Then she sent a blast of wind into the house, and it swept Etain out through the window.

Midhir and Angus waited a while for Fuamach to come and join them. When she did not come they grew uneasy, and Angus hurried back to Brugh na Boinn. He found the sunny house empty. He went looking for Fuamach, and he found her with Etarlaim the Druid, and struck her head off there and then.

For seven years Etain was blown to and fro through Ireland in great misery. A fly, on the wind. For seven years.

At last she came to the house of Etar, of Inver Cechmaine, where there was a feast going on. She fell from a beam of the roof into the golden cup that stood beside Etar's wife. Etar's wife drank her down with the wine. And at the end of nine months she was born again, as Etar's daughter.

She had the same name as before: Etain. She was reared as a king's daughter, and fifty young girls, daughters of princes, were brought up with her to keep her company.

One day Etain and the other young girls were bathing in the bay at Inver Cechmaine, and from the water they saw a man of very high looks coming towards them across the plain, riding a bay horse with curled mane and tail. He wore a long green cloak, and a shirt woven with threads of red gold, and a brooch of gold that reached across to his shoulders on either side. On his back was a shield of silver with a rim of gold and a boss of gold, and in his hand a sharp-pointed spear covered with rings of gold from heel to socket. He had fair yellow hair coming over his forehead, bound with a golden band to keep it from loosening.

When he came near them he got down from his horse and sat on the bank, and this is what he said:

"It is here Etain is today, at the Mound of Fair Women. It is among little children her life is, on the strand of Inver Cechmaine.

"It is she healed the eye of the king from the well of Loch da Lig; it is she was swallowed in a heavy drink by the wife of Etar.

"Many great battles will happen for your sake to Echaid of Midhe; destruction will fall upon the Sidhe, and war on thousands of men."

When he had said that, he vanished, and nobody knew where he went. And they did not know that the man who had come to them was Midhir of Bri Leith.

He had waited all that time. He had found her.

When Etain was grown into a beautiful young woman, she was seen by Eochaid Feidlech, High King of Ireland. This is how it happened.

He was crossing the fair green of Bri Leith once, and he saw a woman beside a well. She had a bright comb of gold and silver, and she was washing in a silver basin with four golden birds on it and little bright purple stones set in its rim. She wore a beautiful purple cloak with silver fringes, and a gold brooch, and under it a dress of green silk with a long hood, embroidered in red gold, and wonderful clasps of gold and silver on her breast and at her shoulder. The sunlight was falling on her, so that the gold and the green silk shone out. She had two plaits of hair, with four locks in each plait and a bead at the point of every lock, and the colour of her hair was like yellow flags in summer, or like red gold after it has been rubbed.

There she was, letting down her hair to wash it, with her arms out through the sleeve-holes of her shift. Her soft hands were as white as the snow of a single night. Her eyes were as blue as any blue flower, and her lips as red as rowan-berries, and her body as white as the foam of a wave. There was the bright light of the moon in her face, and the highness of pride in her eyebrows, a dimple of delight in each of her cheeks, the light of wooing in her eyes. And when she walked, she walked with a step as steady and even as a queen's.

Eochaid sent his people to bring her to him, and asked her name. She told him her name was Etain, daughter of Etar, King of the Riders of the Sidhe. Eochaid gave her his love, and paid the bride-price, and brought her home to Teamhair as his wife, and there was a great welcome for her there.

A while after that there was a great feast at Teamhair. All the chief men of Ireland came to it, and it lasted from the fortnight before Samhain to the fortnight after.

King Eochaid's brother Ailell came to that feast — he who was afterwards called Ailell Anglonach, Ailell of the Only Fault. When he saw his brother's wife Etain he fell in love with her that moment, and all through the feast he could not be content unless he was looking at her.

A woman noticed it: the daughter of Luchta Lamdearg, Luchta of the Red Hand. "What far thing are you looking at, Ailell?" she said. "It's my opinion that looking the way you're looking is a sign of love."

Ailell checked himself, and did not look towards Etain again.

But when the feast was over and the gathering broken up, a great desire and envy came on Ailell, so that he fell sick, and they carried him to a house in Teffia. He stayed there a whole year, wasting away, and he told no one the cause of his sickness.

At the end of the year Eochaid came to visit his brother. He passed his hand over his breast, and Ailell groaned.

"How are you?" said Eochaid. "Are you getting any easier? You mustn't let this illness come to a bad end."

"By my word," said Ailell, "I'm not easier. I'm worse and worse every day and every night."

"What is it ails you? What is it that's coming against you?"

"By my word, I can't tell you that."

"I'll bring someone here who will know the cause of your sickness," said the king.

He sent Fachtna, his own physician, to Ailell. Fachtna passed his hand over Ailell's heart, and at that Ailell groaned again.

"This sickness won't be your death," said Fachtna. "And I know well where it comes from. It's either from the pains of jealousy, or from love you have given and found no way out of."

But Ailell was ashamed, and would not admit to the physician that he was right. So Fachtna went away and left him.

As for King Eochaid, he went off to visit all the provinces of Ireland under his kingship, and left Etain behind.

"Good Etain," he said, "take tender care of Ailell as long as he's living. And if he should die on us, make a sodded grave for him, and raise a pillar-stone over it, and write his name on it in Ogham."

And with that he went away on his journey.

One day Etain went into the house where Ailell lay in his sickness, and they talked together, and then she made a little song for him. This is what she said:

"What is it ails you, young man? It is a long time you are wasted with this sickness, and it is not the hardness of the weather that has stopped your light footstep."

Ailell answered her the same way. "I have good cause for my hurt. The music of my own harp doesn't please me. There's no food that's pleasant to me, and so I'm wasted away."

"Tell me what it is that ails you," said Etain, "for I'm a woman who is wise. Tell me if there's anything that would cure you, so that I can help you to it."

"O kind, beautiful woman," said Ailell, "it isn't good to tell a secret to a woman. But sometimes it may be known through the eyes."

"Though it's bad to tell a secret," said Etain, "it ought to be told now. How else can help be given to you?"

"My blessing on you, fair-haired Etain," said Ailell. "I'm not fit to be spoken to. My wits have been no help to me. My body is a rebel against me. All Ireland knows, O king's wife, there's sickness in my head and in my body."

"If there's a woman among the fair-faced women of Ireland tormenting you like this," said Etain, "she must come to you here, if it pleases you. I'll woo her for you myself."

"Woman," said Ailell, "it would be easy for you yourself to take my sickness from me. My desire is a desire as long as a year. But it's love given to an echo, grief spent on a wave, a lonely fight with a shadow. That is what my love and my desire have been to me."

Then Etain knew what the sickness was that was on him, and it was a heavy trouble to her.

But she came to him every day to tend him, and to make his food ready, and to pour water over his hands. She did everything she could for him, for it grieved her that he should wither away and be lost for her sake.

At last one day she said to him, "Get up, Ailell, son of a king, man of high deeds, and I'll do your healing."

He put his arms around her, and she kissed him.

"Come tomorrow morning at the break of day to the house outside the dun," she said, "and I'll give you all your desire."

That night Ailell lay without sleeping until the morning was nearly there. And at the very moment he should have got up to go to her, sleep settled down on him, and he slept on until the full light of day.

Etain went to the house outside the dun. She had not been there long when she saw a man coming towards her who looked like Ailell, sick and tired and worn. But when he came near and she looked at him closely, she saw it was not Ailell at all. Then he went away, and after she had waited a while she went back into the dun herself.

It was then that Ailell woke. When he knew the morning had gone by, he would sooner have had death than life, and he fretted terribly. Etain came in, and he told her what had happened.

"Come tomorrow to the same place," she said.

But the same thing happened the next day.

And when it happened on the third day, and the same man came to meet her, Etain said to him: "It isn't you at all I come here to meet. Why is it you come to meet me? And as for the one I did come to meet, it isn't for gain or out of lightness I told him to come to me, but to heal him of the sickness he's lying under for my sake."

"It would be more fitting for you to come to meet me than anyone else," said the man. "In the time long ago, I was your first husband, and your first man."

"What are you saying?" she said. "Who are you?"

"That's easy to tell," he said. "I am Midhir of Bri Leith."

"And what parted us, if I was your wife?"

"It was Fuamach's sharp jealousy, and the spells of Bresal Etarlaim the Druid, that parted us. Will you come away with me now?"

"It's not for a man whose kindred is unknown," said Etain, "that I'll give up the High King of Ireland."

She did not remember him. Think of that. He remembered everything, and she remembered nothing, and he had to stand there and be a stranger to her.

"Surely it was I myself put that great desire for you on Ailell," said Midhir. "And it was I kept him from going to meet you, so that you would keep your good name."

When she went back to Ailell's house, she found his sickness gone from him, and his desire with it. She told him everything that had happened.

"It has turned out well for us both," said Ailell. "I'm well of my sickness, and your good name is none the less."

"We give thanks to our gods for that," said Etain. "We are well pleased to have it so."

Just then Eochaid came back from his journey. They told him the whole story, and he was thankful to his wife for the kindness she had shown Ailell.
