A good while after that there was a great fair held at Teamhair, and Etain was out on the green watching the games and the races. She saw a rider coming towards her, and nobody could see him but herself. When he came near, she saw he looked the same as the man who had come and spoken to her and her young girls when they were bathing in the sea at Inver Cechmaine. When he came up to her he began to sing words to her that nobody could hear but her. This is what he said:

"O beautiful woman, will you come with me to the wonderful country that is mine? It is pleasant to look at the people there, beautiful people without any blemish. Their hair is the colour of the flag-flower, their fair bodies are as white as snow, the colour of the foxglove is on every cheek. The young never grow old there. The fields and the flowers are as pleasant to look at as the blackbird's eggs. Warm, sweet streams of mead and of wine flow through that country. There is no care and no sorrow on anyone. We see others, but we ourselves are not seen.

"Though the plains of Ireland are beautiful, you would think little of them after our great plain. Though the ale of Ireland is heady, the ale of the great country is headier. O beautiful woman, if you come to my proud people, it is the flesh of pigs newly killed I will give you for food; it is ale and new milk I will give you to drink; it is feasting you will have with me there; it is a crown of gold you will have upon your hair, O beautiful woman!

"And will you come there with me, Etain?"

Etain said she would not leave Eochaid the High King.

"Will you come," said Midhir, "if Eochaid gives you leave?"

"I will," said Etain.

One day after that, Eochaid the High King was looking out from his palace at Teamhair, and he saw a strange man coming across the plain. He had yellow hair, and eyes blue and shining like the flame of a candle, and a purple dress, and in his hand a five-pronged spear and a shield with gold knobs on it.

He came up to the king, and the king bade him welcome. "Who are you?" he said. "And what have you come for? You're a stranger to me."

"If I'm a stranger to you, you're no stranger to me," said the man. "I've known you a long time."

"What is your name?"

"Nothing very great," he said. "I'm called Midhir of Bri Leith."

"What brings you here?"

"I've come to play a game of chess with you."

"Are you a good player?" said the king.

"A trial will tell you that," said Midhir.

"The chessboard is in the queen's house," said Eochaid, "and she's asleep just now."

"No matter," said Midhir. "I have a chessboard with me as good as your own."

He brought out his chessboard. It was made of silver, with precious stones shining in every corner. Then he brought out the chessmen, made of gold, from a bag woven of shining gold threads.

"Let's play now," said Midhir.

"I won't play without a stake," said the king.

"What stake shall we play for?"

"We can settle that after the game," said the king.

They played, and Midhir was beaten, and the king asked for fifty brown horses. They played a second time, and Midhir was beaten again. This time the king gave him four hard things to do: to make a road over Moin Lamraide, and to clear Midhe of stones, and to cover the district of Tethra with rushes, and the district of Darbrech with trees.

You should be suspicious by now of a stranger who loses at chess. Eochaid was not.

So Midhir brought his people out of Bri Leith to do those things, and it was hard work they had doing them. Eochaid used to go out and watch them, and he noticed that when the men of the Sidhe yoked their oxen, they yoked them by the neck and the shoulder, not by the forehead and the head. After Eochaid taught his own people to yoke them that way, he was given the name Eochaid Airem — Eochaid of the Plough.

When it was all done, Midhir came to Eochaid again, looking thin and wasted enough from the hard work he had been doing, and asked him to play a third game. Eochaid agreed, and it was settled as before: the winner would name the stake.

Midhir won that time. When the king asked him what he wanted, he said, "It's Etain, your wife, I want."

"I won't give her to you," said the king.

"Then all I'll ask," said Midhir, "is to put my arms around her and kiss her once."

"You may do that," said the king, "if you'll wait until the end of a month."

Midhir agreed, and went away for that time.

At the end of the month he came back and stood in the great hall at Teamhair, and nobody had ever seen him look so comely as he looked that night. Eochaid had gathered all his best fighting men in the hall, and when he saw Midhir come in he shut all the doors of the palace, for fear Midhir would try to carry Etain off by force.

"I've come to be paid what's owed to me," said Midhir.

"I haven't been thinking about it up to now," said Eochaid, and there was anger on him.

"You promised me Etain, your wife," said Midhir.

The red of shame came into Etain's face when she heard that.

"Let there be no shame on you, Etain," said Midhir. "For a whole year I've been asking for your love, and offered you every kind of treasure and riches, and you refused to come to me until your husband gave you leave."

"It's true I said that," said Etain. "I'll go, if Eochaid gives me up to you."

"I won't give you up," said Eochaid. "I'll let him do no more than put his arms round you, here in this place, as was promised him."

"I'll do that," said Midhir.

He took his sword in his left hand, and he took Etain in his right arm, and he kissed her.

All the armed men in the house rushed at him then. But he rose up through the roof, taking Etain with him. And when they rushed out of the house to follow, all they could see was two swans, high up in the air, linked together by a chain of gold.

Eochaid was very angry. He went and searched all through Ireland, but there was no news of them to be had anywhere, for they were in the houses of the Sidhe.

They went first to the Brugh of Angus on the Boinn. After they had stayed there a while they went on to a hill of the Sidhe in Connacht. There was a serving-maid with Etain at that time, Cruachan Croderg by name, and she said to Midhir, "Is this your own place we're in?"

"It isn't," said Midhir. "My own place is nearer the rising of the sun."

She was not well pleased to stay there when she heard that, and to quiet her Midhir said, "Your own name will be put on this place from now on." And the hill has been called the Hill of Cruachan from that day.

Then they went to Bri Leith. Etain's daughter Esa came to them there, bringing a hundred of every kind of cattle with her, and Midhir fostered her for seven years.

All that time Eochaid the High King was searching for them.

At last Codal of the Withered Breast took four rods of yew and wrote Oghams on them, and through them and his enchantments he found out that Etain was with Midhir in Bri Leith.

So Eochaid went there and attacked the place. For nine years he besieged it, and Midhir kept driving him away. Then Eochaid's people began digging into the hill. When they were getting near to where Etain was, Midhir sent out three times twenty beautiful women, every one of them with the appearance of Etain, and told the king to choose her out from among them.

The first one he chose was his own daughter, Esa.

But then Etain called out to him, and he knew her, and brought her home to Teamhair.

Eochaid gave his daughter Esa her choice of a place for herself. She chose it, and built a rath there, and it got the name of Rath Esa. From it she could see three notable places: the Hill of the Sidhe in Broga, and the Hill of the Hostages in Teamhair, and Dun Crimthain on Beinn Edair.

But Midhir and his people were very angry that their hill had been attacked and dug into. It was in revenge for that insult that they brought Conaire, High King of Ireland — the grandson of Eochaid and of Etain — to his death, afterwards, at Da Derga's Inn.

The gods do not forget a hole dug in their hill. They can wait a very long time.

As for Manannan the Proud, son of Lir: when he had made places for the rest of the Tuatha de Danaan to live in, he went away out of Ireland himself.

Some said he was dead. They said he got his death in battle at the hands of Uillenn Faebarderg, Uillenn of the Red Edge. They said the battle was fought at Magh Cuilenn, and that Manannan was buried standing on his feet, and that no sooner was he buried than a great lake burst up under his feet, in a place that had been a red bog until then. The lake got the name of Loch Orbson, from one of Manannan's names. And they said that red Badb was glad at that battle, and many women were sorry.

But he had many places to live, and he was often heard of in Ireland afterwards. Whatever the story says, Manannan was never a god who stayed dead.

It was he who sent a messenger to Etain, the mother of Conaire the High King, when she was hidden in the cowherd's house. It was he who brought up Deirdre's children in Emhain of the Apple Trees, and it was said of that place, "a house of peace is the hill of the Sidhe of Emhain." It was he who taught Diarmuid of the Fianna the use of weapons. It was he who taught Cuchulain the use of the Gae Bulg.

Some say he was Deirdre's father. Some say it was he who brought Conchubar, King of Ulster, to the place where she was hidden, running in the shape of a hare in front of the hounds of the men of Ulster to lead them there.

And this is what they say. When Conchubar had brought the sons of Usnach to Emain Macha, and could not get at them to kill them because of their bravery, it was to Manannan he went for help.

Manannan said he would give him none. He had told Conchubar, at the time he took Deirdre, that she would be the cause of the breaking of his kingdom, and Conchubar had taken her anyway.

But Conchubar asked him to put blindness on the sons of Usnach for a while, or else the whole army would be destroyed by their blows. After a time Manannan consented to that. When the sons of Usnach came out again against the army of Ulster, the blindness came on them, and they struck at one another, not seeing who was near them, and they fell by one another's hands.

But more people say that Manannan had no hand in it, and that it was Cathbad the Druid who put a sea about them and brought them to their death by his enchantments.

Some say Culain the Smith, who gave his name afterwards to Cuchulain, was Manannan himself, for Manannan had many shapes.

Anyway, before Culain came to Ulster he lived in the Island of Falga, which was one of Manannan's places. Once, before Conchubar came into his kingdom, he went to ask a Druid for advice, and the Druid told him to go to the Island of Falga and ask the smith he would find there, Culain, to make weapons for him. Conchubar did that, and the smith promised to make him a sword and a spear and a shield.

While he was at work on them, Conchubar went out early one morning to walk on the strand, and there he saw a sea-woman asleep on the shore. He put bonds on her while she slept, so that she could not escape.

When she woke and saw what had happened, she asked him to set her free.

"I am Tiabhal," she said, "one of the queens of the sea. Tell Culain, who's making your shield, to put my likeness on it and my name around it. Whenever you go into battle with that shield, the strength of your enemies will lessen, and your own strength and the strength of your people will increase."

So Conchubar let her go, and told the smith to do as she had said. And when he went back to Ireland he won the victory wherever he carried that shield.

Then he sent for Culain and offered him a place on the plains of Muirthemne. And whether he was Manannan or not, it is likely he gave Cuchulain good teaching, in the time the boy stayed with him there after killing his great dog.

Manannan had good hounds once. They went hunting after a pig that was destroying the whole country and making a desert of it. They followed it until they came to a lake, and there it turned on them. Not one hound escaped alive. They were all drowned, or maimed. The pig made for an island, that got the name of Muc-inis, the Pig's Island, afterwards. And the lake got the name of Loch Conn, the Lake of the Hounds.

It was through Manannan that the wave of Tuaig, one of the three great waves of Ireland, got its name. This is how that happened.

There was a young girl called Tuag, a fosterling of Conaire the High King. She was reared at Teamhair, and a great company of the daughters of the kings of Ireland were set around her to guard her, so that she would be kept for a king's asking.

But Manannan sent Fer Ferdiad of the Tuatha de Danaan — a pupil of his own, and a Druid — in the shape of a woman of Manannan's household. Fer Ferdiad went to where Tuag was, and sang a sleep-spell over her, and carried her away to Inver Glas. There he laid her down while he went looking for a boat, so that he could carry her away in her sleep to the Land of the Ever-Living Women.

But a wave of the flood-tide came over the girl, and she was drowned.

Manannan killed Fer Ferdiad in his anger. It did not bring back the girl. It never does.

Once Manannan's cows came up out of the sea at Baile Cronin: three of them, a red, and a white, and a black. The people there watched them stand on the strand for a while, as if they were thinking. Then they all walked up together, side by side, away from the strand.

There were no roads in Ireland at that time. The people wondered greatly when they saw a good wide road lying ready in front of the three cows to walk on.

When they were about a mile from the sea, the cows parted. The white cow went north-west, towards Luimnech. The red cow went south-west, and on round the coast of Ireland. The black cow went north-east, towards Lis Mor, in the district of Portlairge. A road opened in front of each of them, and the roads can be seen to this day.

Some say it was Manannan who came to Finn and the Fianna in the shape of the Gilla Decair, the Bad Servant, and carried them off to Land-under-Wave. Anyway, he often went hunting with them on Cnoc Aine, and sometimes he came to their help.

He liked people. That was the strange thing about him. Of all the gods, he liked people best, and he liked to play with them.

A long time after that, Manannan went playing tricks through Ireland again. That was the time he got the name of O'Donnell's Kern.

This is how it happened. Aodh Dubh O'Donnell was holding a feast at Bel-atha Senaig, and his people were boasting of the goodness of his house and of his musicians.

While they were talking, they saw a clown coming towards them. He wore old striped clothes. Puddle-water squelched in his shoes. His sword stuck out naked behind him. His ears poked out through the old cloak he had over his head. In his hand he carried three spears of holly-wood, scorched and blackened.

He wished O'Donnell good health, and O'Donnell wished him the same, and asked where he had come from.

"This is where I've been," he said. "I slept last night at Dun Monaidhe, with the King of Alban. I'm a day in Ile, a day in Cionn-tire, a day in Rachlainn, a day in the Watchman's Seat on Slieve Fuad. A pleasant, rambling, wandering man I am. And it's with you I am now, O'Donnell."

"Bring the gate-keeper to me," said O'Donnell.

When the gate-keeper came, O'Donnell asked him if it was he who had let this man in. The gate-keeper said he had not, and had never seen him before.

"Let him off, O'Donnell," said the stranger. "It was as easy for me to come in as it will be for me to go out again."

They all wondered at that: that any man could come into the house without passing the gate.

Then the musicians began to play. All the best musicians of the country were there, and they played very sweet tunes on their harps.

"By my word, O'Donnell," the stranger called out, "there was never a noise of hammers beating iron in any bad place as bad to listen to as this noise your people are making."

With that he took a harp himself, and he made music that would put women in their pains, and wounded men after a battle, into a sweet sleep.

"Since I first heard talk of the music of the Sidhe that's played in the hills and under the earth below us," said O'Donnell, "I never heard better music than yours. You're a very sweet player."

"One day I'm sweet," said the clown, "another day I'm sour."

O'Donnell told his people to bring him up to sit near himself.

"I've no mind to do that," said the clown. "I'd sooner be as I am, an ugly clown making sport for high-up people."

Then O'Donnell sent him down clothes, a hat and a striped shirt and a coat. He would not have them. "I've no mind," he said, "to let high-up people be boasting that they gave them to me."

By now they were afraid he might leave them. They set twenty armed horsemen and twenty men on foot to keep him from leaving the house, and as many again outside at the gate, for they knew he was not a man of this world.

"What are these men for?" said he.

"They're to keep you here," said O'Donnell.

"By my word, it's not with you I'll be eating my supper tomorrow," he said, "but at Cnoc Aine, where Seaghan, Son of the Earl, is, in Desmumain."

"If I find you giving one stir out of yourself between this and morning," said O'Donnell, "I'll knock you into a round lump there on the ground."

At that the stranger took up the harp again, and made the same sweet music as before. While they were all listening to him, he called out to the men outside: "Here I come! Watch me well now, or you'll lose me."

When the men watching the gate heard that, they raised their axes to strike at him. But in their haste they struck at one another instead, until they were all lying stretched in their blood.

Then the clown said to the gate-keeper: "You ask O'Donnell for twenty cows and a hundred of free land, as a fee for bringing his people back to life. And take this herb, and rub it in the mouth of each man of them, and he'll get up whole and well again."

The gate-keeper did that. He got the cows and the land from O'Donnell, and he brought all the people back to life.

Seaghan, Son of the Earl, was holding a gathering on the green in front of his dun at that time, and he saw the same man coming towards him, dressed the same way, and the water squelching in his shoes. When Seaghan asked who he was, he gave himself the name of a very learned man, Duartane O'Duartane. He said he had come by Ess Ruadh, and by Ceiscorainn, and from there to Corrslieve, and to Magh Lorg of the Dagda, and into the district of Hy'Conaill Gabhra — "until I came to you," he said, "by Cruachan of Magh Ai."

So they brought him into the house, and gave him wine to drink and water to wash his feet, and he slept until sunrise the next day.

Then Seaghan, Son of the Earl, came to see him. "That was a long sleep you had," he said, "and no wonder, after so long a journey yesterday. But I've often heard of your learning in books and of your skill on the harp, and I'd like to hear you this morning."

"I'm good at those arts indeed," said the stranger.

They brought him a book, and he could not read a word of it. Then they brought him a harp, and he could not play a single tune.

"It's likely your reading and your music have gone from you," said Seaghan. And he made a little verse mocking him, saying it was a strange thing that Duartane O'Duartane, with such a great name, could not read a line of a book, or even remember one.

When the stranger heard himself being mocked, he took up the book and read it from the top to the bottom of the page, very well, in a sweet-sounding voice. Then he took the harp and played and sang, the same as he had done in O'Donnell's house the day before.

"You're a very sweet man of learning," said Seaghan.

"One day I'm sweet," said the stranger, "another day I'm sour."

They walked out together on Cnoc Aine. While they were talking there, all in a minute the stranger was gone, and Seaghan, Son of the Earl, could not see where he had gone.

After that he went on, and reached Sligach just as O'Conchubar was setting out with the men of Connacht to avenge the Connacht hag's basket on the hag of Munster. This time he called himself the Gilla Decair, the Bad Servant. He joined the men of Connacht, and they went over the Sionnan westward into Munster. There they hunted and drove every creature that could be made to travel — cattle and horses and flocks — into one place, until they got the hornless bull of the Munster hag and her two speckled cows, and O'Conchubar carried them off to give to the Connacht hag in satisfaction for her basket.

The men of Munster attacked them on the way back. The Gilla Decair asked O'Conchubar whether he would sooner have the cows driven on, or the Munster men held back. O'Conchubar said he would sooner have the Munster men held back. So the Gilla Decair turned on them, and with his bow and twenty-four arrows he kept them off until O'Conchubar and his people were safe out of reach, in Connacht.

But then he took offence, because when they came to O'Conchubar's house O'Conchubar took the first drink himself instead of giving it to him, who had done so much. He took his leave and left them that very moment.

Gods notice who is handed the first cup. They always notice.

After that he went to where Tadg O'Cealaigh was, wearing his old striped clothes and his old shoes as before. When they asked him what art he had, he said, "I'm good at tricks. If you'll give me five marks, I'll show you a trick."

"I'll give that," said Tadg.

The stranger put three rushes on the palm of his hand. "I'll blow away the middle rush now," he said, "and the other two will stay where they are."

They told him to do it. He put the tips of two of his fingers on the two outside rushes, and blew the middle one away.

"There's a trick for you now, Tadg O'Cealaigh," he said.

"By my word, that's not a bad trick," said O'Cealaigh.

But one of O'Cealaigh's men said: "No good luck to the one who did it. Give me half of that money, Tadg, and I'll do the same trick for you myself."

"I'll give you half of what I got, if you'll do it," said the stranger.

So the other man put the rushes on his hand. But when he tried the trick, his two fingertips went through the palm of his hand.

"Ob-ob-ob!" said the stranger. "That's not the way I did the trick. But since you've lost the money, I'll heal you again."

"I could do another trick for you," he said. "I could wag the ear on one side of my head and the ear on the other side would stay still."

"Do it, then," said O'Cealaigh.

So the man of tricks took hold of one of his ears and wagged it up and down.

"That's a good trick indeed," said O'Cealaigh.

"I'll show you another one now," he said.

He took a thread of silk out of his bag and threw it up into the air, so that it caught fast to a cloud. Then he took a hare out of the same bag, and it ran up the thread. Then he took out a little dog and set it after the hare, and it followed, yelping on its track. Then he brought out a little serving-boy and told him to follow the dog and the hare up the thread. Then out of another bag he brought a beautiful, well-dressed young woman, and told her to follow the hound and the boy, and to take care the hare was not torn by the dog.

She went up quickly after them. It was a delight to Tadg O'Cealaigh to watch them, and to listen to the sound of the hunt going on in the air.

Then it was quiet for a long time.

"I'm afraid there's some bad work going on up there," said the man of tricks.

"What's that?" said O'Cealaigh.

"I'm thinking the hound might be eating the hare, and the serving-boy courting the girl."

"That's likely enough," said O'Cealaigh.

The stranger drew in the thread. And this is what he found: the boy making love to the girl, and the hound chewing the bones of the hare.

The man of tricks was very angry when he saw that. He took his sword and struck the boy's head off.

"I don't like a thing of that sort done in my presence," said Tadg O'Cealaigh.

"If it didn't please you, I can set everything right again," said the stranger. He took up the head and threw it at the body, and it joined on, and the young man stood up — but his face was turned backwards.

"It would be better for him to be dead than living like that," said O'Cealaigh.

When the man of tricks heard that, he took hold of the boy and twisted his head straight, and he was as well as before.

And with that the man of tricks vanished, and nobody saw where he went.

That is how Manannan used to go round Ireland, doing tricks and wonders. Nobody could keep him in any place. If he was hanged on a gallows, he would be found safe in the house afterwards, and some other man on the gallows in his place. But he did no harm, and anyone who was put to death by him he brought back to life again with a herb out of his bag.

All the food he ever ate was a vessel of sour milk and a few crab-apples. And there was never any music sweeter than the music he played.

One day sweet, another day sour. It is as good a description of the sea as any.

Some people went to Manannan's country beyond the sea, and gave an account of it afterwards.

Bran, son of Febal, was out by himself one time near his dun, and he heard music behind him. It stayed behind him wherever he went, and at last he fell asleep with the sweetness of it. When he woke, there was a branch of silver lying beside him. It had white blossoms on it, and the whiteness of the silver was the same as the whiteness of the blossoms.

He carried the branch into the royal house. When all his people were gathered with him, they saw a woman in strange clothing standing in the house.

She began to make a song for Bran, and all the people watched her and listened to her. This is what she said:

"I bring a branch of the apple-tree from Emhain, from the far island around which are the shining horses of the Son of Lir. A delight of the eyes is the plain where the hosts hold their games: curragh racing against chariot in the White Silver Plain to the south.

"There are feet of white bronze under it, shining through life and time; a comely level land through the length of the world's age, and many blossoms falling on it.

"There is an old tree there with blossoms, and birds calling from among them. Every colour is shining there; delight is common, and music, in the Gentle-Voiced Plain, in the Silver Cloud Plain to the south.

"Keening is not used there, or treachery, in the tilled, familiar land. There is nothing hard or rough, but sweet music striking on the ear.

"To be without grief, without sorrow, without death, without any sickness, without weakness: that is the sign of Emhain. It is no common wonder.

"There is nothing to liken its mists to. The sea washes the wave against the land. Brightness falls from its hair.

"There are riches, there are treasures of every colour in the Gentle Land, the Bountiful Land. Sweet music to listen to; the best of wine to drink.

"Golden chariots on the Plain of the Sea, rising up to the sun with the tide; silver chariots and bronze chariots on the Plain of Sports.

"Gold-yellow horses on the strand, and crimson horses, and others with wool on their backs, blue like the colour of the sky.

"It is a day of lasting weather; silver is dropping on the land; a pure white cliff on the edge of the sea, getting its warmth from the sun.

"The host races over the Plain of Sports; beautiful, and not weak, is their game. Death will not come to them, nor the ebbing of the tide, in the Many-Coloured Land.

"There will come at sunrise a fair man, lighting up the level lands. He rides upon the plain that is beaten by the waves; he stirs the sea until it is like blood.

"An army will come over the clear sea, rowing to the stone that is in sight, that a hundred sounds of music come from.

"It sings a song to the army; it is not sad through the length of time; it increases music with hundreds singing together. They do not look for death, or for the ebb-tide.

"There are three times fifty far islands in the ocean to the west of us, and every one of them twice or three times the size of Ireland.

"It is not to all of you I am speaking, though I have made all these wonders known. Let Bran listen, out of the crowd of the world, to all the wisdom that has been told him.

"Do not fall upon a bed of sloth. Do not be overcome by drunkenness. Set out on your voyage over the clear sea, and you may chance to come to the Land of Women."

With that the woman left them, and they did not know where she went. She took her branch with her. It leapt out of Bran's hand into hers, and he did not have the strength to hold it.

The next day Bran set out upon the sea, with three companies of nine along with him. One of his foster-brothers and comrades was set over each company of nine.

When they had rowed for two days and two nights, they saw a man coming towards them over the sea in a chariot. The man made himself known to them. He said he was Manannan, son of Lir.

Then Manannan spoke to Bran in a song. This is what he said:

"This is what Bran thinks: he is going in his curragh over the wonderful, beautiful clear sea. But to me, from far off in my chariot, it is a flowery plain he is riding on.

"What is a clear sea to the good boat Bran is in, is a happy plain with many flowers to me in my two-wheeled chariot.

"This is what Bran sees: many waves beating across the clear sea. This is what I myself see: red flowers without any fault.

"The sea-horses are bright in summertime, as far as Bran's eyes can reach. There is a wood of beautiful acorns under the head of your little boat.

"A wood with blossom and with fruit, that has the smell of wine; a wood without fault, without withering, with leaves the colour of gold.

"Let Bran row on steadily. It is not far to the Land of Women. Before the setting of the sun you will reach Emhain, of many-coloured hospitality."

Think about that. The same place. To Bran it was the sea, and to Manannan it was a meadow. Neither of them was wrong.

Bran went on from him, and after a while he saw an island. He rowed around it. There was a crowd of people on it, staring at them and laughing. They were all looking at Bran and at his people, but they would not stop to talk to them. They only went on letting out gusts of laughter.

Bran put one of his men ashore on the island. The man joined the others, and began to stare the same way as the people of the island. Bran went on rowing round the island, and every time they passed their own man his comrades called to him, but he would not answer. He only stared and wondered at them.

So they went away and left him there, on that island. It is called the Island of Joy.

It was not long after that they reached the Land of Women. They saw the chief of the women at the landing-place, and this is what she said: "Come here to land, Bran, son of Febal. Your coming is welcome."

But Bran did not dare to go ashore.

Then the woman threw a ball of thread straight at him. He caught it in his hand, and it stuck fast to his palm. The woman kept the other end of the thread in her own hand, and she pulled the curragh in to the landing-place.

They went into a grand house where there was a bed for every couple: three times nine beds. The food that was put on every dish never came to an end. They had every kind of food and drink they wished for.

It seemed to them that they were only a year there.

Then the longing for home took hold of one of them, Nechtan, son of Collbrain, and his kinsmen begged and prayed Bran to go back with him to Ireland. The woman said they would be sorry if they went. In spite of that, in the end, they set out. She told them not to touch the land when they came to Ireland. And she told them to call at the Island of Joy on the way, and bring with them the man they had left there.

So they went on towards Ireland, until they came to a place called Srub Bruin. There were people on the strand, and they asked who it was coming over the sea.

"I am Bran, son of Febal," said Bran.

"We know of no such man," the people said. "Though the voyage of Bran is in our very old stories."

Then Nechtan, son of Collbrain, leapt out of the curragh. No sooner did he touch the shore of Ireland than he was a heap of ashes, as if he had been lying in the earth for hundreds of years.

Then Bran told the people the whole story of his wanderings, from the beginning. And after that he said farewell to them.

Where he went after that is not known. He could not land. He could not go back. The sea was all there was left for him, and to him it was only ever the sea.

Another who went to Manannan's country was Cormac, grandson of Conn, King of Teamhair. This is how it happened.

He was by himself at Teamhair one time, and he saw an armed man coming towards him: quiet, with high looks, and grey-haired. He wore a shirt ribbed with gold thread next to his skin, and broad shoes of white bronze between his feet and the ground. On his shoulder he carried a shining branch with nine apples of red gold on it.

The sound of that branch was a delight. No one on earth would remember any want, or trouble, or tiredness, when that branch was shaken for him. Whatever trouble was on him, he would forget it at the sound.

Cormac and the armed man greeted each other, and Cormac asked where he came from.

"I come from a country where there is nothing but truth," the man said, "and where there is no age, nor withering, nor heaviness, nor sadness, nor jealousy, nor envy, nor pride."

"It isn't like that with us," said Cormac. "I'd be well pleased to have your friendship."

"I'm well pleased to give it," said the stranger.

"Give me your branch along with it," said Cormac.

"I'll give it," said the stranger, "if you'll give me the three gifts I ask in return."

"I'll give them to you indeed," said Cormac.

This is always how it starts. Somebody agrees to give three things before he knows what they are.

The strange man left the branch and went away, and Cormac did not know where he had gone.

Cormac went back into the royal house, and all the people wondered when they saw the branch. He shook it at them, and it put them all to sleep, from that hour of that day to the same hour of the next.

At the end of a year the strange man came back and asked for the first of his three requests.

"You'll get it," said Cormac.

"Then I'll take your daughter, Aille, today," said the stranger.

He took the girl away with him. The women of Ireland gave three loud cries after the king's daughter. But Cormac shook the branch at them until it put sorrow away from them, and put them all to sleep.

A month from that day the stranger came again, and this time he took Cormac's son, Carpre Lifecar, away with him. There was crying and lamenting without end in Teamhair after the boy. That night no one ate or slept, and they were all in grief and very downhearted. But when Cormac shook the branch, their sorrow went from them.

Then the stranger came the third time, and Cormac asked him what he wanted.

"It's your wife, Ethne, I'm asking for this time," he said.

And he went away, taking Ethne the queen with him.

Cormac would not bear that. He went after them, and all his people followed him. But in the middle of the Plain of the Wall a thick mist came down on them. When it lifted, Cormac found himself alone on a great plain.

There was a great dun in the middle of the plain, with a wall of bronze around it. Inside the dun was a house of white silver, half thatched with the white wings of birds. A great troop of the Riders of the Sidhe were all about the house, with their arms full of white birds' wings for thatching. But as soon as they put the thatch on, a blast of wind came and carried it away again.

Then he saw a man kindling a fire. The man would throw a thick oak-tree onto it. By the time he came back with a second tree, the first was burned out.

"I'll look at you no longer," said Cormac, "for there's nobody here to tell me your story. And I think I could find good sense in your meanings, if I understood them."

He went on to another dun, very large and royal, with another wall of bronze around it and four houses inside. He went in, and saw a great king's house with beams of bronze and walls of silver, thatched with the wings of white birds.

On the green he saw a shining well, with five streams flowing out of it, and the armies drinking the water in turn. The nine lasting purple hazels of Buan grew over it. They were dropping their nuts into the water, and the five salmon caught them and sent the husks floating down the streams. The sound of the flowing of those streams is sweeter than any music that men sing.

Then he went into the palace, and there he found a man and a woman waiting for him, very tall, in clothes of many colours. The man was beautiful in his shape, and his face was a wonder to look at. As for the young woman with him, she was the loveliest of all the women of the world. She had yellow hair and a golden helmet.

There was a bath there, with heated stones going in and out of the water of themselves, and Cormac bathed in it.

"Get up, man of the house," the woman said after that. "This is a comely traveller who's come to us. If you have one kind of food better than another, let it be brought in."

The man rose. "I have only seven pigs," he said. "But I could feed the whole world with them. The pig that's killed and eaten today, you'll find it alive again tomorrow."

Another man came into the house then, with an axe in his right hand, and a log in his left hand, and a pig behind him.

"It's time to make ready," said the man of the house. "We have a high guest with us today."

The man struck the pig and killed it, and cut the logs, and made a fire, and put the pig on it in a cauldron.

"It's time for you to turn it," said the master of the house after a while.

"There'd be no use doing that," said the man. "Never and never will the pig be boiled until a truth is told for every quarter of it."

That is the rule in that house. Remember it. Food there is cooked by truth, and by nothing else.

"Then you tell yours first," said the master of the house.

"One day," said the man, "I found another man's cows on my land, and I drove them into a cattle-pound. The owner of the cows followed me, and said he would give me a reward to let them go free. So I gave them back to him, and he gave me an axe. When a pig is to be killed, it's with that axe it's killed. And the log is cut with it, and there's enough wood to boil the pig, and enough for the palace besides. And that's not all: the log is found whole again in the morning. From that time to this, that's the way they are."

"That story is true indeed," said the man of the house.

They turned the pig in the cauldron, and one quarter of it was found to be cooked.

"Let's tell another true story," they said.

"I'll tell one," said the master of the house. "Ploughing time had come. When we had a mind to plough that field outside, this is how we found it: ploughed, and harrowed, and sown with wheat. When we had a mind to reap it, the wheat was found in the haggard, all in one thatched rick. We've been using it from that day to this, and it's no bigger and no smaller."

They turned the pig, and another quarter was found to be done.

"It's my turn now," said the woman. "I have seven cows and seven sheep. The milk of the seven cows would satisfy all the men of the world, if they were in the plain drinking it. It's enough for all the people of the Land of Promise. And it's from the wool of the seven sheep that all the clothes they wear are made."

At that story, the third quarter of the pig was boiled.

"If these stories are true," Cormac said to the man of the house, "you are Manannan, and this is Manannan's wife. For nobody on the whole ridge of the world owns these treasures but him. It was to the Land of Promise he went looking for that woman, and he got those seven cows with her."

They told Cormac it was his turn now. So Cormac told them how his wife and his son and his daughter had been taken away from him, and how he had followed them until he came to that place.

And with that the whole pig was boiled.

They cut it up, and Cormac's share was set in front of him.

"I've never yet eaten a meal," he said, "with only two people in my company."

The man of the house began to sing to him then, and sang him to sleep. And when he woke, he saw fifty armed men, and his son, and his wife, and his daughter with them.

There was great gladness and courage on him then, and ale and food were given out to them all.

A gold cup was put into the hand of the master of the house, and Cormac wondered at it, for the number of shapes on it and the strangeness of the work.

"There's a stranger thing about it yet," said the man. "Let three lying words be spoken under it, and it will break into three. Then let three true words be spoken under it, and it will be as good as before."

He said three lying words under it, and it broke into three pieces.

"It's best to speak truth under it now," he said, "and mend it. And I give you my word, Cormac, that until today neither your wife nor your daughter has seen the face of a man since they were taken from you out of Teamhair, and your son has never seen the face of a woman."

With that, the cup was whole again, that moment.

"Take your wife and your children away with you now," he said, "and this cup with them, so that you'll have it for judging between truth and untruth. And I'll leave the branch with you for music and delight. But on the day of your death they'll be taken from you again.

"And as for me," he said, "I am Manannan, son of Lir, King of the Land of Promise. I brought you here by enchantments, so that you'd be with me tonight in friendship.

"The Riders you saw thatching the house are the men of art, and the poets, and all who go looking for a fortune in Ireland, gathering cattle and riches. When they go out, everything they leave behind them in their houses goes to nothing, and so they go on for ever.

"The man you saw kindling the fire is a young lord who is more generous than he can afford. Everyone else is served while he's getting the feast ready, and everyone else profits by it.

"And the well you saw is the Well of Knowledge, and the streams are the five streams through which all knowledge goes. No one will have knowledge who doesn't drink a draught out of the well itself, or out of the streams. And the people of many arts are the ones who drink from them all."

In the morning, when Cormac got up, he found himself on the green of Teamhair, and his wife and his son and his daughter with him, and he had his branch and his cup.

It was given the name of Cormac's Cup, and it judged between truth and falsehood among the Gael.

But it did not stay in Ireland after the night of Cormac's death. Manannan had told him it would not. Manannan, in that house at least, told the truth.

It was in the time of the Fianna of Ireland that Ciabhan of the Curling Hair, the King of Ulster's son, went to Manannan's country.

Ciabhan was the most beautiful of the young men of the world at that time. He was as far beyond all other kings' sons as the moon is beyond the stars. Finn liked him well. But the rest of the Fianna grew tired of him, because there was not a woman among their women, wed or unwed, who did not give him her love. In the end Finn had to send him away, for he was in dread of the men of the Fianna because of how great their jealousy was.

Being that beautiful is not only a gift. Sometimes it is an exile.

So Ciabhan went on until he came to the Strand of the Cairn, which is called now the Strand of the Strong Man, between Dun Sobairce and the sea. There he saw a curragh with a narrow stern of copper. Ciabhan got into it.

"Is it Ireland you have a mind to leave, Ciabhan?" his people said.

"It is indeed," he said. "In Ireland I get neither shelter nor protection."

He said goodbye to his people then, and left them very sorrowful behind him, for parting with him was like the parting of life from the body.

Ciabhan went on in the curragh, and great white shouting waves rose up around him, every one of them the size of a mountain. The beautiful speckled salmon that stay down in the sand and the shingle rose up to the sides of the curragh, until great dread came on Ciabhan.

"By my word," he said, "if I were on land I could make a better fight for myself."

He was in that danger until he saw a rider coming towards him on a dark grey horse with a golden bridle. The horse would go under the sea for the length of nine waves and rise up with the tenth, and there would be no wet on the rider at all.

"What reward would you give," said the rider, "to whoever would bring you out of this great danger?"

"Is there anything in my hand worth offering you?" said Ciabhan.

"There is," said the rider. "That you'd give your service to whoever gave you his help."

Ciabhan agreed to that, and put his hand into the rider's hand.

With that the rider drew him up onto the horse, and the curragh came along beside them until they reached the shore of Tir Tairngaire, the Land of Promise. They got off the horse there and came to Loch Luchra, the Lake of the Dwarfs, and to Manannan's city. A feast had been made ready there, and comely serving-boys were going round with smooth horns, and playing on sweet-sounding harps until the whole house was filled with music.

Then clowns came in, long-snouted, long-heeled, lean and bald and red, the ones who did tricks in Manannan's house. One of their tricks was this: a man of them would take nine straight willow rods and throw them up to the rafters of the house, and catch them again as they came down — standing on one leg the while, and with only one hand free. They thought nobody could do that trick but themselves, and they used to ask strangers to try it, so they could watch them fail.

So this night, when one of them had done the trick, he came up to Ciabhan — who was beyond all the Men of Dea and all the Sons of the Gael in the house, in shape, and in walk, and in name — and put the nine rods in his hand.

Ciabhan stood up and did the feat in front of them all, as if he had never learned to do anything else.

Now Gebann, who was a chief Druid in Manannan's country, had a daughter, Cliodna of the Fair Hair, and she had never given her love to any man. But when she saw Ciabhan she gave him her love, and she agreed to go away with him the next day.

They went down to the landing-place and got into a curragh, and went on until they came to Teite's Strand, in the southern part of Ireland. The strand got its name from Teite Brec, Teite the Freckled, who went there once for a wave-game with three times fifty young girls, and they were all drowned in that place.

Ciabhan came ashore and went looking for deer, as was right, under the thick branches of the wood. He left the young girl in the boat on the strand.

But the people of Manannan's house came after them, with forty ships. And Iuchnu, who was in the curragh with Cliodna, did treachery. He played music to her until she lay down in the boat and fell asleep. And then a great wave came up on the strand and swept her away.

The wave got its name from Cliodna of the Fair Hair. It will be long remembered.

Ciabhan had given his service to whoever would help him. He never said what it cost him, coming back from the wood with a deer on his shoulders to an empty strand.

It was probably Manannan who sent his messenger for Connla of the Red Hair, the time Connla went away out of Ireland, for it was to Manannan's country that Connla was brought. This is how he got the call.

He was with his father Conn, King of Teamhair, on the Hill of Uisnach one day, and he saw a woman in wonderful clothing coming towards him.

"Where have you come from?" he asked her.

"I come from Tir-nam-Beo," she said, "the Land of the Ever-Living Ones, where no death comes. We have feasts that last for ever, and we do every kind thing without quarrelling. We are called the people of the Sidhe."

"Who are you talking to, boy?" said Conn. For nobody could see the strange woman but Connla.

"He's talking to a high woman that death and old age will never come to," she said. "I'm asking him to come to Magh Mell, the Pleasant Plain, where the triumphant king lives. There he'll be a king for ever, without sorrow or fret. Come with me, Connla of the Red Hair, of the fair freckled neck and the ruddy cheek. Come with me, and your body won't wither from its youth and its comeliness for ever."

They could all hear the woman's words then, though they could not see her.

"Help me, Coran," Conn said to his Druid, "you who sing the spells of the great arts. There's an attack made on me that's beyond my wisdom and beyond my power. I never knew so strong an attack since the first day I was a king. There's an unseen figure fighting with me. She's using her strength against me to take away my beautiful son. The call of a woman is taking him out of the hands of the king."

Then Coran the Druid began to sing spells against the woman of the Sidhe, so that nobody would hear her voice, and Connla could not see her any more. But as she was being driven away by the Druid's spells, she threw an apple to Connla.

For a whole month after that, Connla ate and drank nothing but that apple, for he thought no other food or drink was worth having. And however much of it he ate, it grew no smaller, but stayed whole the whole time. And there was great trouble on Connla because of the woman he had seen.

At the end of the month Connla was at his father's side in Magh Archomnim, and he saw the same woman coming towards him. This is what she said:

"It's a high place indeed Connla has among dying people, with death ahead of him. But the Ever-Living Living Ones are asking you to take the rule over the people of Tethra. They look at you every day, in the gatherings of your country, among your dear friends."

When Conn the king heard her voice, he said to his people: "Call Coran the Druid to me. I hear the sound of that woman's voice again."

"O Conn, fighter of a hundred," she said, "the wonderful tribes of Traig Mor, the Great Strand, have little love and little respect for Druids. Where its law comes, it scatters the spells on their lips."

Then Conn looked at his son Connla to see what he would say.

"My own people are dearer to me than anything," said Connla. "And yet sorrow has taken hold of me because of this woman."

Then the woman spoke to him again. This is what she said:

"Come now into my shining ship, if you will come to the Plain of Victory. There is another country it would be no worse for you to look for. Though the bright sun is going down, we will reach that country before night. That is the country that delights the mind of everyone who turns to me. There is no living race in it but women and girls only."

When the woman had finished her song, Connla leapt away from his people into the shining boat. They saw him sailing away from them, far off, as if in a mist, as far as their eyes could see.

They went away across the sea. They have never come back. Only the gods know where they went.

Conn had a hundred battles in him, and every one of them he could win. This was the one fight he could not see to fight.

Another who went to the Land of the Ever-Living Ones, and who came back again, was Tadg, son of Cian, son of Olioll. This is how that happened.

Tadg was making his round as next heir, into the west of Munster, and his two brothers, Airnelach and Eoghan, were with him.

At that same time Cathmann, son of Tabarn, king of the beautiful country of Fresen, which lay to the south-east of the Great Plain, was searching the sea for whatever he could find, with nine of his ships. They landed at Beire do Bhunadas, in the west of Munster. The country was quiet, and so they slipped ashore, and nobody noticed them until everything was surrounded, men and cattle both.

Tadg's wife Liban, daughter of Conchubar Abratrudh of the Red Brows, was taken by the foreigners, and his two brothers, and a great many of the people of Munster, and they were carried off to the coasts of Fresen.

Cathmann took Liban to be his own wife. He put hardship on Tadg's two brothers. Eoghan he set to work a common ferry across a channel of the coast. Airnelach he set to cut firewood and keep the fires going for all the people. All the food they got was barley-seed and muddy water.

As for Tadg, he only escaped by his courage and his sword. There was great grief and discouragement on him, with his wife and his brothers carried away. But he had forty of his fighting men left, each of whom had killed one of the foreigners, and they had brought one of them in alive. This man told them about the country he came from.

When Tadg heard that, he made a plan in his own head. He gave orders for a curragh to be built that would be fit for a long voyage. It was very strong, with forty ox-hides on it of hard red leather that had been soaked in bark. It was well fitted with masts and oars and pitch and everything else that was needed. They put every kind of meat and drink and clothing into it, enough to last them the length of a year.

When all was ready and the curragh was out in the tide, Tadg said to his people, "Let's set out now on the high sea, and look for our own people, who've been away from us this long time."

They set out over the stormy, heavy flood until at last they could see no land ahead of them or behind, only the hillsides of the great sea. Farther on they heard the singing of a great flock of birds they did not know. Pleasant white-bellied salmon leapt around the curragh on every side, and big dark seals came after them, breaking through the shining wash of the oars, and great whales after the seals, so that the young men liked to watch them, for they had never seen anything like them.

They rowed on for twenty days and twenty nights. At the end of that time they sighted a high land with a smooth coast. When they reached it they all landed and pulled up the curragh and lit their fires. Food was given out, and they made short work of it. Then they made beds for themselves on the beautiful green grass, and slept well until sunrise the next day.

Tadg got up and put on his weapons and went out, with thirty of his men, to search the whole island.

They went all through it, and found no living thing on it, man or beast, but flocks of sheep. The size of the sheep was past telling. They were as big as horses, and the whole island was full of their wool. There was one great flock beyond all the others, all very big rams, and one of them was the biggest of all. He had nine horns. He charged Tadg's chief men, attacking them and butting them.

They were angry at that, and went at him, and there was a struggle. At first the ram broke through five of their shields. But Tadg took his spear, the spear there was no escape from, and made a lucky throw at the ram, and killed him.

They brought the ram to the curragh and made it ready for the young men to eat. They stayed three nights on the island, and every night they had a sheep for their food. They gathered up a good share of the wool and put it in the curragh, for the wonder and the beauty of it. They found the bones of very big men on the island too, but whether those men had died of sickness or been killed by the rams, they did not know.

They left that island and went on until they found two strange islands with great flocks of wonderful birds on them. The birds were like blackbirds, but some were the size of eagles or cranes, red with green heads, and their eggs were blue and pure crimson. Some of the men began to eat the eggs, and that moment feathers began to grow out of them. But they went bathing afterwards, and the feathers dropped off them as quickly as they had come.

Up to then it was the foreigner they had with them who had set their course, for he had been on that track before. But now they went on for six weeks and never saw land.

"We're astray on the great ocean that has no boundaries," the foreigner said.

Then the wind began to rise with its sharp voice, and there was a sound like the tramping of feet in the sea, and the sea rose up into great mountains, hard to climb. Tadg's people were terrified, for they had never seen anything like it.

But Tadg began to stir them up and rouse them, and told them to meet the sea like men. "Do bravery, young men of Munster," he said, "and fight for your lives against the waves that are rising up and coming at the sides of the curragh."

Tadg took one side of the curragh and his men took the other, and he was able to pull it round against the whole twenty-nine of them, and bail it out and keep it dry at the same time.

After a while they got a fair wind and put up their sail, so that less water came in. Then the sea went down and lay flat and calm, and there were strange birds of many shapes singing all around them. They saw land ahead of them, with a good coast, and courage and gladness came on them.

When they came nearer they found a beautiful inver, a river's mouth, with green hills about it. Its bed was sandy and as bright as silver, and there were red-speckled salmon in it, and pleasant woods with purple treetops edging the stream.

"This is a beautiful country," said Tadg. "It would be a happy man who'd always be in it. Pull up the ship now and dry it out."

A score of them went on into the country, and a score stayed to mind the curragh. And for all the cold and discouragement and bad weather they had come through, they felt no wish at all for food or for fire. The sweet smell of the crimson branches of that place was enough for them.

They went on through the wood, and after a while they came to an apple-garden with red apples in it, and leafy oak-trees, and hazels yellow with nuts.

"It's a wonder to me," said Tadg, "to find summer here, and it winter in our own country."

It was a delightful place, but they went on into another wood, a very sweet-smelling one, with round purple berries in it, each of them bigger than a man's head. Beautiful shining birds were eating the berries, strange birds with white bodies and purple heads and golden beaks. And while they ate the berries they sang sweet music that would have put sick and wounded men into their sleep.

Tadg and his men went on farther until they came to a great smooth flowery plain with a dew of honey over it. There were three steep hills on the plain, and a very strong dun on each of them.

When they reached the nearest hill they found a white-bodied woman, the best of the women of the whole world.

"Your coming is welcome, Tadg, son of Cian," she said, "and there'll be food and provision for you as you need it."

"I'm glad of that welcome," said Tadg. "Tell me now, woman of sweet words, what is that royal dun on the hill, with walls of white marble round it?"

"That is the dun of the royal line of the kings of Ireland," she said, "from Heremon, son of Miled, to Conn of the Hundred Battles, who was the last to go into it."

"What is the name of this country?"

"It is Inislocha, the Lake Island. There are two kings over it, Rudrach and Dergcroche, sons of Bodb."

And she told Tadg the whole story of Ireland, up to the time of the coming of the Sons of the Gael.

"That's well," said Tadg. "You have good knowledge and learning. And tell me now, who lives in that middle dun, the one that's the colour of gold?"

"It's not I will tell you that," she said. "Go on to it yourself and you'll find out."

And she went away from them into the dun of white marble.

Tadg and his men went on until they came to the middle dun. There they found a queen of beautiful shape, wearing a golden dress.

"Health to you, Tadg," she said.

"I thank you for that," said Tadg.

"Your coming on this journey was foretold a long time ago," she said.

"What is your name?"

"I am Cesair," she said, "the first that ever reached Ireland. But since I and the men who were with me came out of that dark, unquiet land, we live for ever in this country."

Ireland: that dark, unquiet land. It is worth remembering that this is how it looks from the other side.

"Tell me, woman," said Tadg, "who lives in that dun with the wall of gold about it?"

"That's not hard to tell," she said. "Every king, and every chief man, and every noble person who was in a high place among all those who had power in Ireland, it's in that dun beyond they are. Parthalon and Nemed, Firbolgs and Tuatha de Danaan."

"You have good knowledge and learning," said Tadg.

"I have good knowledge of the history of the world, indeed," she said. "And this island is the fourth paradise of the world. As for the others, they are Inis Daleb to the south, and Inis Ercandra to the north, and Adam's Paradise in the east of the world."

"Who lives in that dun with the silver walls?" said Tadg.

"I won't tell you that, though I know," said the woman. "Go to the beautiful hill where it stands, and you'll find out."

They went on to the third hill. On the top of it was a very beautiful resting-place, and two sweethearts in it, a boy and a girl, comely and gentle. They had smooth hair shining like gold, and beautiful green clothes of the one kind, and anyone would have thought they had the same father and mother. They had gold chains round their necks, and bands of gold above the chains.

"O bright, comely children," said Tadg, "it's a pleasant place you have here."

They answered him, and praised his courage and his strength and his wisdom, and gave him their blessing.

The young man had a sweet-smelling apple the colour of gold in his hand. He would eat a third of it, and however much he ate, it was never any less. That was the food that nourished the two of them, and neither age nor sorrow could touch them once they had tasted it.

"Who are you?" Tadg asked him.

"I'm son to Conn of the Hundred Battles," he said.

"Is it Connla you are?" said Tadg.

"I am indeed," said the young man. "And it was this girl of many shapes who brought me here."

"I've given him my love and my affection," said the girl. "It's because of that I brought him to this place, so that we might be looking at one another for ever. And beyond that, we have never gone."

"That's a beautiful thing, and a strange thing," said Tadg, "and a thing to wonder at. And who is in that grand dun with the silver walls?"

"There's no one at all in it," said the girl.

"Why is that?"

"It's for the kings who are yet to rule Ireland," she said. "And there'll be a place in it for you, Tadg. Come now and see it."

The lovers went on to the dun, and the green grass hardly bent under their white feet. Tadg and his people went with them.

They came to the great wonderful house that stood ready for the company of the kings. It was a pleasant house, and anyone would have liked to be in it. It had walls of white bronze, set with crystal and with carbuncles that shone through the night as well as through the day.

Tadg looked out of the house, and he saw on one side of him a great sheltering apple-tree, with blossom and ripe fruit on it together.

"What's that apple-tree over there?" said Tadg.

"The fruit of that tree is food for the host in this house," said the girl. "And it was an apple from that tree that brought Connla here to me. It's a good tree, with its white-blossomed branches, and its golden apples that would satisfy the whole house."

Then Connla and the young girl left them, and they saw a troop of beautiful women coming towards them. One among them was the most beautiful of all.

"A welcome to you, Tadg," she said when she came to them.

"I thank you for that welcome," said Tadg. "And tell me, who are you?"

"I am Cliodna of the Fair Hair," she said, "daughter of Gebann, son of Treon, of the Tuatha de Danaan, a sweetheart of Ciabhan of the Curling Hair. It's from me that Cliodna's wave on the coast of Munster got its name. I've been a long time on this island now, and it's the apples of that tree you saw that we eat."

So the wave did not drown her. It brought her here.

Tadg was well pleased to listen to her talk. But after a while he said, "It's best for us to go on now and look for our people."

"We'd be well pleased if you stayed longer with us," said the woman.

While she was saying it, they saw three beautiful birds coming to them. One was blue with a crimson head, and one was crimson with a green head, and the third was speckled with a head the colour of gold. They lit on the great apple-tree, and each of them ate an apple, and then they sang sweet music that would put sick men to sleep.

"Those birds will go with you," said Cliodna. "They'll guide you on your way, and they'll make music for you, and there'll be neither sorrow nor sadness on you, by land or by sea, until you come to Ireland.

"And take this beautiful green cup away with you. There's power in it. If you only pour water into it, it will turn to wine that moment. Don't let it out of your hand, but keep it with you. For whenever it escapes from you, your death won't be far off.

"And this is where you'll meet your death: in the green valley beside the Boinn. A wandering wild deer will give you a wound, and after that, strangers will put an end to you. I myself will bury your body, and there'll be a hill over it, and the name it will get is Croidhe Essu."

That is the price of a visit to the Land of the Ever-Living. You come home knowing exactly how you will die.

They went out of the shining house, and Cliodna of the Fair Hair went with them to the place where they had left their ship. She gave their comrades a kindly welcome, and asked them how long they had been in that country.

"It seems to us we've been here only one day," they said.

"You've been here the whole length of a year," she said, "and in all that time you had neither food nor drink. But however long you stayed here, cold or hunger would never come on you."

"It would be a good thing to live this way always," said Tadg's people when they heard that.

But Tadg said, "It's best for us to go on and look for our people. We must leave this country, though it's hard for us to leave it."

Then Cliodna and Tadg said farewell to one another, and she gave her blessing to him and to his people.

They set out over the ridges of the sea. They were downhearted after leaving that country, until the birds began to sing for them. Then their courage rose, and they were glad and light-hearted.

When they looked back they could not see the island they had come from, because of a Druid mist that came down on it and hid it from them.

Then, by the leading of the birds, they came to the country of Fresen, and they were in a deep sleep for the whole of that voyage.

They attacked the foreigners and got the better of them, and Tadg killed Cathmann the king after a hard fight. Liban his wife made no delay. She came to meet her husband and her sweetheart, and she was glad to see him.

When they had rested a while they faced the sea again — Tadg, and his wife Liban, and his two brothers, and a great many treasures with them — and they came home safely to Ireland at last.

He had chosen the dark, unquiet land over paradise. He had a green cup in his hand, and he knew he must never let it go.

Another who went to Magh Mell, the Happy Plain, was Laegaire, son of the King of Connacht, Crimthan Cass.

He was out one day with the king his father near Loch na-n Ean, the Lake of Birds, and the men of Connacht with them, and they saw a man coming towards them through the mist. He had long golden-yellow hair streaming out behind him, a gold-hilted sword at his belt, two five-barbed darts in his hand, a gold-rimmed shield on his back, and a five-folded crimson cloak about his shoulders.

"Give a welcome to the man coming towards you," said Laegaire to his people. He had the best name of all the men of Connacht. And to the stranger he said, "A welcome to the champion we don't know."

"I'm thankful to you all," said the stranger.

"What have you come for, and where are you going?" said Laegaire.

"I've come to look for the help of fighting men," said the stranger. "My name is Fiachna, son of Betach, of the men of the Sidhe. And this is what ails me: my wife was taken from my pillow and carried off by Eochaid, son of Sal. We fought, and I killed him. Now she's gone to a brother's son of his, Goll, son of Dalbh, king of a people of Magh Mell. I've given him seven battles, and all of them went against me. There's another to be fought this very day, and I've come to ask for help. To everyone who deserves it I'll give a good reward of gold and silver."

And this is what he said:

"The most beautiful of plains is the Plain of the Two Mists. It is not far from here. A host of the men of the Sidhe, full of courage, are stirring up pools of blood upon it.

"We have drawn red blood from the bodies of high nobles; many women are keening them with cries and with tears.

"The men of the host go out in good order ahead of their beautiful king; they march among blue spears, white troops of fighters with curled hair.

"They scatter the troops of their enemies; they destroy every country they attack; they are beautiful in battle, a host with high looks, rushing, avenging.

"It is no wonder they have such strength: every one of them is the son of a king and a queen; they have manes of hair the colour of gold.

"Their bodies are smooth and comely; their eyes blue and far-seeing; their teeth bright like crystal within their thin red lips.

"They have white shields in their hands, patterned with white silver; blue shining swords, red horns set with gold.

"They are good at killing men in battle; good at song-making; good at chess-playing.

"The most beautiful of plains is the Plain of the Two Mists; the men of the Sidhe are stirring up pools of blood on it; it is not far from this place."

"It would be a shameful thing not to help this man," said Laegaire.

Then Fiachna, son of Betach, went down into the lake, for it was out of the lake he had come. Laegaire went down into it after him, with fifty fighting men.

They saw a strong place in front of them, and a company of armed men, with Goll, son of Dalbh, at their head.

"That's well," said Laegaire. "I and my fifty will go out against this troop."

"I'll answer you," said Goll, son of Dalbh.

The two fifties fell on each other. Goll fell. Laegaire and his fifty came out of it with their lives, and made such slaughter of their enemies that not one of them escaped.

"Where's the woman now?" said Laegaire.

"She's inside the dun of Magh Mell, with a troop of armed men guarding it," said Fiachna.

"You stay here," said Laegaire, "and I and my fifty will go there."

So he and his men went on to the dun, and Laegaire called out to the men around it: "Your king has got his death. Your chief men have fallen. Let the woman come out, and I'll give you your lives."

The men agreed, and brought the woman out. And when she came out, she made this lament:

"It is a sorrowful day that swords are reddened for the sake of the dear dead body of Goll, son of Dalbh. It was he loved me; it was he I loved. Little does Laegaire Liban care for that.

"Weapons were hacked and split by Goll. It is to Fiachna, son of Betach, I must go. It is Goll, son of Dalbh, I loved."

That lament got the name of The Lament of the Daughter of Eochaid the Dumb.

Nobody had asked her. Two kings and a hero from the world of men had fought over her, and nobody had once asked her.

Laegaire went back with her until he put her hand in Fiachna's hand. That night Fiachna's daughter, Deorgreine, a Tear of the Sun, was given to Laegaire as his wife, and fifty other women were given to his fifty fighting men, and they stayed with them there until the end of a year.

At the end of that time Laegaire said, "Let's go and ask for news of our own country."

"If you have a mind to go," said Fiachna, "take horses with you. But whatever happens, don't get down off them."

So they set out. When they came back to Ireland they found a great gathering of all the men of Connacht, keening them.

When the men of Connacht saw them coming they rose up to meet them and welcome them. But Laegaire called out, "Don't come near us. It's to bid you farewell we're here."

"Don't leave us again," said Crimthan his father. "I'll give you the rule over the three Connachts, their silver and their gold, their horses and their bridles, and their beautiful women, if you won't leave us."

And this is what Laegaire said:

"In the place we have gone to, the armies move from kingdom to kingdom; they listen to the sweet-sounding music of the Sidhe; they drink from shining cups; we talk with those we love; it is beer that falls instead of rain.

"We have brought from the dun of the Pleasant Plain thirty cauldrons, thirty drinking horns; we have brought the lament that was sung by the Sea, by the daughter of Eochaid the Dumb.

"There is a wife for every man of the fifty; my own wife to me is the Tear of the Sun; I am made master of a blue sword. I would not give, for your whole kingdom, one night of the nights of the Sidhe."

With that Laegaire turned from them and went back to that kingdom. He was made king there along with Fiachna, son of Betach, and his daughter. He has not come out of it yet.


Now, at the time the Tuatha de Danaan chose a king for themselves after the battle of Tailltin, when Lir heard that the kingship had been given to Bodb Dearg, it did not please him. He left the gathering without leave and without a word to anyone, for he thought it was he who had the right to be made king.

But though he went away, Bodb was given the kingship all the same, for not one of the five begrudged it to him except Lir. And the others decided to follow Lir and burn his house down, and attack him with spear and sword, for refusing obedience to the king they had chosen.

"We won't do that," said Bodb Dearg. "That man would defend any place he was in. And besides, I'm none the less king over the Tuatha de Danaan though he doesn't submit to me."

Things went on like that for a good while. But at last a great misfortune came on Lir. His wife died, after a sickness of three nights. It came very hard on him, and there was heaviness on his mind after her. There was great talk of the death of that woman in her own time.

The news of it was told all through Ireland, and it came to the house of Bodb, where the best of the Men of Dea were with him.

"If Lir had a mind for it," said Bodb, "my help and my friendship would be good for him now, since his wife is gone from him. For I have here with me the three young girls of the best shape, and the best appearance, and the best name in all Ireland: Aobh, Aoife, and Ailbhe, the three daughters of Oilell of Aran, my own three nurselings."

The Men of Dea said it was a good thought, and that what he said was true.

So messages and messengers went from Bodb Dearg to where Lir was, to say that if he had a mind to join with the Son of the Dagda and acknowledge his lordship, Bodb would give him one of his foster-children. Lir thought well of the offer. The next day he set out with fifty chariots from Sidhe Fionnachaidh, and went by every short way until he came to Bodb's dwelling-place at Loch Dearg. There was a welcome for him there, and all the people were merry and pleasant to him, and he and his people were well attended that night.

The three daughters of Oilell of Aran were sitting on the one seat with Bodb Dearg's wife, the queen of the Tuatha de Danaan, their foster-mother.

"You may have your choice of the three young girls, Lir," said Bodb.

"I can't say which of them is my choice," said Lir. "But whichever of them is the eldest is the noblest, and it's best for me to take her."

"If that's so," said Bodb, "Aobh is the eldest, and she'll be given to you, if it's your wish."

"It is my wish," he said.

He took Aobh as his wife that night, and stayed there a fortnight, and then he brought her to his own house, to make a great wedding-feast.

In the course of time Aobh gave birth to two children, a daughter and a son, and their names were Fionnuala and Aodh. After a while she was brought to bed again, and this time she gave birth to two sons, and they called them Fiachra and Conn.

She died at their birth.

That weighed very heavy on Lir, and if his mind had not been set on his four children, he would have come near to dying of grief.

The news came to Bodb Dearg's place, and all the people gave three loud, high cries, keening their nursling. When they had keened her, Bodb Dearg said: "It's a grief to us that our daughter has died, for her own sake and for the sake of the good man we gave her to, for we're thankful for his friendship and his faithfulness. But our friendship won't be broken. I'll give him her sister Aoife for a wife."

When Lir heard that, he came for the girl and married her and brought her home to his house.

At first Aoife had honour and affection for her sister's children. Indeed, nobody at all could see those four children without giving them the heart's love.

Bodb Dearg often came to Lir's house for the sake of those children, and would bring them to his own place for a good while, and then let them go back home again. And the Men of Dea were holding the Feast of Age in each hill of the Sidhe in turn at that time, and when they came to Lir's hill, those four children were their joy and delight for the beauty of their looks. The children slept in beds in sight of their father Lir. He would rise at the break of every morning, and go and lie down among his children.

But this is what came of all that. A fire of jealousy was kindled in Aoife, and she came to dislike her sister's children, and then to hate them.

She pretended to have a sickness, and it lasted nearly a whole year. And at the end of that time she did a deed of jealousy and cruel treachery against the children of Lir.

One day she had her chariot yoked, and took the four children into it, and they set out towards the house of Bodb Dearg. Fionnuala had no wish to go with her. She knew by Aoife that she had some plan for their death or their destruction, and she had seen in a dream that there was treachery against them in Aoife's mind. But for all that, she could not escape what was ahead of her.

On the way Aoife said to her people: "Kill the four children of Lir now — for whose sake their father has given up my love — and I'll give you your own choice of reward out of all the good things of the world."

"We won't do that indeed," they said. "It's a bad deed you've thought of, and harm will come to you out of it."

When they would not do as she said, she took out a sword herself to put an end to the children. But she was a woman with no good courage, and no great strength in her mind, and she was not able to do it.

They went on west to Loch Dairbhreach, the Lake of the Oaks, and the horses were stopped there. Aoife told the children of Lir to go out and bathe in the lake, and they did as she told them.

As soon as Aoife saw them out in the lake she struck them with a Druid rod, and put on them the shape of four swans, white and beautiful.

And this is what she said: "Out with you, children of the king. Your luck is taken from you for ever. Sorrowful will the story be to your friends. It's with flocks of birds your cries will be heard, for ever."

And Fionnuala said: "Witch, we know your name now. You've struck us down with no hope of relief. But though you drive us from wave to wave, there are times we'll touch the land. We'll get help when we're seen — help, and all that's best for us. Even if we have to sleep on the lake, our minds will be going abroad early."
