Then the four children of Lir turned towards Aoife, and Fionnuala said: "It's a bad deed you've done, Aoife, and a bad fulfilling of friendship, to destroy us without cause. Vengeance for it will come on you, and you'll fall in satisfaction for it. Your power to destroy us is not greater than the power of our friends to avenge it on you. Now set some bounds to the time this enchantment is to stay on us."

She is the eldest, and she is a child, and she is a swan, and she is the one who thinks to ask. Remember that.

"I'll do that," said Aoife, "and it's worse for you that you asked it of me. The bounds I set to your time are these: until the Woman from the South and the Man from the North come together. And since you ask to hear it of me: no friends and no power you have will be able to bring you out of these shapes through the length of your lives, until you've been three hundred years on Loch Dairbhreach, and three hundred years on Sruth na Maoile between Ireland and Alban, and three hundred years at Irrus Domnann and Inis Gluaire. Those are to be your journeys from now on."

But then repentance came on Aoife, and she said: "Since there's no other help I can give you now, you may keep your own speech. And you'll sing sweet music of the Sidhe that would put the men of the earth to sleep, and there'll be no music in the world to equal it. And your own sense and your own nobility will stay with you, so it won't weigh so heavy on you to be in the shape of birds.

"And go away out of my sight now, children of Lir, with your white faces and your stammering Irish. It's a great curse on tender lads to be driven out on the rough wind. Nine hundred years to be on the water — it's a long time for anyone to be in pain. It was I put this on you through treachery. It's best for you to do as I tell you now.

"Lir, who got victory with so many a good cast, his heart is a kernel of death in him now. The groaning of the great hero is a sickness to me, though it's I that have well earned his anger."

Then the horses were caught for Aoife, and the chariot yoked for her, and she went on to the palace of Bodb Dearg. The chief people of the place welcomed her. The Son of the Dagda asked her why she had not brought the children of Lir with her.

"I'll tell you that," she said. "It's because Lir has no liking for you, and he won't trust you with his children, for fear you'd keep them from him altogether."

"I wonder at that," said Bodb Dearg, "for those children are dearer to me than my own children."

In his own mind he thought the woman was deceiving him. So he sent messengers north to Sidhe Fionnachaidh. Lir asked them what they had come for.

"For your children," they said.

"Didn't they go to you with Aoife?"

"They didn't," they said. "And Aoife said it was you who wouldn't let them come."

Lir was downhearted and sorrowful at that news, for he understood well that it was Aoife who had destroyed his children, or made an end of them. Early the next morning his horses were caught, and he set out on the road to the south-west.

When he had got as far as the shore of Loch Dairbhreach, the four children saw the horses coming towards them.

"A welcome to the troop of horses I see coming near the lake," said Fionnuala. "The people they carry are strong, and there's sadness on them. It's us they're following, it's us they're looking for. Let's move over to the shore, Aodh, Fiachra, and comely Conn. The ones who are coming can be nobody else in the world but Lir and his household."

Lir came to the edge of the lake, and he saw that the swans had the voices of living people, and he asked them why they had that voice.

"I'll tell you that, Lir," said Fionnuala. "We are your own four children, destroyed by your wife, the sister of our own mother, through the force of her jealousy."

"Is there any way to put you back in your own shapes?" said Lir.

"There's no way," said Fionnuala. "All the men of the world couldn't help us until we've gone through our time. And that won't be until the end of nine hundred years."

When Lir and his people heard that, they gave three great heavy shouts of grief and sorrow and crying.

"Have you a mind to come to us on the land," said Lir, "since you still have your own sense and your memory?"

"We haven't the power to live with any person at all from now on," said Fionnuala. "But we have our own language, the Irish, and we have the power to sing sweet music, and it's enough to satisfy the whole race of men to listen to that music. Stay here tonight, and we'll make music for you."

So Lir and his people stayed there listening to the music of the swans, and they slept quietly there that night.

Lir rose early the next morning and made this lament:

"It is time to go out from this place. I do not sleep, though I am lying down. To be parted from my dear children, it is that is tormenting my heart.

"It was a bad net I put over you, bringing Aoife, daughter of Oilell of Aran, to the house. I would never have followed that advice if I had known what it would bring on me.

"O Fionnuala, and comely Conn, O Aodh, O Fiachra of the beautiful arms; I am not ready to go away from you, from the border of the harbour where you are."

Then Lir went on to the palace of Bodb Dearg, and there was a welcome for him there, and Bodb Dearg reproached him for not bringing his children with him.

"My grief!" said Lir. "It wasn't I who wouldn't bring my children. It was Aoife there beyond, your own foster-child and the sister of their mother, who put them in the shape of four white swans on Loch Dairbhreach, in the sight of all the men of Ireland. But they have their sense still, and their reason, and their voice, and their Irish."

Bodb Dearg gave a great start when he heard that, and he knew what Lir said was true. He gave Aoife a very sharp reproach.

"This treachery will be worse for you in the end, Aoife," he said, "than for the children of Lir. What shape would you think worst to be in?"

"I'd think worst of being a witch of the air," she said.

"That's the shape I'll put you into now," said Bodb.

He struck her with a Druid wand, and she was turned into a witch of the air there and then. She went away on the wind in that shape. She is in it yet, and she will be in it to the end of life and time.

Nine hundred years for the children. For ever, for her. The gods have their own arithmetic.

As for Bodb Dearg and the Tuatha de Danaan, they came to the shore of Loch Dairbhreach and made their camp there, to listen to the music of the swans.

The Sons of the Gael came from every part of Ireland as well as the Men of Dea to hear them, for there never was any music or any delight heard in Ireland to compare with the music of those swans. The swans told stories and talked every day with the men of Ireland, and with their teachers and their fellow-pupils and their friends. Every night they sang very sweet music of the Sidhe, and whoever heard it would sleep sound and quiet, whatever trouble or long sickness was on him. Everyone who heard the music of those birds was happy and contented after it.

Those two gatherings, of the Tuatha de Danaan and of the Sons of the Gael, stayed there around Loch Dairbhreach for three hundred years.

Then Fionnuala said to her brothers, "Do you know that we've spent all we have to spend of our time here, except this one night?"

The sons of Lir were greatly grieved when they heard that. Talking with their friends and companions on Loch Dairbhreach had seemed to them almost the same as being living people again, compared with going out on the cold, fretful sea of the Maoil in the north.

Early the next day they came to speak with their father and their foster-father, and said farewell to them, and Fionnuala made this lament:

"Farewell to you, Bodb Dearg, the man with whom all knowledge is in pledge. And farewell to our father along with you, Lir of the Hill of the White Field.

"The time has come, as I think, for us to part from you, O pleasant company. My grief, it is not on a visit we are going to you.

"From this day out, O friends of our heart, our comrades, it is on the tormented course of the Maoil we will be, without the voice of any person near us.

"Three hundred years there, and three hundred years in the bay of the men of Domnann: it is a pity for the four comely children of Lir, that the salt waves of the sea should be their covering by night.

"O three brothers, with the ruddy faces gone from you, let them all leave the lake now, the great troop that loved us. Sorrowful is our parting."

After that lament they took flight, lightly, airily, until they came to Sruth na Maoile, between Ireland and Alban. That was a grief to the men of Ireland, and they gave out an order that from then on no swan was to be killed anywhere in Ireland, whatever chance there might be of killing one.

Sruth na Maoile was a bad dwelling-place for the children of Lir. When they saw the wide coast around them they were filled with cold and with sorrow, and they thought nothing of all they had been through before, compared with what they went through on that sea.

One night while they were there a great storm came on them.

"My dear brothers," said Fionnuala, "it's a pity we aren't making ready for this night, for it's certain the storm will separate us. Let's settle on some place where we can meet afterwards, if we're driven apart in the night."

"Let's settle to meet at Carraig na Ron, the Rock of the Seals," said the others, "for we all know it."

When midnight came, the wind came with it, and the noise of the waves grew, and lightning flashed, and a rough storm came sweeping down, so that the children of Lir were scattered over the great sea, and the wideness of it set them astray, and none of them could tell which way the others had gone.

After the storm a great quiet came on the sea, and Fionnuala was alone on Sruth na Maoile. When she found her brothers were gone, she lamented them greatly, and made this lament:

"It is a pity for me to be alive in the state I am. My wings are frozen to my sides. It is little that the wind has not broken the heart in my body, with the loss of Aodh.

"To be three hundred years on Loch Dairbhreach without going into my own shape — it is worse to me, the time I am on Sruth na Maoile.

"The three I loved, och, the three I loved, that slept under the shelter of my feathers: until the dead come back to the living I will see them no more for ever.

"It is a pity I should stay after Fiachra, and after Aodh, and after comely Conn, with no account of them. My grief, to be here to face every hardship this night."

She stayed all night on the Rock of the Seals until sunrise, looking out over the sea on every side. At last she saw Conn coming to her, his feathers soaked through and his head hanging, and her heart gave him a great welcome. Then Fiachra came, wet and perished and worn out, and he could not say a word they could understand for the cold and the hardship he had gone through. Fionnuala put him under her wings.

"We'd be well off now," she said, "if only Aodh would come to us."

It was not long after that they saw Aodh coming, his head dry and his feathers beautiful. Fionnuala gave him a great welcome, and put him in under the feathers of her breast, and Fiachra under her right wing, and Conn under her left, so that she could put her feathers over them all.

"And och, my brothers," she said, "this was a bad night for us, and there are many like it ahead of us from now on."

They stayed there a long time after that, suffering cold and misery on the Maoil, until at last a night came on them the like of which they had never known, for frost and snow and wind and cold. They cried and lamented the hardship of their life, and the cold of the night, and the depth of the snow, and the hardness of the wind.

After they had suffered cold to the end of a year, a worse night again came on them, in the middle of winter. They were on Carraig na Ron, and the water froze round them, and as they rested on the rock their feet and their wings and their feathers froze to it, so that they could not move. They struggled so hard to get away that they left the skin of their feet, and their feathers, and the tips of their wings on the rock behind them.

"My grief, children of Lir," said Fionnuala, "our state is bad now. We can't bear the salt water to touch us, and there are bonds on us not to leave it. If the salt water gets into our sores, we'll get our death."

And she made this lament:

"It is keening we are tonight, without feathers to cover our bodies. Cold are the rough, uneven rocks under our bare feet.

"Bad was our stepmother to us, the time she played enchantments on us, sending us out like swans upon the sea.

"Our washing-place is on the ridge of the bay, in the foam of the flying manes of the sea. Our share of the ale-feast is the salt water of the blue tide.

"One daughter and three sons; it is in the clefts of the rocks we are; it is on the hard rocks we are; it is a pity, the way we are."

All the same they came out onto the course of the Maoil again, and the salt water was sharp and rough and bitter to them, but they could neither avoid it nor find shelter from it. They stayed by the shore in that hardship until their feathers grew again, and their wings, and their sores were entirely healed. After that they used to go every day to the shore of Ireland or of Alban, but they had to come back to Sruth na Maoile every night.

One day they came to the mouth of the Banna, in the north of Ireland, and they saw a troop of riders, beautiful, all of one colour, with well-trained pure white horses under them, travelling straight along the road from the south-west.

"Do you know who those riders are, sons of Lir?" said Fionnuala.

"We don't," they said. "But it's likely they're some troop of the Sons of the Gael, or of the Tuatha de Danaan."

They moved closer to the shore to see who they were, and when the riders saw them they came to meet them, until they could talk together.

The chief men among them were two sons of Bodb Dearg: Aodh Aithfhiosach, Aodh of the Quick Wits, and Fergus Fithchiollach, Fergus of the Chess. A third part of the Riders of the Sidhe were with them. They had been looking for the swans for a long time, and when they came together they gave each other a kind and loving welcome.

The children of Lir asked for news of all the Men of Dea, and above all of Lir, and Bodb Dearg, and their people.

"They're well," they said, "and they're all together in your father's house at Sidhe Fionnachaidh, keeping the Feast of Age pleasantly and happily, with no unease on them except for being without you, and not knowing what happened to you from the day you left Loch Dairbhreach."

"It hasn't been that way with us," said Fionnuala. "We've gone through great hardship and unease and misery on the tides of the sea until this day."

And she made this lament:

"There is delight tonight with the household of Lir! Plenty of ale with them, and of wine — though it is in a cold dwelling-place, this night, are the four children of the king.

"Our bedclothes are without a spot, our bodies covered over with curved feathers. But often we were dressed in purple, drinking pleasant mead.

"This is our food and our drink: the white sand and the bitter water of the sea. Often we drank mead of hazel-nuts from round four-lipped drinking cups.

"These are our beds: bare rocks out of the power of the waves. Often there were spread out for us beds of the breast-feathers of birds.

"Though it is our work now to be swimming through the frost and through the noise of the waves, often a company of the sons of kings rode after us to the Hill of Bodb.

"This is what has wasted my strength: to be going and coming over the current of the Maoil, the way I was never used to, and never to be in the sunshine on the soft grass.

"Fiachra's bed and Conn's bed is under the cover of my wings on the sea. Aodh has his place under the feathers of my breast, the four of us side by side.

"The teaching of Manannan without deceit, the talk of Bodb Dearg on the pleasant ridge, the voice of Angus, his sweet kisses: it is by their side I used to be without grief."

After that the riders went on to Lir's house, and told the chief men of the Tuatha de Danaan all that the birds had gone through, and the state they were in.

"We have no power over them," said the chief men. "But we're glad they're still living, for they'll get help at the end of time."

The gods could do nothing. That is worth saying plainly. All that power, and they could do nothing but be glad.

The children of Lir went back to their old place on the Maoil, and stayed there until the time they had to spend in it was spent.

Then Fionnuala said, "The time has come for us to leave this place. It's to Irrus Domnann we must go now, after our three hundred years here. There'll be no rest for us there, or any standing-ground, or any shelter from the storms. But since it's time to go, let's set out on the cold wind, so we won't go astray."

So they set out, and left Sruth na Maoile behind them, and went to the point of Irrus Domnann, and there they stayed. It was a life of misery and cold they led there. Once the sea froze around them so that they could not move at all, and the brothers were lamenting, and Fionnuala was comforting them, for she knew help would come to them in the end.

They stayed at Irrus Domnann until the time they had to spend there was spent.

Then Fionnuala said, "The time has come for us to go back to Sidhe Fionnachaidh, where our father is, with his household and all our own people."

"It pleases us well to hear that," they said.

So they set out, flying lightly through the air until they came to Sidhe Fionnachaidh.

This is how they found the place: empty in front of them, with nothing in it but green hillocks and thickets of nettles. No house. No fire. No hearthstone.

The four pressed close to one another, and gave three sorrowful cries, and Fionnuala made this lament:

"It is a wonder to me, this place, without a house, without a dwelling-place. To see it the way it is now — ochone! — it is bitterness to my heart.

"Without dogs, without hounds for hunting, without women, without great kings; we never knew it to be like this when our father was in it.

"Without horns, without cups, without drinking in the lighted house; without young men, without riders; the way it is tonight is a foretelling of sorrow.

"The people of the place to be as they are now — ochone! — it is grief to my heart. It is plain to my mind tonight that the lord of the house is not living.

"Och, house where we used to see music and playing and the gathering of people! I think it a great change to see it lonely the way it is tonight.

"The greatness of the hardships we have gone through, going from one wave of the sea to another, we never heard of the like of them coming on any other person.

"It is seldom this place had its share of grass and bushes. The man is not living who would know us. It would be a wonder to him to see us here."

All the same, the children of Lir stayed that night in their father's place and their grandfather's, where they had been reared, and they sang very sweet music of the Sidhe.

They rose early the next morning and went to Inis Gluaire, and all the birds of the country gathered near them on Loch na-n Ean, the Lake of the Birds. They used to go out every day to feed in the far parts of the country, to Inis Geadh, and to Accuill, where Donn, son of Miled, and his people who were drowned were buried, and to all the western islands of Connacht. And they went back to Inis Gluaire every night.

It was about that time that they met a young man of good family named Aibric. He often watched the birds, and their singing was sweet to him, and he loved them greatly, and they loved him. It was this young man who told the whole story of all that had happened to them, and put it in order.

And this is the story he told of what happened to them at the end.

It was after the faith of Christ and blessed Patrick came into Ireland that Saint Mochaomhog came to Inis Gluaire. On the first night he came to the island, the children of Lir heard the sound of his bell ringing near them. The brothers started up in fright when they heard it.

"We don't know what that weak, unpleasing voice is that we hear," they said.

"That's the voice of the bell of Mochaomhog," said Fionnuala. "And it's through that bell you'll be set free from pain and from misery."

They listened to the music of the bell until matins were done, and then they began to sing the low, sweet music of the Sidhe.

Mochaomhog listened to them, and prayed to God to show him who was singing that music, and it was shown to him that it was the children of Lir. The next morning he went to the Lake of the Birds and saw the swans ahead of him on the lake, and he went down to them at the brink of the shore.

"Are you the children of Lir?" he said.

"We are indeed," they said.

"I give thanks to God for that," he said. "It's for your sakes I came to this island above any other island. Come to land now, and put your trust in me, so that you may do good deeds and part from your sins."

They came to land after that, and put their trust in Mochaomhog, and he brought them to his own dwelling-place, and they used to hear Mass with him. He got a good smith and had him make chains of bright silver for them. He put a chain between Aodh and Fionnuala, and a chain between Conn and Fiachra. The four of them lifted his heart and gladdened his mind, and no danger and no distress that had been on the swans before troubled them now.

The King of Connacht at that time was Lairgnen, son of Colman, son of Cobthach, and his wife was Deoch, daughter of Finghin. And that was the coming together of the Man from the North and the Woman from the South that Aoife had spoken of.

Deoch heard talk of the birds, and a great desire came on her to have them. She told Lairgnen to bring them to her, and he said he would ask Mochaomhog for them.

She gave her word she would not stay another night with him unless he brought them to her, and she set out from the house there and then. Lairgnen sent messengers after her to bring her back, and they did not overtake her until she was at Cill Dun. She went home with them then, and Lairgnen sent messengers to ask Mochaomhog for the birds, and he did not get them.

Lairgnen was very angry. He went himself to where Mochaomhog was, and asked whether it was true he had refused him the birds.

"It's true indeed," said Mochaomhog.

At that Lairgnen got up and took hold of the swans, and pulled them off the altar, two birds in each hand, to carry them off to Deoch.

No sooner had he laid his hands on them than their bird-skins fell away. And what was in their place was three lean, withered old men and a thin, withered old woman, without blood or flesh.

Nine hundred years. They had been children when it started.

Lairgnen gave a great start at that, and went out of the place.

Then Fionnuala said to Mochaomhog: "Come and baptize us now, for it's not long till our death comes. And it's certain you don't think worse of parting with us than we do of parting with you. Make our grave afterwards, and lay Conn at my right side, and Fiachra at my left side, and Aodh in front of my face, between my two arms. And pray to the God of Heaven that you may be able to baptize us."

The children of Lir were baptized then, and they died, and they were buried as Fionnuala had asked: Fiachra and Conn one on each side of her, and Aodh in front of her face. A stone was put over them, and their names were written on it in Ogham, and they were keened there, and heaven was gained for their souls.

That is the fate of the children of Lir, so far.

She had held them under her wings for nine hundred years. She held them there still.

When Finn was born, his father was already dead.

His father was Cumhal, of the sons of Baiscne, Head of the Fianna of Ireland, and he had been killed in battle by the sons of Morna, who were fighting him for the leadership. Finn's mother was beautiful long-haired Muirne, daughter of Tadg, son of Nuada of the Tuatha de Danaan, and of Ethlinn, the mother of Lugh of the Long Hand. So there was god-blood in the boy, on his mother's side. It did not keep him safe.

Muirne did not dare to keep him with her. Two women came and took him away to care for him: Bodhmall, the woman Druid, and Liath Luachra.

They took him to the woods of Slieve Bladhma, and nursed him there in secret, because of his father's enemies, the sons of Morna. They kept him there a long time.

Muirne took another husband, who was King of Carraighe. But at the end of six years she came to see Finn, travelling through every lonely place until she came to the wood. There she found the little hunting-cabin, and the boy asleep in it. She lifted him up in her arms and kissed him, and sang him a little sleepy song. Then she said goodbye to the women, and went away again.

That is all she had of him. One song, in a cabin, in a wood.

The two women went on caring for him until he came to sensible years. One day he went out and saw a wild duck on the lake with her clutch, and he made a throw at her that cut off her wings so that she could not fly, and he brought her back to the cabin. That was his first hunt.

They gave him good training in running and leaping and swimming. One of them would run round a tree with a thorn switch, and Finn after her with another switch, each trying to hit the other. They would leave him in a field with hares, and tell him not to let the hares leave the field, but to keep in front of them whichever way they went. And to teach him swimming, they would throw him into the water and let him make his own way out.

After a while he went away with a troop of poets, to hide from the sons of Morna, and they hid him on the mountain of Crotta Cliach. But there was a robber in Leinster then, Fiacuil, son of Codhna, and he came to where the poets were in Fidh Gaible and killed them all. He spared the child, and took him to his own house, which was in a cold marsh. After a while the two women, Bodhmall and Liath, came looking for him, and Fiacuil gave him up to them, and they brought him back to the same place he had been before.

He grew up there, straight and strong and fair-haired and beautiful.

One day he was out on Slieve Bladhma with the two women, and they saw a herd of the wild deer of the mountain ahead of them.

"It's a pity," said the old women, "that we can't get a deer of those deer."

"I'll get one for you," said Finn.

He went after the herd, and caught two stags, and brought them home to the hunting-cabin. After that he hunted for them every day.

But at last they said to him: "It's best for you to leave us now. The sons of Morna are watching again, to kill you."

So he went off by himself, and did not stop until he came to Magh Lifé. There he saw young lads swimming in a lake, and they called to him to swim against them. He went into the lake, and he beat them at swimming.

"Fair he is, and well shaped," they said, watching him swim. And from that time on he had the name of Finn, which means Fair.

But they grew jealous of his strength, and he went away and left them.

He went on until he came to Loch Lein, and took service there with the King of Finntraigh. There was no hunter like him.

"If Cumhal had left a son," the king said, "you would be that son."

He left that king afterwards and went into Carraighe, and took service there with the king who had taken his mother Muirne to wife. One day they were playing chess together, and Finn won seven games, one after another.

"Who are you at all?" said the king.

"I'm the son of a countryman of the Luigne of Teamhair," said Finn.

"You are not," said the king. "You're the son that Muirne my wife bore to Cumhal. Don't stay here any longer, or you'll be killed while you're under my protection."

From there he went into Connacht, looking for his father's brother, Crimall, son of Trenmor. On his way he heard a lone woman crying. He went to her and looked at her, and there were tears of blood on her face.

"Your face is red with blood, woman," he said.

"I have reason for it," she said. "My only son has just been killed by a great fighting man who came on us."

Finn went after the big champion and fought him and killed him. And the man he killed was the same man who had given Cumhal his first wound in the battle where he got his death, and who had carried off his treasure-bag.

As for that treasure-bag: it was made of a crane's skin. The skin had once been Aoife, the beautiful sweetheart of Ilbrec, son of Manannan, who was put into the shape of a crane through jealousy. The bag used to hang in Manannan's house, and there were treasures kept in it: Manannan's shirt and his knife, and the belt and the smith's hook of Goibniu, and the shears of the King of Alban, and the helmet of the King of Lochlann, and a belt made of the skin of a great fish, and the bones of Asal's pig that had been brought to Ireland by the sons of Tuireann. All those treasures would be in the bag at full tide, but at the ebbing of the tide it would be empty. It passed from Manannan to Lugh, son of Ethlinn, and after that to Cumhal, who was husband to Muirne, Ethlinn's daughter.

Finn took the bag and carried it with him until he found Crimall. Crimall was an old man now, living in a lonely place, and some of the old men of the Fianna were with him, and went hunting for him. Finn gave him the bag, and told him his whole story.

Then he said goodbye to Crimall, and went on to learn poetry from Finegas, a poet who lived by the Boinn. The poets always thought it was on the brink of water that poetry was revealed to them. Finn did not give him his own name. He called himself Deimne.

Finegas had been seven years at the Boinn, watching for the salmon. It was in the prophecy that he would eat the salmon of knowledge that would come there, and after that he would have all knowledge. When at last the salmon of knowledge came, he brought it to Finn and told him to roast it, but told him not to eat any of it.

After a while Finn brought him the salmon.

"Did you eat any of it at all, boy?" said Finegas.

"I did not," said Finn. "But I burned my thumb pressing down a blister that rose on the skin, and after I did that I put my thumb in my mouth."

"What is your name, boy?" said Finegas.

"Deimne."

"It is not. Your name is Finn. And it's to you, and not to me, the salmon was given in the prophecy."

Seven years of waiting. And he gave the boy the whole of the salmon anyway. That is a better thing than it sounds.

From that time Finn had the knowledge that came from the nuts of the nine hazels of wisdom that grow beside the well below the sea.

Besides the wisdom he got then, a second wisdom came to him at another time, and this is how it happened. There was a well of the moon belonging to Beag, son of Buan, of the Tuatha de Danaan. Whoever drank from it would get wisdom, and after a second drink he would get the gift of foretelling. The three daughters of Beag, son of Buan, had charge of the well, and they would not part with a vessel of its water for anything less than red gold. One day Finn happened to be hunting in the rushes near the well, and the three women ran out to keep him from it. One of them had a vessel of the water in her hand, and she threw it at him to stop him, and some of the water went into his mouth. From then on he had all the knowledge that water could give.

He learned the three ways of poetry. And this is the poem he made to show that he had got his learning well:

"The month of May is the pleasant time; its face is beautiful. The blackbird sings his full song; the living wood is his holding; the cuckoos are singing and ever singing. There is a welcome before the brightness of the summer.

"Summer is lessening the rivers; the swift horses are looking for the pool; the heath spreads out its long hair; the weak white bog-down grows. A wildness comes on the heart of the deer; the sad, restless sea is asleep.

"Bees with their little strength carry a load reaped from the flowers; the cattle go up muddy to the mountains; the ant has a good full feast.

"The harp of the woods is playing music; there is colour on the hills, and a haze on the full lakes, and entire peace upon every sail.

"The corncrake is speaking, a loud-voiced poet; the high lonely waterfall is singing a welcome to the warm pool; the talking of the rushes has begun.

"The light swallows are darting; the loudness of music is around the hill; the fat soft mast is budding; there is grass on the trembling bogs.

"The bog is as dark as the feathers of the raven; the cuckoo makes a loud welcome; the speckled salmon is leaping; as strong is the leaping of the swift fighting man.

"The man is gaining; the girl is in her comely growing power; every wood is without fault from the top to the ground, and every wide good plain.

"Pleasant is the colour of the time; rough winter is gone; every plentiful wood is white; summer is a joyful peace.

"A flock of birds pitches in the meadow; there are sounds in the green fields; there is in them a clear rushing stream.

"There is a hot desire on you for the racing of horses; twisted holly makes a leash for the hound; a bright spear has been shot into the earth, and the flag-flower is golden under it.

"A weak, lasting little bird is singing at the top of his voice; the lark is singing clear tidings; May without fault, of beautiful colours.

"I have another story for you. The ox is lowing; the winter is creeping in; the summer is gone. High and cold the wind, low the sun; cries are about us; the sea is quarrelling.

"The ferns are reddened and their shape is hidden; the cry of the wild goose is heard; the cold has caught the wings of the birds. It is the time of ice-frost, hard, unhappy."

After that, while Finn was still only a young lad, he made himself ready and went up at Samhain to the gathering of the High King at Teamhair.

It was the law of that gathering that nobody should raise a quarrel or bring out any grudge against anyone for the whole time it lasted. The king and his chief men were sitting at a feast in the great house of the Middle Court, and Goll, son of Morna, who was now Head of the Fianna, was with them, and Caoilte, son of Ronan, and Conan, son of Morna, of the sharp words. The young lad came in and took his place among them, and not one of them knew who he was.

The High King looked at him. The horn of meetings was brought to the king, and he put it into the boy's hand and asked him who he was.

"I am Finn, son of Cumhal," he said. "Son of the man who used to be head over the Fianna, and king of Ireland. I've come to get your friendship, and to give you my service."

He said it in a hall full of the men who had killed his father. Under the Samhain peace, nobody could lift a hand.

"You are the son of a friend, boy," said the king, "and the son of a man I trusted."

Then Finn stood up and made his agreement of service and of faithfulness to the king. The king took him by the hand and sat him down beside his own son, and they gave themselves to drinking and pleasure for a while.

Now, every year at Samhain for nine years, a man of the Tuatha de Danaan had come out of Sidhe Finnachaidh in the north and burned Teamhair to the ground. His name was Aillen, son of Midhna. This is how he came. He played music of the Sidhe, and all who heard it fell asleep. When they were all asleep, he let a flame of fire out of his mouth, and blew on the flame until all Teamhair was burned.

After a while the king rose at the feast with his smooth horn in his hand. "If I could find among you, men of Ireland," he said, "any man who would keep Teamhair until the break of day tomorrow without its being burned by Aillen, son of Midhna, I would give him whatever inheritance is right for him to have, whether it be much or little."

The men of Ireland made no answer. They knew well that at the sound of the sweet, pitiful music of that comely man of the Sidhe, even women in their pains and wounded men would fall asleep.

It was then Finn stood up and spoke to the King of Ireland.

"Who will be your sureties that you'll fulfil this?"

"The kings of the provinces of Ireland," said the king, "and Cithruadh with his Druids."

So they gave their pledges, and Finn undertook to keep Teamhair safe until the break of day.

There was a fighting man among the followers of the King of Ireland, Fiacha, son of Conga, whom Cumhal, Finn's father, had been very fond of.

"Well, boy," he said to Finn, "what reward would you give me if I brought you a deadly spear that no false cast was ever made with?"

"What reward are you asking?" said Finn.

"Whatever your right hand wins at any time, a third of it to be mine," said Fiacha. "And a third of your trust and your friendship to be mine."

"I'll give you that," said Finn.

Then Fiacha brought him the spear, without the sons of Morna or anyone else knowing.

"When you hear the music of the Sidhe," he said, "strip the covering off the head of the spear, and put it to your forehead. The power of the spear won't let sleep come on you."

That is the rule of the spear. Hold the blade to your own head. The pain keeps you awake. There are worse ways to stay awake, and very few better.

Then Finn stood up in front of all the men of Ireland and made a round of the whole of Teamhair.

It was not long before he heard the sorrowful music. He stripped the covering off the head of the spear, and held the power of it to his forehead.

Aillen went on playing his little harp until he had put everyone to sleep as he always did. Then he let a flame of fire out of his mouth to burn Teamhair.

Finn held up his fringed crimson cloak against the flame. The flame fell down through the air and went into the ground, and carried the four-folded cloak deep into the earth with it.

When Aillen saw his spells were broken, he went back to Sidhe Finnachaidh on the top of Slieve Fuad. But Finn followed him there, and as Aillen was going in at the door, Finn threw the spear, and it went through his heart. Then Finn struck off his head and brought it back to Teamhair, and fixed it on a crooked pole, and left it there until the sun rose over the heights and the river-mouths of the country.

Aillen's mother came to where his body was lying. There was great grief on her, and she made this lament:

"Ochone! Aillen is fallen, chief of the Sidhe of Beinn Boirche; the slow clouds of death have come on him. Och! he was pleasant; och! he was kind: Aillen, son of Midhna of Slieve Fuad.

"Nine times he burned Teamhair. It is a great name he was always looking for. Ochone, ochone, Aillen!"

He had burned Teamhair nine times, and to his mother he was pleasant and kind. Both things were true.

At the break of day, the king and all the men of Ireland came out onto the lawn at Teamhair, where Finn was.

"King," said Finn, "there is the head of the man who burned Teamhair, and the pipe and the harp that made his music. And it's my opinion that Teamhair and everything in it is saved."

Then they all came together into the place of counsel, and they agreed that the headship of the Fianna of Ireland should be given to Finn.

"Well, Goll," the king said to Goll, son of Morna, "is it your choice to leave Ireland, or to put your hand in Finn's hand?"

"By my word," said Goll, "I'll give Finn my hand."

When the charms that bring good luck had done their work, the chief men of the Fianna stood up and struck their hands into Finn's hand. And Goll, son of Morna, was the first to give him his hand, so that there would be less shame on the rest for doing it.

Goll had killed Finn's father. And he was the first to kneel. That is Goll. Remember him.

Finn kept the headship of the Fianna until the end. The place he lived in was Almhuin of Leinster, where Nuada of the Tuatha de Danaan had built the white dun — as white as if all the lime in Ireland had been put on it. It got its name from a great herd of cattle that died fighting once around the well there, and left their horns behind them, speckled horns and white.

As for Finn himself: he was a king and a seer and a poet, a Druid and a man of knowledge, and everything he said was sweet-sounding to his people. A better fighting man than Finn never struck his hand into a king's hand, and whatever anyone ever said of him, he was three times better.

It was said of his justice that if his enemy and his own son had come before him to be judged, he would have given a fair judgment between them.

It was said of his generosity that he never refused any man anything as long as that man had a mouth to eat with and legs to carry away what he was given. He left no woman without her bride-price, and no man without his pay. He never promised at night what he would not fulfil in the morning, and he never promised in the day what he would not fulfil at night. And he never forsook his right-hand friend.

If he was quiet in peace, he was angry in battle, and Oisin his son and Osgar his son's son followed him in that.

A young man of Ulster came once and claimed kinship with them, saying they were of the one blood.

"If that's so," said Oisin, "it's from the men of Ulster we took the madness and the angry heart we have in battle."

"That is so indeed," said Finn.

In those days the Fianna of Ireland numbered seven score and ten chief men, and every one of them had three times nine fighting men under him.

Every man of them was bound to three things. To take no cattle by oppression. Not to refuse any man, whether it was cattle or riches he asked for. And never to fall back before nine fighting men.

No man was taken into the Fianna until his tribe and his kindred gave securities for him that, even if they themselves were all killed, he would not look for satisfaction for their deaths. And if he himself did harm to others, that harm was not to be avenged on his people.

No man was taken into the Fianna until he knew the twelve books of poetry.

And these were the tests. Before any man was taken, he was put into a deep hole in the ground up to his middle, with his shield and a hazel rod in his hand. Nine men went off the length of ten furrows from him and threw their spears at him all at the one time. If he got a wound from any of them, he was not thought fit to join the Fianna.

After that his hair was fastened up, and he was set to run through the woods of Ireland, and the Fianna came after him to see whether they could wound him, with only the length of a branch between him and them when they started. If they caught him and wounded him, he was not let join. Nor was he, if his spears had trembled in his hand, or if a branch of a tree had undone the plaiting of his hair, or if he had cracked a dry stick under his foot as he ran.

And they would not take him among them until he had leapt over a stick the height of himself, and stooped under one the height of his knee, and pulled a thorn out of his foot with his nail — all while running his fastest.

If he had done all those things, he was one of Finn's people.

The wages Finn and the Fianna got in those days were good: a townland in every district, and in every house the fostering of a pup or a whelp from Samhain to Beltaine, and a great many other things besides. But however good the pay was, the hardships and dangers they went through for it were greater. They had to keep strangers and robbers from beyond the seas, and every bad thing, from coming into Ireland. They had hard work enough doing it.

Besides the fighting men, Finn had with him his five Druids, the best that ever came into the west. One of them was Cainnelsciath, of the Shining Shield, who used to bring knowledge down out of the clouds in the sky for Finn, and who could foretell battles. He had his five wonderful physicians, four of them from Ireland and one who came over the sea from the east. He had his five high poets, and his twelve musicians, and among them were Daighre, son of Morna, and Suanach, son of Senshenn, Finn's teller of old stories, the sweetest that ever took a harp in his hand in Ireland or in Alban. He had his three cup-bearers and his six door-keepers, and his horn-players, and the stewards of his house, and his huntsman, Comhrag of the five hundred hounds, and his serving-men, who were under Garbhcronan, of the Rough Buzzing. And a great troop of others with them.

Fifty of the best sewing-women in Ireland were gathered together in a rath on Magh Feman, under the charge of a daughter of the King of Britain, and they made clothing for the Fianna the whole year round. Three of them, who were a king's daughters, made music for the rest on a little silver harp. There was a very great candlestick of stone in the middle of the rath, because they would not kindle a fire more than three times in the year, for fear the smoke and the ashes might harm the needlework.

Of all his musicians, the one Finn thought most of was Cnu Deireoil, the Little Nut, who came to him from the Sidhe.

Finn was at Slieve-nam-ban for hunting the time he came. He was sitting on the turf-built grave that is there, and when he looked around him he saw a small little man, about four feet tall, standing on the grass. He had light yellow hair hanging down to his waist, and he was playing music on his harp. There was no fault at all in the music he made, and it was a wonder the whole of the Fianna did not fall asleep with the sweetness of it.

The little man came up and put his hand in Finn's hand.

"Where do you come from, little one," said Finn, "you and your sweet music?"

"I've come out of the place of the Sidhe in Slieve-nam-ban," he said, "where ale is drunk and made. I've come here to be in your company for a while."

"You'll get good rewards from me," said Finn, "and riches, and red gold, and my full friendship. I like you well."

"That's the best luck that ever came to you, Finn," said all the rest of the Fianna, for they were well pleased to have him with them.

They gave him the name of the Little Nut. He was good at speaking, and his memory was so good he never forgot anything he heard, east or west. There was nobody who did not have to stop and listen to his music, and all the Fianna liked him well. Some said he was a son of Lugh Lamh-Fada, of the Long Hand.

The five musicians of the Fianna were brought to him to learn the music of the Sidhe that he had brought from that other place, for there was never any music heard on earth that his was not better than.

These were the three best things Finn ever got: Bran and Sceolan, who were without fault, and the Little Nut from the House of the Sidhe in Slieve-nam-ban.

Two of those three were hounds. That is a story too.

This is the story of the birth of Bran.

Finn's mother, Muirne, came once to Almhuin, and brought her sister Tuiren with her.

Iollan Eachtach, a chief man of the Fianna of Ulster, was at Almhuin at the time. He gave his love to Tuiren, and asked for her in marriage, and took her to his own house. But before they went, Finn made him give his word that he would bring her back safe and sound if ever Finn asked for her, and told him to find sureties for himself among the chief men of the Fianna. Iollan did that. The sureties he got were Caoilte and Goll and Lugaidh Lamha, and it was Lugaidh who gave her into the hand of Iollan Eachtach.

But before Iollan made that marriage he had had a sweetheart of the Sidhe, Uchtdealb of the Fair Breast. A great jealousy came on her when she learned he had taken a wife.

She put on the appearance of Finn's woman-messenger and came to the house where Tuiren was.

"Finn sends health and long life to you, queen," she said, "and he bids you make a great feast. And come with me now until I speak a few words with you, for I'm in a hurry."

So Tuiren went out with her. When they were away from the house, the woman of the Sidhe took her dark Druid rod out from under her cloak and struck Tuiren a blow with it that changed her into a hound — the most beautiful hound that was ever seen.

Then she went on, bringing the hound with her, to the house of Fergus Fionnliath, king of the harbour of Gallimh.

Fergus was the most unfriendly man to dogs in the whole world. He would not let one stay in the same house with him.

"Finn wishes you life and health, Fergus," said Uchtdealb, "and he tells you to take good care of his hound until he comes himself. Mind her well, for she's with young. Don't let her go hunting when her time is near, or Finn will be no way thankful to you."

"I wonder at that message," said Fergus, "for Finn knows well there's no man in the world has less liking for dogs than I have. But all the same, I won't refuse Finn the first time he's sent a hound to me."

When he took the hound out to try her, she was the best he had ever known. She never saw a wild creature she did not run down. And Fergus took a great liking to hounds from then on.

When her time came near, they did not let her go hunting any more, and she gave birth to two whelps.

As for Finn: when he heard that his mother's sister was not living with Iollan Eachtach, he called on Iollan to fulfil the pledge he had given the Fianna. Iollan asked for time to go looking for Tuiren, and gave his word that if he did not find her he would give himself up in satisfaction for her.

They agreed to that, and Iollan went to the hill where Uchtdealb was, his sweetheart of the Sidhe, and told her how things stood with him, and the promise he had made to give himself up to the Fianna.

"If that's so," she said, "and if you'll give me your pledge to keep me as your sweetheart to the end of your life, I'll free you from that danger."

So Iollan gave her his promise. She went to the house of Fergus Fionnliath and brought Tuiren away, and put her own shape back on her, and gave her up to Finn. And Finn gave her to Lugaidh Lamha, who asked for her in marriage.

As for the two whelps, they stayed with Finn always. The names he gave them were Bran and Sceolan.

They were his cousins. He never forgot it, and neither, in their way, did they.

Finn and his men were coming back from hunting one time when a beautiful fawn started up in front of them. They followed it, men and dogs, until at last they were all tired and fell back — all but Finn himself, and Bran and Sceolan.

Suddenly, as they were going through a valley, the fawn stopped and lay down on the smooth grass. Bran and Sceolan came up with it. They did not harm it at all. They played about it, licking its neck and its face.

Finn wondered at that. He went on home to Almhuin, and the fawn followed him, playing with the hounds, and came with them into the house.

Late that evening, when Finn was alone, a beautiful young woman in a rich dress came before him. She told him she herself was the fawn he had been hunting that day.

"It was for refusing the love of Fear Doirche, the Dark Druid of the Men of Dea, that I was put into this shape," she said. "For three years I've lived the life of a wild deer in a far part of Ireland, and I'm hunted like a wild deer. A serving-man of the Dark Druid took pity on me. He said that if I were once inside the dun of the Fianna of Ireland, the Druid would have no more power over me. So I ran, and I never stopped the whole length of a day until I came into the district of Almhuin. And I never stopped then until there was no one after me but Bran and Sceolan, who have human wits. I was safe with them, for they knew my nature was like their own."

Then Finn gave her his love, and took her as his wife, and she stayed in Almhuin. Her name was Sadbh.

So great was his love for her that he gave up his hunting and all the things he used to take pleasure in, and gave his mind to nothing else but her.

Finn, who never refused any man. Finn, who was never still. For a while, he was only a husband. It was the happiest he was ever to be.

But at last the men of Lochlann came against Ireland. Their ships came into the bay below Beinn Edair, and they landed there.

Finn and the battalions of the Fianna went out against them and drove them back. At the end of seven days Finn came home. He went quickly over the plain of Almhuin, thinking to see Sadbh his wife looking out from the dun. There was no sign of her.

When he came to the dun, all his people came out to meet him, and they had a very downcast look.

"Where is the flower of Almhuin?" he asked them. "Where is beautiful, gentle Sadbh?"

And this is what they said.

"While you were away fighting, your likeness, and the likeness of Bran and of Sceolan, appeared in front of the dun, and we thought we heard the sweet call of the Dord Fiann. And Sadbh, who was so good and so beautiful, came out of the house and went out through the gates. She wouldn't listen to us, and we couldn't stop her.

"'Let me go and meet my love,' she said, 'my husband, the father of the child that isn't born.'

"And she went running out towards the shadow of you that was in front of her, with its arms stretched out to her. But no sooner did she touch it than she gave a great cry. And the shadow lifted up a hazel rod, and that moment it was a fawn standing on the grass.

"Three times she turned and made for the gate of the dun. But the two hounds the shadow had with him went after her and took her by the throat and dragged her back to him.

"And by your hand of valour, Finn, we made no delay, but went out on the plain after her. But — our grief — they had all vanished. There was no woman to be seen, nor fawn, nor Druid. But we could hear the quick tread of feet on the hard plain, and the howling of dogs. And if you asked every one of us which quarter he heard those sounds from, each one would tell you a different one."

When Finn heard that, he said no word at all. He struck his breast over and over again with his closed fists. Then he went into his own inner room, and his people did not see him again that day, or until the sun rose over Magh Lifé the next morning.

For seven years after that, whenever he was not out fighting the enemies of Ireland, he went searching, and searching, in every far corner of the country for beautiful Sadbh. There was great trouble on him the whole time, unless he could throw it off for a while in hunting or in battle. And in all that time he never took any hounds out hunting but the five he trusted most — Bran and Sceolan and Lomaire and Brod and Lomluath — so that there would be no danger to Sadbh if ever he came on her track.

He never found her.

At the end of seven years, Finn and some of his chief men were hunting on the sides of Beinn Gulbain, and they heard a great outcry among the hounds, which had gone into some narrow place. When they followed them in, they saw Finn's five hounds in a ring, keeping the other hounds back. In the middle of the ring was a young boy with high looks, naked, with long hair.

He was not frightened by the noise of the hounds. He did not look at them at all. He was looking at the men who were coming up.

As soon as the fight was stopped, Bran and Sceolan went up to the little lad and whined and licked him, so that anyone would think they had forgotten their master.

Finn and the others came up to him then, and put their hands on his head, and made much of him. They brought him to their own hunting-cabin, and he ate and drank with them, and before long he lost his wildness and was the same as they were. And as for Bran and Sceolan, they never tired of playing about him.

Finn thought there was some look of Sadbh in his face, and that he might be her son, and he kept him always beside him.

Little by little, as the boy learned their speech, he told them all he could remember.

He had lived with a deer, he said, whom he loved very much, and who cared for him and sheltered him. They lived in a wide place with hills and valleys and streams and woods in it, but it was shut in with high cliffs on every side, so that there was no way out. He ate fruits and roots in the summer, and in the winter there was food left for him in the shelter of a cave.

A dark-looking man used to come to that place. Sometimes he spoke to the deer softly and gently, and sometimes in a loud, angry voice. But whichever way he spoke, she always drew away from him, as if in great dread, and the man would go away in a great rage.

The last time the boy saw the deer, his mother, the dark man talked to her for a long time, from softness to anger. At the end he struck her with a hazel rod. With that she was forced to follow him, and she kept looking back at the child the whole time, crying out after him so that anyone would have pitied her. He tried hard to follow her, and made every attempt, and cried out with grief and rage. But he had no power to move. And when he could hear his mother no more, he fell down on the grass, and his wits went from him.

When he woke, he was on the side of the hill where the hounds found him. He searched a long time for the place where he had been brought up, but he could not find it.

The name the Fianna gave him was Oisin, which means Little Fawn. He was their maker of poems afterwards, and their good fighter.

He would outlive them all. But that was a long way off yet.

While Oisin was still in his early youth, Finn had other good men with him, and the best of them were Goll, son of Morna, and Caoilte, son of Ronan, and Lugaidh's Son.

Goll was of Connacht. He was very tall and light-haired, and some say he was the strongest of all the Fianna. Finn made a poem in praise of him once, when some stranger was asking what kind of man he was. He said how hardy Goll was and how brave in battle, as strong as a hound or as the waves; and with all that, how kind and gentle, and open-handed, and sweet-voiced, and faithful to his friends.

This was the man who had killed Finn's father. Finn made a poem for him anyway. That is the kind of thing that was possible, once.

Goll's chessboard was called the Solustairtech, the Shining Thing. Some of the chessmen were made of gold and some of silver, and each of them was as big as the fist of the biggest man of the Fianna. After the death of Goll it was buried in Slieve Baune.

Caoilte was a grey, thin man, and he was the best runner of them all. He did a good many great deeds. He killed a big man of the Fomor once. He killed a five-headed giant in a wheeling door. Another time he made an end of an enchanted boar that nobody else could get near. And he killed a grey stag that had escaped the Fianna for twenty-seven years.

Another time he brought Finn out of Teamhair, where the High King was keeping him by force because of some rebellion the Fianna had stirred up.

When Caoilte heard that Finn had been carried off to Teamhair, he went out to avenge him. The first man he killed was Cuireach, a king of Leinster with a great name, and he carried his head up to the hill above Buadhmaic. After that he made a great rout through Ireland, bringing sorrow into every house for Finn's sake, killing a man in every place, and killing the calves along with the cows. Every door the red wind from the east blew on, he threw open, and went in and destroyed everything in front of him, setting fire to the fields, and giving one man's wife to another.

When he came to Teamhair, he went to the palace and took the clothes off the door-keeper. He left his own sword, worn thin with use, in the king's sheath, and took the king's sword, which had great power in it. Then he went into the palace disguised as a servant, to see how best to free Finn.

When evening came, Caoilte held the candle at the king's feast in the great hall.

After a while the king said, "You'll wonder at what I tell you, Finn. The two eyes of Caoilte are in my candlestick."

"Don't say that," said Finn, "and don't put reproach on my people, even if I myself am your prisoner. As for Caoilte, that's not his way. He has a high mind, and he only does high deeds. He wouldn't stand serving with a candle for all the gold of the whole world."

After that Caoilte was serving drink to the King of Ireland, and as he stood beside him he let out a high, sorrowful lament.

"There's the smell of Caoilte's skin on that lament," said the king.

When Caoilte saw he was known, he spoke out. "Tell me how I can get freedom for my master."

"There's only one way to get freedom for him," said the king, "and it's a thing you can never do. If you can bring me together a pair of every one of the wild creatures of Ireland, I'll give your master up to you then."

When Caoilte heard that, he made no delay. He set out from Teamhair and went through the whole of Ireland to do that work for Finn's sake. He started with the flocks of birds, though they were scattered in every part, and from them he went on to the beasts. And he gathered together two of every kind.

Two ravens from Fiodh da Bheann. Two wild ducks from Loch na Seillein. Two foxes from Slieve Cuilinn. Two wild oxen from Burren. Two swans from blue Dobhran. Two owls from the wood of Faradhruim. Two polecats from the branchy wood on the side of Druim da Raoin, the Ridge of the Victories. Two gulls from the strand of Loch Leith. Four woodpeckers from white Brosna. Two plovers from Carraigh Dhain. Two thrushes from Leith Lomard. Two wrens from Dun Aoibh. Two herons from Corrain Cleibh. Two eagles from Carraig of the Stones. Two hawks from Fiodh Chonnach. Two sows from Loch Meilghe. Two water-hens from Loch Erne. Two moor-hens from Monadh Maith. Two sparrow-hawks from Dubhloch. Two stonechats from Magh Cuillean. Two tomtits from Magh Tuallainn. Two swallows from Sean Abhla. Two cormorants from Ath Cliath. Two wolves from Broit Cliathach. Two blackbirds from the Strand of the Two Women. Two roebucks from Luachair Ire. Two pigeons from Ceas Chuir. Two nightingales from Leiter Ruadh. Two starlings from green-sided Teamhair. Two rabbits from Sith Dubh Donn. Two wild pigs from Cluaidh Chuir. Two cuckoos from Drom Daibh. Two lapwings from Leanain na Furraich. Two woodcocks from Craobh Ruadh. Two hawks from the Bright Mountain. Two grey mice from Luimneach. Two otters from the Boinn. Two larks from the Great Bog. Two bats from the Cave of the Nuts. Two badgers from the province of Ulster. Two landrail from the banks of the Sionnan. Two wagtails from Port Lairrge. Two curlews from the harbour of Gallimh. Two hares from Muirthemne. Two deer from Sith Buidhe. Two peacocks from Magh Mell. Two more cormorants from Ath Cliath. Two eels from Duth Dur. Two goldfinches from Slieve na-n Eun. Two birds of slaughter from Magh Bhuilg. Two bright swallows from Granard. Two redbreasts from the Great Wood. Two rock-cod from Cala Chairge. Two sea-pigs from the great sea. Two wrens from Mios an Chuil. Two salmon from Eas Mhic Muirne. Two clean deer from Gleann na Smoil. Two cows from Magh Mor. Two cats from the Cave of Cruachan. Two sheep from bright Sidhe Diobhlain. Two pigs of the pigs of the son of Lir. A ram and a crimson sheep from Innis.

And along with all these he brought ten hounds of the hounds of the Fianna, and a horse and a mare of the beautiful horses of Manannan.

When Caoilte had gathered all of them, he brought them to the one place. But when he tried to keep them together, they scattered away from him in every direction. The raven went off southward, and that vexed him badly, but he caught it again in Gleann da Bheann, beside Loch Lurcan. Then his wild duck went off, and it was not easy to get back. He followed it through every stream as far as grey Accuill, until he took it by the neck and brought it back, and it not at all willing.

For the rest of his life Caoilte remembered well everything he went through that time with the birds, big and little, travelling over hills and ditches and struggling to bring them with him, so that he could set Finn his master free.

When he came to Teamhair he had more to go through yet. The king would not let him bring them in before morning, but gave him a house with nine doors to keep them in for the night. No sooner were they put in than they raised a loud screech all together, for a little ray of light was coming in to them through fifty openings, and they were all trying to escape. If they were not easy inside the house, Caoilte was not easy outside it, watching every door until sunrise.

When he brought his troop out, the people called them Caoilte's Rabble. And no wonder.

But all the profit the King of Ireland got from them was to see them together that one time. For no sooner did Finn get his freedom than the whole of them scattered, and no two of them left Teamhair by the same road.

That was one of the best things Caoilte, son of Ronan, ever did.

Another time he ran from the wave of Cliodna in the south to the wave of Rudraige in the north. Colla his son was a very good runner too. Once he ran a race backwards against the three battalions of the Fianna, for a chessboard. He won the race. But he went backwards over Beinn Edair into the sea.

Caoilte had very good hearing. One time he heard the King of the Luigne of Connacht at his hunting, and Blathmec, who was with him, said: "What hunt is that, Caoilte?"

"A hunt of three packs of hounds," he said, "and three kinds of wild creature in front of them. The first hunt is after stags and large deer. The second hunt is after swift small hares. The third is a furious hunt after heavy boars."

"And what's the fourth hunt, Caoilte?" said Blathmec.

"It's the hunting of heavy-sided, low-bellied badgers."

Then they heard, coming after the hunt, the shouts of the lads, and of the readiest of the men, and of the serving-men who were best at carrying burdens. Blathmec went out to see the hunting, and it was exactly as Caoilte had told him.

He understood the use of herbs, too. Once he met two women who were very downhearted because their husbands had left them to take other wives. Caoilte gave them Druid herbs, and they put them in the water of a bath and washed in it. The love of their husbands came back to them, and the husbands sent away the new wives they had taken.

As for Lugaidh's Son, he was of Finn's blood, and another of the best men of the Fianna. He was put into Finn's arms as a child, and reared by Duban's daughter, who had reared eight hundred fighting men of the Fianna, until his twelfth year. Then she gave him all he wanted of weapons and armour, and he went to Chorraig Conluain and the mountains of Slieve Bladhma, where Finn and the Fianna were at that time.

Finn gave him a very gentle welcome. The boy struck his hand in Finn's hand and made his agreement of service with him, and stayed a year with the Fianna.

But he was somehow sluggish that whole time, so that under his leadership no more than nine of the Fianna got to kill so much as a boar or a deer. And he used to beat both his servants and his hounds.

At last the three battalions of the Fianna went to Finn at the Point of the Fianna, on the edge of Loch Lein, and made their complaint against Lugaidh's Son.

"Make your choice now," they said. "Will you have us with you, or will you have Lugaidh's Son by himself?"

Then Lugaidh's Son came to Finn, and Finn asked him, "What is it has put the whole of the Fianna against you?"

"By my word," said the lad, "I don't know the reason — unless it's that they don't like me doing my feats and throwing my spears among them."

Then Finn gave him advice. This is what he said:

"If you have a mind to be a good champion, be quiet in a great man's house; be surly in the narrow pass. Don't beat your hound without a cause. Don't bring a charge against your wife without knowledge of her guilt. Don't hurt a fool in fighting, for he's without his wits. Don't find fault with high-up persons. Don't stand up to take part in a quarrel. Have no dealings with a bad man or a foolish man.

"Let two-thirds of your gentleness be shown to women, and to little children creeping on the floor, and to men of learning who make the poems; and don't be rough with the common people.

"Don't give your reverence to everyone. Don't be ready to share one bed with your companions. Don't threaten or talk big, for it's a shameful thing to speak stiffly unless you can carry it out afterwards.

"Don't forsake your lord as long as you live. Don't give up any man who puts himself under your protection, for all the treasures of the world. Don't speak against others to their lord; that's not work for a good man. Don't be a bearer of lying stories, or a tale-bearer that's always chattering. Don't talk too much. Don't find fault hastily. However brave you are, don't raise factions against you.

"Don't be going to drinking-houses, or finding fault with old men. Don't meddle with low people. This is right conduct I'm telling you.

"Don't refuse to share your meat. Don't have a miser for your friend. Don't force yourself on a great man, or give him occasion to speak against you. Hold fast to your weapons until the hard fight is well ended. Don't give up your opportunity — but with it, follow after gentleness."

That was good advice, and Finn was well able to give it. It was said of him that he had all the wisdom of a little child who is busy about the house, when his mother herself doesn't understand what he's doing — and that's the time she's proudest of him.

As for Lugaidh's Son, that advice stayed with him always, and he changed his ways. After a while he got a great name among the poets of Ireland and of Alban, and whenever they praised Finn in their poems, they praised him too.

Aoife, daughter of the King of Lochlann, who was married to Mal, son of Aiel, King of Alban, heard the great praise the poets were giving Lugaidh's Son, and she set her love on him for the sake of those stories.

One time Mal her husband and his young men went hunting to Slieve-mor-Monaidh, in the north of Alban. While he was gone, Aoife made a plan, in the sunny house where she was, to go over to Ireland, she and her nine foster-sisters. They set out over the manes of the sea until they came to Beinn Edair, and landed there.

It happened that on that day there was a hunt going on from Slieve Bladhma to Beinn Edair. Finn was in his hunting-seat, with his fosterling, brown-haired Duibhruinn, beside him. The little lad was looking about him on every side, and he saw a ship coming in to the strand, and a queen with modest looks in the ship, and nine women with her.

They landed and came up to where Finn was, bringing every kind of present with them, and Aoife sat down beside him. Finn asked her news, and she told him the whole story: how she had given her love to Lugaidh's Son, and had come over the sea looking for him. And Finn made her welcome.

When the hunting was over, the chief men of the Fianna came back to where Finn was, and every one of them asked who the queen with him was. Finn told them her name and what had brought her to Ireland.

"We welcome her who made that journey," they all said. "There's no better man in Ireland or in Alban than the man she's come looking for, unless it's Finn himself."

As for Lugaidh's Son, he had been hunting on the far side of Slieve Bladhma that day, and he was the last to come in. He went into Finn's tent, and when he saw the woman beside him he asked Finn the same as the others had, and Finn told him the whole story.

"And it's to you she's come," he said. "Here she is for you, out of my hand, and all the war and the battles she brings with her. But it won't fall heavier on you than on the rest of the Fianna."

She was with Lugaidh's Son a month and a year without anyone coming to ask for her.

Then one day the three battalions of the Fianna were on the Hill of the Poet in Leinster, and they saw three armed battalions, equal to themselves, coming against them. They asked who was leading them.

"It's Mal, son of Aiel, leading them," said Finn, "to avenge his wife on the Fianna. And it's a good time they've come, when we're all gathered together in the one spot."

Then the two armies went towards each other. Mal, son of Aiel, took hold of his weapons, and three times he broke through the Fianna, and every time a hundred fell by him. In the middle of the battle he and Lugaidh's Son met, and they fought each other with spear and sword. Whether the fight was short or long, it was Mal who fell at the last, by the hand of Lugaidh's Son.

Aoife stood on a hill near by for as long as the battle lasted.

From that day on she belonged to Lugaidh's Son, and was a mother of children to him.

She had crossed the sea for a man she knew only from poems. It is the kind of thing poems do.

Besides all the men Finn had in his household, there were some who came and joined him from one place or another.

Once a young man wearing a dress of skins came to Finn's house at Almhuin, with his wife, and asked to take service with Finn.

In the morning, as they were going out to hunt, the Lad of the Skins said to Finn: "Let me have no one with me but myself. Let me go into one part of the country alone, and you with all your men go to another."

"Will you go on the dry ridges," said Finn, "or in the deep bogs and marshes, where there's danger of drowning?"

"I'll go in the deep boggy places," he said.

So they all went out from Almhuin, Finn and the Fianna to one part, and the Lad of the Skins to another, and they hunted all day. When they came back at evening, the Lad of the Skins had killed more than Finn and all his men together.

When Finn saw that, he was glad to have so good a servant.

But Conan said to him, "The Lad of the Skins will destroy us and the whole of the Fianna of Ireland, unless you find some way to rid yourself of him."

"I never had a good man with me yet, Conan," said Finn, "but you wanted me to put him away. And how could I put away a man like that?"

"The way to put him away," said Conan, "is to send him to the King of the Floods, to take from him the great cauldron that's never without meat, but always has enough in it to feed the whole world. And let him bring that cauldron back here to Almhuin."

This is Conan. You will get to know him. There is one in every company.

So Finn called the Lad of the Skins and said, "Go from me now to the King of the Floods, and get the great cauldron that's never empty from him, and bring it here to me."

"As long as I'm in your service I must do your work," said the Lad of the Skins.

He set out, leaping over the hills and valleys until he came to the shore of the sea. There he picked up two sticks and laid one across the other, and a great ship rose up out of the two sticks.

The Lad of the Skins went into the ship and put up the sails and set out over the sea. He heard nothing but the whistling of eels in the sea and the calling of gulls in the air until he came to the house of the King of the Floods. There were hundreds of ships waiting near the shore. He left his own ship outside them all, and stepped from ship to ship until he stood on land.

There was a great feast going on in the king's house. The Lad of the Skins went up to the door, but he could get no farther because of the crowd. So he stood outside the door a while, and nobody looked at him, and at last he called out: "This is a hospitable house indeed, and these are mannerly ways, not to ask a stranger if there's hunger on him or thirst."

"That's true," said the king. "Give the cauldron of plenty to this stranger now, until he eats his fill."

His people did that. The moment the Lad of the Skins got hold of the cauldron, he ran off to the ship and put it safe inside.

But when he had done it he said: "There's no use taking the pot by my swiftness if I don't take it by my strength."

So he turned and went back to land. The whole army of the King of the Floods was ready to fight. So was the Lad of the Skins. He went through them and over them all until the whole place was quiet.

Then he went back to his ship and raised the sails and set out again for Ireland, and the ship went rushing back to the place where he had made it. When he got there he gave the ship a touch of his hand, and there was nothing left of it but the two sticks he had made it from, lying on the strand in front of him, and the cauldron of plenty with them. He took the cauldron up on his back and brought it to Finn, son of Cumhal, at Almhuin. And Finn thanked him for the work he had done.

One day Finn was washing himself at the well, and a voice spoke out of the water.

"You must give back the cauldron, Finn, to the King of the Floods," it said, "or you must give him battle in place of it."

Finn told that to the Lad of the Skins. But the answer he got was that the Lad's time was up, and he could not serve on time that was past.

"But if you want me to go with you," he said, "watch my wife through the night. She is Manannan's daughter. In the middle of the night, when she's combing her hair, whatever request you make of her, she can't refuse it. And the request you'll make is that she'll let me go with you to the King of the Floods, to bring the cauldron to his house and bring it back again."

So Finn watched Manannan's daughter through the night. When he saw her combing her hair, he made his request.

"I have no power to refuse you," she said. "But you must promise me one thing: to bring my husband back to me, alive or dead. If he's alive, put up a grey-green flag on the ship coming back. If he's dead, put up a red flag."

Finn promised to do that. And he and the Lad of the Skins set out together for the dun of the King of the Floods, bringing the cauldron with them.

No sooner did the king see them than he told all his armies to make ready. But the Lad of the Skins went at them and overthrew them, and went into the king's dun, and Finn with him, and they overcame the king, and carried off the cauldron that was never empty a second time.

But as they were going back to Ireland they saw a great ship coming towards them.

When the Lad of the Skins looked at it he said, "I think there's an old enemy of mine in that ship, trying to bring me to my death, because of my wife, who refused him her love."

When the ship came alongside, the man in it called out: "I know you well — and it's not by your clothes I know you, son of the King of the Hills."

With that he leapt onto their ship, and the two of them fought a great battle together, and they took every shape. They began young, like two little boys, and fought until they were two old men. They fought from being two young pups until they were two old dogs; from being two young horses until they were two old horses. Then they began to fight in the shape of birds, and it was in that shape they killed each other at the last.

Finn threw the one bird into the water. But the other, which was the Lad of the Skins, he brought with him in the ship. And when he came in sight of Ireland he raised a red flag, as he had promised the woman.

When he came to the strand she was there before him. When she saw Finn, she said, "It's dead you've brought him back to me."

Finn gave her the bird, and she asked if that was what she was to get in place of her husband. She was crying over the bird. She took it into a little boat with her, and told Finn to push the boat out to sea.

He pushed it out. It was driven by wind and waves until at last she saw two birds flying with a dead one between them. The two living birds set the dead one down on an island. It was not long before it rose up alive, and the three went away together.

When Manannan's daughter saw that, she said, "There might be some cure for my man on that island, the way there was for that dead bird."

The sea brought the boat to the island, and she went searching around it, but all she could find was a tree with green leaves.
