"It might be in these leaves the cure is," she said.

She took some of the leaves and brought them to where the Lad of the Skins lay, and put them about him. And that moment he stood up, as well and as sound as he had ever been.

Finn had brought him home dead. It was his wife who found the way to bring him back.

They went back to Ireland then, and came to Almhuin at midnight, and the Lad of the Skins knocked at the door.

"Put out my wages to me," he said.

"There's no man living or dead has wages owing from me but the Lad of the Skins," said Finn. "And I'd sooner see him here tonight than the wages of three men."

"If that's so, get up and you'll see him," said he.

So Finn got up and saw him, and gave him a great welcome, and paid him his wages.

After that he went away, and his wife with him, to wherever his own country was. Some said he had gone to the country of his wife's father, Manannan, Son of the Sea.

Finn was hunting one time near Teamhair of the Kings, and he saw three strange men coming towards him, and asked them their names.

"Dubh and Dun and Glasan — Black, Brown, and Grey — are our names," they said. "We've come to find Finn, son of Cumhal, Head of the Fianna, and to take service with him."

So Finn took them into his service. When evening came he said: "Let each of you watch through a third part of the night."

There was a tree-trunk there, and he told them to cut it into three equal parts, and he gave a part to each of the three men.

"When each of you begins his watch," he said, "let him set fire to his own log. As long as the wood burns, let him watch."

That is the rule. The log is the watch. When the log is ash, the watch is over, and not before.

They drew lots, and the lot fell to Dubh to take the first watch. He set fire to his log and went out around the place, and Bran with him.

He went farther and farther until at last he saw a bright light. When he came to the place it was coming from, he saw a large house. He went inside. There was a great company of very strange-looking men in it, all drinking out of a single cup. One of them, who seemed to be the highest, gave the cup to the man nearest him, and when that man had drunk his fill he passed it on to the next, and so on to the last.

While it was going round, the highest one said: "This is the great cup that was taken from Finn, son of Cumhal, a hundred years ago. However many men are together, every one of them can drink his fill from it, of whatever drink he has a mind for."

Dubh was sitting near the door, on the edge of the crowd. When the cup came to him he took a drink from it, and then slipped away in the dark, taking it with him. When he came back to where Finn was, his log had burned out.

Then it was Dun's turn, for the second lot had fallen on him. He set light to his log and went out, and Bran with him.

He walked on through the night until he saw a fire shining out of a large house, and when he went in he saw a crowd of men fighting. A very old man, sitting in a high place above the rest, called out: "Stop fighting now. I have a better gift for you than the one you lost tonight."

With that he drew a knife out of his belt and held it up. "This is the wonderful knife, the small knife of division, that was stolen from Finn, son of Cumhal, a hundred years ago. You have only to cut on a bone with this knife, and you'll get your fill of the best meat in the world."

He gave the knife to the man nearest him, with a bare bone, and the man began to cut, and slices of the best meat in the world came off the bone.

The knife and the bone were passed round from man to man until they came to Dun. As soon as he had the knife in his hand he slipped out unnoticed and hurried back. He had just got to the well where Finn was when his part of the log burned out.

Then Glasan lit his log and went out on his watch, until he came to the house the same way the others had.

He looked in, and he saw the floor covered with dead bodies.

"There must be some great wonder here," he thought. "If I lie down on the floor and pull some of the bodies over me, I'll be able to see everything that happens."

So he lay down and pulled some of the bodies over him. He had not been there long when he saw an old hag come into the house. She had one leg, and one arm, and one upper tooth, and the tooth was long enough to serve her as a crutch.

When she came inside the door she picked up the first dead body she met and threw it aside, for it was lean. As she went on, she took two bites out of every fat body she came to, and threw away every lean one.

She had had her fill of flesh and blood before she reached Glasan. She dropped down on the floor and fell asleep, and Glasan thought every breath she drew would bring the roof down on his head.

He got up then and looked at her, and wondered at the bulk of her body. At last he drew his sword and struck her a slash that killed her. But when he did, three young men leapt out of her body. Glasan struck a blow that killed the first of them, and Bran killed the second. The third escaped.

Glasan made his way back. Just as he got to where Finn was, his log burned out, and the day was beginning to break.

When Finn got up in the morning he asked the three watchers for their news. They gave him the cup and the knife and told him everything they had seen. He gave great praise to Dubh and to Dun. But to Glasan he said:

"It might have been as well for you to have left that old hag alone. I'm afraid the third young man may bring trouble on us all."

Twenty-one years went by.

At the end of twenty-one years, Finn and the Fianna were hunting in the hills, and they saw a Red-Haired Man coming towards them. He spoke to no one, but came and stood in front of Finn.

"What are you looking for?" said Finn.

"I'm looking for a master for the next twenty-one years," he said.

"What wages are you asking?"

"No wages at all. Only, if I die before the twenty-one years are up, to bury me on Inis Caol, the Narrow Island."

"I'll do that for you," said Finn.

So the Red-Haired Man served Finn well for twenty years. But in the twenty-first year he began to waste and wither away, and he died.

When he was dead, the Fianna were not at all inclined to go to Inis Caol to bury him. But Finn said he would break his word for no man, and that he would take the body there himself. He took an old white horse that had been turned loose on the hills — and that had grown younger, not older, since it was put out — and put the Red-Haired Man's body on its back, and let it go its own way. He followed it himself, with twelve men of the Fianna.

When they came to Inis Caol, there was no trace of the horse or of the body. There was an open house on the island, and they went in. There were seats inside for every man of them, and they sat down to rest a while.

When they tried to get up, they could not. There was enchantment on them.

And in that moment they saw the Red-Haired Man standing in front of them.

"The time has come now," he said, "for me to get satisfaction from you for the death of my mother and my two brothers, who were killed by Glasan in the house of the dead bodies."

Twenty-one years he had waited. Twenty years he had served them well, and eaten their bread, and waited.

He began to attack them, and he would have made an end of them all, but Finn got hold of the Dord Fiann and blew a great blast on it.

Before the Red-Haired Man had killed more than three of them, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, who had heard the sound of the Dord Fiann, came into the house and made an end of him, and broke the enchantment.

And Finn came back to Almhuin with the nine that were left of the Fianna.

One day the three battalions of the Fianna came to Magh Femen, and there they saw three young men waiting for them, with a hound. There was not a colour in the world that was not on that hound, and it was bigger than any other hound.

"Where do you come from, young men?" said Finn.

"Out of the greater Iruath, in the east," they said. "Our names are Dubh, the Dark, and Agh, the Battle, and Ilar, the Eagle."

"What have you come for?"

"To enter your service, and for your friendship."

"What good will it do us to have you with us?" said Finn.

"We are three," they said, "and you can make a different use of each of us."

"What uses are those?"

"I'll do the watching for all the Fianna of Ireland and of Alban," said one of them.

"I'll take the weight of every fight and every battle that comes to them," said the second, "so they can keep themselves in quiet."

"I'll meet every troublesome thing that might come to my master," said the third. "Let all the wants of the world be told to me, and I'll satisfy them. And I have a pipe with me, and all the men of the world would sleep at the sound of it, even in their sickness. As for the hound, as long as there are deer in Ireland he'll get provision for the Fianna every second night. And I myself will get it on the other nights."

"What will you ask of us, to be with us like that?" said Finn.

"We'll ask three things," they said. "That no one comes near the place where we lodge after nightfall. That nothing is given out to us, but we provide for ourselves. And that the worst places are given to us in the hunting."

"Tell me on your oath," said Finn, "why you won't let anyone see you after nightfall."

"We have a reason," they said. "But don't ask it of us, whether we're a short time or a long time on the one path with you. We'll tell you this much: every third night, one of us three is dead, and the other two are watching over him. And we have no mind for anyone to be looking at us."

Every third night, one of them died. They said it as plainly as that, and asked for privacy, and it was given.

Finn promised it. But some of the Fianna were not well pleased with the ways of those three men, living by themselves as they did, with a wall of fire about them, and they would have made an end of them if Finn had not protected them.

About that time seven men of poetry came from the people of Cithruadh, asking the fee for a poem: three times fifty ounces of gold and the same of silver, to bring back to Cithruadh at Teamhair.

"However we get it, we must find some way to get that," said a man of the Fianna.

"Well, men of learning," said the three young men from Iruath, "would you sooner get the fee for your poem tonight or tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow will be time enough," they said.

The three young men went to the place a little way off from the rath where the hound had its bed. The hound brought up out of its mouth in front of them three times fifty ounces of gold and three times fifty of silver. They gave it to the men of poetry, and the poets went away.

Another time Finn said: "What can the three battalions of the Fianna do tonight, with no water?"

"How many drinking-horns do you have with you?" said one of the men of Iruath.

"Three hundred and twelve," said Caoilte.

"Give me the horns into my hand," said the young man, "and whatever you find in them after that, you may drink."

He filled the horns with beer, and they drank it. He did it a second time and a third, and by the third filling they were talkative and their wits were confused.

"This is a wonderful mending of the feast," said Finn.

And they gave the place where all that happened the name of the Little Rath of Wonders.

Some time after that, three bald red clowns came to Finn, holding three red hounds and three deadly spears. There was poison on their clothes, and on their hands and feet, and on everything they touched. Finn asked who they were.

They said they were the three sons of Uar, son of Indast, of the Tuatha de Danaan. Their father had been killed by a man of the Fianna, Caoilte, son of Ronan, in the battle of the Tuatha de Danaan on Slieve nan Ean, the Mountain of Birds, in the east.

"Let Caoilte, son of Ronan, give us the blood-fine for him now," they said.

"What are your names?" said Finn.

"Aincel and Digbail and Espaid," they said. "Ill-Wishing and Harm and Want. And what answer do you give us now, Finn?"

"Nobody before me ever gave a blood-fine for a man killed in battle," said Finn, "and I won't give it."

"Then we'll do revenge and robbery on you," they said.

"What revenge is that?"

"This is what I'll do," said Aincel. "If I meet with two or three or four of the Fianna, I'll take their feet and their hands from them."

"This is what I'll do," said Digbail. "I won't let a day go by without the loss of a hound, or a serving-boy, or a fighting man to the Fianna of Ireland."

"And I'll always be leaving them in want," said Espaid, "of people, or of a hand, or of an eye."

"Unless we get some help against them," said Caoilte, "there won't be one of us living at the end of a year."

"Well," said Finn, "we'll make a dun and stay here a while. I won't go through Ireland with these men following after me, until I find out who is the stronger, they or we."

So the Fianna made little raths for themselves all about Slieve Mis, and stayed there a month and a quarter and a year. And all that time the three red bald-headed men were doing every kind of hurt and harm to them.

But the three sons of the King of Iruath came to speak with Finn.

"It's our wish, Finn," they said, "to send the hound that's with us to go round you three times every day. However many people are trying to hurt you or rob you, they won't have the power to do it after that. But let there be no fire, and no weapons, and no other dog, in the house he goes into."

"I'll let none of those things into the same house as him," said Finn, "and he'll go safe back to you."

So every day the hound was sent to Finn, with its chain of ridges of red gold around its neck. It went three times round Finn, and three times it put its tongue on him. To the people nearest the hound when it came into the house, it seemed as if a vat of mead was being strained; and to others there came the sweet smell of an apple-garden.

Every harm and sickness the three sons of Uar brought on the Fianna, the three sons of the King of Iruath took off them again with their herbs and their help and their healing.

After a while the High King of Ireland came to Slieve Mis with a great troop of his men, to join Finn and the Fianna. They told the High King the whole story: how the sons of Uar were destroying them, and how the three sons of the King of Iruath were helping them against them.

"Why wouldn't men who can do all that find some good spell to drive the sons of Uar out of Ireland?" said the High King.

With that Caoilte went looking for the three young men from Iruath and brought them to the High King.

"These are comely men," said the High King, "good in their shape and with a good name. Could you find any charm, my sons, that will drive out these three enemies who are destroying the Fianna of Ireland?"

"We'd do that if we could find those men near us," they said. "And this is where they are now: at Daire's Cairn, at the end of the raths."

"Where are Garb-Cronan, the Rough Buzzing One, and Saltran of the Long Heel?" said Finn.

"Here we are, King of the Fianna," they said.

"Go out to those men beyond, and tell them I'll give satisfaction for their father according to the judgment of the King of Ireland."

The messengers went out and brought them in, and they sat down on the bank of the rath.

Then the High King said: "Rise up, Dubh, son of the King of Iruath, and command these sons of Uar with a spell to leave Ireland."

Dubh rose up and said: "Go out through the strength of this spell and this charm, you three enemies of the Fianna — one-eyed, lame-thighed, left-handed, of the bad race. Go out on the deep bitter sea, and let each of you strike a blow of his sword on the head of his brothers. For it's long enough you've been doing harm and destruction on the King of the Fianna, Finn, son of Cumhal."

With that the hound sent a blast of wind under them that carried them out into the fierce green sea. Each of them struck a blow on the heads of the others. And that was the last that was seen of the three destroying sons of Uar, Aincel and Digbail and Espaid.

But after the time of the Fianna there came, three times in the one year, into West Munster, three flocks of birds from the western sea, with beaks of bone and fiery breath, and the wind from their wings was as cold as a wind of spring. The first time they came was at reaping-time, and every one of them carried off an ear of corn from the field. The next time they came they did not leave an apple on a tree, or a nut on a bush, or a berry on the rowan. The third time they spared no living thing they could lift from the ground — young bird, or fawn, or silly little child. And the first day they came was the same day of the year that the three sons of Uar were put out on the sea.

When Caoilte — one of the last of the Fianna, and still living — heard of them, he remembered the sons of Uar. He made a spell that drove them out into the sea again, and they perished there, by one another.

Ill-Wishing and Harm and Want. You can drive them out. They come back, a long time later, with wings.

The three sons of the King of Iruath stayed about a year with Finn.

At the end of that time Donn and Dubhan, two sons of the King of Ulster, came out of the north to Munster. One night they kept watch for the Fianna, and three times they made a round of the camp.

The young men from Iruath always stayed in a place by themselves, apart from the Fianna, with their hound between them, and at nightfall a wall of fire rose around them, so that nobody could look at them.

The third time the sons of the King of Ulster made the round of the camp, they saw the fiery wall.

"It's a wonder," said Donn, "the way those three young men have been a year now, and their hound with them, and nobody allowed to look at them."

With that he and his brother took their weapons in their hands and went inside the wall of fire, and began looking at the three men and at the hound.

The great hound they saw every day at the hunting was no bigger now than a lap-dog that would belong to a queen or a high person. One of the young men was watching over the dog with his sword in his hand. Another was holding a vessel of white silver to the dog's mouth. Whatever drink any of the three asked for, the dog would bring it up out of its mouth into the vessel.

Then one of the young men said to the hound: "Well, noble one, and brave one, and just one, take notice of the treachery that is done to you by Finn."

When the dog heard that it turned to the King of Ulster's sons, and a dark Druid wind rose up and blew the shields from their shoulders and the swords from their sides into the wall of fire. Then the three men came out and made an end of them. When that was done, the dog came and breathed on them, and they turned to ashes that moment, and no blood or flesh or bone of them was ever found afterwards.

The three battalions of the Fianna divided themselves into companies of nine and went searching through every part of Ireland for the King of Ulster's two sons.

As for Finn, he went to Teamhair Luachra, with nobody with him but the serving-lads and the followers of the army. The companies of nine who were looking for the King of Ulster's sons all came back to him there on the one night. They brought no word of them, dead or living.

And as for the three sons of the King of Iruath and the hound that was with them, they were seen no more by Finn and the Fianna.

Finn had given his word. It was broken, and not by him. That did not matter. It never matters, to the ones who leave.

There was another young man who came and served Finn for a while. He came out of Connacht, and he was very daring, and the name they gave him was the Red Ridge.

He nearly left Finn once, because his wages were too long in coming to him. The three battalions of the Fianna came to try to quiet him, but he would not stay for them.

At last Finn himself came. He had a power: if he made only three verses, he could quiet anyone. And this is what he said:

"Daring Red Ridge, good in battle: if you go from me today with your great name, it is a good parting for us. But once, at Rath Cro, I gave you three times fifty ounces in the one day; and at Cam Ruidhe I gave you the full of my cup of silver and of yellow gold. And do you remember the time we were at Rath Ai, when we found the two women, and when we ate the nuts — you and I were there together."

After that the young man said no more about leaving him.

It was not the gold that kept him. It was the nuts, and the two women, and the being there together. Finn knew that. It was why he said it last.

Another helper came to Finn once when he was fighting at a ford, and all his weapons were used up or worn out with the force of the fight. A daughter of Mongan of the Sidhe came to him, bringing a flat stone with a chain of gold on it. He took the stone and did great deeds with it. After the fight the stone fell into the ford, and the ford got the name of Ath Liag Finn, the Ford of Finn's Stone.

That stone will never be found until the Woman of the Waves finds it and brings it to land on a Sunday morning.

And seven years from that day, the world will come to an end.

So if you are ever by that ford, and you see something glinting under the water, leave it where it is.

Of all the great battles the Fianna fought to keep the foreigners out of Ireland, the greatest was the one fought at Finntraigh, the White Strand, in Munster. This is the whole story of it, and of how the Fianna came to have so great a name.

Once the enemies of Ireland gathered together under Daire Donn, High King of the Great World. They meant to take Ireland and put it under tribute.

The King of Greece was among them, and the King of France, and the King of the Eastern World. There was Lughman of the Broad Arms, King of the Saxons, and Fiacha of the Long Hair, King of the Gairean, and Tor, son of Breogan, King of the Great Plain, and Sligech, son of the King of the Men of Cepda. There was Comur of the Crooked Sword, King of the Men of the Dog-Heads, and Caitchenn, King of the Men of the Cat-Heads, and Caisel of the Feathers, King of Lochlann, and Madan of the Bent Neck, son of the King of the Marshes. There were three kings from the rising of the sun in the east. There was Ogarmach, daughter of the King of Greece, the best woman-warrior that ever came into the world. And a great many other kings and great lords.

The whole world, more or less, against one island.

"Who can give me knowledge of the harbours of Ireland?" asked the King of the World.

"I'll do that for you," said Glas, son of Bremen, "and I'll bring you to a good harbour." Finn had put Glas out of Ireland for some treachery he had done.

The armies set out in their ships. They had not gone far when the wind rose, and the waves, and they could hear nothing but the wild playing of the sea-women, and the screams of frightened birds, and the breaking of ropes and of sails. But after a while, when the wind found no weakness in the heroes, it rose up off them and went back to its own high place. Then the sea grew quiet, and the waves grew tame, and the harbours friendly, and they stopped a while at an island called the Green Rock.

"It's not a harbour like this you promised me, Glas, son of Bremen," said the King of the World, "but a shore of white sand, where my armies could hold their fairs and their gatherings when they weren't fighting."

"I know a harbour of that kind in the west of Ireland," said Glas. "The Harbour of the White Strand, in Corca Duibhne."

So they went back into their ships, and went on over the sea towards Ireland.

They were coming to hold fairs on our beach. That is what they thought a war would be.

As for Finn, when it was shown to him that the enemies of Ireland were coming, he called together the seven battalions of the Fianna.

The place where they gathered was the hill called Fionntulach, the White Hill, in Munster. They often stayed on that hill a while, and spear-shafts with spells on them were brought to them there. They had every kind of food: beautiful blackberries, haws of the hawthorn, nuts of the hazels of Cenntire, tender twigs of the bramble-bush, sprigs of wholesome gentian, watercress at the beginning of summer. To their cooking-pots were brought birds out of the oak-woods, and squirrels from Berramain, and speckled eggs from the cliffs, and salmon out of Luimnech, and eels of the Sionnan, and woodcocks of Fidhrinne, and otters from the hidden places of the Doile, and fish from the coasts of Buie and Beare, and dulse from the bays of Cleire.

As they were about to set out southward, they saw one of their young men, Cael, grandson of Nemhnain, coming towards them.

"Where have you come from, Cael?" Finn asked him.

"From Brugh na Boinne," he said.

"What were you asking for there?"

"I was asking to speak with Muirenn, daughter of Derg, who was my own nurse."

"For what cause?"

"It was about a high marriage, and a woman of the Sidhe who was shown to me in a dream. It was Credhe I saw, daughter of the King of Ciarraighe Luachra."

"Do you know this, Cael," said Finn, "that she's the greatest deceiver of all the women of Ireland? There's hardly a precious thing in Ireland but she has coaxed it away to her own great dun."

"Do you know what she asks of every man who comes asking for her?" said Cael.

"I know it," said Finn. "She'll let nobody come unless he can make a poem setting out the report of her bowls and her horns and her cups, her grand vessels and all her palaces."

"I have all that ready," said Cael. "It was given to me by my nurse, Muirenn, daughter of Derg."

The whole world was sailing against Ireland. And the Fianna put off the battle for the time being, and went courting.

They went on over every hilly place and every stony place until they came to Loch Cuire, in the west. They came to the door of the hill of the Sidhe and knocked on it with the shafts of their long gold-socketed spears. Young girls with yellow hair came to the windows of the sunny houses. And Credhe herself came out to speak with them, with three times fifty women.

"We've come to ask you in marriage," said Finn.

"Who is it that's asking for me?" said she.

"It's Cael, the hundred-killer, grandson of Nemhnain, son of the King of Leinster in the east."

"I've heard talk of him, but I've never seen him," said Credhe. "And has he any poem for me?"

"I have that," said Cael. He stood up, and sang his poem:

"A journey I have to make, and no easy journey, to the house of Credhe against the breast of the mountain, at the Paps of Dana. There I must go through hardships for the length of seven days. Pleasant is her house, with men and boys and women, with Druids and musicians, with cup-bearer and door-keeper, with a horse-boy who does not leave his work, with a distributor to share out food; and Credhe of the Fair Hair in command over them all.

"It would be delightful to me in her dun, with coverings and with down, if she has only a mind to listen to me.

"A bowl she has with the juice of berries in it to make her eyebrows black; crystal vats of fermenting grain; beautiful cups and vessels. Her house is the colour of lime; there are rushes for beds, and many silken coverings and blue cloaks; red gold is there, and bright drinking-horns. Her sunny house is beside Loch Cuire, made of silver and yellow gold; its ridge is thatched without any fault with the crimson wings of birds. The doorposts are green; the lintel is of silver taken in battle. Credhe's chair on the left is the delight of delights, covered with gold of Elga; at the foot of the pleasant bed it stands, the bed that was made of precious stones by Tuile in the east. Another bed there is on the right, of gold and silver, made without any fault; it has curtains the colour of the foxglove, hanging on rods of copper.

"The people of her house, they are the ones who have delight. Their cloaks are not faded white, they are not worn smooth; their hair is fair and curling. Wounded men in their blood would sleep, hearing the birds of the Sidhe singing in the eaves of the sunny house.

"If I have any thanks to give to Credhe, for whom the cuckoo calls, she will get better praise than this. If this love-service I have done is pleasing to her, let her not delay; let her say, 'Your coming is welcome to me.'

"A hundred feet there are in her house from one corner to another; twenty feet, fully measured, is the width of her great door. Her roof has its thatch of the wings of blue and yellow birds; the border of her well is of crystals and carbuncles.

"There is a vat there of royal bronze; the juice of pleasant malt is running from it; over the vat is an apple-tree with its heavy fruit. When Credhe's horn is filled from the vat, four apples fall into it together.

"She who owns all these things, both at low water and at flood, Credhe from the Hill of the Three Peaks: she is beyond all the women of Ireland by the length of a spear-cast.

"Here is this song for her. It is no sudden bride-gift, no hurried asking. I bring it to Credhe of the beautiful shape, that my coming may be very bright to her."

Then Credhe took him for her husband. The wedding-feast was made, and the whole of the Fianna stayed there for seven days, drinking and taking their pleasure and having every good thing.

It was a good wedding. Remember it. Remember that they were happy, for seven days, at the foot of the Paps of Dana.

When Finn turned off his road to go to Credhe's house, he had sent watchmen out to every landing-place, to give warning when the ships of the strangers came in sight. The man keeping watch at the White Strand was Conn Crither, son of Bran, from Teamhair Luachra.

He watched a long time. Then one night, west of the Round Hill of the Fianna that is called Cruachan Adrann, he fell asleep.

While he slept, the ships came.

What woke him was the noise of shields breaking, and the clash of swords and spears, and the cries of women and children, and of dogs and horses under the flames, that the strangers were attacking.

Conn Crither started up when he heard it. "It's great trouble has come on the people through my sleep," he said. "I won't stay living after this for Finn and the Fianna of Ireland to see me. I'll rush into the middle of the strangers, and they'll fall by me until I fall by them."

One man. One sleep. He did not make excuses for it. He did not look for someone to blame. He picked up his weapons.

He put on his battle-suit and ran down towards the strand. On the way he saw three women ahead of him, dressed in battle-clothes, and however fast he ran he could not catch them. He took his spear to throw at the nearest one, but she stopped that moment.

"Hold your hand and don't harm us," she said. "We haven't come to harm you, but to help you."

"Who are you?" said Conn Crither.

"We are three sisters," she said, "and we've come from Tir nan Og, the Country of the Young. All three of us have given you our love, and none of us loves you less than the others, and it's to give you our help we've come."

"How will you help me?"

"We'll give you good help," she said. "We'll make Druid armies around you out of stalks of grass and the tops of the watercress. They'll cry out at the strangers, and strike the weapons out of their hands, and take away their strength and their eyesight. And we'll put a Druid mist around you now, that will hide you from the armies of the strangers, so they won't see you when you attack them. And we have a well of healing at the foot of Slieve Iolair, the Eagle's Mountain. Its waters will cure every wound made in battle. After bathing in that well you'll be as whole and as sound as the day you were born. And bring whatever man you like best with you, and we'll heal him along with you."

Conn Crither thanked them, and hurried on to the strand.

At that time the armies of the King of the Great Plain were taking spoils from Traigh Moduirn in the north to Finntraighe in the south. Conn Crither came on them, with the Druid army at his side. He took their spoils from them, and the Druid army took their sight and their strength from them, and they were routed. They ran to where the King of the Great Plain was, and Conn Crither followed, killing and destroying.

"Stop and stand with me, king-hero," said the King of the Great Plain, "so I can fight you for my people's sake, since there isn't one of them who'll turn and stand against you."

So the two of them set their banners in the earth and went at each other, and fought a good part of the day, until Conn Crither struck off the king's head.

He lifted the head up, boasting of what he had done.

"By my word," he said, "I won't let myself be parted from this body until some of the Fianna, few or many, come to me."

The King of the World heard that.

"That's a big word that man is saying," he said. "Get up now, Glas, son of Dremen, and see which of the Fianna of Ireland it is that's saying it."

Glas left the ship and went to where Conn Crither was, and asked who he was.

"I am Conn Crither, son of Bran, from Teamhair Luachra," he said.

"If that's so," said Glas, "you're of the one blood with me. I am Glas, son of Bremen, from Teamhair Luachra."

"Then it's not right for you to come fighting against me on the side of those foreigners," said Conn.

"It's a pity indeed," said Glas. "If Finn and the Fianna hadn't driven me out from them, I wouldn't fight against you, or against one of them, for all the treasures of the whole world."

"Don't say that," said Conn. "I swear by my hand of valour: if you had killed Finn's own son, and the sons of his people along with him, you'd have no need to be in dread of him, if only you came under his word and his protection."

That is what Finn's word was worth, in those days. You could stake your life on it. People did.

"I think indeed the day has come for me to fight beside you," said Glas. "I'll go back and tell that to the King of the World."

He went back to the king, and the king asked him which of the men of the Fianna it was.

"It's a kinsman of my own, High King," said Glas. "And my heart is weak at his being alone. I have a great desire to go and help him."

"If you go," said the King of the World, "what I ask of you is to come and tell me every day how many of the Fianna of Ireland have fallen by me. And if a few of my own men should fall, come and tell me who it was they fell by."

"And what I ask of you," said Glas, "is not to let your armies land until the Fianna come to us, but to let only one man at a time come to fight with each of us until then."

So two of the strangers were sent against them that day, and they got their death by Glas and by Conn Crither. Then the two asked to have two men sent against each of them, and that was done, and three times nine fell by them before night.

Conn Crither was covered with wounds by the end of the day.

"Three women came to me from the Country of the Young," he said to Glas, "and they promised to put me in a well of healing for my wounds. You watch the harbour tonight, and I'll go and look for them."

So he went to them, and they bathed him in the well of healing, and he was whole of his wounds.

As for Glas, son of Dremen, he went down to the harbour.

"O King of the World," he called, "there's a friend of mine in the ships, Madan of the Bent Neck, son of the King of the Marshes. He said in the great world in the east that he alone would be enough to take Ireland for you, and would bring it under tribute to you one way or another. I ask you to let him come alone against me tonight, until we see which of us will fight best for Ireland."

So Madan came ashore, and the two went at each other and made a very hard fight. But it was not in the prophecy that Glas would find his death there. It was the son of the King of the Marshes who got his death by him.

Not long after, Conn Crither came back to Glas, and gave him great praise for all he had done.

A traitor had brought the whole world to the White Strand. And now there were two men on it, standing between the whole world and Ireland, and one of them was the traitor.

Then Taistellach, one of Finn's messengers, came to the White Strand asking for news. Conn told him to go back to where Finn was and tell him how things stood.

But Taistellach would not go until he had wetted his sword in the blood of one of the enemies of Ireland, as the others had done. He sent a challenge to the ships. Coimhleathan, a very big, tall champion, came and fought with him on the strand, and took him up in his arms to carry him alive back to the High King's ship. But Taistellach struck his head off in the sea, and brought the head back to land.

"Victory and blessing be with you!" said Conn Crither. "Go now, tonight, to the house of Bran, son of Febal, my father, at Teamhair Luachra, and tell him to gather all the Tuatha de Danaan to help us. And go on tomorrow to the Fianna of Ireland."

So Taistellach went on to Bran's house, and told him the whole story, and gave him the message.

Then Bran, son of Febal, went out to gather the Tuatha de Danaan. He went to Dun Sesnain in Ui Conall Gabra, where they were holding a feast. He found three of the best young men of the Tuatha de Danaan there: Ilbrec the Many-Coloured, son of Manannan, and Nemanach the Pearly, son of Angus Og, and Sigmall, grandson of Midhir. They made him welcome and asked him to stay with them.

"There's a greater thing than this for you to do, Men of Dea," said Bran. And he told them the whole story, and how things were with Conn Crither his son.

"Stay with me tonight," said Sesnan, "and my son Dolb will go to Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, and gather the Tuatha de Danaan in to us."

So Bran stayed there, and Dolb, son of Sesnan, went to Sidhe Bean Finn above Magh Femen, where Bodb Dearg was at that time, and gave him his message.

"Young man," said Bodb Dearg, "we're in no way bound to help the men of Ireland out of that strait."

"Don't say that," said Dolb. "There isn't a king's son, or a prince, or a leader of the Fianna of Ireland, who doesn't have a wife, or a mother, or a foster-mother, or a sweetheart, of the Tuatha de Danaan. And they've given you good help every time you needed it."

That is the truth of it. The gods had lost Ireland to the Gael. Then they had married them.

"I give my word," said Bodb Dearg, "it's right to give a good answer to so good a messenger."

With that he sent word to the Tuatha de Danaan in every place where they were, and they gathered to him. From there they went on to Dun Sesnain and stayed the night. They rose in the morning and put on their shirts of the costliest silk and their embroidered coats of rejoicing, and took their green shields and their swords and their spears.

Their leaders then, besides Bodb Dearg, were Midhir of Bri Leith, and Lir of Sidhe Finnachaidh, and Abarthach, son of Ildathach, and Ilbrec, son of Manannan, and Fionnbhar of Magh Suil, and Argat Lamh, the Silver Hand, from the Sionnan, and the Man of Sweet Speech from the Boinn.

The whole army of them came into Ciarraighe Luachra, and to red-haired Slieve Mis, and from there to the harbour of the White Strand.

"O Men of Dea," said Abarthach, "let a high mind and high courage rise in you now in the face of the battle. For the doings of every one of you will be told until the end of the world. So fulfil now the big words you've spoken in the drinking-houses."

"Get up, Glas, son of Dremen," said Bodb Dearg, "and tell the King of the World I've come to do battle."

Glas went to the King of the World.

"Are those the Fianna of Ireland I see?" said the king.

"They are not," said Glas. "They're another part of the men of Ireland, who don't dare to be on the face of the earth, but who live in hidden houses under the earth. It's to give warning of battle from them I've come."

"Who will answer the Tuatha de Danaan for me?" said the King of the World.

"We'll go against them," said two of the kings who were with him: Comur Cromchenn, King of the Men of the Dog-Heads, and Caitchenn, King of the Men of the Cat-Heads.

They had five red-armed battalions with them, and they went up the shore like great red waves.

"Who is there to match the King of the Dog-Heads for me?" said Bodb Dearg.

"I'll go against him," said Lir of Sidhe Finnachaidh, "though I've heard there's no man in the world with stronger hands."

"Who'll be a match for the King of the Cat-Heads?"

"I'll be a match for him," said Abarthach, son of Ildathach.

So Lir and the King of the Dog-Heads went at each other and made a hard fight of it. But after a while Lir was getting the worst of it.

"It's a pity, the way Lir is," said Bodb Dearg. "Let some of you get up and help him."

Then Ilbrec, son of Manannan, went to his help, but he got a wound himself and could do nothing. Then Sigmal, grandson of Midhir, went to help him, and after him the five sons of Finnaistucan, and others of the Men of Dea. They were all driven off by the King of the Dog-Heads.

Lir, whose children had been nine hundred years on the water. It is hard to know what he was fighting, that day.

But by then Abarthach had made an end of the King of the Cat-Heads. He rose up on his spear and made a leap, and came down between Lir and his enemy.

"Leave off now, and watch the fight," he said to Lir. "Leave it to me and the foreigner."

He took his sword in his left hand and thrust with his spear in through the king's armour. As the king raised his shield, Abarthach struck at him with the sword in his left hand, and cut off both his legs at the knees. The king let his shield fall then, and Abarthach struck off his head.

With the two kings dead, their people broke and ran. The Men of Dea followed them and made an end of them all. But they lost a good many of their own men doing it.

The gods do not die. Some of them died on the White Strand anyway.

Finn and the Fianna were still at Credhe's house when they saw Taistellach coming towards them.

It was Finn's custom, when he sent anyone out for news, that the news should be told to him first. That way, if it was bad news, he could pretend not to mind it. And if it was good news, he would have the satisfaction of telling it himself.

That is a thing a leader learns. Bad news is heard alone. Good news is shared.

So Taistellach told him how the foreigners had come to the harbour of the White Strand.

Then Finn turned to his chief men. "Fianna of Ireland," he said, "there never came harm or danger to Ireland to compare with this great danger that has come against us now. You get great tribute and great service from the chief men of Ireland. If you take that from them, it's right for you to defend them now."

The Fianna all said they would not go back one step from the defence of Ireland.

Credhe gave every one of them a battle-dress. They were taking their leave of her when Finn said, "Let the woman come with us, until we know whether the end of this journey is good or bad."

So she came with them, bringing a great herd of cattle. For the whole length of the battle — and it lasted a year and a day — she had new milk for them, and it was to her house that the wounded were brought for healing.

Then the Fianna set out. They went to the borders of Ciarraighe Luachra, and across by the shores of the Bannlid, with Slieve Mis on their left hand, and made shelters for themselves that night and kindled fires.

But Caoilte and Oisin and Lugaidh's Son said to one another that they would go on ahead to the harbour, so that they would have time to redden their hands in the blood of the foreigners before the rest of the Fianna came.

At that time the King of the World was telling some of his chief men to go ashore and bring him back spoils. They went to land and gave a great shout, and the people in the ships gave a great shout at the same time.

"I swear by the oath my people swear by," said Caoilte, "I've gone round the whole world, and I never heard so many voices together in one place."

With that he and Oisin and Lugaidh's Son attacked the strangers and struck great blows at them. When Conn Crither and Glas, son of Bremen, heard the noise of those blows, they knew they were being struck by some of the Fianna of Ireland. They came and joined them, and did great destruction on the strangers, until there was not one left of all that had come to land.

Five men on a beach, now. It was a start.

In the morning they saw Finn and all his people coming to the rath above the harbour.

"My father Finn," said Oisin, "let's fight the whole of the foreigners now, all together."

"That's not my advice," said Finn. "The number of their armies is too great for us, and we couldn't stand against them. But every day we'll send out some son of a king or of a leader against some king of the kings of the world who's equal in blood to ourselves. And let none of you redden your weapons at first except on a king or a chief man. When a king has fallen, his people are more inclined to give way. Now, who'll give out a challenge of battle for me?"

"I'll do that," said the son of Cuban, leader of the Fianna of Munster.

"Don't go, my son," said Finn. "It isn't shown to me that you'll have good luck in the battle. And I never sent out any man to fight without knowing he'd come back safe to me."

"Don't say that," said Cuban's son. "I wouldn't go back from a fight for the treasure of the whole world because of a bad foretelling. And since it's my own country they did their robbing in first, I'll defend it for you."

"I'm sorrowful for that," said Finn. "For whichever of the kings of the world meets you today, you and he will fall together."

This is what it is to be Finn, who drank from the salmon. He knows. He says so. They go anyway.

Glas, son of Dremen, gave out the challenge from Cuban's son, and the King of Greece answered it. The two fought hand to hand. The King of Greece made a great cast of his thick spear at Cuban's son, and it went through his body and broke his back in two. But Cuban's son did not take that blow as a gift. He paid for it with a strong cast of his own golden spear, and it went through the ringed armour of the King of Greece. And those two fell together, sole to sole, and lip to lip.

"There's grief on me that Cuban's son has fallen," said Finn. "No one ever went from his house unsatisfied. A man that I wouldn't keep, or that the High King of Ireland wouldn't keep for a week, he would keep in his house for the length of a year. Let Follamain, his son, be called to me now, and I'll give him his father's name and place."

They stayed there until the next morning.

"Who'll go and fight today?" said Finn.

"I will," said Goll Garb, son of the King of Alban and of the daughter of Goll, son of Morna.

He put on his battle-dress, and there came against him the three kings from the rising of the sun in the east, with their three battalions. Goll Garb rushed in among their men and wounded and maimed and destroyed them, and blinded their eyes for ever, so that their wits went from them, and they called out to him to stop his deadly sword for a while. He did that. And they agreed to take their three kings and hand them over to Goll Garb, so that he would stop the destruction of his sword.

"Who'll go out and fight today?" said Finn, the next morning.

"I'll go," said Oisin, "and the chief men of the sons of Baiscne with me. We get the best share of all the pleasant things of Ireland, and we should be first to defend her."

"I'll answer that challenge," said the King of France. "It's against Finn I came to Ireland, because of my wife that he carried off from me. These men will fall by me now, and Finn himself at the last. When the branches of a tree are cut off, it's not hard to cut down the tree itself."

So the King of France and Oisin met at the eastern end of the strand. They struck their banners of soft silk into the green hill, and bared their swords, and made a quick attack on each other. At one point the king struck such a great blow that he knocked a groan out of Oisin. But he was worsted in the end all the same. A great fear came on him, like the fear of a hundred horses at the sound of thunder. He ran from Oisin, and rose up like a swallow, so that his feet never touched the earth at all, and he never stopped until he came to Gleann na-n Gealt, the Valley of Wild Men.

Ever since then, people who have lost their wits make for that valley. Every mad person in Ireland, if he had his way, would go there within twenty-four hours.

Great cries of lamentation rose from the armies of the World when they saw him go, and the Fianna of Ireland raised great shouts of joy.

When night was coming on, Finn said: "The King of the World is sad and gloomy tonight. It's likely he'll make an attack on us. Which of you will keep watch over the harbour through the night?"

"I will," said Oisin, "with the same number that fought with me today. It's not too much for us to fight for the Fianna of Ireland through a day and a night."

So they went down to the harbour. Just then the King of the World was saying: "It seems to me, men of the World, that our luck of battle wasn't good today. Let a share of you get up now and make an attack on the Fianna of Ireland."

Then the nine sons of Garb, King of the Sea of Icht, got up — they were smiths — and sixteen hundred of their people with them. They all went ashore except Dolar Durba, who was the eldest.

The sons of Baiscne were ready for them, and they fought a great battle until the early light of the next day. And not one man on either side was left alive who could hold a weapon, except Oisin and one of the sons of Garb.

Those two made rushes at each other, and threw their swords out of their hands, and closed their arms round each other and wrestled together, so that it would have been worth coming from the east of the world to the west to see the fight of those two.

Then the foreigner gave Oisin a sudden great fall to bring him into the sea. He was a great swimmer, and he thought he would get the better of him there. And Oisin thought it would not be worthy of him to refuse any man his own place of fighting.

So they went into the water together, and tried to drown each other, until they came to the sand and the gravel of the clear sea-bottom. It was a torment to the heart of the Fianna to see Oisin in that strait.

"Get up, Fergus of the Sweet Lips," said Finn, "and go and praise my son and encourage him."

So Fergus went down to the edge of the sea and called out: "It's a good fight you're making, Oisin, and there are many watching it. The armies of the whole world are looking at you, and the Fianna of Ireland. Show them now your ways and your greatness — for you never went into any place yet but some woman of high beauty, or some king's daughter, set her love on you."

That is a poet's job in a battle. Not to fight. To remind the fighter who he is.

Then Oisin's courage rose, and anger came on him. He locked his hands behind the foreigner's back and put him down on the sand under the sea, face upward, and did not let him rise until the life was gone out of him. Then he brought the body ashore, and struck off the head, and brought it to the Fianna.

But there was great grief and anger on Dolar Durba, the eldest of the sons of Garb, who had stayed in the ship. He swore a great oath that he would have satisfaction for his brothers. He went to the High King and said:

"I'll go alone to the strand, and I'll kill a hundred men every day until I've made an end of the whole of the armies of Ireland. And if any of your own men comes to interfere with me, I'll kill him along with them."

The next morning Finn asked who would lead the battle that day.

"I will," said Dubhan, son of Donn.

"Don't," said Finn. "Let someone else go."

But Dubhan went to the strand, and a hundred men with him. There was nobody there before him but Dolar Durba, and Dolar Durba said he was there to fight the whole of them.

Dubhan's men gave a great shout of laughter when they heard that.

Then Dolar Durba rushed at them, and made an end of the whole hundred, without one of them being able to put a scratch on him.

Then he took a hurling-stick and a ball. He threw up the ball and kept it in the air with the hurl from the west end of the strand to the east, without letting it touch the ground once. Then he put the ball on his right foot and kicked it high into the air, and when it was coming down he gave it a kick with his left foot, and kept it in the air like that, rushing like a blast of March wind from one end of the strand to the other.

When he had done that, he walked up and down the strand making great boasts, and challenging the men of Ireland to do the like of those feats.

And every day he killed a hundred of the men who were sent against him.

It happened at that time that news of the great battle reached the court of the King of Ulster.

The king's son was only twelve years old, and he was the comeliest of all the young men of Ireland.

"Let me go to help Finn, son of Cumhal, and his men," he said to his father.

"You're not old enough or strong enough, boy," said the king. "Your bones are too soft."

When the boy kept on asking, his father shut him up in a closed place, and put twelve young men, his foster-brothers, in charge of him.

A great anger came on the lad then.

"It was through courage and daring that my father won a great name for himself in his own early youth," he said to his foster-brothers. "Why does he keep me from winning a name for myself? Help me now, and I'll be a friend to you for ever."

He went on talking to them and persuading them until he had won them all round, and they agreed to go with him to join Finn and the Fianna. When the king was asleep they went into the house where the weapons were kept, and every lad of them took a shield and a sword and a helmet and two spears and two greyhound whelps.

They went across Ess Ruadh in the north, and through Connacht of many tribes, and through Caille an Chosanma, the Woods of Defence, which were called the choice of every king and the true honour of every poet, and into Ciarraighe, and so on to the White Strand.

When they got there Dolar Durba was on the strand, boasting in front of the men of Ireland.

Oisin was getting up to go against him. He said he would sooner die fighting him than watch the destruction he was doing on his people every day. And all the wise men and the fighting men and the poets and the musicians of the Fianna gave a great cry of sorrow when they heard Oisin say it.

The King of Ulster's son went to Finn and stood in front of him and greeted him. Finn asked him who he was and where he had come from.

"I am the son of the King of Ulster," he said. "I've come here with my twelve foster-brothers to give you what help we can."

"I give you a welcome," said Finn.

Just then they heard the voice of Dolar Durba, very loud and boastful.

"Who is that I hear?" said the king's son.

"It's a man of the foreigners, asking for a hundred of my men to go and meet him," said Finn.

When the twelve foster-brothers heard that, they said no word. They went down to the strand, without the king's son or Finn knowing.

"You're not a grown man," Conan said to the king's son. "Neither you nor your comrades are fit to face any fighting man at all."

"I never saw the Fianna of Ireland until today," said the young lad. "But I know well that you're Conan Maol, who never says a good word of any man. And you'll see now whether I'm in dread of that man on the strand, or of any man in the world. I'll go out against him by myself."

But Finn held him back and was talking with him. Then Conan began again.

"Dolar Durba has made an end of many men," he said, "and there wasn't a man of all of them who couldn't have killed a hundred of the like of you every day."

When the king's son heard that, a great anger came on him and he leapt up. Just then Dolar Durba gave a great shout on the strand.

"What's he shouting for?" said the king's son.

"He's shouting for more men to come against him," said Conan. "He's just after killing your twelve comrades."

"That's a sorrowful story," said the king's son.

He was twelve. He said it the way a king would say it.

He took hold of his weapons, and nobody could hold him or stop him, and he rushed down to the strand where Dolar Durba was.

All the armies of the strangers gave a great shout of laughter. They thought all Finn's men must be finished, if he was sending a young lad like that against their best champion.

When the boy heard the laughter, his courage grew greater. He fell on Dolar Durba and gave him many wounds before Dolar Durba even knew he was being attacked. They fought a very hard fight together, until their shields and their swords were broken in pieces. That did not stop the battle. They grappled together, and fought and wrestled that way, until the tide came in over them and drowned them both.

When the sea went over them, the armies on both sides gave a great, sorrowful cry.

After the ebb-tide the next day, the two bodies were found, cold and quiet, each held fast by the other. But Dolar Durba was underneath the king's son. So they knew it was the young lad who had been the better, and had won.

They buried him, and put a flagstone over his grave, and keened him there.

Nobody has kept his name. Only that he was the King of Ulster's son, and that he was twelve, and that he was on top.

Then Finn said he would send out a challenge himself to Daire Donn, the King of the Great World.

But Caoilte asked leave to do that day's fighting himself. Finn said he would agree to it if Caoilte could find enough men to go with him. Finn gave him a hundred men himself, and Oisin did the same, and so on with the rest.

Caoilte gave out his challenge, and it was the son of the King of the Great Plain who answered it.

While they were in the heat of the fight, a fleet of ships came into the harbour. Finn thought they had come to help the foreigners.

But Oisin looked at them. "It's seldom your knowledge fails you, Finn," he said, "but those are friends of our own: Fiachra, son of the King of the Fianna of the Bretons, and Duaban Donn, son of the King of Tuathmumain, with his own people."

When the people in the ships came ashore, they saw Caoilte's banner going down before the son of the King of the Great Plain. They all went hurrying to his help, and between them they made an end of the king's son and of all his people.

"Who'll keep watch tonight?" said Finn then.

"We will," said the nine Garbhs of the Fianna: of Slieve Mis, and Slieve Cua, and Slieve Clair, and Slieve Crot, and Slieve Muice, and Slieve Fuad, and Slieve Atha Moir, and Dun Sobairce, and Dundealgan.

They had not been long watching when they saw the King of the Men of Dregan coming towards them, and they fought a fierce battle. At the end of the night only three of the Garbhs were left standing, and the King of the Men of Dregan. They fought until their wits were gone from them. And those four fell together, sole against sole, and lip against lip.

The fight went on from day to day and from week to week, with great losses on both sides.

When Fergus of the Sweet Lips saw how many of the Fianna had fallen, he asked nobody's leave but went to Teamhair of the Kings, where the High King of Ireland was, and told him how it was with Finn and his people.

"That's good," said the High King, "Finn being in that strait. There's no labouring man dares touch a pig or a deer or a salmon, even if he finds it lying dead in front of him, because of the Fianna. There's no man but is afraid to go from one place to another without leave from Finn, or to take a wife until he knows whether she has a sweetheart among the Fianna of Ireland. Finn has often given bad judgments against us. It would be better for us if the foreigners won the day than he did."

That is a king, too. Not all of them are Nuada.

Then Fergus went out to the lawn where the High King's son was playing ball.

"It's no good help you're giving to Ireland," said Fergus, "playing a game that brings no lasting profit, while strangers are taking your country away from you."

He went on urging him and blaming him, until great shame came on the young man. He threw away his hurling-stick and went through the people of Teamhair and gathered all the young men who were there — a thousand and twenty of them. They asked no leave and no advice of the High King, but set out, and went on until they came to Finntraigh.

Fergus went to where Finn was and told him the son of the High King of Ireland had come with him. All the Fianna rose up before the young man and welcomed him.

"Young man," said Finn, "we would sooner see you coming at a time when there'd be musicians and singers and poets and high-up women to make pleasure for you, than at a time when we're in the straits of battle the way we are now."

"It's not for playing I've come," said the young man, "but to give you my service in battle."

"I never brought a lad who was new to the work into the breast of battle," said Finn. "Often a lad coming like that finds his death, and I wouldn't wish him to fall through me."

"I give my word," said the young man, "I'll do battle with them on my own account, if I may not do it on yours."

Then Fergus of the Sweet Lips went out to give a challenge of battle from the son of the High King of Ireland to the King of the World.

"Who'll answer the King of Ireland's son for me?" said the King of the World.

"I'll go against him," said Sligech, King of the Men of Cepda.

He went ashore, and his three red battalions with him. The High King's son went against them, with his comrades near him.

"Take a good heart into the fight now," they said to him, "for the Fianna will be no better pleased if it goes well with you than if it goes well with the foreigner."

When the High King's son heard that, he made a rush through the army of the foreigners and began killing and overthrowing them, until their chief men were all made an end of. Then Sligech their king came to meet him, very angry, destroying as he came. They struck at each other and made a great fight. But at the last the King of Ireland's son got the upper hand, and killed the King of the Men of Cepda, and struck off his head.

His father had hoped the Fianna would lose. His son had just made sure they would not. That is how it goes with fathers and sons.

The fighting went on from day to day, and at last Finn said to Fergus of the Sweet Lips: "Go out, Fergus, and see how many of the Fianna are left for the fight today."

Fergus counted them. "There's only one battalion of the Fianna left in good order," he said. "But some men in it are able to fight three, and some are able to fight nine, or thirty, or a hundred."

"If that's so," said Finn, "get up and go to where the King of the World is, and tell him to come out to the great battle."

So Fergus went to the King of the World. He was lying on his bed, listening to the music of harps and pipes.

"King of the World," said Fergus, "it's a long time you're in that sleep. And that's no shame to you, for it'll be your last sleep. The whole of the Fianna have gone out to their place of battle. Go out and answer them."

"In my opinion," said the King of the World, "there's not a man of them able to fight me. How many are left of the Fianna of Ireland?"

"Only one battalion in good order," said Fergus.

"And how many of the armies of the World are left?" said the king. "Thirty battalions came with me to Ireland. Twenty of them have fallen by the Fianna, and what's left is ten red battalions in good order. And there are eight good fighters among them who would put down the men of the whole world if they were against me. That is: myself; and Conmail my son; and Ogarmach, the daughter of the King of Greece, who is the best hand in battle in the whole world after me; and Finnachta of the Teeth, the chief of my household; and the King of Lochlann, Caisel Clumach of the Feathers; and his three sons, Tocha, and Forne of the Broad Shoulders, and Mongach of the Sea."

"I swear by the oath of my people," said the King of Lochlann, "if any man of the armies goes out against the Fianna before me and my three sons, we won't go at all. We wouldn't get the satisfaction we're used to, unless our swords get their fill of blood."

"I'll go out against them alone," said Forne, the youngest son of the King of Lochlann.

He put on his battle-suit and went in among the Fianna of Ireland, with a red-edged sword in each of his hands. He destroyed the young men who were sent against him, and made the strand narrow with their bodies.

Finn saw it, and it was a torment to his heart, and a danger of death and loss of his wits to him. He kept encouraging the men of Ireland against Forne.

And Fergus of the True Lips stood up and said: "Fianna of Ireland, it's a pity the way you are under hardship, defending Ireland. One man is taking her away from you today. You're like nothing but a flock of little birds looking for shelter in a bush from a hawk that's after them. It's into the shelter of Finn and Oisin and Caoilte you're going. Not one of you is better than another, and none of you sets his face against the foreigner."

"By my oath," said Oisin, "all that's true. None of us tries to do better than the rest at keeping him off."

"There's not one of you better than another," said Fergus.

Then Oisin gave a great shout against the King of Lochlann's son. "Stay here with me, king's son," he said, "until I fight you for the Fianna."

"I give my word, the delay will be short," said Forne.

He and Oisin went at each other, and for a while it seemed the battle was going against Oisin.

"By my word, Man of Poetry," said Finn to Fergus of the True Lips, "it's a pity the way you sent my son against the foreigner. Get up and praise him and hearten him now."

So Fergus went down to where the fight was, and called out: "There's great shame on the Fianna, Oisin, seeing you so low in this fight. There's many a foot-messenger and many a horseman from the daughters of the kings and princes of Ireland watching you now."

Great courage rose in Oisin then, and he drove his spear through the body of Forne, the King of Lochlann's son. And he came back to the Fianna of Ireland.

The armies of the World gave a great cry, keening Forne. There was anger on his brothers, not fear, for they thought it no right thing that he should have fallen by a man of the Fianna.

Tocha, the second son of the King of Lochlann, went ashore to avenge his brother. He went straight into the middle of the Fianna and gave his sword good feeding on their bodies, until they broke away in front of him and made no stand — until Lugaidh's Son turned round against him.

Those two fought a great fight, until their swords were bent and their spears crumbled away and they had lost their golden shields. At last Lugaidh's Son made a stroke of his sword that cut through the foreigner's sword, and then another stroke that cut his heart in two halves. And he came back, high and proud, to the Fianna.

Then the third son of the King of Lochlann, Mongach of the Sea, stood up, and all the armies stood up with him.

"Stay here, Men of the World," he said. "It's not you but I that has to go and ask satisfaction for the bodies of my brothers."

So he went ashore. This is how he was armed. He had a strong iron flail in his hand. It had seven balls of pure iron on it, and fifty iron chains, and fifty apples on every chain, and fifty deadly thorns on every apple.

He rushed through the Fianna to break them up entirely and tear them into strings, and they gave way before him.

Great shame came on Fidach, son of the King of the Bretons. "Come here and praise me, Fergus of the True Lips," he said, "until I go out and fight the foreigner."

"It's easy to praise you, son," said Fergus, and he praised him for a long time.

Then the two of them looked at each other and used fierce, proud words. Mongach of the Sea raised his iron flail and made a great blow at the King of the Bretons' son. But Fidach made a quick leap to one side and gave him a blow of his sword that cut off his two hands at the wrist. He did not stop at that, but struck at his middle and cut him into two halves.

But as Mongach fell, an apple of the flail, with its deadly thorns, went into Fidach's comely mouth and through his brain. And those two fell foot to foot, and lip to lip.

Nobody wins against a weapon like that. At best, you go down together.

The next to come to fight on the strand was the King of Lochlann himself, Caisel of the Feathers.

He came to the battle with his shield on his arm. The smith of the Fomor had made that shield for him. Red flames came out of it, and if it were put under the sea itself, not one of its flames would stop blazing. While he had that shield on his arm, no man could come near him.

There was never such destruction done on the men of Ireland as on that day. The flames he sent out of his shield went through the bodies of men until they blazed up like a splinter of oak that has hung a whole year in the smoke of a chimney. And anyone who touched a man who was burning caught fire himself. Every other harm that had ever come into Ireland before was small beside this.

Then Finn said: "Lift up your hands, Fianna of Ireland, and give three shouts of blessing to whoever will stop this foreigner."

The Fianna gave those three shouts. And the King of Lochlann gave a great laugh when he heard them.

Druimderg, grandson of the Head of the Fianna of Ulster, was near him. He had with him a deadly spear, the Croderg, the Red-Socketed, which had come down from one to another of the sons of Rudraighe.

He looked at the King of Lochlann, and could see no part of him that was not armoured — except his mouth, which was wide open, laughing at the Fianna.

Druimderg threw the Croderg. It hit him in the open mouth, and he fell. His shield fell along with its master, and its flame went out.

Druimderg struck the head from his body, and made great boasts of the things he had done.

He was entitled. It is not every day a man finds the one weak place in a king, and it is his mouth, and he is laughing.

Then Fergus of the True Lips set out again, and went through the length of Ireland until he came to the house of Tadg, son of Nuada, who was Finn's grandfather.

There was great grief on Muirne, Finn's mother, and on Labran of the Long Hand, her brother, and on all her people, when they knew the great danger Finn was in.

Tadg asked his wife who she thought would come out alive from the great fighting at the White Strand.

"It's a pity, the way they are there," she said. "If all the living men of the world were on one side, Daire Donn, the King of the World, would put them all down. For there are no weapons in the world that will ever be reddened on him. On the night he was born, the smith of the Fomor made a shield and a sword, and it's in the prophecy that he'll fall by no weapons but those. And he gave them to the King of the Country of the Fair Men to keep, and it's with him they are now."

That is the rule. He cannot be killed. Except by the one sword and the one shield made for him on the night he was born. Remember the rule, because the story does.

"If that's so," said Tadg, "you might be able to get help for Finn, son of Cumhal, the only son of your daughter. Tell Labran Lamfada to go and ask those weapons of him."

"Don't ask me to go against Daire Donn," she said. "He was brought up in my father's house."

But after they had talked a while, they went out onto the lawn, and they sent Labran looking for the weapons in the shape of a great eagle.

He went on from sea to sea until at noon the next day he came to the dun of the King of the Country of the Fair Men. He went into the dun in his own shape and greeted the king. The king made him welcome and asked him to stay a while.

"There's a thing I want more than that," said Labran. "The wife of a champion of the Fianna has given me her love, and I can't get her without fighting for her. It's the loan of that sword and that shield you have in your keeping I've come to ask for."

It was a lie. It was a good lie. It was told for Finn.

There were seven rooms in the king's house, opening one into the next. The first door had one lock, and the second two locks, and so on to the door of the last room, which had seven locks. It was in that room that the sword and the shield made by the smith of the Fomor were kept.

They were brought out and given to Labran, and stalks of luck were put with them, and they were bound together with shield-straps.

Then Labran of the Long Hand went back across the seas, and reached his father's dun between cockcrow and full daylight, and the weakness of death came on him.

"That's a good errand you've done, my son," said Tadg. "No one ever went that far in so short a time."

"It's little profit to me," said Labran, "when I'm not able to bring them to Finn in time for the fight tomorrow."

Just then one of Tadg's people saw Aedh, son of Aebinn. Aedh was as quick as the wind over a plain until the middle of every day; and after midday, there was no man quicker.

"You've come at a good time," said Tadg, and gave him the sword and the shield to bring to Finn for the battle.

So Aedh, son of Aebinn, went with the swiftness of a hare, or a fawn, or a swallow, until at daybreak the next morning he came to the White Strand.

Just then Fergus of the True Lips was rousing up the Fianna for the great fight. "Fianna of Ireland," he was saying, "if there were seven days' length in one day, you'd have work to fill it now. For there never was, and there never will be, a day's work done in Ireland like the work of today."

The Fianna of Ireland stood up, and saw Aedh, son of Aebinn, coming towards them at his quick run, and Finn asked him for news.

"I've come from the dun of Tadg, son of Nuada," he said, "and I'm sent to you, to ask how it is you haven't reddened your weapons yet on the King of the World."

"I swear by the oath of my people," said Finn, "if I don't redden my weapons on him, I'll crush his body inside his armour."

"I have here for you, King of the Fianna," said Aedh, "the deadly weapons that will bring him to his death. It was Labran of the Long Hand who got them for you, by his Druid arts."

He put them in Finn's hand, and Finn took the coverings off them. Flashes of fire rose out of them, and deadly bubbles, and not one of the Fianna could bear to look at them. But it put great courage into them to know that Finn had them.

"Get up now," said Finn to Fergus of the True Lips, "and go to where the King of the World is, and tell him to come out to the place of the great fight."

Then the King of the World came to the strand, and all his armies with him. All that were left of the Fianna went out against them. They were like two thick woods meeting. They made great strokes, and swords crashed against bones, and bodies were hacked, and eyes were blinded, and many a mother was left without her son, and many a comely wife without her comrade.

Then the creatures of the high air answered the battle, foretelling the destruction that would be done that day. The sea chattered of the losses. The waves gave heavy shouts, keening them. The water-beasts roared to one another. The rough hills creaked with the danger of the battle. The woods trembled, mourning the heroes. The grey stones cried out at their deeds. The wind sobbed, telling them. The earth shook, foretelling the slaughter. And the cries of the grey armies put a blue cloak over the sun, and the clouds were dark. The hounds and the whelps and the crows, and the witches of the valley, and the powers of the air, and the wolves of the forests, howled from every quarter and on every side of the armies, urging them on against each other.

Everything knew. Everything in Ireland knew what that day was.

It was then that Conan, son of Morna, remembered that he and his kindred had done great harm to the sons of Baiscne. He wished to do some good thing for them because of it, and he raised his sword and did great deeds.

Finn was above the battle, encouraging the Fianna, and the King of the World was on the other side, encouraging the foreigners.

"Get up now, Fergus," said Finn, "and praise Conan for me, so his courage will be greater. It's good work he's doing on my enemies."

So Fergus went to where Conan was. Conan was hot with the dust of the fight, and had gone outside it to let the wind get at him.

"It's well you remember the old quarrel between the sons of Morna and the sons of Baiscne, Conan," said Fergus. "You'd be ready to go to your own death if it would bring harm on the sons of Baiscne."

"For the love of your good name, Man of Poetry," said Conan, "don't speak against me without cause. I'll do good work on the foreigners when I get back into the battle."

"By my word," said Fergus, "that would be a good thing for you to do."

Then he sang a verse of praise for him, and Conan went back into the battle, and his deeds were no worse this time than before. And Fergus went back to Finn.

It is hard to praise Conan. Fergus managed it. That is what a poet is for.

"Who's best in the battle now?" said Finn.

"Duban, son of Cas, a champion of your own people," said Fergus. "He never gives more than one stroke to any man, and no man escapes with his life from that stroke. Three times nine and eighty men have fallen by him so far."

Duban Donn, great-grandson of the King of Tuathmumhain, was there listening to him.

"By my oath, Fergus," he said, "all you say is true. There's no son of a king or of a lord better in the battle than Duban, son of Cas. And I'll go to my own death if I don't go beyond him."

With that he went rushing through the battle like flames over a high hill thick with furze. Nine times he made a round of the battle, and he killed nine times nine in every round.

"Who's best in the battle now?" said Finn, after a while.

"It's Duban Donn, who just went from us," said Fergus. "There's been no one ahead of him since he was in his seventh year, and there's no one ahead of him now."

"Get up and praise him, so his courage will be greater," said Finn.

"It's right to praise him," said Fergus, "with the foreigners running from him on every side as they'd run from a heavy drenching of the sea."

So Fergus praised him a while, and then went back to Finn.

"Who's best in the battle now?" said Finn.

"It's Osgar is best in it now," said Fergus. "He's fighting alone against two hundred Franks and two hundred of the men of Gairian, and the King of the Men of Gairian himself. They're all beating at his shield, and not one of them has given him a wound but he's given a wound back for it."

"How is Caoilte, son of Ronan?" said Finn.

"He's in no great strait, after the red slaughter he's made," said Fergus.

"Then go to him," said Finn, "and tell him to keep off a share of the foreigners from Osgar."

So Fergus went to him. "Caoilte," he said, "your friend Osgar is in great danger under the blows of the foreigners. Get up and give him some help."

Caoilte went to where Osgar was, and struck a straight blow of his sword at the man nearest him, and made two halves of him.

Osgar raised his head and looked at him.

"It's likely, Caoilte," he said, "you didn't dare redden your sword on anyone until you struck down a man who was in front of my sword. It's a shame for you — all the men of the great world and the Fianna of Ireland in the one battle, and you not able to make a fight for yourself without coming to take a share of my share of it. I give my oath, I'd be glad to see you put down in your bed of blood for that."
