That is Osgar. He would rather die than be helped. He would get his wish, in the end, on another field.

Caoilte's mind changed when he heard that. He turned again to the army of the foreigners with the red of anger on his white face, and eighty fighting men fell in that rout.

"How is the battle now?" said Finn.

"It's a pity," said Fergus, "there never came and there never will come anyone who could tell how it is now. By my word, the treetops of the thickest forest in the whole of the western world aren't closer together than the armies are now, for the bosses of their shields are in each other's hands. There's fire coming off the edges of their swords, and blood raining down like a shower on a day of harvest. And there were never as many leaves torn by the wind from a great forest as there are locks of long golden hair, and of black curled hair, cut off by sharp weapons and blowing up into the clouds at this moment. And nobody could tell one man from another now, unless it might be by their voices."

With that he went into the very middle of the fight to praise and hearten the men of the Fianna.

"Who's first in the battle now, Fergus?" said Finn, when he came back.

"By my oath, it's no friend of yours that's first in it," said Fergus. "It's Daire Donn, the King of the World. It's you he's searching for through the battle, and three times fifty of his own people were with him. Two of the men of your Fianna fell on them — Cairell the Battle-Striker, and Aelchinn of Cruachan — and made an end of them. But they weren't able to wound the King of the World, and the two of them fell together by him."

Then the King of the World came towards Finn. There was nobody near Finn but Arcallach of the Black Axe, the first man who ever brought a wide axe into Ireland.

"I give my word," said Arcallach, "I'd never let Finn go before me into any battle."

He rose up and struck a terrible great blow of his axe at the king. It went through his royal crown to the hair of his head. But it did not take one drop of blood out of him. The edge of the axe turned, and balls of fire went out over the plain from that blow.

And the King of the World struck back at Arcallach, and made two halves of him.

Then Finn and the King of the World turned on each other.

When the king saw the sword and the shield in Finn's hand, he knew those were the weapons that were to bring him to his death. Great dread came on him. His comeliness left him. His fingers shook, and his feet were unsteady, and the sight of his eyes was weakened.

This is what it is to know the rule of your own death, and to see it walking towards you.

Then the two of them fought a great fight, striking at each other like two days of judgment for the possession of the world.

But the king, who had never had a wound before, began to weaken badly in the fight. Finn struck great strokes that broke his shield and his sword, and cut off his left foot. And at the last he struck off his head.

But when he did, Finn himself fell into a faint of weakness from the force of the wounds he had got.

Then Finnachta of the Teeth, the first man of the household of the King of the World, took hold of the king's royal crown, and brought it to Conmail his son, and put it on his head.

"May this bring you success in many battles, my son," he said. And he gave him his father's weapons with it.

The young man went through the battle looking for Finn, and three fifties of the men of the Fianna fell by him. Then Goll Garbh the Rough, son of the King of Alban, saw him and attacked him, and they fought a hard fight. But the King of Alban's son gave him a blow under the shelter of the shield, in his left side, that made an end of him.

Finnachta of the Teeth saw that. He made another rush at the royal crown, and brought it to where Ogarmach was, the daughter of the King of Greece.

"Put on that crown, Ogarmach," he said. "It's in the prophecy that the world will be owned by a woman. And it will never be owned by any woman higher than you."

She went to look for Finn in the battle. Fergus of the True Lips saw her, and he went to where Finn was.

"O King of the Fianna," he said, "bring to mind the good fight you made against the King of the World, and all your victories before that. For a great danger is coming to you now. It's Ogarmach, daughter of the King of Greece."

With that the woman-warrior came towards him.

"O Finn," she said, "you're little satisfaction to me for all the kings and lords who've fallen by you and your people. But for all that, there's nothing better for me to get than yourself, and whatever's left of your people."

"You won't get that," said Finn. "I'll lay your head in its bed of blood the same as I did to every other one."

Then those two went at each other as if there had risen up to smother one another the flooded wave of Cliodna, and the seeking wave of Tuaigh, and the big brave wave of Rudraighe.

The woman-warrior fought for a long time. She was the best hand in battle in the whole world, after the King of the World, and she proved it. But at last a blow from Finn reached her, and cut through the royal crown, and with a second blow he struck her head off.

Then he fell himself in his bed of blood, and was the same as dead — except that he rose again.

The armies of the World and the Fianna of Ireland had fallen side by side there. There were none left fit to stand but Cael, son of Crimthan of the Harbours, and the chief man of the household of the King of the World, Finnachta of the Teeth.

Finnachta went among the dead bodies and lifted up the body of the King of the World and carried it with him to his ship.

"Fianna of Ireland," he said, "bad as this battle was for the armies of the World, it was worse for you. And I'm going back to tell that in the East of the World."

Finn heard him say it, lying on the ground in his blood with the best men of the sons of Baiscne around him.

"It's a pity I didn't find death before I heard the foreigner say those words," he said. "Nothing I've done, or the Fianna of Ireland, is worth anything, since there's a man of the foreigners left alive to go back into the great world and tell that story. Is there anyone left living near me?"

"I am," said Fergus of the True Lips.

"How is the battle now?" said Finn.

"It's a pity, the way it is," said Fergus. "By my word, since the armies met today, no man of the foreigners or of the men of Ireland has taken one step backward from the other, until they all fell foot to foot and sole to sole. There's not so much as a blade of grass or a grain of sand to be seen for the bodies of fighting men stretched on them. And there's no man of the two armies who isn't stretched in that bed of blood, except the chief man of the household of the King of the World, and your own foster-son, Cael, son of Crimthan of the Harbours."

"Get up and go to him," said Finn.

So Fergus went to Cael and asked him how he was.

"It's a pity, the way I am," said Cael. "I swear by my word that if my helmet and my armour were taken off me, there's no part of my body but would fall away from the rest. And by my oath, it's worse to me to see that man over there going away alive than to be the way I am myself. I leave you my blessing, Fergus. Carry me on your back to the sea, so I can swim after the foreigner. I'd be glad for the foreigner to fall by me before the life goes out of my body."

Fergus lifted him up and carried him to the sea, and set him swimming after the foreigner.

Finnachta waited for him to reach the ship, for he thought he was one of his own people.

Cael raised himself up when he came alongside the ship. Finnachta stretched out his hand to him. Cael took it by the wrist, and clasped his fingers round it, and gave a very strong pull that brought Finnachta over the side.

Then their arms locked across each other's bodies, and they went down together to the sand and the gravel of the clear sea.

Nobody went home to the East of the World to tell the story. That is why we are the ones telling it.

And Credhe was waiting, with the cattle, at the edge of the strand.

Then the women came, and the musicians and the singers and the physicians of the Fianna of Ireland, to search out the kings and princes of the Fianna and to bury them. Everyone who might be healed was carried to a place of healing.

Credhe, wife of Cael, came with the others. She went looking through the bodies for her comely comrade, crying as she went.

As she was searching, she saw a crane of the meadows with her two nestlings, and the cunning beast the fox watching the nestlings. When the crane covered one of the birds to save it, the fox would make a rush at the other, so that she had to stretch herself out over both. She would sooner have got her own death from the fox than let her nestlings be killed by him.

Credhe watched that. "It's no wonder I have such love for my comely sweetheart," she said, "when the bird is in that distress over her nestlings."

Then she heard a stag on Druim Ruighlenn above the harbour, making great lamentation for his hind from place to place. They had been nine years together, and had lived in the wood at the foot of the harbour, Fidh Leis. Finn had killed the hind. The stag had gone nineteen days without tasting grass or water, lamenting after her.

"It's no shame for me," said Credhe, "to die of grief after Cael, when the stag is shortening his life sorrowing after the hind."

Then she met Fergus of the True Lips.

"Have you news of Cael for me, Fergus?" she said.

"I have news," said Fergus. "He and the last man left of the foreigners, Finnachta Fiaclach, have drowned each other in the sea."

By then the waves had put Cael back on the strand. The women and the men of the Fianna who were looking for him lifted him up and carried him to the south end of the White Strand.

Credhe came to where he was. She keened him and cried over him, and she made this lament:

"The harbour roars, O the harbour roars, over the rushing race of the Headland of the Two Storms: the drowning of the hero of the Lake of the Two Dogs, that is what the waves are keening on the strand.

"Sweet-voiced is the crane, O sweet-voiced is the crane in the marshes of the Ridge of the Two Strong Men. It is she cannot save her nestlings; the wild dog of two colours is taking her little ones.

"Pitiful the cry, pitiful the cry the thrush is making in the Pleasant Ridge; sorrowful is the cry of the blackbird in Leiter Laeig.

"Sorrowful the call, O sorrowful the call of the deer in the Ridge of Two Lights. The doe is lying dead in Druim Silenn; the mighty stag cries after her.

"Sorrowful to me, O sorrowful to me, the death of the hero who lay beside me: the son of the woman of the Wood of the Two Thickets, to be with a bunch of grass under his head.

"Sore to me, O sore to me, that Cael is a dead man beside me, that the waves have gone over his white body. It is his pleasantness that has put my wits astray.

"A woeful shout, O a woeful shout the waves are making on the strand. They that took hold of comely Cael — a pity it is he went to meet them.

"A woeful crash, O a woeful crash the waves are making on the strand to the north, breaking against the smooth rock, crying after Cael now he is gone.

"A sorrowful fight, O a sorrowful fight the sea is making with the strand to the north. My beauty is lessened; the end of my life is measured.

"A song of grief, O a song of grief is made by the waves of Tulcha Leis. All I had is gone since this story came to me. Since the son of Crimthann is drowned I will love no one after him for ever. Many a king fell by his hand; his shield never cried out in the battle."

When she had made that lament, Credhe lay down beside Cael, and died of grief after him.

They were put in the one grave, and it was Caoilte who raised the stone over them.

She had asked him for a poem about her cups and her bowls and her beds. He had given her one. It was the poem that brought him to her door. It is hers that we remember.

After that great battle of the White Strand, which lasted a year and a day, many a sword and shield was left broken, and many a dead body lying on the ground, and many a fighting man left with a foolish smile on his face.

The great name that had been on the armies of the World went from them to the Fianna of Ireland. They took the ships and the gold and the silver and all the spoils of the armies of the World. And from that time on the Fianna had charge of the whole of Ireland, to keep it from the Fomor and from anyone else who might come against it.

They never lost that power, from that time until their last battle: the sorrowful battle of Gabhra.

Arthur, son of the King of Britain, came once to take service with Finn, with three times nine men.

They went hunting one day on Beinn Edair. Finn took his place on the Cairn of the Fianna, between the hill and the sea, and Arthur took his stand between the hunt and the sea, so that the deer would not escape by swimming.

While Arthur was there he took notice of three of Finn's hounds: Bran, and Sceolan, and Adhnuall. And he made a plan in his mind to go away across the sea with his three nines, and take those three hounds with him.

He did it. He and his men took the hounds and crossed the sea, and the place they landed was Inver Mara Gamiach, on the coast of Britain. After they landed they went to the mountain of Lodan, son of Lir, to hunt on it.

As for the Fianna, when their hunting was done they gathered together on the hill, and, as the custom was, all Finn's hounds were counted. He had three hundred full-grown hounds and two hundred whelps, and the poets used to say that counting them was like counting the branches on a tree.

On this day when they were counted, Bran and Sceolan and Adhnuall were missing, and Finn was told. He told his people to search again through the three battalions of the Fianna. However hard they searched, the hounds were not to be found.

Then Finn sent for a long basin of pale gold with water in it. He put his face in the water, and his hand over his face, and what had happened was shown to him.

"The King of Britain's son has taken the hounds," he said. "Let nine men be chosen to follow them."

So nine men were chosen: Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne; Goll, son of Morna; Oisin, son of Finn; Faolan, the friend of the hounds, son of a woman who had come over the sea to give her love to Finn; Ferdoman, son of Bodb Dearg; two sons of Finn, Raighne Wide-Eye and Cainche the Crimson-Red; Glas, son of Enchered Bera; and with them Caoilte and Lugaidh's Son. Those nine put their helmets on their heads and took their long spears in their hands, and they felt sure they were a match for any four hundred men from the east of the world to the west.

They set out, and came to the mountain of Lodan, son of Lir, and they had not been there long when they heard talk of men hunting in that place.

Arthur of Britain and his people were sitting on a hunting-mound just then. The nine men of the Fianna attacked them, and killed them all except Arthur. Goll, son of Morna, put his two arms around Arthur and saved him from death.

Goll, again. The one who holds back the killing stroke.

Then they turned to go back to Ireland, bringing Arthur with them, and the three hounds. As they were going, Goll happened to look round, and he saw a dark-grey horse with a bridle fitted with worked gold. Then he looked to the left and saw a bay mare that was not easy to catch, with a bridle of silver rings and a golden bit. Goll took hold of the two of them and gave them into Oisin's hand, and Oisin gave them on to Diarmuid.

They went back to Finn, bringing his three hounds, and the King of Britain's son as a prisoner. Arthur made bonds with Finn, and was his follower until he died.

As for the horse and the mare, they gave them to Finn. The mare foaled eight times, eight foals at every birth. All the horses of the fair Fianna of the Gael came of that stock, for they had used no horses up to that time.

That was not the only time Finn was robbed of his hounds.

There was a daughter of Roman who was woman-Druid to the Tuatha de Danaan, and she set her love on Finn. But Finn said that as long as there was another woman to be found in the world, he would not marry a witch.

Once, three times fifty of Finn's hounds passed by the hill where she was. She breathed on the hounds and shut them up in the hill, and they never came out again. It was to spite Finn she did it. And the place got the name of Duma na Conn, the Mound of the Hounds.

Finn could be careless with his words, when it came to women. It cost him, more than once. It was going to cost him more.

As for Adhnuall, one of the hounds Finn thought most of, who was brought back from the King of Britain's son: this is how he came to his death afterwards.

There was a great fight once between the Fianna and Macoon, son of Macnia, somewhere in the province of Leinster, and a great many of the Fianna were killed. The hound Adhnuall went wandering northward from the battle and went astray. Three times he went round the whole of Ireland. Then he came back to the place of the battle, to a hill where three young men of the Fianna who had fallen there were buried, and three daughters of a King of Alban who had died for love of them.

When Adhnuall came to that hill, he gave three loud howls, and stretched himself out, and died.

Three times round Ireland, looking. And then home, to the grave.

Finn called for a great hunt once, on the plains of Magh Chonaill and in the forest parts of Cairbre of the Nuts. He himself went up to the top of Ceiscoran, with his two dogs, Bran and Sceolan.

The Fianna were shouting through the whole country where they hunted, so that the deer were roused in their wild places, and the badgers in their holes, and the foxes in their wanderings, and the birds on the wing.

Conaran, son of Imidd, of the Tuatha de Danaan, ruled in Ceiscoran at that time. When he heard the shouting and the cry of the hounds all around, he told his three daughters — who had a great share of enchantments — to take vengeance on Finn for his hunting.

The three women went to the opening of a cave in the hills and sat down there together. They put three strong enchanted hanks of yarn on crooked holly-sticks, and began to reel them off outside the cave.

They had not been there long when Finn and Conan came towards them, and saw the three ugly old hags at their work: their coarse hair tossed, their eyes red and bleary, their teeth sharp and crooked, their arms very long, their nails like the tips of cows' horns, and the three spindles in their hands.

Finn and Conan passed through the hanks of yarn, to get a better look at the hags.

The moment they did it, a deadly trembling came on them, and a weakness. And the bold hags took hold of them and bound them tight.

That is the rule of the yarn. Walk through it, and your strength is gone. It does not matter who you are.

Two other men of the Fianna came up then, with the sons of Menhann, and went through the spindles to where Finn and Conan were. Their strength went from them the same way, and the hags tied them fast and carried them into the cave.

They had not been there long when Caoilte and Lugaidh's Son came to the place, and with them the best men of the sons of Baiscne. The sons of Morna came too. The moment they saw the hanks, their strength and their bravery went out of them, the same as it had gone from the others.

In the end the whole number of them, gentle and simple, were put in bonds by the hags, and carried into the cave.

And there began at the mouth of the cave a great outcry of hounds, calling for the masters who had left them there. And lying on the hillside was a great heap of deer and wild pigs and hares and badgers, dead and torn, that the hunters now tied up in the cave had brought as far as that.

Then the three women came in with swords in their hands, to the place where the Fianna lay, to make an end of them. But first they looked out, to see whether there was any other man of the Fianna left to bring in and make an end of with the rest.

They saw a very tall man coming towards them. It was Goll, son of Morna, the Flame of Battle.

When the three hags saw him they went out to meet him, and they fought a hard battle with him. A great anger came on Goll, and he struck great strokes at the witches, and at last he raised his sword and with one blow cut the two nearest him through and through.

Then the eldest of the three women wound her arms round Goll, and he turned to face her, and they wrestled together, until at last Goll gave her a great twist and threw her on the ground. He tied her fast with the straps of a shield, and took his sword to make an end of her.

"O champion who was never worsted," said the hag, "strong man who never went back in battle, I put my body and my life under the protection of your bravery. It's better for you to get Finn and the Fianna back safe and whole than to have my blood. And I swear by the gods my people swear by, I'll give them back to you."

With that Goll set her free, and they went together into the hill where the Fianna were lying.

"Loose the fastenings first from Fergus of the True Lips, and from the other learned men of the Fianna," said Goll. "After that, from Finn, and Oisin, and the twenty-nine sons of Morna, and from all the rest."

The poets first. Then his old enemy. Then his own kin. That is Goll's order of things, and it is a good one.

She took off the fastenings, and the Fianna made no delay, but got up and went out and sat down on the side of the hill. And Fergus of the Sweet Lips looked at Goll, son of Morna, and made great praises of him, and of all that he had done.

Every man of the Fianna had walked through the yarn. Goll alone had come too late to be caught. Sometimes that is what saves a people: one man, late.

Once the Fianna were hunting on the island of Toraig, north of Ireland, and they roused a fawn that was very wild and beautiful. It made for the coast, and Finn and six of his men followed it through the whole country, until they came to Slieve-nam-Ban. There the fawn put down its head and vanished into the earth, and none of them knew where it had gone.

Then a heavy snow began to fall, bending the tops of the trees like willow-rods, and the courage and strength went out of the Fianna with the force of the bad weather.

"Is there anywhere we can find shelter tonight?" Finn said to Caoilte.

Caoilte made himself supple, and went over the elbow of the hill southward. When he looked around him he saw a house full of light, with cups and horns and bowls of different kinds in it.

He stood a good while in front of the door of the house, which he knew was a house of the Sidhe, wondering whether it would be best to go in and find out about it, or to go back to Finn and the few men with him. He made up his mind to go in. He sat down on a shining chair in the middle of the floor, and looked around.

On one side he saw eight-and-twenty armed men, each with a well-shaped woman beside him. On the other side he saw six nice young girls, yellow-haired, in shaggy gowns from their shoulders. And in the middle was another young girl sitting in a chair with a harp in her hand, playing and singing. Every time she stopped, one of the men would give her a horn to drink from, and she would give it back to him, and they were all making merry around her.

She spoke to Caoilte. "Caoilte, my life," she said, "give us leave to attend on you now."

"Don't," said Caoilte. "There's a better man than me outside, Finn, son of Cumhal, and he has a mind to eat in this house tonight."

"Get up, Caoilte, and go for Finn," said a man of the house. "He never refused any man in his own house, and he'll get no refusal from us."

Caoilte went back to Finn. "You were a long time away from us, Caoilte," said Finn when he saw him. "Since the day I first took weapons in my hands, I never had a night that put so much hardship on me as this one."

The six of them went into the lighted house, with their shields and their weapons. They sat down on the edge of a seat, and a girl with yellow hair came and brought them to a shining seat in the middle of the house. The newest of every food and the oldest of every drink were put in front of them.

When the sharpness of their hunger and thirst was eased, Finn said: "Which of you may I question?"

"Question whoever you like," said the tallest of the men near him.

"Who are you yourself, then?" said Finn. "I didn't think there were so many champions in Ireland I didn't know."

"Those eight-and-twenty armed men you see over there," said the tall man, "had the one father and mother with me. We're the sons of Midhir of the Yellow Hair, and our mother is Fionnchaem, the fair, beautiful daughter of the King of the Sidhe of Monaid in the east.

"At one time the Tuatha de Danaan held a gathering and gave the kingship to Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, at his bright, hospitable place. He began asking hostages of me and my brothers. We said we wouldn't give them until all the rest of the Men of Dea had given theirs. Then Bodb Dearg said to our father, 'Unless you put away your sons, we'll wall up your dwelling-place on you.'

"So the eight-and-twenty brothers of us came out to look for a place for ourselves. We searched all Ireland until we found this secret hidden place, and we've been here ever since. My own name is Donn, son of Midhir. Every one of us had ten hundred armed men of his own, but they're all worn away now, and only the eight-and-twenty of us are left."

"What is it that's wearing you away?" said Finn.

"The Men of Dea," said Donn, "who come three times every year to give battle to us on the green outside."

So the gods fight the gods. They never stopped. They only stopped doing it where we could see.

"What's the long new grave we saw on the green outside?" said Finn.

"It's the grave of Diangalach, a man of enchantments of the Men of Dea," said Donn. "That was the greatest loss that's come on them yet. It was I who killed him."

"What was the next loss after that?"

"All the Tuatha de Danaan had of jewels and riches and treasures, horns and vessels and cups of pale gold, we took from them at the one time."

"And the third greatest loss they had?"

"It was Fethnaid, daughter of Feclach, the woman-harper of the Tuatha de Danaan, their music and the delight of their minds," said Donn.

"And tomorrow," he said, "they'll be coming to attack us, and there's no one left but me and my brothers. We knew we'd be in danger, and that we could make no stand against them. So we sent that bare-headed girl over there to Toraig in the north, in the shape of a foolish fawn, and you followed her here. It's that girl washing herself, with the green cloak around her, who went looking for you.

"And the empty side of the house belonged to our people that the Men of Dea have killed."

They spent that night drinking and taking their pleasure. When they got up the next morning Donn, son of Midhir, said to Finn: "Come out with me now on the lawn and see the place where we fight the battles every year."

They went out and looked at the graves and the flagstones.

"It's as far as this the Men of Dea come to meet us," said Donn.

"Which of them come here?" said Finn.

"Bodb Dearg with his seven sons," said Donn. "And Angus Og, son of the Dagda, with his seven sons. And Finnbharr of Cnoc Medha with his seventeen sons. Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh with his twenty-seven sons and their sons. Tadg, son of Nuada, out of the beautiful hill of Almhuin. Donn of the Island and Donn of the Vat. The two called Glas, from the district of Osraige. Dobhran Dubthaire from the hill of Liamhain of the Smooth Shirt. Aedh of the Island of Rachrainn in the north. Ferai and Aillinn and Lir and Fainnle, sons of Eogobal, from Cnoc Aine in Munster. Cian and Coban and Conn, three sons of the King of Sidhe Monaid in Alban. Aedh Minbhreac of Ess Ruadh with his seven sons. The children of the Morrigu, the Great Queen, her six-and-twenty women-warriors. The two Luaths from Magh Life. Derg and Drecan out of the hill of Beinn Edair in the east. And Bodb Dearg himself with his great household, ten hundred, ten score and ten. Those are the chief leaders of the Tuatha de Danaan who come to destroy our hill every year."

Tadg, son of Nuada, was on that list. Finn's own grandfather. Finn heard it, and said nothing about it.

Finn went back into the hill and told all that to his people.

"My people," he said, "the sons of Midhir are in great need and under great oppression, and we've come into great danger ourselves. Unless we make a good fight now, it's likely we'll never see the Fianna again."

"Good Finn," every one of them said, "did you ever see any drawing back in any of us, that you give us that warning?"

"I give my word," said Finn, "if I went through the whole world with only this many of the Fianna of Ireland with me, I'd know neither fear nor fright. Good Donn, is it by day or by night the Men of Dea come against you?"

"It's at nightfall they come," said Donn, "so they can do us the most harm."

So they waited until night came on. Then Finn said: "Let one of you go out on the green now and keep watch, so the Men of Dea won't come on us without word or warning."

The man they set to watch had not gone far when he saw five strong battalions of the Men of Dea coming towards him. He went back to the hill and said: "It's my opinion the troops that have come against us this time, and are standing now around the grave of the Man of Enchantments, are a match for any fighting men."

Finn called to his people. "These are good fighters come against you, with strong red spears," he said. "Let you all do well in the battle now. And what you have to do is keep the little troop of brothers, the sons of Midhir, safe in the fight. It would be treachery to friendship if any harm came on them, after our joining them. Caoilte and I are the oldest among you. Leave the rest of the battle to us."

Then from the covering-time of evening to the edge of the morning they fought the battle. The loss of the Tuatha de Danaan was no less than ten hundred, ten score and ten men.

Then Bodb Dearg and Midhir and Fionnbhar said to each other: "What are we to do with all these? Let Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh give us advice, since he's the oldest of us."

"This is what I advise," said Lir. "Let every one carry away his friends and his fosterlings, his sons and his brothers, to his own place. And as for those of us who stay here, let a wall of fire be made around us on one side, and a wall of water on the other."

Then the Men of Dea raised a great heap of stones, and carried away their dead. And of all the great slaughter that Finn and his men and the sons of Midhir had made, not enough was left for a crow to perch on.

As for Finn and his men, they went back into the hill, hurt and wounded and worn out.

They stayed in the hill with the sons of Midhir for a whole year, and three times in the year the Men of Dea attacked the hill, and a battle was fought.

Conn, son of Midhir, was killed in one of those battles. As for the Fianna, there were so many wounds on them that their clothing had to be held off their bodies with bent hazel sticks as they lay in their beds, and two of them were near to dying.

Finn and Caoilte and Lugaidh's Son went out on the green.

"It was a bad journey we made coming to this hill," said Caoilte, "to leave two of our comrades behind us."

"It's a pity for whoever will face the Fianna of Ireland," said Lugaidh's Son, "after leaving his comrades behind."

"Whoever goes back and leaves them, it won't be me," said Finn.

Then Donn, son of Midhir, came to them.

"Good Donn," said Finn, "do you know of any physician who can cure our men?"

"I only know one physician who could do that," said Donn, "a physician the Tuatha de Danaan have with them. Unless a wounded man has the marrow of his back cut through, he'll get relief from that physician, so that he'll be sound at the end of nine days."

"How can we bring that man here," said Finn, "when the people he's with are no good friends of ours?"

"He goes out every morning at break of day," said Donn, "to gather healing herbs while the dew is on them."

"Find someone, Donn, to show me that physician," said Caoilte, "and living or dead, I'll bring him back with me."

Then Aedh and Flann, two of the sons of Midhir, stood up. "Come with us, Caoilte," they said.

They went ahead of him to a green lawn with the dew on it. When they got there they saw a strong young man, armed, with a cloak made of the wool of the seven sheep of the Land of Promise. The cloak was full of herbs of healing he had been gathering for the Men of Dea who had been wounded in the battle.

"Who's that man?" said Caoilte.

"That's the man we came looking for," said Aedh. "Mind him well now, so he doesn't get away from us back to his own people."

They ran at him together, and Caoilte took him by the shoulders, and they carried him away with them to the ford of the Slaine in the great plain of Leinster, where most of the Fianna were at that time. A Druid mist rose about them so that they could not be seen.

They went up on a little hill above the ford, and saw in front of them four young men in crimson fringed cloaks, with gold-hilted swords, and four good hunting hounds with them. The physician could not see them because of the mist. But Caoilte saw that they were his own two sons, Colla and Faolan, and two other young men of the Fianna. He could hear them talking together, saying it was a year now since Finn, son of Cumhal, had gone from them.

"What will the Fianna of Ireland do from now on," said one of them, "without their lord and their leader?"

"There's nothing for them to do," said another, "but go to Teamhair and break up there, or find another leader for themselves."

There was heavy sorrow on them for the loss of their lord. It was a grief to Caoilte to be watching them, his own sons, and not able to say a word.

He and the two sons of Midhir went back by the Lake of the Two Birds to Slieve-nam-Ban, and went into the hill.

Finn and Donn gave a great welcome to Luibra the physician, and showed him their two comrades lying in their wounds.

"Those men are brothers to me," said Donn. "Tell me how they can be cured."

Luibra looked at their wounds. "They can be cured," he said, "if I get a good reward."

"You'll get that indeed," said Caoilte. "Tell me now, how long will it take to cure them?"

"It will take nine days."

"It's a good reward you'll get," said Caoilte, "and this is what it is: your own life left to you. But if these young men aren't healed, it's my own hand will strike off your head."

Within nine days the physician had cured them, and they were as well and as sound as before.

It was after that time that the High King sent a messenger to bring the Fianna to the Feast of Teamhair. They all gathered to it, men and women, boys and heroes and musicians. Goll, son of Morna, was sitting at the feast beside the king.

"It's a great loss you've had, Fianna of Ireland," said the king, "losing your lord and your leader, Finn, son of Cumhal."

"It's a great loss indeed," said Goll.

"There's been no greater loss fallen on Ireland since the loss of Lugh, son of Ethne," said the king.

"What orders will you give the Fianna now, king?" said Goll.

"To you, Goll," said the king, "I'll give the right of hunting over all Ireland, until we know whether the loss of Finn is lasting."

"I won't take Finn's place," said Goll, "until he's been missing from us for three years, and until no one in Ireland has any hope of seeing him again."

The place he had once held himself, that Finn had taken from him. He would not take it back. Not yet. Not while there was hope.

Then Ailbe of the Freckled Face said to the king: "What should the seventeen queens of Finn's household do?"

"Let a safe, secret, sunny house be given to every one of them," said the king. "Let her stay there with her women, and let provision be given her for a month and a quarter and a year, until we know whether Finn is alive or dead."

Then the king stood up with a smooth drinking-horn in his hand.

"It would be a good thing, men of Ireland," he said, "if any one of you could get us news of Finn — in hills, or in secret places, or in rivers or river-mouths, or in any house of the Sidhe in Ireland or in Alban."

With that Berngal, the cow-owner from the borders of Slieve Fuad, who was divider to the King of Ireland, spoke.

"The day Finn came out of the north following a deer of the Sidhe, with his five comrades, he put a sharp spear with a shining head into my hand, and a hound's collar with it, and told me to keep them until he met me again in the same place."

Berngal showed the spear and the collar to the king and to Goll. They looked at them, and the king said: "The man who owned this collar and this spear is a great loss to the men of Ireland. Were his hounds with him?"

"They were," said Berngal. "Bran and Sceolan were with Finn, and Breac and Lainbhui with Caoilte, and Conuall and Comrith with Lugaidh's Son."

The High King called for Fergus of the True Lips.

"Do you know how long Finn has been away from us?"

"I know that well," said Fergus. "It's a month and a quarter and a year since we lost him. And indeed he's a great loss to the Fianna of Ireland, himself and the men who were with him."

"It's a great loss indeed," said the king. "And I have no hope at all of finding those six, who were the best men of Ireland or of Alban."

Then he called to Cithruadh the Druid. "Finn gave you many riches and many treasures," he said. "Tell us now: is he living, or is he dead?"

"He's living," said Cithruadh. "But as to where he is, I'll give no news of that, for he himself wouldn't want me to."

There was great joy among them when they heard that, for everything Cithruadh had ever foretold had come true.

"Tell us when he'll come back," said the king.

"Before the Feast of Teamhair is over," said the Druid, "you'll see the Leader of the Fianna drinking at it."

As for Finn and his men, they stayed in the House of the Two Birds until they had taken hostages from the Tuatha de Danaan on behalf of Donn, son of Midhir. And on the last day of the Feast of Teamhair, they came back to their people.

And from that time on, the Fianna of Ireland had no more dealings with the people who live in houses than they had with the People of the Gods of Dana.

They had been inside the hill. You do not come all the way back from that.

One day Finn and Oisin and Caoilte and Diarmuid and Lugaidh's Son went up to the top of Cairn Feargall, with their five hounds: Bran and Sceolan, Sear Dubh, Luath Luachar, and Adhnuall.

They had not been there long when they saw a giant coming towards them, very tall and rough, with an iron fork on his back and a squealing pig between the prongs of the fork. Behind the giant was a beautiful, eager young girl, shoving him along in front of her.

"Let someone go and speak with those people," said Finn.

So Diarmuid went towards them, but they turned away before he reached them. Then Finn and the rest got up and went after them. But before they reached the giant and the girl, a dark Druid mist rose up and hid the road.

When the mist cleared, Finn and the rest looked about them and saw a good, light-roofed house at the edge of a ford close by. They went to the house. There was a green lawn in front of it, and on the lawn two wells. On the edge of one well was a rough iron vessel, and on the edge of the other a copper vessel.

They went into the house. There they found a very old, white-haired man standing to the right of the door, and the beautiful young girl they had seen before, sitting near him, and the great rough giant beside the fire, boiling a pig. On the other side of the fire was an old countryman with dark-grey hair and twelve eyes in his head, and his twelve eyes were twelve sons of battle. There was a ram in the house with a white belly and a very black head and dark-blue horns and green feet. And there was a hag at the end of the house in a worn grey gown. There was nobody else in the house.

The man at the door gave them a welcome, and the five of them sat down on the floor of the house, with their hounds.

"Let great respect be shown to Finn, son of Cumhal, and to his people," said the man at the door.

"It's the way I am," said the giant, "always to be asking and getting nothing." But all the same he got up and showed respect to Finn.

Presently a great thirst came on Finn. Nobody noticed it but Caoilte, and he began to complain loudly about it.

"Why are you complaining, Caoilte?" said the man at the door. "You have only to go out and get a drink for Finn at whichever of the wells you choose."

So Caoilte went out and brought the full of the copper vessel to Finn. Finn drank from it. There was the taste of honey on it while he was drinking, and the taste of gall on it afterwards, so that fierce windy pains and the signs of death came on him, and his looks changed so that he could hardly be known.

Caoilte complained louder than before at the state he was in, until the man at the door told him to go out and bring him a drink from the other well. Caoilte did that, and brought in the full of the iron vessel.

Finn never went through such hardship in any battle as he did drinking that draught, from the bitterness of it. But no sooner had he drunk it than his own colour and looks came back to him, and he was as well as before, and his people were very glad to see it.

Then the man of the house asked whether the pig in the cauldron was ready.

"It's ready," said the giant, "and leave the dividing of it to me."

"How will you divide it?" said the man of the house.

"I'll give one hind-quarter to Finn and his dogs," said the giant, "and the other hind-quarter to Finn's four comrades, and the fore-quarter to myself, and the chine and the rump to the old man there by the fire and the hag in the corner, and the entrails to yourself and the young girl beside you."

"I give my word," said the man of the house, "you've shared it well."

"I give my word," said the ram, "it's a bad division for me, for you've forgotten my share."

With that the ram took hold of the quarter that was in front of the Fianna, and carried it off into a corner and began to eat it.

The four of them attacked him with their swords. But with all the hard strokes they gave him they could not harm him at all. The swords slid off his back as they would off a rock.

"On my word, it's a pity for anyone who has the like of you for comrades," said the man with the twelve eyes, "letting a sheep take your food from you."

With that he went up to the ram and took him by the feet and threw him out through the door, so that he fell on his back, and they saw him no more.

Not long after that, the hag got up and threw her pale grey gown over Finn's four comrades. They turned into four old men, weak and withered, their heads hanging.

When Finn saw that a great dread came on him. The man at the door saw it, and told him to come over to him and put his head on his breast and sleep. Finn did that. And the hag took her covering off the four men, so that when Finn woke they were in their own shape again, and he was well pleased to see it.

"Do you wonder, Finn," said the man at the door, "at the ways of this house?"

"I never wondered more at anything I ever saw," said Finn.

"Then I'll tell you what they mean," said the man.

"The giant you saw first, with the squealing pig in the prongs of his fork — Sluggishness is his name. And the girl here beside me who was shoving him along is Liveliness. For liveliness pushes sluggishness on, and liveliness goes farther in the winking of an eye than the foot can travel in a year.

"The old man over there with the twelve bright eyes stands for the World. He's stronger than anyone, and he showed it when he made nothing of the ram.

"The ram you saw stands for the Desires of Men.

"The hag is Old Age, and her gown withered up your four comrades.

"And the two wells you drank the two draughts from stand for Lying and Truth. For it's sweet to people to tell a lie, but it's bitter in the end.

"And as for me, my name is Cuanna from Innistuil. It's not here I usually am. But I took a very great love for you, Finn, because of your wisdom and your great name, and so I put these things in your way, so that I might see you. The Hospitality of Cuanna's House to Finn will be the name of this story to the end of the world. Now come together, you and your men, and sleep till morning."

So they did that. And when they woke in the morning they were on the top of Cairn Feargall, with their dogs and their weapons beside them.

Swords could not touch the ram. Only the World could throw it out of doors. And even the Fianna could not stand up against Old Age; the best they could do was sleep, and be let wake again. There is no other story in this book that is so plainly about everyone.

Nine of the Fianna set out once looking for a pup they wanted, and they searched through many places before they found it.

They searched all through Magh Leine, and through the Valley of the Swords, and through the storm of Druim Cleibh — and pleasant the Plain of the Life looked after it — but not a pup could they find. Then they went searching through Durlass of the generous men, and great Teamhair, and Dun Dobhran, and Ceanntsaile, men and dogs searching the whole of Ireland, and not a pup could they find.

While they were going from place to place, with their people, they saw the three armies of the sons of the King of Ruadhleath coming towards them. One army was Cat-Headed, and the one beside it was Dog-Headed, and the men of the third army were White-Backed.

When the Fianna saw them coming, Finn held up his shining spear, and light-hearted Caoilte let out a great shout that was heard in Almhuin, and in Magh Leine, and in Teamhair, and in Dun Reithlein. And that shout was answered by Goll, son of Morna, and by Faolan, Finn's son, who was with him, and by the Stutterers from Burren, and by the two sons of Maith Breac, and by Iolunn of the Sharp Edge, and by Cael of the Sharp Sword, who never gave his ear to tale-bearers.

Pleasant was the sound then of the spears and the armies, and of the silken banners raised up in the gusty wind of the morning.

These were the banners.

Finn's banner was the Dealb-Greine, the Sun-Shape, and it had the likeness of the sun on it.

Goll's banner was the Fulang Duaraidh, and it was the first to move in a battle and the last.

Faolan's banner was the Coinneal Catha, the Candle of Battle.

Oisin's banner was the Donn Nimhe, the Dark Deadly One.

Caoilte's was the Lamh Dearg, the Red Hand.

Osgar's was the Sguab Gabhaidh. It had a Broom of rowan branches on it, and when the fight was at its hottest, the only thing anyone asked was: where is the Broom?

Merry Diarmuid's banner was the Liath Loinneach, the Shining Grey.

The Craobh Fuileach, the Bloody Branch, was the banner of Lugaidh's Son.

And as for Conan, he had a briar on his banner, because he was always for quarrels and for trouble. It used to be said of him that he never saw a man frown without striking him, or a door left open without going in through it.

When the Fianna had raised their banners they attacked the three armies. First they killed the whole of the Cat-Heads. Then they took the Dog-Heads in hand and made an end of them, and of the White-Backs along with them.

After that they went to a little hill to the south with a double dun on it, and it was there they found a hound they were able to get a pup from.

By that time they had searched the whole of Ireland, and they had not found in the whole of it a hundred men who could match their nine.

As well as their banners, some of the Fianna had swords that had names. Mac an Luin, Son of the Waves, belonged to Finn. Ceard-nan Gallan, the Smith of the Branches, was Oisin's. Caoilte had Cruadh-Chosgarach, the Hard Destroying One. Diarmuid had Liomhadoir, the Burnisher. And Osgar had Cosgarach Mhor, the Great Triumphant One.

This is how they got those swords.

There came one time to where Finn and Caoilte and some others of the Fianna were, a young man, very big and ugly, with only one foot and one eye. He had a cloak of black skins over his shoulders, and in his hand a blunt ploughshare that was turning red. He told them he was Lon, son of Liobhan, one of the three smiths of the King of Lochlann.

Whether he meant to get away from the Fianna, or to lead them to his smithy, he started running, and they followed him all through Ireland: to Slieve-na-Righ, and to Luimnech, and to Ath Luain, and by the right side of Cruachan of Connacht, and to Ess Ruadh and to Beinn Edair, and so to the sea.

Wherever it was they found the smithy, they went into it. Inside there were four smiths working, and every one of them had seven hands. Finn and Caoilte and the rest stayed there watching them until the swords were made. Then they took them away with them, and they made good use of them afterwards.

Besides his sword Mac an Luin, Finn had a shield called the Sgiath Gailbhinn, the Storm Shield. When it called out, it could be heard all through Ireland.

And whether or not it was the Storm Shield, Finn had a wonderful shield that he did great deeds with, and this is its story.

At the time of the Great Battle of Magh Tuireadh, after Lugh had struck the head off Balor of the Evil Eye, he hung it in the fork of a hazel-tree. The tree split, and the leaves fell off it, with the force of the poison that dripped from the head. For fifty years that tree was a dwelling-place of crows and ravens.

At the end of that time Manannan, son of Lir, was passing by, and he noticed the tree, split and withered, and told his men to dig it up. When they began to dig, a mist of poison rose up out of the roots. Nine of the men got their death from it, and another nine after them, and the third nine were blinded.

Luchtaine the Carpenter made a shield out of the wood of that hazel, for Manannan. After a while Manannan gave it, and a set of chessmen with it, to Tadg, son of Nuada. And from him it came to his grandson, Finn, son of Muirne and of Cumhal.

So Finn carried Balor's death on his arm. Balor, his great-great-grandfather. It is a small country, Ireland, and the dead in it are never very far away.

Finn took a wife once from the Luigne of Midhe. At the same time there was a fool in his household, named Lomna.

Finn went into Tethra, hunting with the Fianna, but Lomna stayed at the house. After a while he saw Coirpre, a man of the Luigne, go secretly in to where Finn's wife was.

When the woman knew he had seen it, she begged and prayed Lomna to hide it from Finn. Lomna agreed. But it preyed on him to have a hand in treachery against Finn.

After a while he took a four-sided rod and wrote an Ogham on it. These are the words he wrote:

"An alder stake in a paling of silver; deadly nightshade in a bunch of cresses; a husband of a lewd woman; a fool among the well-taught Fianna; heather on bare Ualann of Luigne."

He had promised not to tell. He did not tell. He wrote it down in riddles, and left it where it would be found. That is how a fool keeps a promise.

Finn saw the message, and there was anger on him against the woman. She knew well it was from Lomna he had heard the story, and she sent a message to Coirpre telling him to come and kill the fool.

So Coirpre came and struck his head off, and took the head away with him.

When Finn came back in the evening he saw the body without a head.

"Let's find out whose body this is," said the Fianna.

Then Finn did the divination of rhymes, and this is what he said: "It is the body of Lomna. It is not by a wild boar he was killed. It is not by a fall he was killed. It is not in his bed he died. It is by his enemies he died. It is no secret to the Luigne the way he died. Now let the hounds out on their track."

So they let the hounds out and put them on Coirpre's track, and Finn followed them. They came to a house with Coirpre in it, and three times nine of his men, cooking fish on a spit. Lomna's head was on a spike beside the fire.

Coirpre divided the first fish that was cooked among his men, but he put no bite into the mouth of the head. Then he made a second division in the same way.

That was against the law of the Fianna. Everyone at the fire gets a share. Everyone.

And the head spoke. "A speckled, white-bellied salmon that grows from a small fish under the sea," it said. "You have shared a share that is not right. The Fianna will avenge it upon you, Coirpre."

"Put the head outside," said Coirpre. "That's an evil word for us."

Then the head spoke from outside: "It is in many pieces you will be. It is great fires will be lighted by Finn in Luigne."

And as it said that, Finn came in. And he made an end of Coirpre and of his men.

Nobody tells us what became of the wife. The head of the fool, at least, got the last word.

Caoilte was hunting once on Beinn Gulbain, and he went on to Ess Ruadh.

When he came near the hill of the Sidhe that is there, he saw a young man waiting for him. He wore a crimson fringed cloak, with a silver brooch on his breast. He had a white shield worked with linked beasts of red gold. His hair was rolled into a ball at the back and covered with a golden cup. He carried heavy green weapons, and he held two hounds on a silver chain.

When Caoilte came up to him the young man gave him three loving kisses and sat down beside him on the grass.

"Who are you, young champion?" said Caoilte.

"I'm Derg, son of Eoghan, of the people of Usnach," he said, "and your own foster-brother."

Then Caoilte knew him. "And what's your life like with your mother's people, the Tuatha de Danaan, in Sidhe Aedha?"

"There's nothing wanting to us there of food or clothing," said the young man. "But for all that, I'd sooner live the life of the worst-treated of the serving-boys of the Fianna than the life I'm living in the hill of the Sidhe."

Food and clothing and no age and no death. And he would give it all to carry water for the Fianna.

"Lonely as you are at your hunting today," said Caoilte, "I often saw you coming to the Valley of the Three Waters in the south, where the Siuir and the Beoir and the Berba come together, with a great company around you: fifteen hundred young men, fifteen hundred serving-boys, and fifteen hundred women."

"That was so," said Derg. "And though my gentle hound and I are living in the hill of the Sidhe, my mind is always on the Fianna. I remember well the time you won the race against Finn's lasting black horse. Come into the hill now, for the dark of the night is coming on."

So he brought Caoilte into the hill with him, and they were set in their right places.

At that time there was great war between Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh and Ilbrec of Ess Ruadh. A bird with an iron beak and a tail of fire used to come every evening to a golden window of Ilbrec's house, and shake itself there, until there was not a sword left on a pillow, or a shield on a peg, or a spear in a rack — they would all come down on the heads of the people of the house. And whatever they threw at the bird fell on the heads of some of themselves.

On the night Caoilte came in, the hall was made ready for a feast, and the bird came in again and did the same destruction as before, and nothing they threw at it touched it at all.

"Has the bird been doing this long?" said Caoilte.

"For a whole year now," said Derg, "since we went to war with Sidhe Fionnachaidh."

Then Caoilte put his hand inside the rim of his shield and took out a copper rod he kept there. He threw it at the bird, and it brought the bird down on the floor of the hall.

"Did anyone ever make a better cast than that?" said Ilbrec.

"By my word," said Caoilte, "there's no one of us in the Fianna has any right to boast against another."

Then Ilbrec took down from its place a sharp spear with thirty rivets of gold in it. "That's the Spear of Fiacha, son of Congha," he said. "It was with that Finn made an end of Aillen, son of Midhna, who used to burn Teamhair. Keep it beside you now, Caoilte, until we see whether Lir will come to avenge his bird on us."

So the spear that saved Teamhair had ended up in a hill of the Sidhe. Weapons wander. The good ones always come back to the hand that needs them.

Then they took up their horns and their cups and were at drinking and pleasure.

"Well, Caoilte," said Ilbrec, "if Lir comes to avenge his bird on us, who will you put in command of the battle?"

"I'll give the command to Derg over there," said Caoilte.

"Will you take it in hand, Derg?" said the people of the hill.

"I'll take it," said Derg, "with its loss and its gain."

That is how they spent the night. It was not long into the morning before they heard the blowing of horns, and the rattling of chariots, and the clashing of shields, and the uproar of a great army coming all round the hill. They sent some of their people out to see how many there were, and they saw three brave armies of one size.

"It would be a great vexation to me," said Aedh Nimbrec, the Speckled, "for us to get our death and Lir's people to take the hill."

"Did you never hear, Aedh," said Caoilte, "that the wild boar sometimes escapes both hounds and wolves, and the stag in the same way gets away from the hounds with a sudden start? What man are you most in dread of in the battle?"

"The man who is the best fighter of all the Men of Dea," they all said. "Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh."

"The thing I've done in every battle I won't give up today," said Caoilte: "to meet the best man in it hand to hand."

"The two next to him in fighting," they said, "are Donn and Dubh."

"I'll put down those two," said Derg.

Then the host of the Sidhe went out to the battle, and the armies went at each other with wide green spears and little casting-spears and great stones, and the fight went on from the rising of the day until midday.

Then Caoilte and Lir met, and made a very fierce fight of it, and at the last Lir of Sidhe Fionnachaidh fell by the hand of Caoilte.

Lir. The father of Fionnuala and Aodh and Fiachra and Conn. So he died, or went wherever the gods go, in a quarrel over a bird, at the hands of a man.

Then the two good champions Dubh and Donn, sons of Eirrge, decided to go on with the battle. This is how they fought: Dubh at the front of the whole army, and Donn behind all of it, guarding the rear. Derg saw that. He put his finger into the thong of his spear and threw at the one nearest him. It broke his back and went on into the body of the other, so that the one cast made an end of the two.

That ended the battle, and all that was left of the great army of Lir went wearing away to the north. There was great rejoicing in the hill at Ess Ruadh. Ilbrec took the spoils of the beaten army for his people, and to Caoilte he gave the enchanted spear of Fiacha, with nine rich cloaks, and nine long swords with hilts and guards of gold, and nine hounds for hunting.

They said farewell to each other. Caoilte left his blessing with the people of the hill, and took their thanks away with him. And hard as the battle had been, it was harder for Derg to part from his comrade. The day he was parted from Finn and from all the Fianna was no sadder to him than that day.

It was a long time after that Caoilte went again to the hill of Ilbrec at Ess Ruadh, and this is how it happened.

In a battle at Beinn Edair, in the east, Mane, son of the King of Lochlann, threw a deadly spear at him in the middle of the fighting. He heard the whistling of the spear rushing at him, and lifted his shield to protect his head and his body. That did not save him. It struck into his thigh and left its poison there, so that he had to go looking for healing.

This is where he went: to the hill of the Sidhe at Ess Ruadh, to ask the help of Bebind, daughter of Elcmar of Brugh na Boinne, who had the drink of healing of the Tuatha de Danaan, and all that was left of the ale of Goibniu, which she used to give out to them.

Caoilte called Cascorach the Musician, son of Caincenn, and told him to bring his harp and come with him. They stayed a night in the hill of the Sidhe of Druim Nemed, in Luigne of Connacht. From there they went on by Ess Dara, the Fall of the Oaks, and Druim Dearg na Feinne, the Red Ridge of the Fianna, and Ath Daim Glas, the Ford of the Grey Stag, and to Beinn Gulbain, and northward into the plain of Ceitne, where the Men of Dea used to pay their tribute to the Fomor; and up to the Footstep of Ess Ruadh, and the High Place of the Boys, where the boys of the Tuatha de Danaan used to play their hurling.

Aedh of Ess Ruadh and Ilbrec of Ess Ruadh were at the door of the hill, and they gave Caoilte a true welcome.

"I'm glad of that welcome," said Caoilte.

Then Bebind, daughter of Elcmar of Brugh na Boinne, came out with three times fifty comely women around her. She sat down on the green grass and gave three loving kisses to each of the three — to Caoilte, and to Cascorach, and to Fermaise, who had come with them out of the hill of the Sidhe in Luigne of Connacht.

All the people of the hill welcomed them. "Your friendship would be worth little," they said, "if you wouldn't come to help us when we're in need of help."

"It wasn't for bravery I was asked to come," said Cascorach. "But when the right time comes, I'll make music for you, if you've a mind to hear it."

"It's not for deeds of bravery we've come," said Fermaise. "But we'll give you our help if you need it."

Then Caoilte told them why he had come.

"We'll heal you well," they said.

Then they all went into the hill, and stayed there three days and three nights at drinking and pleasure.

It was good help Caoilte and Cascorach gave them after that.

There was a woman-warrior who used to come every year with the ships of the men of Lochlann to attack the Tuatha de Danaan. She had been reared by a woman who knew all enchantments, and there was no precious thing in all the hills of the Sidhe that she did not know of, and carry off. Just at this time a messenger came to the door of the hill with news that the harbour was full of ships, and a great army had landed, and the woman-warrior with it.

It was Cascorach the Musician who went out against her, with a shield he had borrowed from Donn, son of Midhir. She used high words when she saw so young a man coming to fight her, and alone. But he made an end of her for all her high talk, and left her lying on the strand with the sea-foam washing up to her.

The harper. Not the hero. The harper went.

As for Caoilte, he went out in a chariot belonging to Midhir of the Yellow Hair, son of the Dagda, and a spear was given to him that was called Ben-badb, the War-Woman. He threw it, and it struck the King of Lochlann, so that he fell in the middle of his army and the life went from him.

Fermaise went looking for the king's brother, Eolus, who was the comeliest of all the men of the world. He knew him by the band of gold around his head, and his green armour, and his red shield, and he killed him with a cast of a five-pronged spear.

When the men of Lochlann saw their three leaders were gone, they went into their ships and back to their own country. There was great joy through the whole country, among both the men of Ireland and the Tuatha de Danaan, that the men of Lochlann had been driven away by the deeds of Caoilte and Fermaise and Cascorach.

That was not all they did. At that time three flocks of beautiful red birds came from Slieve Fuad in the north and began eating the green grass in front of the hill of the Sidhe.

"What birds are those?" said Caoilte.

"They're three flocks that come and destroy the green every year," said Ilbrec, "eating it down to the bare flagstones, until they leave us no place for our races."

Caoilte and his comrades took up three stones and threw them at the flocks and drove them away.

"Power and blessings to you," said the people of the Sidhe. "That's good work you've done. And there's another thing you can do for us. Three ravens come to us every year out of the north, and when the young lads of the hill are playing their hurling, each of the ravens carries off a boy. And it's tomorrow the hurling will be."

When the full light of day came the next morning, the whole of the Tuatha de Danaan went out to watch the hurling. Every six men of them were given a chessboard, and every five a board for some other game, and every ten men a little harp, and every hundred men a harp, and every nine men pipes that were sharp and powerful.

Then they saw the three ravens from the north coming over the sea. The ravens settled on the great tree of power that stood on the green, and gave three gloomy screeches — screeches that, if such a thing were possible, would have brought the dead up out of the earth, or the hair off the heads of the listeners. As it was, they took the courage out of the whole gathering.

Then Cascorach, son of Caincenn, took one of the chessmen and threw it at one of the ravens. It struck the bird in the beak and the throat and made an end of it. Fermaise killed the second, and Caoilte the third, the same way.

"Let my cure be done now," said Caoilte. "I've paid my fee for it, and it's time."

"You've paid it indeed," said Ilbrec. "Where is Bebind, daughter of Elcmar?"

"I'm here," she said.

"Bring Caoilte, son of Ronan, with you into some hidden place," he said, "and do his cure, and let him be well served, for he's driven every danger away from the Men of Dea and from the Sons of the Gael. Let Cascorach make music for him, and let Fermaise, son of Eogabil, watch him and guard him and attend him."

So Elcmar's daughter went to the House of Arms, and her two sons with her, and a bed of healing was made ready for Caoilte. A bowl of pale gold was brought to her, full of water. She took a crystal vessel and put herbs into it, and bruised them and put them in the water, and gave the bowl to Caoilte. He drank a great drink of it, and it made him throw up the poison of the spear that was in him. He took five drinks of it, and after that she gave him new milk to drink. But with the force of the retching he was left without strength for three days and three nights.

"Caoilte, my life," she said then, "in my opinion you've got relief."

"I've got it indeed," he said, "except that the weakness of my head is troubling me."

"The washing of Flann, daughter of Flidais, will be done for you now," she said. "The head that washing is done for will never be troubled with pain, or baldness, or weakness of sight."

So that cure was done for him for a while. And the people of the hill divided themselves into three parts — one part of their best men and great nobles, another of their young men, and another of their women and poets — to visit him and make mirth with him as long as he was on his bed of healing. Everything that was best from their hunting, it was to him they brought it.

One day, when Elcmar's daughter and her two sons and Cascorach and Fermaise were with Caoilte, they heard a sound of music coming towards them from the waters of Ess Ruadh. Anyone would leave the music of the whole world for that music. They put their harps on the corners of the pillars and went out, and Caoilte wondered that they had left him.

He noticed that his strength, and the strength of his hands, had not come back to him yet.

"I went into many a rough battle and many a hard fight," he said, "and now there isn't strength enough in me even to go out with the rest."

And he cried.

Caoilte, the runner. The one who ran from the wave of Cliodna to the wave of Rudraige. He could not get out of his bed to hear the music, and he lay there and cried, and the story does not look away from it.

The others came back to him, and he asked them for news.

"What was that sound of music we heard?"

"It was Uaine, out of the hill of the Sidhe at the Wave of Cliodna in the south," they said, "and with her the birds of the Land of Promise. She's musician to the whole of that country. Every year she goes to visit one of the hills of the Sidhe, and this time it's our turn."

Then the woman from the Land of Promise came into the house, and the birds came in with her and settled on the pillars and the beams. Thirty of them came in to where Caoilte was, and began singing together. And Cascorach took his harp, and whatever he played, the birds sang to it.

"I've heard much music," said Caoilte, "but I never heard music as good as that before."

After that Caoilte asked to have the healing of his thigh done, and the daughter of Elcmar gave herself to that. Everything bad was sucked out of the wound by her serving-people until it was healed. Caoilte stayed where he was for three nights after that.

Then the people of the hill got up and went into the stream to swim.

"What's to stop me going to swim now," said Caoilte, "since my health has come back to me?"

And he went into the water.

Afterwards they went back into the hill, and a great feast was made that night.

After that Caoilte said farewell to them, and so did Cascorach, but Fermaise stayed with them a while. The people of the hill gave good gifts to Caoilte: a fringed crimson cloak of the wool of the seven sheep of the Land of Promise; and a fish-hook called Aicil mac Mogha, that could not be set in any river or river-mouth without taking fish; and along with those, a drink of remembrance. After that drink there would be no place he ever saw, and no battle or fight he was ever in, but it would stay in his memory.

"That's a good help from kinsmen and from friends," said Caoilte.

Then Caoilte and Cascorach went out of the hill, and the people of it made a great lamentation after them.

He had been given the gift of never forgetting. He would live long enough to learn what that gift cost.

Caoilte was at Cruachan of Connacht once, with Cascorach. There he saw a man sitting on a heap of stones, with very rough grey hair, in a dark brown cloak fastened with a pin of bronze, and a long stick of white hazel in his hand. There was a herd of cattle in front of him in a fenced field.

Caoilte asked him for news.

"I'm steward to the King of Ireland," said the old man, "and it's from him I hold this land. We have great troubles on us in this district."

"What troubles are those?" said Caoilte.

"I have many herds of cattle," he said, "and every year at Samhain a woman comes out of the hill of the Sidhe of Cruachan and takes away nine of the best out of every herd. As for my name, I'm Bairnech, son of Carbh of Collamair of Bregia."

"Who was the best man that ever came out of Collamair?" said Caoilte.

"I know, and the men of Ireland and of Alban know," said he. "It was Caoilte, son of Ronan. And do you know where that man is now?"

"I am that man myself," said Caoilte, "and your own kinsman."

When Bairnech heard that he gave him a great welcome, and Caoilte gave him three kisses.

"It seems to me that tonight is Samhain night," said Caoilte.

"If that's so," said Bairnech, "it's tonight the woman will come to rob us."

"Let me go tonight to the door of the hill of the Sidhe," said Cascorach.

"You may do that," said Caoilte, "and bring your weapons with you."

So Cascorach went, and it was not long before he saw the girl come out past him from the hill of Cruachan. She had a beautiful cloak of one colour about her, and a gown of yellow silk tied up with a knot between her thighs, and two spears in her hands, and she was in dread of nothing in front of her or behind her.

Cascorach blew a blast against her. Then he put his finger into the thong of his spear and threw it at the girl, and it went through her. That is how she was made an end of by Cascorach of the Music.

Then Bairnech said to Caoilte: "Caoilte, do you know the other oppression that's on me in this place?"

"What oppression is that?"

"Three she-wolves that come out of the Cave of Cruachan every year and destroy our sheep and our wethers. We can do nothing against them, and they go back into the cave again. It'll be a good friend who rids us of them."

"Well, Cascorach," said Caoilte, "do you know what the three wolves are that are robbing this man?"

"I know well," said Cascorach. "They're the three daughters of Airetach, of the last of the people of oppression of the Cave of Cruachan. It's easier for them to do their robbing as wolves than as women."

"And will they come near anyone?"

"They'll come near only one kind," said Cascorach. "If they see men of the world with harps for music, they'll come near them. What if I went tomorrow to the cairn over there, and brought my harp with me?"

So in the morning he got up and went to the cairn and stayed on it, playing his harp until the mists of evening came. While he was there he saw the three wolves coming towards him. They lay down in front of him, listening to the music. But Cascorach found no way to attack them, and at the end of the day they went back into the cave.

Cascorach went back to Caoilte and told him what had happened.

"Go up tomorrow to the same place," said Caoilte, "and tell them it would be better for them to be in the shape of women for listening to music, than in the shape of wolves."

So the next day Cascorach went out to the same cairn and set his people around it, and the wolves came there and stretched themselves out to listen to the music.

"If you were ever women," Cascorach said to them, "it would be better for you to listen to the music as women than as wolves."

They heard that. And they threw off the dark trailing coverings that were around them, for they liked the sweet music of the Sidhe very much.

When Caoilte saw them there side by side, elbow to elbow, he threw his spear. It went through the three women, so that they were like a skein of thread drawn together on the spear.

That is how he made an end of the strange, unknown three. And the place got the name of the Valley of the Shapes of the Wolves.

They had come out of their wolf-skins to hear the music better. It is the one tender thing we are told about them, and it was the thing that killed them.

Finn and the Fianna made a great hunt once on the hill of Torc, above Loch Lein and Feara Mor.

They went on hunting until they came to pleasant green Slieve Echtge, and from there it spread over other green-topped hills, and through thick tangled woods, and rough red-headed hills, and over the wide plains of the country. Every chief man among them chose the place he liked, and the gap of danger he was used to. The shouts they gave at the turns of the hunt were heard in the woods all around, so that they started the deer in the wood, and sent the foxes wandering, and the little red beasts climbing the rocks, and the badgers out of their holes, and the birds flying, and the fawns running their best. Then they let out their angry, small-headed hounds and set them hunting. Red were the hands of the Fianna that day, and proud they were of their hounds, torn and wounded before evening.

It happened that day that nobody stayed with Finn but Diorraing, son of Domhar.

"Well, Diorraing," said Finn, "you watch for me while I sleep. I rose early today — and it's an early rising a man makes when he can't see the shadow of his five fingers between himself and the light of day, or tell the leaves of the hazel from the leaves of the oak."

With that he fell into a quiet sleep that lasted until the yellow light of evening. And the rest of the Fianna, not knowing where he had gone, gave up the hunt.

The time was long to Diorraing while Finn slept, and he woke him and told him the Fianna must have given up the hunt, for he could not hear a cry or a whistle from them.

"The end of the day has come," said Finn, "and we won't follow them tonight. Go to the wood now and bring timber and dead branches for a shelter, and I'll go looking for food for the night."

So Diorraing went to the wood. He had not gone far when he saw a fine, well-lighted house of the Sidhe in front of him, on the edge of the wood close by. He went back to Finn with the news.

"Let's go to it," said Finn. "We shouldn't be working in this place, with people living so near."

They went to the door of the house and knocked, and the door-keeper came.

"Whose house is this?" said Diorraing.

"It belongs to Conan of Ceann Slieve," said the door-keeper.

"Tell him there are two of the Fianna of the Gael at the door."

The door-keeper went in and told Conan there were two men of the Fianna at the door.

"One of them," he said, "is young and strong, quiet and fair-haired, and more beautiful than the rest of the men of the world. He has in his hand a small-headed, white-breasted hound, with a collar of rubbed gold and a chain of old silver. The other is brown and ruddy and white-toothed, and he's leading a yellow-spotted hound on a chain of bright bronze."

"You've made a good report of them," said Conan, "and I know them by it. The man you spoke of first is Finn, son of Cumhal, Head of the Fianna of Ireland, with Bran in his hand. And the other is Diorraing, with Sceolan. Go quickly now and let them in."

So Finn and Diorraing were brought in and well attended to. Their weapons were taken from them, and a grand feast was made ready that pleased them well. Conan's wife sat on one side of Finn, and his daughter Finndealbh, of the Fair Shape, on the other. They talked a great deal together. At last, seeing her so beautiful, with the colour of gold on her curled hair and her eyes as blue as flowers, and a soft four-cornered cloak fastened at her breast with a silver pin, Finn asked Conan for her as his wife.

"Leave off asking that, Finn," said Conan. "Your own courage isn't greater than the courage of the man she's promised to."

"Who's that?" said Finn.

"He's Fatha, son of the King of Ess Ruadh," said Conan.

"Your wounds and your danger on yourself," said Diorraing. "It would be right for that stammering tongue that gave out those words to be tied and shortened for ever, and a drink of death to be given to you. For if the whole of the Men of Dea could be put into the one body, Finn would be better than all of them."

"Leave off, Diorraing," said Finn. "It's not fighting I'm here for, but asking for a wife. And I'll get her, whether the Men of Dea think well or badly of it."

A girl is promised to a man of the Sidhe, and Finn wants her, and says so, and means it. He has done this before. It has never once gone well.

"I won't quarrel with you," said Conan. "But I put you under bonds, as a true hero, to answer everything I'm going to ask you."

"I'll do that," said Finn.

So Conan questioned Finn about his birth and his rearing, and the deeds he had done since he came to the Fianna, and Finn gave full answers to them all.

At last Finn said: "Let's go on with this no longer. If you have musicians with you, let them be brought to us now. It's not my custom to go a single night without music."

"Tell me this first," said Conan. "Who made the Dord Fiann, the Mutterer of the Fianna, and when was it made?"

"I'll tell you the truth of that," said Finn. "It was made in Ireland by the three sons of Cearmait Honey-Mouth. Nine men used to sound it, and since it came to me I have fifty men sounding it."

"And tell me this," said Conan. "What music pleased you best of all you ever heard?"

"I'll tell you that," said Finn. "When the seven battalions of the Fianna are gathered in the one place, and raise their spear-shafts over their heads, and the sharp whining of the clear cold wind goes through them — that's very sweet to me.
