And when the drinking-hall is set out in Almhuin, and the cup-bearers give out the bright cups to the chief men of the Fianna, that's very sweet to me. And it's sweet to me to listen to the voice of the sea-gull and the heron, and the noise of the waves of Traig Liath, the song of the three sons of Meardha, the whistle of Lugaidh's Son, and the voice of the cuckoo at the beginning of summer, and the grunting of the pigs on the Plain of Eithne, and the shouting of laughter in Doire."

And this is what he said:

"The Dord in the green-topped woods; the lasting wash of the waves against the shore; the noise of the waves at Traig Liath meeting with the river of the White Trout; the three men that came to the Fianna, a man of them gentle and a man of them rough, another man of them ploughing the clouds — they were sweeter than any other thing.

"The grey mane of the sea, when a man cannot follow its track; the swell that brings the fish to the land; it is sleep-music, its sound is sweet.

"Feargall, son of Fionn, a man who was ready-handed, long was his leap, well marked is his track; he never gave a story that did not do away with secrets; it is his voice was the music of sleep to me."

When Finn had answered all the questions so well, Conan said he would give him his daughter, and that he would have a wedding-feast ready at the end of a month.

They spent the rest of the night in sleep. But Finn saw a dreadful vision in his sleep that made him start up from his bed three times.

"What makes you start from your bed, Finn?" said Diorraing.

"It was the Tuatha de Danaan I saw," he said, "taking up a quarrel against me, and making a great slaughter of the Fianna."

As for the Fianna, they rested at Fotharladh of Moghna that night, and they were downhearted, having no news of Finn. Early the next morning two of them, Bran Beag and Bran Mor, got up and went to Mac-an-Reith, son of the Ram, who had the gift of true knowledge, and asked him where Finn had spent the night. Mac-an-Reith was somehow unwilling to tell them, but at last he said it was at the house of Conan of Ceann Slieve.

The two Brans went on to Conan's house, and Finn made them welcome. But they blamed him when they heard he was taking a wife with none of his people with him.

"Tell all the Fianna to come to the feast at the end of a month," said Conan.

So Finn and Diorraing and the two Brans went back to where the Fianna were and told them all that had happened, and they went on to Almhuin.

That night, when they were in the drinking-hall at Almhuin, they saw the son of the King of Ireland coming to where they were.

"It's a pity the king's son has come," said Finn. "He won't be satisfied without ordering everything in the hall his own way."

"We won't take his orders," said Oisin. "We'll leave half the hall to him and keep the other half ourselves."

So they did that. But it happened that in the half of the house given up to the King of Ireland's son there were sitting two of the Men of Dea, Failbhe Mor and Failbhe Beag. And they said it was because they were sitting on that side of the hall that it was given up.

"It's a pity," said Failbhe Beag, "that this shame and this great insult have been put on us tonight. And it's likely Finn has a mind to do more than that to us again. He's going to carry off the woman who's promised to the third best man of the Tuatha de Danaan, against the will of her father and mother."

This is how wars start. A seat in a hall. A girl. Two men sitting on the wrong side of a room, who were never asked where they would like to sit.

Those two went away early in the morning to Fionnbhar of Magh Feabhail, and told him of the insults Finn and the Fianna of Ireland meant to put on the Tuatha de Danaan.

When Fionnbhar, who was king over the Tuatha de Danaan, heard that, he sent messengers through the length of Ireland to gather them all to him. Six good battalions came to him on the edge of Loch Derg Dheirc at the end of a month. It was the same day Conan had the wedding-feast made ready for Finn and his people.

Finn was at Teamhair Luachra at that time. When he heard the feast was ready he set out to go to it. It happened that most of the men he had with him were of the sons of Morna.

On the way Finn said to Goll: "O Goll, I never felt any fear going to a feast until now. There are only a few of my people with me. I know there's no good thing ahead of me, but that the Men of Dea are going to raise a quarrel against me and kill my people."

"I'll defend you against anything they may do," said Goll.

Goll, again. He always says it the same way.

They went on to Conan's house, and there was a welcome for them. They were brought into the drinking-hall, and Finn was put in the place beside the door, with Goll on his right and Finndeilb, of the Fair Shape, on his left, and all the rest in the places they were used to.

As for Fionnbhar of Magh Feabhail and the Tuatha de Danaan, they put a Druid mist about themselves and went on, hidden and armed, in sixteen battalions, to the lawn in front of Conan's house.

"There's little profit in our being here," they said, "with Goll beside Finn against us."

"Goll won't protect him this time," said Ethne, the woman-Druid. "I'll entice Finn out of the house, however well he's watched."

She went to the house and took her stand outside, in front of Finn.

"Who is that in front of me?" she said.

"It's I," said Finn.

"I put you under the bonds a true hero never broke," she said, "to come out to me here."

When Finn heard that he made no delay but went out to her. For all the people in the house, not one of them noticed him going except Caoilte, and he followed him out.

That is the trouble with being a true hero. Anyone who knows the words can call you out of a lit room into the dark.

At the same time the Tuatha de Danaan let loose a flock of blackbirds with fiery beaks. They settled on the breasts of all the people in the house, and burned them and destroyed them, until the young lads and the women and children of the place ran out on every side. And the woman of the house, Conan's wife, was drowned in the river outside the dun.

As for Ethne, the woman-Druid, she asked Finn whether he would race her.

"It's to run a race against you I called you out," she said.

"What length of race?" said Finn.

"From Doire da Torc, the Wood of the Two Boars, to Ath Mor, the Great Ford."

So they set out, and Finn got over the ford first. Caoilte was following after them, and Finn was urging him on.

"You should be ashamed of your running, Caoilte," he said, "with a woman going past you."

At that Caoilte made a leap forward, and when he was ahead of the witch he turned and gave her a blow of his sword that made two equal halves of her.

"Power and good luck to you, Caoilte!" said Finn. "Many a good blow you've struck, but you never struck a better one than this."

They went back to the lawn in front of Conan's dun, and there they found the whole company of the Tuatha de Danaan, who had put the Druid mist off them.

"It seems to me, Caoilte," said Finn, "that we've come into the middle of our enemies."

With that they stood back to back, and they were attacked on all sides, until groans of weakness from the unequal fight were forced out of Finn.

When Goll, inside the house, heard that, he said: "It's a pity the Tuatha de Danaan have enticed Finn and Caoilte away from us. Let's go to their help, and make no delay."

He rushed out, and all the Fianna who were there with him, and Conan of Ceann Slieve and his sons. A great anger came on Goll, so that he looked like a tall mountain under his grey shield in the battle. He broke through the Tuatha de Danaan until he reached Fionnbhar, their leader, and they went at each other, cutting and wounding, until at last Fionnbhar of Magh Feabhail fell by the strokes of Goll.

A great many others fell in that battle, and there was never a harder battle fought in Ireland. No man on either side had a mind to go back one step before whoever he was fighting. They were the two hardest-fighting troops to be found in the four parts of the world: the strong, hardy Fianna of the Gael, and the beautiful Men of Dea. And they came near to being all destroyed in that battle.

But after a while they saw the rest of the Fianna, who had not been in the battle, coming from all parts of Ireland. When the Tuatha de Danaan saw them coming they put the Druid mist about themselves again and went away.

Clouds of weakness came on Finn himself, and on those with him, from the force of the fight. Many men of the Fianna were lost in that battle. As for the rest, they stayed a long time in Almhuin of Leinster, until their wounds were entirely healed.

The story does not say whether Finn ever married Finndealbh of the Fair Shape. It does not say what became of her at all. Her mother was drowned on her wedding-day, and after that nobody mentions her again.

Finn had no great luck, going to look for a wife that time. And he had no better luck another time he asked for a wife from among the Sidhe. This is how that happened.

He was hunting on the mountain of Bearnas Mor, and a great wild pig turned on the hounds of the Fianna and killed most of them. Then Bran attacked it and got the better of it.

The pig began to scream. With that a very tall man came out of the hill and asked Finn to let the pig go free. When Finn agreed, the man brought them into the hill of the Sidhe at Glandeirgdeis. When they came to the door of the house he struck the pig with his Druid rod, and that moment it changed into a beautiful young woman. The name he called her by was Scathach, the Shadowy One.

He made a great feast for the Fianna. Finn asked for the young girl in marriage, and the tall man, her father, said he would give her to him that very night.

But when night came on, Scathach asked for the loan of a harp, and it was brought to her.

It had three strings. One was of iron, and one of bronze, and one of silver.

When the iron string was played, it set all the hosts of the world crying, and crying without end.

When the bright bronze string was played, it set them all laughing, from one day to the same hour the next.

When the silver string was played, all the men of the whole world fell into a long sleep.

It was the sleepy silver string the Shadowy One played, until Finn and Bran and all his people were in their heavy sleep.

When they woke at sunrise the next morning, they were outside on the mountain of Bearnas, where they had first seen the wild pig.

She had not said no. She had not had to. She had only chosen which string to play.

Finn and the Fianna came once to a ford of the Slaine, and sat down there for a while.

As they sat there they saw, on the round rock above the ford, a young woman in a dress of silk, with a green cloak about her and a golden brooch in the cloak, and on her head the golden crown that is the sign of a queen.

"Fianna of Ireland," she said, "let one of you come and speak with me now."

Sciathbreac, of the Speckled Shield, went towards her. "Who is it you want?" he said.

"Finn, son of Cumhal," she said.

Finn went over to talk with her. "Who are you?" he said. "And what is it you want?"

"I am Daireann, daughter of Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda," she said. "I've come to be your wife, if you'll give me the bride-gift I ask."

"What bride-gift is that?"

"Your promise," she said, "that I'll be your only wife for the length of a year, and have half your time after that."

"I won't give that promise to any woman of the world," said Finn, "and I won't give it to you."

At that the young woman took a cup of white silver from under a covering and filled it with strong drink, and gave it to Finn.

"What's this?" said Finn.

"It's very strong mead," she said.

Now there were bonds on Finn not to refuse anything that belonged to a feast. So he took the cup, and drank what was in it.

That was the rule, and she knew the rule. It is always the rules they use against you, the ones who know you best.

That moment he was like a man gone mad. He turned his face towards the Fianna, and every harm and every fault and every misfortune in battle that he knew of against any one of them, he sprang it on them, through the mad drunkenness the young woman had put on him.

Then the chief men of the Fianna of Ireland got up and left the place to him, every one of them setting out for his own country, until there was nobody left on the hill but Finn and Caoilte.

Caoilte got up and followed after them.

"Fianna of Ireland," he said, "don't leave your lord and your leader because of the arts and the tricks of a woman of the Sidhe."

Thirteen times he went after them, bringing them back to the hill like that.

With the end of the day and the fall of night, the bitterness went out of Finn's tongue. By the time Caoilte had brought back the whole of the Fianna, his sense and his memory had come back to him. And he would sooner have fallen on his sword and got his death than have stayed living.

Think of it. To wake from a drunkenness and know every word you said, and to whom, and that every word was true.

That was the hardest day's work Caoilte ever did — unless it was the day he brought the flock of beasts and birds to Teamhair, to ransom Finn from the High King of Ireland.

Another time Maer, wife of Bersa of Berramain, fell in love with Finn. She made nine nuts of Segair with love-charms in them, and sent them to Finn, and told him to eat them.

"I won't," said Finn. "They're not nuts of knowledge, but nuts of ignorance. And there's no knowing what they are, unless they're an enchantment for drinking love."

So he buried them a foot deep in the earth.

He had learned something, then. It had only cost him one very long day.

The Fianna were at Almhuin once with no great work to do. There came a very misty morning, and Finn was afraid sluggishness would come on his men. He got up and said, "Make yourselves ready, and we'll go hunting to Gleann-na-Smol."

They all said the day was too misty for hunting. But there was no use talking. They had to do as Finn told them. So they made themselves ready and went on towards Gleann-na-Smol. They had not gone far when the mist lifted and the sun came out.

When they were on the edge of a little wood, they saw a strange beast coming towards them with the quickness of the wind, and a Red Woman on its track. The beast had narrow feet, and a head like the head of a boar, with long horns on it. But the rest of it was like a deer, and there was a shining moon on each of its sides.

Finn stopped. "Fianna of Ireland," he said, "did you ever see a beast like that one before?"

"We never did indeed," they said. "It would be right for us to let the hounds out after it."

"Wait a while," said Finn, "until I speak with the Red Woman. But don't let the beast get past you."

They tried to hold the beast back by going in front of it, but they could hardly hinder it at all, and it went away through them.

When the Red Woman came up to them, Finn asked her the name of the beast she was following.

"I don't know that," she said, "though I've been on its track since I left the borders of Loch Dearg a month ago, and I've never lost sight of it since. The two moons on its two sides shine over the country all round at night. And I must follow it until it falls, or I'll lose my own life and the lives of my three sons, who are the best fighting men in the whole world."

"We'll take the beast for you, if you like," said Finn.

"Don't try to do that," she said. "I'm swifter than you are myself, and I can't come up with it."

"We won't let it go until we know what kind of beast it is," said Finn.

"If you or your share of men go after it," she said, "I'll bind you hand and foot."

"That's stiff talk," said Finn. "Don't you know I'm Finn, son of Cumhal? And there are fourscore fighting men with me who were never beaten yet."

"I give little heed to you or your share of men," said the Red Woman. "And if my three sons were here, they'd stand up against you."

"It will be a bad day indeed," said Finn, "when the threat of a woman puts fear on me or on the Fianna of Ireland."

With that he sounded his horn. "Let us all follow now, men and dogs, after that beast we saw."

No sooner had he said it than the woman made a great water-worm of herself and attacked Finn. She would have killed him then and there if Bran had not been with him.

Bran took a grip of the worm and shook it. Then it wound itself round Bran's body, and would have crushed the life out of her, but Finn thrust his sharp sword into its throat.

"Hold back your hand," said the worm, "and you won't have the curse of a lonely woman on you."

"It's my opinion," said Finn, "that you wouldn't leave me my life if you could take it. But go out of my sight now, and let me never see you again."

Then she made herself into a Red Woman again and went away into the wood.

While Finn was talking and fighting with the Red Woman, all the Fianna had gone off on the beast's track, and he did not know where they were. He went after them, he and Bran. It was late in the evening when he caught up with a share of them, still on the track of the beast.

The dark of the night was coming on, but the two moons on the sides of the beast gave a bright light, and they never lost sight of it. They kept following it. About midnight they were pressing close on it, and it began to scatter blood behind it, and before long Finn and his men were red from head to foot. That did not stop them. They followed it on until they saw it going in at the foot of Cnoc-na-righ at the break of day.

When they came to the foot of the hill, the Red Woman was standing there in front of them.

"You didn't take the beast," she said.

"We didn't take it," said Finn, "but we know where it is."

She took a Druid rod and struck a blow on the side of the hill, and that moment a great door opened, and they heard sweet music coming from inside.

"Come in now," said the Red Woman, "and see the wonderful beast."

"Our clothes aren't clean," said Finn, "and we wouldn't like to go in among a company the way we are."

Covered in blood from head to foot, and his worry was whether he was fit to go to a party. That is Finn too.

She put a horn to her mouth and blew it, and that moment ten young men came to her.

"Bring water for washing," she said, "and four times twenty suits of clothes, and a beautiful suit and a crown of shining stones for Finn, son of Cumhal."

The young men went away and came back at the end of a minute with water and with clothing.

When the Fianna were washed and dressed, the Red Woman brought them into a great hall where there was the brightness of the sun and of the moon on every side. From there she brought them into another great room. Finn and his men had seen many grand things up to that time, but they had never seen anything as grand as what they saw there.

There was a king sitting in a golden chair, in clothes of gold and of green, and his chief people were sitting around him, and his musicians were playing. Nobody could say what colour the musicians' clothes were, for every colour of the rainbow was in them. There was a great table in the middle of the room with every kind of thing on it, each better than the last.

The king rose and welcomed Finn and his men, and told them to sit down at the table. They ate and drank their fill, and they needed it after the hunt they had made.

Then the Red Woman stood up. "King of the Hill," she said, "if it's your will, Finn and his men have a mind to see the wonderful beast. They spent a long time following it, and that's what brought them here."

The king struck a blow on his golden chair, and a door opened behind him, and the beast came through and stood before the king. It bowed down before him and spoke.

"I'm going on towards my own country now," it said. "There's no runner in the world as good as me, and the sea is the same to me as the land. Let whoever can catch me come now, for I'm going."

With that the beast went out of the hill as quick as a blast of wind, and all the people who were in the hill went after it. It was not long before Finn and his men were ahead of the rest, at the front of the hunt, gaining on the beast.

About midday Bran made the beast turn, and then she forced it to turn a second time. It began to cry out, and before long its strength began to flag. At last, just at sunset, it fell dead, and Bran was at its side when it fell.

Then Finn and his men came up. But instead of a beast, it was a tall man they saw lying dead in front of them.

The Red Woman came up at the same time.

"High King of the Fianna," she said, "that's the King of the Firbolgs you've killed. His people will put great troubles on this country in the time to come, when you, Finn, and your people are under the sod. And I'm going now to the Country of the Young, and I'll bring you with me if you like."

"We thank you for that," said Finn. "But we wouldn't give up our own country if we were to get the whole world as an estate, and the Country of the Young along with it."

Remember that he said this. Remember that it was Finn who said it, with the whole of his life in front of him. Someone else would be asked the same question, later, and answer differently.

"That's well," said the Red Woman. "But you're going home empty after your hunt."

"It's likely we'll find a deer in Gleann-na-Smol," said Finn.

"There's a fine deer at the foot of that tree over there," said the Red Woman, "and I'll rouse it for you."

With that she gave a cry, and the deer started out and away, and Finn and his men after it. It never stopped until it came to Gleann-na-Smol, and they could not catch it.

Then the Red Woman came to them. "I think you're tired now with following the deer," she said. "Call off your hounds, and I'll let out my own little dog after it."

So Finn sounded a little horn he had at his side, and that moment the hounds came back to him. Then the Red Woman brought out a little hound as white as the snow of the mountains and set it after the deer. It was not long before it had caught the deer and killed it. Then it came back and leapt in under the Red Woman's cloak.

Finn wondered greatly at that. But before he could ask the Red Woman a question, she was gone out of sight.

As for the deer, Finn knew there was enchantment on it, and he left it lying there.

Tired and empty were the Fianna, going back to Almhuin that night.

Finn went to a gathering once at Aonach Clochair, and a great many of the men of Munster crowded to it. The horses of the Fianna were brought there, and the horses of the men of Munster, and they raced against each other.

Fiachu, son of Eoghan, was there. When the games were over he gave good presents to Finn: a lasting black horse that won the three prizes of the gathering, and a chariot, and a horse for the chariot-driver, and a spear with a deadly spell on it, and weapons of silver, and three comely hounds — Feirne and Derchaem and Dialath — with collars of yellow gold and chains of white bronze.

Finn stood up and thanked Fiachu, son of Eoghan. Then he and his people set out for the house of Cacher at Cluain-da-loch. They stayed three days feasting in Cacher's house, and then Finn gave him the price of his feast and his ale: fifty rings, and fifty horses, and fifty cows.

He and the Fianna went on from there over Luachair to the strand at Berramain. Finn was trying out his black horse on the strand, and Caoilte and Oisin raced against him. But it was only folly for them to do it. He gave his horse a blow and away with him, to Traigh Liath, and over the Plain of Health to the Old Yew of the Old Valley, and to the mouth of the Flesc and the mouth of the Lemain to Loch Lein, until he came to the hill of Bairnech, with Caoilte and Oisin after him.

"Night's coming on us," said Finn. "Go and look for some place where we can sleep."

He looked round at the rocks on his left hand and saw a house, and a fire shining out from it in the valley below.

"I never knew of a house in this valley," he said.

"It's best for us to go and see it," said Caoilte. "There are many things we don't know about."

The three of them went on to the house, and they heard screams and crying coming from it. When they came to the house, the people in it were very fierce and rough. A big grey man took hold of their horses and brought them in, and shut the door of the house with iron hooks.

"My welcome to you, Finn of the great name," he said. "You were a long time coming here."

They sat down on the hard boards of a bed. The grey man kindled a fire and threw logs of elder-wood on it, until they were nearly smothered with the smoke.

Then they saw a hag in the house with three heads on her lean neck. And on the other side there was a man without a head, with one eye, and the eye was in his breast.

"Get up, you that are in the house," said the grey man, "and make music for the King of the Fianna."

With that nine bodies rose up out of the corner nearest the Fianna, and nine heads rose up on the other side of the bed, and they gave nine harsh screeches together that nobody would want to listen to. Then the hag answered them, and the headless man answered. And harsh as all that music was, there was none of it you would not rather hear than the music of the one-eyed man. The music that was sung came near to breaking the bones of their heads. It was no sweet music.

Then the big grey man got up and took the axe that was for cutting logs, and began striking at the horses, flaying them and destroying them. Fifty pointed spits of the rowan-tree were brought, and he put a piece of the horses' flesh on each spit and set them on the hearth. But when he took the spits from the fire and put them in front of Finn, the flesh on them was still raw.

"Take your food away," said Finn. "I've never eaten meat that was raw, and I never will, just for being a day without food."

"If you've come into our house to refuse our food," said the grey man, "we'll surely go against you, Finn and Caoilte and Oisin."

With that everyone in the house attacked the three. They were driven back into the corner, and the fire was put out, and the fight went on through the whole night in the dark. And but for Finn and the way he fought, they would have been put down.

When the sun rose and lit up the house the next morning, a mist came into the head of each of the three, so that they fell down as if dead on the floor.

After a while they got up again. There was nothing to be seen of the house, or of the people of the house. They had all vanished. But their horses were there, and they took them and went on, very weak and tired, for a long way, until they came to the strand of Berramain.

The ones who had fought them were the three Shapes out of the Valley of the Yew Tree, who had come to avenge their sister, Cuillen of the Wide Mouth.

As for Cuillen: she was a daughter of the King of Munster, and her husband was the King of Ulster's son. They had a son who was called Fear Og, the Young Man, and there was hardly a man in Ireland as good as he was in shape and courage and spear-casting.

Once he joined a game with the Fianna, and did better than all of them, and Finn gave him a great reward. After that he went out on a hunt they made, and it was by him, and by none of the Fianna, that the first blood was drawn of pig or of deer.

When they came back, a heavy sickness fell on the young man, through the eyes and the envy of the Fianna. It left him without life at the end of nine days.

He was buried under a green hill, and the shining stone he used to hold in his hand while he did his feats was put over his head.

His mother, Cuillen, came to his grave keening him every day for the length of a year. And one day she died there, of grief after her son, and they put her into the same green hill.

The Fianna had killed him by looking at him too hard. Nobody lifted a hand. Envy is a weapon too, and the story is honest enough to say whose it was.

As for Finn, he was afraid of no earthly thing. He killed many great serpents in Loch Cuilinn and Loch Neathach and at Beinn Edair; and Shadow-Shapes at Loch Lein and Drom Cleib and Loch Liath; and a serpent and a cat in Ath Cliath.

Angus Og, son of the Dagda, made a feast once at Brugh na Boinne for Finn and the Fianna of the Gael. There were ten hundred of them there, wearing green clothes and crimson cloaks. As for the people of Angus's house, their clothes were of red silk.

Finn sat beside Angus in the beautiful house, and it is a long time since the like of those two were seen in Ireland. Any stranger would have wondered to see the way the golden cups went from hand to hand.

Then Angus said, in a loud voice that everyone could hear: "This is a better life than hunting."

Anger came on Finn. "It's a worse life than hunting," he said, "to be here — without hounds, without horses, without battalions, without the shouting of armies."

"Why are you talking like that, Finn?" said Angus. "As for the hounds you have, they wouldn't kill so much as one pig."

"Neither you nor the whole host of the Tuatha de Danaan," said Finn, "has a pig that ever went on dry land that Bran and Sceolan wouldn't kill."

"I'll send you a pig," said Angus, "that will get away from you and your hounds, and that will kill them in the end."

This is how it goes with gods and heroes, at a feast, with drink in them. Nobody means it. Everybody means it.

The steward of the house called out in a loud voice: "Let everyone go to his bed now, before the lightness of drunkenness comes on you."

But Finn said to his people: "Let's make ready and leave this place. We're only a few among the Men of Dea."

So they set out and went westward until they came to Slieve Fuad, where the Fianna were at that time.

For the whole length of a year after that, the Tuatha de Danaan boasted of how they would get the better of the Fianna, and the Fianna thought about how they could do best in the hunt.

At the end of that time Angus sent messengers to Finn, asking him with great respect whether he was ready to keep his word. Finn said he was.

The hounds were brought out. Finn himself held Bran and Sceolan, one in each hand. Caoilte had Adhnuall, and Oisin had Ablach, and merry Bran Beag had Lonn, and Diarmuid held Eachtach, and Osgar held Mac an Truim. Garraidh was held by Faolan, and Rith Fada, of the Long Run, by hungry Conan.

They had not been there long with their hounds when they saw a terrible herd of great pigs on the plain to the east, every one of them the height of a deer. One pig, out in front of the rest, was blacker than a smith's coal, and the bristles on its head were like a thicket of thorn-trees.

Then Caoilte let Adhnuall go, and she was the first to kill a pig of the herd. Then Bran broke away from the leash Finn was holding. The pigs ran their best, but she caught up with them and took hold of a pig.

At that Angus said: "O Bran, fosterling of fair-haired Fergus, it's not a right thing you're doing, killing my own son."

When Bran heard that, her ways changed, and it was like an enemy she took hold of the pig. She did not let it go. She held her breath and kept it for the Fianna.

She had been told it was her own foster-brother. She held on anyway. For Finn. There is nothing more to say about Bran than that, and nothing less.

The hunt went over Slieve Cua and Slieve Crot, and from Magh Cobha to Cruachan, and to Fionnabraic and to Finnias. At evening, when the hunt was over, there was not one pig of the whole herd without a hurt, and there were only a hundred and ten pigs left living. But if the hunt brought destruction on Angus, it brought losses on the Fianna too. Ten hundred of their men were missing, besides serving-lads and dogs.

"Let's go to Brugh na Boinne and get satisfaction for our people," said Oisin.

"That's the advice of a man without sense," said Finn. "If we leave these pigs the way they are, they'll come to life again. Let's burn them, and throw their ashes into the sea."

That is the rule of the pigs of the Sidhe. Killed today, alive tomorrow. Unless they are burned.

So the seven battalions of the Fianna made seven fires to every battalion. But for all they could do, they could not set fire to one pig.

Then Bran, who had great sense and knowledge, went away. She came back bringing three logs with her, and no one knows what wood they came from. When the logs were put on the fire they lit up like a candle, and it was with them the pigs were burned. And after that their ashes were thrown into the sea.

Then Oisin said again: "Let's go now to Brugh na Boinne and avenge the death of our people."

So the whole of the Fianna set out for Brugh na Boinne, and every step they took could surely be heard through the whole of the skies.

Angus sent messengers out to where Finn was, offering him any one thing if he would spare his people.

"I'll take no gift at all from you, Angus of the slender body," said Finn, "as long as there's a room left in your house, north or east, without being burned."

"Though you think it bad, the loss of the fine people you rule," said Angus, "yet, O Finn, father of Oisin, the loss of my own good son is sorrowful to me. For the black pig that came before you on the plain was no common pig, but my own son. And along with him there fell the son of the King of the Narrow Sea, and the son of the King of the Sea of Gulls, and the son of Ilbhrec, son of Manannan, and seven score of the comely sons of kings and queens. And what destroyed my strength and my honour entirely was that they were burned away from me in a far place.

"And it's a pity for you, sweet, daring Bran, fosterling of Fergus of the thirty woods and plains, that you didn't do something worth praise before killing your own foster-brother. I'll put a curse on you, Bran, beyond every hound in Ireland: that you'll never see with your eyes any deer you ever kill."

Anger came on Finn when he heard that. "If you put a curse on Bran, Angus," he said, "there won't be a room left, east or west, in the whole of your great house without being burned."

"If you do that," said Angus, "I'll put trees and stones in front of you in every battle. And I'll know the number of men you have in your armies by looking at them through my ring."

Then Oisin, who was wise, said: "It's best for you to agree between yourselves now. Let's be helpful to one another, and pay whatever fines are due."

So they agreed to that and made peace, and gave children to be fostered by each other: a son of Finn's to Angus, and a son of Angus Og to the Fianna.

But for all that, Angus was not very friendly to Finn afterwards, at the time Finn was following Diarmuid and Grania through the whole length of Ireland.

That story is coming. It is the longest in the book, and the saddest. Angus had not forgotten the black pig. Gods never do.

Finn was out on the green of Almhuin once, and he saw what looked like a grey fawn running across the plain.

He called and whistled for his hounds. Neither hound nor man heard him or came to him — only Bran and Sceolan. He set them after the fawn. Close as they kept to her, he kept closer to them, until at last they came to Slieve Cuilinn, in the province of Ulster.

No sooner were they at the hill than the fawn vanished from them, and they did not know where she had gone. Finn went looking for her eastward, and the two hounds went west.

It was not long before Finn came to a lake. Sitting on the brink of it was a young girl, the most beautiful he had ever seen, with hair the colour of gold and skin as white as lime, and eyes like the stars in a time of frost. But she seemed somehow sorrowful and downhearted.

Finn asked her whether she had seen his hounds pass that way.

"I didn't see them," she said. "And it's little I'm thinking of your hounds or your hunting, but of the cause of my own trouble."

"What ails you, woman of the white hands?" said Finn. "Is there any help I can give you?"

"What I'm fretting after," she said, "is a ring of red gold I lost off my finger in the lake. And I put you under bonds, Finn of the Fianna, to bring it back to me out of the lake."

Bonds again. Finn never learned to walk past a beautiful woman at the edge of water.

With that Finn stripped off his clothes and went into the lake at the woman's bidding. He went three times round the whole lake, and left no part of it unsearched, until he brought back the ring. He handed it up to her out of the water. And no sooner had he done it than she gave a leap into the water and vanished.

When Finn came up on the bank of the lake he could not even reach the place where his clothes were. For in that moment he — the head and the leader of the Fianna of Ireland — was nothing but a grey old man, weak and withered.

Bran and Sceolan came up to him then. They did not know him. They went on round the lake, searching for their master.

At Almhuin, when he was missed, Caoilte began asking after him.

"Where is Finn," he said, "of the gentle rule and of the spears?"

But nobody knew where he had gone, and there was grief on the Fianna when they could not find him.

But this is what Conan said: "I never heard music that pleased me better than to hear that the son of Cumhal is missing. May he stay missing the whole year, and I'll be king over you all."

Downhearted as they were, they could hardly keep from laughing when they heard Conan say it.

Then Caoilte and the rest of the chief men of the Fianna set out looking for Finn, and they got word of him, and at last they came to Slieve Cuilinn. There they saw a withered old man sitting beside the lake, and they took him for a fisherman.

"Tell us, old man," said Caoilte, "did you see a fawn go by, and two hounds after her, and a tall fair-faced man with them?"

"I did see them," he said, "and it's not long since they left me."

"Tell us where they are now."

But Finn made no answer. He did not have the courage to tell them that he himself was Finn, their leader, being what he was: an ailing, downhearted old man, without leaping, without running, without a walk, grey and sorrowful.

This is the most frightening thing in any story about Finn. Not a giant, not a war. A man who cannot bear to be seen by his friends.

Caoilte drew his sword from its sheath. "It won't be long before you know what death is," he said, "unless you tell us what happened to those three."

Then Finn told them the whole story. And when the seven battalions of the Fianna heard him, and knew that it was Finn, they gave three loud, sorrowful cries. And they gave the lake the name of Loch Doghra, the Lake of Sorrow.

But Conan of the sharp tongue began abusing Finn and all the Fianna in turn.

"You never gave me right praise for my deeds, Finn, son of Cumhal," he said, "and you were always the enemy of the sons of Morna. But we're living in spite of you. And I have only the one fault to find with your shape, and that's that it wasn't put on the whole of the Fianna the same as on you."

Caoilte went at him. "Bald, senseless Conan," he said, "I'll break your mouth to the bone."

But Conan ran in among the rest of the Fianna and asked for their protection, and peace was made again.

As for Finn, they asked him whether there was any cure to be found for him.

"There is," he said. "I know well the enchantment was put on me by a woman of the Sidhe, Miluchradh, daughter of Cuilinn, through jealousy of her sister Aine. Bring me to the hill that belongs to Cuilinn of Cuailgne. He's the only one who can give me my shape again."

They gathered round him and lifted him gently on their shields, and carried him on their shoulders to the hill of the Sidhe in Cuailgne. But nobody came out to meet them.

Then the seven battalions began digging and rooting up the whole hill, and they went on digging for three nights and three days.

At the end of that time Cuilinn of Cuailgne — some say he was Manannan, son of Lir — came out of the hill, holding a vessel of red gold in his hand. He gave the vessel into Finn's hand.

No sooner had Finn drunk what was in the vessel than his own shape and his looks came back to him.

Only his hair, which used to be so fair and so beautiful, like a woman's hair, never got its own colour back. The lake Cuilinn's daughter had made for Finn would have turned every man in the world grey if they had gone into it.

When Finn had drunk all that was in the vessel, it slipped from his hand into the earth, which was loosened with the digging, and he never saw it again. But in the place where it went into the earth a tree grew up. Anyone who looked at the branches of that tree in the morning, fasting, would know everything that was going to happen that day.

That is how Finn came by his grey hair: through the jealousy of Miluchradh of the Sidhe, because he had not given his love to her, but to her sister Aine.

He had been an old man for a few days. He never quite stopped being one after.


As for Oisin, who was so brave and so comely, who could overtake a deer at its greatest speed and see a thistle-thorn on the darkest night: the wife he took was Eibhir of the plaited yellow hair, who had been the foreign sweetheart of the High King of Ireland.

She lived beyond the sea, in a very sunny place. Her father's name was Iunsa. Her sunny house was thatched with the feathers of birds, and the doorposts were of gold, and the doors of ribbed grass. Oisin went there looking for her, and he fought for her against the High King, and against an army of the Firbolgs the High King had helping him. He got the better of them all, and brought Eibhir of the yellow hair away to Ireland.

He had a daughter, and she married the son of Oiliol, son of Eoghan and of Beara, daughter of the King of Spain.

That Eoghan was driven out of Ireland once, and it was to Spain he went for safety. Beara, the daughter of the King of Spain, was very shining and beautiful, and her father wanted to know who her husband would be. He sent for his Druid and asked him.

"I can tell you that," said the Druid. "The man who is to be her husband will come to land in Spain this very night. Let your daughter go eastward to the river Eibhear. She'll find a crimson-spotted salmon in that river, with shining clothing on him from head to tail. Let her strip that clothing off him and make a shining shirt out of it for her husband."

So Beara went to the river Eibhear, and found the golden salmon as the Druid had said, and stripped him of his crimson clothing, and made a shining shirt of it.

As for Eoghan, the waves of the shore put a welcome in front of him, and he came to the king's house that same night. The king gave him a friendly welcome. Everyone said there was never a comelier man seen than Eoghan, or a more beautiful woman than Beara, and that it was fitting for them to come together. Eoghan's own people said they would not be sorry to have been sent out of Ireland, if only Eoghan could get her for his wife.

After a while the king sent his Druid to ask Eoghan why he did not ask for Beara.

"I'll tell you that," said Eoghan. "It wouldn't be fitting for me to be refused a wife. I'm only an exile in this country, and I've brought no treasures or goods with me out of Ireland to give to learned men and poets. But for all that, the king's daughter is dear to me, and I think I have the king's friendship."

The Druid went back with that message.

"That's the answer of a king," said the King of Spain. "Tell my daughter to sit at Eoghan's right hand, and I'll give her to him this very night."

When Beara, the king's daughter, heard that, she sent her serving-maid to bring the shirt she had made for Eoghan. He put it on over his armour, and its shining was seen in every place. It was from wearing that shirt that he got the name of Eoghan the Bright.

Oiliol was the first son they had. It was he who had his ear bitten off by Aine of the Sidhe in revenge for her brother. And it was his son who married Oisin's daughter afterwards.

As for Osgar, Oisin's son: of all the young men of the Fianna he was the best in battle.

When he was only a young child the whole of the Fianna made much of him. It was for him they kept the marrow-bones, and they did not like to put any hardship on him. He grew up tall and idle, and nobody thought he would turn out as strong as he did.

One day a troop of the Fianna was attacked, and everyone in it went out to fight, and they left Osgar behind. When he knew the fight was going on, he took a log of wood, the first thing he could find, and attacked the enemy and made a great slaughter, and they gave way and ran before him. From then on there was no battle he did not go into. He was said to be the strongest of all the Fianna, though the people of Connacht said that Goll was the strongest.

He and Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, were comrades and dear friends. It was Diarmuid who taught him feats of arms and of skill, and chess-playing. Oisin his father took great pride in him, and so did his grandfather Finn.

Once Finn was holding a feast at Almhuin, and he asked the chief men of the Fianna there what music they thought was best.

"Playing at games," said Conan. "That's the best music I ever heard." For though Conan was a good hand against an enemy, there never was a man with less sense.

"The music I like best is talking with a woman," said Diarmuid.

"My music is the outcry of my hounds when they're putting a deer to its last stand," said Lugaidh's Son.

"The music of the woods is best to me," said Oisin. "The sound of the wind, and of the cuckoo and the blackbird, and the sweet silence of the crane."

Then Osgar was asked.

"The best music," he said, "is the striking of swords in a battle."

It is likely he took after Finn in that. For in spite of all the sweet sounds Finn gave an account of, the time he was at Conan's house at Ceann Slieve, the Fianna used to say that the music Finn liked best was the music of what happens.

Of all the answers, it is the one that has lasted.

This is how Osgar met his wife.

Finn and his men came once to Slieve Crot, and they saw a woman waiting for them there, with a crimson fringed cloak, and a gold brooch in it, and a band of yellow gold on her forehead. Finn asked her name and where she came from.

"Etain of the Fair Hair is my name," she said, "daughter of Aedh of the White Breast, of the hill of the Sidhe at Beinn Edair, son of Angus Og."

"What brought you here, girl?" said Finn.

"To ask a man of the Fianna of Ireland to run a race with me."

"What kind of runner are you?" said Diarmuid.

"I'm a good runner," said the girl. "It's all the same to me whether the ground under my feet is long or short."

All of the Fianna who were there set out to run with her. They ran to the height over Badhamair, and on to Ath Cliath, and from there on to the hill of the Sidhe at Beinn Edair.

There was a good welcome for them there. Meat was brought to them, and wine to drink, and water to wash their feet. After a while they saw a nice fair-haired girl in front of the vats, with a cup of white silver in her hand, giving out drink to everyone.

"It seems to me that's the girl who came asking the Fianna to race her at Slieve Crot," said Finn.

"It is not," said Aedh of the White Breast. "That's the slowest woman there is among us."

"Who was it, then?"

"It was Be-mannair, daughter of Ainceol, the woman-messenger of the Tuatha de Danaan. She's the one who changes herself into every shape. She'll take the shape of a fly, or of a true lover, and everyone leaves their secret with her. It was she outran you coming from the east, and not this other girl, who was drinking and making merry here in the hall."

"What's her name?" said Finn.

"Etain of the Fair Hair," he said. "A daughter of my own, and a darling of the Tuatha de Danaan. And the way it is with her, she has a lover among the men of the Fianna."

"That's well," said Finn. "And who is that lover?"

"It's Osgar, son of Oisin," said Aedh. "It was she herself sent her messenger for you, in her own shape, to Slieve Crot in the south. The son of the High King of Ireland has offered a great bride-price to the Men of Dea for her: three hundreds of the land nearest to Bregia and to Midhe, and to put himself and his weight in gold into a balance, and give it all to her. But we didn't take it, since she had no mind or wish for it herself. So we made no bargain or agreement about her."

"Well," said Finn, "and what conditions will you ask of Osgar?"

"Never to leave me for anything at all but my own fault," said the girl.

"I'll make that agreement with you indeed," said Osgar.

"Give me sureties for it," she said. "Give me the surety of Goll for the sons of Morna, and of Finn, son of Cumhal, for the Fianna of Ireland."

So they gave those sureties, and the wedding-feast was made, and they stayed there twenty nights. At the end of that time Osgar asked Finn where he should bring his wife.

"Bring her to wide Almhuin for the first seven years," said Finn.

But some time after that, in a great battle at Beinn Edair, Osgar got so heavy a wound that Finn and the Fianna were as if they had lost their wits.

When Etain of the Fair Hair came to the bed where Osgar lay, and saw the way he was, and that the great king-like shape he had was gone from him, greyness and darkness came over her. She raised pitiful cries, and went to her bed, and her heart broke in her like a nut. And she died of grief for her husband and her first love.

But it was not then that Osgar got his death. That was afterwards, in the battle of Gabhra.

She did not live to see it. She was spared that much.

Diarmuid was the son of Donn, son of Duibhne, of the Fianna. His mother was Crochnuit, who was near in blood to Finn. At the time he was born, Donn had been banished from the Fianna because of some quarrel, and Angus Og took the child from him to rear him at Brugh na Boinne.

After a while Crochnuit bore another son, to Roc Diocain, who was Head Steward to Angus. Roc Diocain went to Donn and asked whether he would rear his son for him, the way Angus was rearing Donn's son. But Donn said he would not take the son of a common man into his house, and it would be best for Angus to take him. So Angus took that child into Brugh na Boinne too, and he and Diarmuid were reared together.

Two boys. Half-brothers. Same mother, same house, same god for a foster-father.

One day Finn was on the great Hill at Almhuin of Leinster, with nobody but Donn and a few of the poets and learned men of the Fianna, and their hounds and dogs. Bran Beag came in and asked whether he remembered that there were bonds on him not to stay in Almhuin for ten nights together. So Finn asked the people around him where he should go to be entertained that night.

"I'll bring you to the house of Angus, son of the Dagda," said Donn, "where my young son is being reared."

So they went together to the house of Angus at Brugh na Boinne. The child Diarmuid was there, and Angus had great love for him. The Steward's son was with him that night, and the people of the household made as much of him as Angus made of Diarmuid. And there was great vexation on Donn when he saw that.

After a while a great fight broke out between two of Finn's hounds over some broken meat that was thrown to them. The women and the common people of the place ran from them, and the others got up to part them. In running away, the Steward's child ran between Donn's knees. And Donn gave the child a strong squeeze between his two knees that killed him that moment. Then he threw him under the feet of the hounds.

There is no reason given. There is only a man who did not like to see another man's son loved as much as his own.

When the Steward came after that and found his son dead, he gave a long, very pitiful cry.

"There isn't a man in the house tonight has suffered more from this uproar than I have," he said to Finn. "I had only one son, and he's been killed. What satisfaction will I get from you for that, Finn?"

"See if you can find the mark of a tooth or of a nail of one of the hounds on him," said Finn. "If you can, I'll give you satisfaction for him."

So they looked at the child, and there was no scratch on him and no mark of a tooth at all.

Then the Steward put Finn under the destroying bonds of the Druid cave of Cruachan to tell him who it was that had killed his son. Finn asked for a chessboard, and for water to be brought to him in a basin of pale gold, and he searched, and it was shown to him truly that it was Donn who had killed the Steward's son between his two knees.

When Finn knew that, he said he would take the fine on himself. But the Steward would not consent to it, and forced him to say who had done him the wrong.

When he knew it was Donn who had killed the child, he said: "There's no man in the house it's easier to get satisfaction from than him. His own son is here. I have only to put him between my two knees. And if I let him go from me safe, I'll forgive the death of my son."

Angus was vexed at what the Steward said. As for Donn, he meant to strike the Steward's head off, until Finn pushed him back.

Then the Steward came again, with a Druid rod in his hand. He struck his own dead son with the rod, and made him into a wild boar, without bristle or ear or tail.

"I put you under bonds," he said, "to bring Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, to his death. And your own life will be no longer than his."

With that the wild boar got up and ran out through the open door. He was called afterwards the Boar of Slieve Guillion. And it was by him Diarmuid came to his death at the last.

That is the rule of the boar. It will kill Diarmuid. And when Diarmuid dies, it dies. The two lives are knotted together, one brother's to the other's, and there is no untying them.

When Diarmuid came to his full strength he was given a place among the Fianna of Ireland. All women loved him. He did many great deeds, fighting the enemies of the Fianna and of Ireland. Once he fought a wild ox for seven days and seven nights on the top of the Mountain of Happiness.

Somewhere in the woods of Ireland, a boar without ears was growing old, and waiting.

Diarmuid and Conan and Goll and Osgar went hunting one day, and they went so far that they could not get home in the evening. They spent the first part of the night walking through the woods, pulling berries and eating them.

About midnight they saw a light. They went towards it and found a little house in front of them, with the light shining out of it. They went in. There was an old man there, and he welcomed them and called each of them by his name. They saw nobody else in the house but the old man, and a young girl, and a cat.

The old man told the girl to make food ready for the Fianna of Ireland, for there was great hunger on them.

When the food was ready and on the table, a great wether that was tied up at the back of the house broke loose and got up on the table where they were eating. When they saw that they looked at one another.

"Get up, Conan," said Goll, "and tie that wether where it was before."

Conan got up and took hold of it. But the wether gave itself a shake that threw Conan down under one of its feet.

The rest were watching that. "Get up, Diarmuid," said Goll, "and tie up the wether."

So Diarmuid got up and took hold of it. It gave itself a shake the same as before, and when Diarmuid was down, it put one of its feet on him.

Goll and Osgar looked at each other, and shame came on them that a wether should have done so much.

Osgar got up. The wether put him down under one of its feet, so that it had the three men under it now.

Then Goll got up and took hold of it and threw it down. But it got up again in spite of him, and put Goll under its fourth foot.

"It's a great shame," said the old man, "for such a thing to be done to the Fianna of Ireland. Get up now, cat, and tie the wether in the place where it was."

The cat got up and took hold of the wether, and brought it over, and tied it in its place at the end of the house.

The men got up then. But they had no mind to go on eating, for there was shame on them at what the wether had done to them.

"You may go on eating," said the old man, "and when you're done, I'll show you that you are now the bravest men in the world."

So they ate their fill, and then the old man spoke to them.

"Goll," he said, "you are the bravest of all the men of the world. For you have wrestled with the world, and you threw it down. The strength of the world is in the wether. But death will come to the world itself. And that is death," he said, and he showed them the cat.

A cat. Death is a cat, sitting by the fire in a small house in the woods. It gets up when it is asked. It is never in a hurry.

They talked together then, and when they had eaten their food, the old man said their beds were ready and they could go to sleep. The four of them went into the one room. When they were in their beds, the young girl came to sleep in the same room with them. The light of her beauty was shining on the walls as if it were the light of a candle.

When Conan saw her he went over to the side of the bed where she was.

Now, the young girl was Youth.

When she saw Conan coming to her she said, "Go back to your bed, Conan. I belonged to you once, and I'll never belong to you again."

Conan went back to his bed. Then Osgar had a mind to go over to her.

"Where are you going?" she said.

"I'm going over to you for a while," he said.

"Go back again, Osgar," she said. "I belonged to you once, and I'll never belong to you again."

Then Diarmuid got up to go to her.

"Where are you going, Diarmuid?" she said.

"I'm going over to you for a while," he said.

"O Diarmuid," she said, "that can't be. I belonged to you once, and I can never belong to you again. But come over here to me, Diarmuid, and I'll put a love-spot on you, so that no woman will ever see it without giving you her love."

So Diarmuid went over to her. She put her hand on his forehead and left the love-spot there. And no woman who ever saw him after that was able to refuse him her love.

It sounds like a gift. So does most of what the Sidhe give you.

One snowy night of winter the Fianna had come into the house after their hunting. About midnight they heard a knocking at the door, and a woman came in, very wild and ugly, with her hair hanging down to her heels.

She went to where Finn was lying and asked him to let her in under the edge of his covering. When he saw how strange she was, and how ugly and wild-looking, he would not let her in.

She gave a great cry, and went to where Oisin was, and asked him to let her shelter under the edge of his covering. Oisin refused her the same way.

Then she gave another great scream and went over to where Diarmuid was.

"Let me in," she said, "under the edge of your covering."

Diarmuid looked at her. "You're strange-looking and wild and ugly," he said, "and your hair is down to your heels. But come in for all that."

So she came in under the edge of his covering.

"O Diarmuid," she said, "I've been travelling over sea and ocean for seven years, and in all that time I never got shelter any night until this night. Let me come to the warmth of the fire now."

So Diarmuid brought her over to the fire. All the Fianna who were sitting there went away from it, seeing her so ugly and so dreadful to look at.

She had not been long at the fire when she said, "Let me under the warmth of the covering with you now."

"You're asking too much," said Diarmuid. "First it was to come under the edge you asked, and then to come to the fire, and now it's under the bedclothes with me you want to be. But for all that, you may come."

So she came in under the covering, and he turned a fold of it between them.

It was not long before he looked at her. What he saw was a beautiful young woman beside him, asleep.

He called the others to come over. "Isn't this the most beautiful woman that ever was seen?" he said.

"She is that," they said. And they covered her up and did not wake her.

The same woman. They had turned her away. It is worth remembering that they were the ones who turned her away.

After a while she stirred. "Are you awake, Diarmuid?" she said.

"I'm awake," he said.

"Where would you like to see the best house that ever was built?"

"Up there on the hillside, if I had my choice," he said. And with that he fell asleep.

In the morning two men of the Fianna came in and said they had just seen a great house up on the hill, where there had never been a house before.

"Get up, Diarmuid," said the strange woman. "Don't lie there any longer. Go up to your house. Look out now and see it."

So he looked out and saw the great house, standing ready.

"I'll go to it," he said, "if you'll come with me."

"I'll do that," she said, "if you'll make me a promise: not to say to me three times how I was when I came to you."

"I'll never say it to you, for ever," said Diarmuid.

That is the rule. Three times, and she is gone. You have heard rules like it before. You know how they go.

They went up to the house, and it was ready for them, with food and servants, and they had everything they could wish for. They stayed there three days. When the three days were over, she said: "You're getting sorrowful because you're away from your comrades of the Fianna."

"I'm not sorrowful indeed," said Diarmuid.

"It will be best for you to go to them," she said. "And your food and your drink will be no worse when you come back than they are now."

"Who'll take care of my greyhound bitch and her three pups if I go?" said Diarmuid.

"There's no fear for them," she said.

When he heard that he took leave of her and went back to the Fianna, and there was a great welcome for him. But all the same they were not well pleased. They were somehow envious that Diarmuid had got that grand house, and her love, from the woman they themselves had turned away.

As for the woman, she was outside the house for a while after Diarmuid went away, and she saw Finn, son of Cumhal, coming towards her. She bade him welcome.

"You're vexed with me, Queen?" he said.

"I'm not indeed," she said. "Come in now and take a drink of wine from me."

"I'll go in if I get my request," said Finn.

"What request is there that you wouldn't get?"

"What I'm asking is one of the pups of Diarmuid's greyhound bitch."

"That's no great thing to ask," she said. "Whichever of them you choose, you may take it away."

So he got the pup, and took it away with him.

At nightfall Diarmuid came back to the house. The greyhound met him at the door and gave a yell when she saw him. He looked for the pups, and one of them was gone.

Anger came on him, and he said to the woman: "If you'd remembered the way you were when I let you in, with your hair hanging, you wouldn't have let the pup be taken from me."

That was once.

"You ought not to say that, Diarmuid," she said.

"I ask your pardon for saying it," said Diarmuid.

They forgave each other, and he spent the night in the house.

The next day Diarmuid went back to his comrades, and the woman stayed at the house. After a while she saw Oisin coming towards her. She welcomed him and asked him into the house. He said he would come if he got his request. And what he asked for was another of the greyhound's pups.

She gave it to him, and he went away with it. When Diarmuid came back that night the greyhound met him and cried out twice. He knew that another pup was gone. And he said to the greyhound, with the woman standing there: "If she'd remembered the way she was when she came to me, she wouldn't have let the pup be taken."

That was twice.

The next day he went back to the Fianna again. When he was gone the woman saw Caoilte coming towards her, and he would not come in to take a drink from her until he had got the promise of one of the pups, the same as the others.

When Diarmuid came back that night the greyhound met him and gave three yells, the most terrible that were ever heard. There was great anger on him when he saw all the pups were gone.

And he said it the third time: "If this woman remembered the way she was when I found her, with her hair down to her heels, she wouldn't have let the pup go."

"O Diarmuid," she said, "what is it you've said?"

He asked her forgiveness then. He went to go into the house. But the house was gone, and the woman was gone, that moment. And it was on the bare ground he woke the next morning.

The three pups went to Finn and Oisin and Caoilte. His friends. They had turned her away themselves, and then they came, one after another, and took what was his.

There was great sorrow on him, and he said he would search every place until he found her again.

He set out through the lonely valleys. The first thing he saw was the greyhound lying dead. He put her on his shoulder and would not leave her, because of the love he had for her.

After a while he met a cowherd and asked him whether he had seen a woman going that way.

"I saw a woman early in the morning yesterday, walking hard," said the cowherd.

"Which way was she going?"

"Down that path there to the strand. I saw her no more after that."

So he followed the path she had taken down to the strand, until he could go no farther. Then he saw a ship. He leaned on the handle of his spear and made a light leap onto the ship, and it went on until it came to land. He got out and lay down on the side of a hill and fell asleep. When he woke there was no ship to be seen.

"It's a pity for me to be here," he said. "I see no way of getting away again."

After a while he saw a boat coming, with a man in it rowing. He went down and got into the boat and brought the greyhound with him. The boat went out over the sea, and then down under it. And Diarmuid, when he went down, found himself on a plain.

He walked along it, and before long he came on a drop of blood. He picked it up and put it in a napkin. "The greyhound lost this," he said. After a while he came on another drop of blood, and then a third, and he put them in the napkin.

After that he saw a woman gathering rushes as if she had lost her wits. He went towards her and asked her what news she had.

"I can't tell it till I've gathered the rushes," she said.

"Tell it while you're gathering them," said Diarmuid.

"There's great haste on me," she said.

"What is this place we're in?" said Diarmuid.

"It's Land-under-Wave," she said.

"And what use have you for the rushes when they're gathered?"

"The daughter of King Under-Wave has come home," she said. "She was seven years under enchantment. There's sickness on her now, and all the physicians are gathered, and none of them can do her any good. A bed of rushes is what she finds wholesomest."

"Will you show me where the king's daughter is?" said Diarmuid.

"I'll do that," said the woman. "I'll put you in the sheaf of rushes, and put the rushes under you and over you, and carry you to her on my back."

"That's a thing you can't do," said Diarmuid.

But she put the rushes around him and lifted him onto her back. When she got to the room she let the bundle down.

"O come here to me," said the daughter of King Under-Wave.

Diarmuid went over to her, and they took each other's hands, and they were very joyful at that meeting.

"Three parts of my sickness are gone from me now," she said. "But I'm not well yet, and I never will be. For every time I thought of you on my journey, Diarmuid, I lost a drop of the blood of my heart."

Not the greyhound's blood. Hers. Every time she thought of him.

"I have those three drops here in this napkin," said Diarmuid. "Take them now in a drink, and you'll be healed of your sickness."

"They'd do nothing for me," she said, "since I haven't got the one thing in the world I want. And that's the thing I'll never get."

"What thing is that?"

"It's the thing you'll never get, nor any man in the world," she said. "They've failed a long time to get it."

"If it's anywhere on the whole ridge of the world," said Diarmuid, "I'll get it."

"It's three draughts from the cup of the King of Magh an Ionganaidh, the Plain of Wonder," she said. "No man ever got it, and no man ever will."

"Tell me where that cup is to be found," said Diarmuid, "for there aren't as many men on the whole ridge of the world as will keep it from me."

"That country isn't far from the boundary of my father's country," she said. "But there's a little river between. You'd be sailing on that river in a ship, with the wind behind it, for a year and a day before you'd reach the Plain of Wonder."

Diarmuid set out. He came to the little river, and walked beside it a good while, and saw no way to cross it.

At last he saw a low-sized, reddish man standing in the middle of the river.

"You're in straits, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne," he said. "Come here and put your foot in the palm of my hand, and I'll bring you through."

Diarmuid did as he told him and put his foot in the red man's palm, and the red man carried him across the river.

"It's to the King of the Plain of Wonder you're going," he said, "to bring away his cup from him. I'll go with you myself."

They went on until they came to the king's dun. Diarmuid called out that the cup should be sent out to him, or else champions to fight him.

It was not the cup that was sent out, but twice eight hundred fighting men. In three hours there was not one of them left to stand against him. Then twice nine hundred better fighters were sent out against him, and within four hours there was not one of them left to stand against him.

Then the king himself came out and stood in the great door.

"Where did the man come from who has brought destruction on my whole kingdom?" he said.

"I'll tell you that," said he. "I'm Diarmuid, a man of the Fianna of Ireland."

"It's a pity you didn't send a messenger telling me that," said the king, "and I wouldn't have wasted my men on you. For seven years before you were born, it was in the prophecy that you would come and destroy them. What is it you're asking for now?"

"It's the cup of healing from your own hand I'm asking for," said Diarmuid.

"No man ever got that cup from me but you," said the king. "But it's easy for me to give it to you, whether there's healing in it or not."

So the King of the Plain of Wonder gave Diarmuid the cup, and they parted. Diarmuid went on until he came to the river. It was only then he thought of the red man, whom he had given no thought to while he was at the king's house. But the red man was there before him. He took Diarmuid's foot in the palm of his hand and carried him over the river.

"I know where you're going, Diarmuid," he said. "It's to heal the daughter of King Under-Wave, whom you've given your love to. I'll give you the signs of a well. Go to it, and bring a share of the water of that well with you. When you come to where the woman is, this is what you have to do: put that water in the cup, and one of the drops of blood in it, and she'll drink it. Then the same with the second drop, and the third. And her sickness will be gone from her from that time on.

"But there's another thing will go along with it," he said, "and that's the love you have for her."

That is the rule of the cure. It heals her. It takes his love away. Both. There is no having one without the other.

"That won't go from me," said Diarmuid.

"It will go from you," said the man. "And it will be best for you to make no secret of it, for she'll know, and the king will know, that you think no more of her then than of any other woman. King Under-Wave will come to you and offer you great riches for healing his daughter. But take nothing from him. Ask only for a ship to bring you home to Ireland. And do you know who I am?"

"I don't know," said Diarmuid.

"I'm the messenger from beyond the world," he said. "And I came to your help because your own heart is hot to come to the help of another."

So Diarmuid did as he told him. He brought the water and the cup and the drops of blood to the woman, and she drank them, and at the third draught she was healed.

And no sooner was she healed than the love he had for her was gone, and he turned away from her.

"O Diarmuid," she said, "your love is gone from me."

"O, it's gone indeed," he said.

Then there was music made through the whole place, and the lamenting stopped, because the king's daughter was healed. As for Diarmuid, he would take no reward and he would not stay there, but asked for a ship to bring him home to Ireland, to Finn and the Fianna.

When he came to where they were, there was a joyful welcome for him.

He had gone to the bottom of the sea for her, and brought back the one cup that could save her, knowing what it would cost. It is the kindest thing Diarmuid ever did. It is the thing to remember about him, later, when the story is less kind.

The Fianna went hunting once in the two proud provinces of Munster.

They went out from Almhuin by the nearest paths until they came to the Brosna river in Slieve Bladhma, and from there to the twelve mountains of Eiblinne, and on to Aine Cliach, the harp of Aine.

Then they scattered themselves and hunted through the borders of the forest called Magh Breogain, through blind, trackless places and through broken lands, over beautiful level plains and the high hills of Desmumum, under pleasant Slieve Crot and smooth Slieve na Muc, along the level banks of the blue Siuir, and over the green plain of Feman and the rough plain of Eithne, and the dark woods of Belach Gabrain.

Finn was on the side of a hill with the chief men of the Fianna, watching the hunting. They liked to listen to the outcry of the hounds, and the hurried cries of the boys, and the noise and the whistling and the shouts of the strong men.

Finn asked which of the men with him would go and keep watch on the side of the hill where they were. Finnbane, son of Bresel, said he would go. He went up to the top of the hill, where he could see about him on every side.

He had not been there long when he saw coming from the east a very big man, ugly and gloomy and deformed. This is how he was. He had a dark-coloured shield on his back, and a wide sword on his crooked left thigh, and two spears on his shoulder, and a torn, loose cloak over his limbs, which were as black as a quenched coal.

He had a sulky horse with him that had no good look about it: bony and thin in the body and weak in the legs. He was leading it by a rough iron halter. It was a great wonder that the horse's head was not pulled off its body, or its owner's arms pulled out of him, with the sudden stands and stops and jerks it made. The big man was beating the horse with an iron cudgel, to try to knock some going into it, and the sound of the blows was like the breaking of strong waves.

When Finnbane saw all that, he thought it would not be right to let a stranger like that come up to Finn and the Fianna unannounced. He ran back in haste to where they were and told them everything he had seen.

When he had told his story, they saw the big man coming towards them. But short as the distance was, he was a long time coming, from the badness of his walk and his going.

When he came into Finn's presence he greeted him, and bowed his head and bent his knee, making signs of humility.

Finn raised his hand over his head and asked him for news, and whether he was of the noble or of the mean blood of the great world.

He answered that he did not know whom he came from, only that he was a man of the Fomor, travelling in search of wages from the kings of the earth. "And I heard," he said, "that Finn never refused wages to any man."

"I never did indeed," said Finn, "and I won't refuse you. But why are you without a boy to mind your horse?"

"I have a good reason for that," said the big man. "There's nothing in the world worse to me than a boy being with me. It takes a hundred men's share of food to serve me for one day, and I think it little enough, and I'd begrudge a boy sharing it with me."

"What name do you have?" said Finn.

"The name I have is the Gilla Decair, the Hard Servant."

"Why did you get that name?"

"There's a good reason for that," said the big man. "There's nothing in the world harder for me than to do anything at all for my master, or for whoever I'm with. And tell me this, Conan, son of Morna: who gets the best wages, a horseman or a man on foot?"

"A horseman gets twice as much," said Conan.

"Then I call you to witness, Conan, that I'm a horseman, and that it was as a horseman I came to the Fianna. Now give me your guarantee, Finn, son of Cumhal, and the guarantee of the Fianna, and I'll turn my horse out with your horses."

"Let him out, then," said Finn.

The big man pulled the iron halter off his horse. It went off as hard as it could go until it came to where the horses of the Fianna were, and began to tear and kick and bite at them, killing and maiming.

"Take your horse out of that, big man," said Conan. "By the earth and the sky, if it weren't on the guarantee of Finn and the Fianna you took the halter off him, I'd let his brains out through the windows of his head. Many a bad prize Finn has found in Ireland, but he never got one as bad as you."

"And I swear by earth and sky as well as you," said the big man, "I'll never bring him out of that. I've no serving-boy to do it for me, and it's not work for me to be leading my horse by the hand."

So Conan, son of Morna, got up and took the halter and put it on the horse, and led it back to where Finn was, and held it with his hand.

"You'd never have done a horse-boy's service for any one of the Fianna, Conan," said Finn, "however far above this Fomor he might be. If you'll take my advice, you'll get up on the horse now and search out every hill and hollow and flowery plain of Ireland with him, until his heart is broken in his body, as payment for the way he destroyed the horses of the Fianna."

Conan leapt onto the horse and struck his heels hard into it. For all that, the horse would not stir.

"I know what ails him," said Finn. "He won't stir until he has the same weight of horsemen on him as the weight of the big man."

At that thirteen men of the Fianna got up behind Conan. The horse lay down with them, and got up again.

"I think you're mocking my horse and me," said the big man. "It's a pity for me to spend the rest of the year with you, after all the humbugging I've seen in you today, Finn. I know well now that everything I heard about you was nothing but lies, and there was no cause for the great name you have through the world. I'll leave you now, Finn."

With that he went away from them, slow and weak, dragging himself along until he had put a little hill between himself and the Fianna. As soon as he was on the other side of it, he tucked his cloak up to his waist and away with him, as quick as a swallow or a deer, and the rush of his going was like a blast of loud wind going over plains and mountains in springtime.

When the horse saw his master going from him, he could not bear it. Great as his load was, he set out at full gallop after him.

When Finn and the Fianna saw the thirteen men behind Conan, son of Morna, on the horse, and the horse starting off, they shouted with mocking laughter.

When Conan found he could not get down off the horse, he screeched and shouted to them not to let him be carried off by the big man they knew nothing about, and he began abusing and reproaching them.

"A cloud of death over water on you, Finn," he said, "and may some son of a slave or a robber of the bad blood — someone who's a worse son of a father and mother even than you — take everything that might protect your life, and your head along with it, unless you follow us to whatever place or island the big man carries us to, and bring us back to Ireland again."
