Finn and the Fianna got up then and followed the Gilla Decair over every bald hill and through every valley and every river, on to pleasant Slieve Luachra, into the borders of Corca Duibhne. The big man, who was up on the horse now with Conan and the rest, turned towards the deep sea.

Liagan Luath of Luachar took hold of the horse's tail with his two hands, thinking to drag it back by the hair of it. But the horse gave a great tug, and away with him over the sea, and Liagan along with him, holding on to his tail.

It was a heavy care to Finn that those fourteen men of his people had been carried away from him, and he himself under bonds to bring them back.

"What can we do now?" Oisin asked him.

"What should we do," said Finn, "but follow our people to whatever place or island the big man has brought them, and, whatever way we do it, bring them back to Ireland?"

"What can we do, having neither a ship nor any kind of boat?" said Oisin.

"We have this," said Finn. "The Tuatha de Danaan left it as a gift to the children of the Gael: that whoever had to leave Ireland for a while had only to go to Beinn Edair, and however many went with him, they'd find a ship that would hold them all."

Then Finn looked towards the sea, and saw two strong armed men coming towards him. The first had a shield on his back, ribbed and many-coloured, engraved with the shapes of strange, wonderful beasts; a heavy sword at his side, and two thick spears on his shoulders; a cloak of lasting crimson about him, with a gold brooch on the breast; a band of white bronze on his head, and gold under each of his feet. The other was dressed the same way.

They made no delay until they came to where Finn was. They bowed their heads and bent their knees before him, and Finn raised his hand over their heads and told them to give an account of themselves.

"We are sons of the King of the Eastern World," they said, "and we've come to Ireland asking to be taken into Finn's service. We heard there wasn't a man in all Ireland better than you to judge the skill we have."

"What are your names, and what skill is that?" said Finn.

"My name is Feradach, the Very Brave," said one. "I have a carpenter's axe and a sling. If there were as many as thirty hundred of the men of Ireland with me in one spot, with three blows of the axe on the sling-stick I could get a ship that would hold them all. And I'd ask no more help of them than to bow down their heads while I was striking those three blows."

"That's a good art," said Finn. "And what can the other man do?"

"I can do this," said the other. "I can follow the track of the teal over nine ridges and nine furrows until I come on her in her bed. And it's all the same to me whether I do it on sea or on land."

"That's a good art," said Finn, "and it would be a great help to us if you'd come following a track with us now."

"What's gone from you?" said one of the men. And Finn told them the whole story of the Hard Servant.

Then Feradach, the Very Brave, struck three blows on his sling-stick with his axe. The whole of the Fianna bowed their heads. And that moment the whole bay and the harbour were filled with ships and fast boats.

"What'll we do with that many ships?" said Finn.

"We'll do away with all you don't use," he said.

Caoilte got up then and let out three great shouts, and all the Fianna of Ireland, wherever they were, heard them, and thought Finn and his people must be in some kind of danger from men from beyond the sea.

They came in small companies, as they happened to be, until they reached the stepping-stones of the Cat's Head in the western part of Corca Duibhne. They asked Finn what had happened that he had called them away from their hunting, and Finn told them all of it.

Then Finn and Oisin took counsel together, and this is what they agreed. Since only fifteen of his people had been carried off from Finn, he would go on their track with fifteen others. And Oisin would be left at the head of the Fianna to guard Ireland.

They said farewell to one another. A grand ship was made ready for Finn and his people, with food put in it for eating and gold for giving away. The young men and the heroes took their seats and took hold of the oars, and they set out over the restless hills and the dark valleys of the great sea.

The sea rose up and bellowed, and there was madness on the broken green waters. But to Finn and his people the roaring and crooning that went on for ever about the sides of the ship was a call in the morning and a lullaby at night.

They went on like that for three days and three nights, and saw no country and no island. At the end of that time one of them went up into the head of the ship and saw ahead of them a great, rough, grey cliff. They went on towards it. On the edge of the cliff they saw a high rock, round-shaped, with sides more slippery than an eel's back. And they found the track of the Hard Servant as far as the foot of the rock.

Then Fergus of the True Lips said to Diarmuid: "It's no brave thing you're doing, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, holding back like this. It was with Manannan the Powerful, son of Lir, you were reared and got your learning, in the Land of Promise and on the coasts of the harbours, and with Angus Og, the Dagda's son. Are you without any share of their skill and their daring now, that would bring Finn and his people up this rock?"

Diarmuid's face reddened when he heard those words. He took hold of Manannan's staves of power, which he had with him, and reddened again. Then he rose on the staves and gave a leap, and got a standing-place for his two feet on the overhanging rock.

He looked down from there at Finn and his people. But however much he wished to bring them up to where he was, he was not able to do it.

He left the rock behind him, and he had not gone far when he saw a wild, tangled place in front of him, with thick woods. Of all the woods he had ever walked in, it was the leafiest, and the fullest of the sounds of wind and streams and birds, and the humming of bees.

He went walking on over the plain, and as he was looking about him he saw a great tree with many twigs and branches, and a rock beside it, and a smooth-pointed drinking-horn on the rock, and a beautiful fresh well at its foot. There was a great thirst on Diarmuid after the sea-journey, and he had a mind to drink a hornful of the water. But when he stooped to it he heard a great noise coming towards him, and he knew there was enchantment in the water.

"I'll drink my fill of it all the same," he said.

It was not long after that that he saw a Man of Enchantments coming towards him, armed, with no friendly look. And it was in no friendly way he spoke to Diarmuid when he came up to him, but abused him greatly.

"It's no right thing," he said, "to be walking through my thickets and drinking up my share of water."

With that they faced each other angrily, and they fought until the end of the day.

Then the Enchanter thought it best to leave off fighting, and he made a leap into the bottom of the well, away from him. And Diarmuid was vexed to be left like that.

He looked around him and saw a herd of deer coming through the scrub. He went towards them and threw a spear that went through the nearest stag and drove the bowels out of it. He kindled a fire and cut thin bits of the flesh and put them on spits of white hazel. That night he had his fill of meat and of the water of the well.

He got up early the next morning, and found the Enchanter at the well before him.

"It seems to me, Grandson of Duibhne," he said, "it's not enough for you to be walking my scrub and my woods, without killing my deer as well."

With that they started again, blow for blow and thrust for thrust and wound for wound, until the end of the day came on them. Diarmuid killed another great deer that night, and in the morning the fight began again. But in the evening, when the Enchanter was making his leap into the well, Diarmuid threw his arms round his neck, thinking to stop him. And this is what happened: he fell in himself. And when he was at the bottom of the well, the Enchanter left him.

Diarmuid went after the Enchanter. He found in front of him a beautiful, wide, flowery plain, and a comely royal city on the plain, and on the green in front of the dun a great army. When they saw Diarmuid following the Enchanter, they left a way open, a royal road, for the Enchanter to pass through until he got inside the dun. Then they shut the gates, and the whole army turned on Diarmuid.

That put no fear or cowardice on him. He went through them and over them as a hawk goes through little birds, or a wild dog through a flock of sheep, killing everything in front of him, until some of them ran off to the woods and the wastes, and another share of them in through the gates of the dun, and they shut the gates of the dun and the gates of the city behind them.

Diarmuid, full of hurts and wounds after the hard fight, lay down on the plain.

Then a very strong, daring champion came and kicked at him from behind. At that Diarmuid roused himself and put out his brave, ready hand for his weapons.

"Wait a while, Grandson of Duibhne," said the champion. "It's not to do you any hurt or harm I've come, but to tell you it's a bad sleeping-place you have, on your ill-wisher's lawn. Come with me now and I'll give you a better resting-place."

Diarmuid followed him, and they went a long, long way from there, until they came to a high-topped city. There were three times fifty brave champions in it, and three times fifty modest women, and another young woman on a bench, with blushes in her cheeks and delicate hands, and a silken cloak about her, and a dress sewn with gold threads, and on her head the flowing veil of a queen.

There was a good welcome for Diarmuid, for his own sake and for his people's. He was put in a house of healing in the city, and good herbs were put on his hurts until he was smooth and sound again.

Then a feast was made. The tables and the benches were set, and no high person was put in the place of the low, or low in the place of the high, but every one in his own place, according to his nobility, or his descent, or his art. Plenty of good food was brought to them, and well-tasting strong drinks. They spent the first part of the night in drinking, and the second part in music and delight and rejoicing of the mind, and the third part in sound sleep that lasted until the sun rose over the heavy-sodded earth the next day.

Diarmuid stayed three days and three nights in that city, and the best feast he ever found was given to him the whole time. At the end of that time he asked what place he was in, and who was the head of it.

The champion who had brought him there told him it was Land-Under-Wave, and that the man who had fought with him was its king.

"And he's an enemy of the Red Hand to me," he said. "As for me, I was once taking wages from Finn, son of Cumhal, in Ireland, and I never put a year over me that pleased me better. Now tell me, what's the journey or the work in front of you?"

And Diarmuid told him the story of the Hard Servant from beginning to end.

As for Finn and his people, when they thought Diarmuid had been away from them too long, they made ladders of the ship's ropes and put them against the rock, and went looking for him.

After a while they found the leavings of the meat he had eaten. For Diarmuid never ate meat without leaving some behind him.

That is a small thing to tell about a man, and it tells you everything. He always left some for whoever came after.

Finn looked about him on every side, and saw a rider coming towards him over the plain on a dark, beautiful horse with a bridle of red gold. Finn greeted him when he came up, and the rider bowed his head and gave Finn three kisses, and asked him to come with him. They went on a long way until they came to a wide, large dwelling-place full of weapons, with a great troop of armed men on the green in front of the fort. Finn and his people stayed three nights and three days in the dun, and the best feast they ever had was served out to them.

At the end of that time Finn asked what country he was in. The man who had brought him there told him it was the land of Sorcha, and that he himself was its king.

"And I was with you once, Finn, son of Cumhal," he said, "taking your wages for the length of a year in Ireland."

Then Finn and the King of Sorcha called a great gathering of the people, and a great meeting. While it was going on they saw a woman-messenger coming towards them through the crowd, and the king asked her for news.

"I have news indeed," she said. "The whole of the bay and the harbour is full of ships and boats, and there are armies all through the country robbing everything in front of them."

"I know well," said the king, "it's the High King of Greece. He has a mind to put the entire world under him, and to get hold of this country like every other."

The King of Sorcha looked at Finn, and Finn understood it was help he was asking for.

"I take the protection of this country on myself," Finn said, "as long as I'm in it."

He and his people got up then, and the King of Sorcha with them, and they went looking for the strange army. When they came up with it they made great slaughter of its champions. Those they did not kill ran before them and made no better stand than a flock of frightened birds, until there were hardly enough of them left to tell the story.

Then the High King spoke. "Who has done this great slaughter of my people?" he said. "I never heard any talk before of the courage or the doings of the men of Ireland, either now or in the old times. But from now on I'll banish the Sons of the Gael for ever to the very ends of the earth."

But Finn and the King of Sorcha raised a green tent in view of the ships of the Greeks.

Then the King of the Greeks called for help against Finn and the King of Sorcha, to get satisfaction for the shame that had been put on his people. The sons of kings of the eastern and southern world came to his help. But they could make no stand against Finn and Osgar and Oisin and Goll, son of Morna. And at last the King of Greece brought all his people back home, so that no more of them would be made an end of.

Then Finn and the King of Sorcha called another great gathering. While it was going on, they saw a great troop of champions coming towards them, bearing flags of many-coloured silk, with grey swords at their sides and high spears raised over their heads. And at the front of them was Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne.

When Finn saw him, he sent Fergus of the True Lips to ask him for news, and they told each other everything that had happened.

It would take too long to tell, and it would tire the hearers, how Finn made the Hard Servant bring home the fifteen men he had carried off. When the Hard Servant had brought them back to Ireland, the whole of the Fianna were watching to see him ride away again, he and his long-legged horse. But while they were watching him, he vanished from them. All they could see was a mist, stretching out towards the sea.

That is the story of the Hard Servant, and of Diarmuid's adventures on the island Under-Wave.

Some say the Hard Servant was Manannan himself. If so, he had got what he wanted: a long look at the Fianna, and at Diarmuid, whom he had reared, going over a rock that no one else could climb.

The Fianna would often have been badly off without Diarmuid's help. It was he who came to their help the time Miodac, the son of the King of Lochlann, brought them into the enchanted House of the Quicken Trees.

He brought them in by treachery. He gave himself out to be a poet, and made poems for Finn to find the meaning of.

He made a verse about a great army he had seen riding over the plains to victory, robbing everything in front of it, and the riders had no horses but plants and branches.

"I understand that," said Finn. "It was an army of bees you saw, gathering riches from the flowers as it went."

Another verse Miodac made was about a woman in Ireland who was swifter than the swiftest horse.

"I know that," said Finn. "That woman is the River Boinn. Slow as she goes, she's swifter in the end than the swiftest horse, for her going never stops."

He made other verses about Angus's house at Brugh na Boinn. Finn made them all out.

After that Miodac said he had a feast ready for them, and told them to go into his House of the Quicken Trees until he brought it. They did that, and went in. It was a beautiful house, with walls of every colour, and foreign coverings of every colour on the floor, and a fire that gave out a very pleasant smoke. They sat down there.

After a while Finn said, "It's a wonder, such a beautiful house to be here."

"There's a greater wonder than that," said Goll. "That fire that was so pleasant when we came in is giving out the worst stench in the world now."

"There's a greater wonder than that," said Glas. "The walls that were every colour are only rough boards joined together now."

"There's a greater wonder than that," said Fiacha. "Where there were seven high doors to the house, there's only one little door now, and it shut."

"There's a more wonderful thing than that, indeed," said Conan. "We sat down on beautiful coverings, and now there's nothing between us and the bare ground, and it as cold as the snow of one night."

He tried to get up. He could not stir, and neither could any of the rest of them. There was an enchantment holding them where they were.

That is how a trap works, in the old stories. Everything gets slowly worse, and you notice one thing at a time, and by the time you have noticed enough, you cannot stand.

It was the treachery of Miodac, and the spells of the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods, that had brought them into that danger. Finn knew by his divination that their enemies were gathering to make an end of them. He told his people there was no use in complaining, but to sound the music of the Dord Fiann.

Some of the Fianna who were waiting for him not far off heard that sorrowful music, and came fighting against Miodac and his armies. They fought well, but they could not stand against them.

At last it was Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, who made an end of Miodac, who was so treacherous, and of the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods. And he took the enchantment off the floor of the House of the Rowan Trees with their blood.

While he was freeing the Fianna, Conan called out, asking him to bring him a share of the feast Miodac had made ready for his own friends, for there was hunger on him.

When Diarmuid took no notice of him, he said: "If it was a comely woman speaking to you, Diarmuid, you wouldn't refuse to listen."

For if many women loved Diarmuid, there were many he gave his own love to. He was often called Diarmuid the Brave, or the Hardy, or the Comely, or the Hawk of Ess Ruadh. And he was often called as well the friend and the coaxer of women: Diarmuid-na-man.

Conan meant it as an insult. Conan usually did. But he was not wrong, and the next story is the proof of it.

Finn rose early one morning at Almhuin of Leinster, and sat out alone on the green lawn, without a boy or a servant with him.

Oisin followed him out, and Diorraing the Druid.

"What's the cause of your early rising, Finn?" said Oisin.

"It's not without cause I rise early," said Finn. "I'm without a wife or a companion since Maighneis, daughter of Black Garraidh, died from me. Quiet sleep doesn't come to a man who's without a fitting wife."

He was grey. He was lonely. He was the greatest man in Ireland. All three were true, and it is the first that matters in what follows.

"Why should you be like that?" said Oisin. "There isn't a woman in all green Ireland you'd throw a look at but we'd bring her to you, willing or unwilling."

"I could find a wife myself who'd be fitting for you," said Diorraing.

"Who's that?" said Finn.

"It's Grania, daughter of the High King of Ireland," said Diorraing. "She's the woman of the best make and shape and the best speech of all the women of the whole world."

"By my word, Diorraing," said Finn, "there's been strife and disagreement between the High King and me this long time, and it wouldn't be pleasing to me to get a refusal from him. It's best for you two to go together and ask his daughter in marriage for me. That way, if he gives a refusal, it'll be to you and not to me he gives it."

"We'll go," said Oisin, "even if we get little profit by it. And let nobody at all know of our going until we've come back."

So the two of them said farewell to Finn and set out, and nothing is told of what they did until they came to Teamhair.

The King of Ireland was holding a gathering on the green of Teamhair at that time, and the chief nobles of his people were with him. Oisin and Diorraing were given a friendly welcome. The king put off the gathering until the next day, for he was sure it was some pressing thing that had brought these two men of the Fianna to Teamhair. Oisin went aside with him and told him they had come from Finn, Head of the Fianna of Ireland, to ask for his daughter Grania in marriage.

This is what the king said: "There isn't a son of a king or of a great prince, there isn't a champion in Ireland, that my daughter hasn't given a refusal to. And it's on me they all lay the blame for it. I'll give you no answer at all until you go to her yourselves. It's better for you to get her own answer than to be displeased with me."

So they went together to the sunny house of the women. The king sat down at the head of the high seat beside Grania.

"Here, Grania," he said, "are two of the people of Finn, son of Cumhal, come to ask you as a wife for him. What answer have you a mind to give them?"

And this is what Grania said: "If he's a fitting son-in-law for you, why wouldn't he be a fitting husband for me?"

Listen to what she said. She did not say yes. She said he was fit for her father. They heard what they wanted to hear.

They were satisfied, and a feast was made for them that night in Grania's sunny house, and the king set a meeting a fortnight from then between himself and Finn at Teamhair.

So Oisin and Diorraing went back to Almhuin and told Finn their story from beginning to end. And as everything wears away, so did that time of waiting.

Then Finn gathered the seven battalions of the Fianna from every part where they were to Almhuin, and they set out in great bands and troops until they came to Teamhair.

The king was out on the green in front of them, with the great people of the men of Ireland, and there was a great welcome for Finn and the Fianna.

But when Grania saw grey-haired Finn, she said: "It's a great wonder it wasn't for Oisin Finn asked me. He'd be more fitting for me than a man who's older than my father."

But they talked together for a while, and Finn put questions to Grania, for she had the name of being very quick with answers.

"What's whiter than snow?" he said.

"The truth," said Grania.

"What's the best colour?"

"The colour of childhood."

"What's hotter than fire?"

"The face of a hospitable man when he sees a stranger coming in, and the house empty."

"What has a taste more bitter than poison?"

"The reproach of an enemy."

"What's best for a champion?"

"His doings to be high, and his pride to be low."

"What's the best of jewels?"

"A knife."

"What's sharper than a sword?"

"The wit of a woman between two men."

"What's quicker than the wind?" said Finn.

"A woman's mind," said Grania.

She was telling no lie when she said it.

And for all their talk together, she had no liking for Finn. She felt the blood in her heart rising against him.

She had answered every question he asked. He had not once asked the one that mattered.

Then the wedding-feast was made ready, and they all went into the king's feasting-house in the Middle Court. The king sat down to take his share of drinking and pleasure, with his wife at his left side and Grania beside her; and Finn, son of Cumhal, at the king's right hand, and Oisin on the other side of Finn, and everyone else according to his nobility and his birth.

Then Daire of the Poems stood up in front of Grania and sang her the songs and the good poems of her fathers. Sitting near Grania was a knowledgeable man, a Druid of Finn's people, and it was not long before they began to talk together.

"Tell me now," said Grania, "who's that man on the right hand of Oisin?"

"That's Goll, son of Morna," said the Druid, "the ready fighter."

"Who's that beside Goll?"

"Osgar, son of Oisin."

"And who's that thin-legged man beside Osgar?"

"That's Caoilte, son of Ronan."

"Who's that proud, hasty man beside Caoilte?"

"Lugaidh's Son of the Strong Hand."

"Who's that sweet-worded man," she said, "with the dark hair, and cheeks like the rowan-berry, on the left side of Oisin, son of Finn?"

"That's Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne," said the Druid. "The best lover of women in the whole world."

"That's a good company," said Grania.

After the feast had gone on a while, the dogs outside were given their own feast. They began to fight one another, and the noise was heard in the hall, and the chief men of the Fianna went out to drive them apart.

Now, Diarmuid always kept his cap over the love-spot the woman had left on his forehead, for no woman could see that spot without giving him her love.

It happened, while he was driving the dogs apart, that the cap fell off him. Grania was looking out at him as it fell. And a great love for him came on her there and then.

That is the rule of the love-spot. She saw it. That is all. Whatever came after, remember that she did not choose it, and neither did he.

She called her serving-maid and told her to bring the great golden cup from the sunny house, the one that held drink for nine times nine men. When the serving-maid brought the cup, Grania filled it with wine that had enchantment in it.

"Give the cup to Finn first," she said, "and tell him to take a drink from it, and tell him it was I myself sent it to him."

The serving-maid did that. Finn took the cup and drank from it, and no sooner had he drunk than he fell into a deep sleep. Then the cup was given to the king, and the queen, and the sons of kings, and the whole company — all but Oisin and Osgar and Caoilte and Diarmuid, and Diorraing the Druid. And everyone who drank from it fell into the same heavy sleep.

When they were all asleep, Grania rose up softly from her seat and turned her face to Diarmuid.

"Will you take my love, Diarmuid, son of Duibhne," she said, "and will you bring me away out of this house tonight?"

"I won't," said Diarmuid. "I won't meddle with the woman who's promised to Finn."

"If that's so," said Grania, "I put you under Druid bonds to bring me out of this house tonight, before Finn and the King of Ireland wake from their sleep."

"It's under bad bonds you're putting me, Grania," said Diarmuid. "And why is it you put them on me more than on the great men and sons of kings who are in the Middle Court tonight? There isn't one of them but is as well worthy of a woman's love as I am."

"By my hand, Diarmuid, it's not without cause I laid those bonds on you," said Grania. "I was at the door a while ago when you were parting the dogs, and my eyes fell on you, and I gave you there and then the love I never gave to any other, and never will give, for ever."

"It's a wonder you should give that love to me and not to Finn," said Diarmuid. "There isn't a man in Ireland is a better lover of a woman than he is. And do you know this, Grania: the night Finn is in Teamhair, it's he himself is the keeper of its gates. So we can't leave the town."

"There's a side door of escape at my sunny house," said Grania, "and we'll go out by it."

"It's a thing I'll never do," said Diarmuid, "go out by any side door of escape at all."

"That may be so," said Grania. "But I've heard it said that every fighting man has leave to pass over the walls of any dun or any strong place at all by the shafts of his spears. I'll go out through the door, and you follow me like that."

With that she went out.

Diarmuid spoke to his people. "O Oisin, son of Finn," he said, "what must I do with these bonds that are laid on me?"

"You're not guilty if the bonds were laid on you," said Oisin. "I tell you to follow Grania, and keep yourself well out of Finn's hands."

Finn's own son. That is what he said.

"Osgar, son of Oisin," said Diarmuid, "what must I do with these bonds that are put on me?"

"I tell you to follow Grania," said Osgar. "It's a pitiful man who'd break his bonds."

"What advice do you give me, Caoilte?"

"This is what I say," said Caoilte. "I have a fitting wife myself. And it would be better to me than all the riches of the world for Grania to have given me that love."

"What advice do you give me, Diorraing?"

"I tell you to follow Grania," said Diorraing, "though you'll get your death by it, and that's bad to me."

"Is that the advice you all give me?" said Diarmuid.

"It is," said Oisin, and all the rest with him.

With that Diarmuid stood up and stretched out his hand for his weapons. He said farewell to Oisin and the others, and every tear he shed was the size of a mountain berry.

He went out to the wall of the dun and put the shafts of his two spears under him, and rose with a light leap, and came down on the grassy earth outside. Grania met him there.

"It's a bad journey you've come on, Grania," said Diarmuid. "It would be better for you to have Finn, son of Cumhal, as a lover than me. I don't know any part or any western corner of Ireland that will hide you. And if I do bring you with me, it's not as a wife I'll bring you. I'll keep my faith to Finn. Turn back now to the town, and Finn will never get news of what you've done."

"It's certain I won't turn back," said Grania. "And I'll never part from you until death parts us."

"If that's so, let's go on, Grania," said Diarmuid.

They went on. They had not gone far out from the town when Grania said, "I'm getting tired, indeed."

"It's a good time to be tired," said Diarmuid. "Go back again to your own house now. For I swear by the word of a true champion, I'll never carry you or any other woman, to the end of life and time."

"That's not what you have to do," said Grania. "My father's horses are in a grass field by themselves, and chariots with them. Turn back now and bring two horses of them, and I'll wait in this place until you come to me again."

So Diarmuid went back for the horses. We have no knowledge of their journey until they reached the ford on the Sionnan that is called Ath-luain now.

"It's easier for Finn to follow our track," said Diarmuid, "with the horses along with us."

"If that's so," said Grania, "leave the horses here, and I'll go on foot from now on."

Diarmuid went down to the river and brought one horse over the ford with him, and left the other horse on the far side of the river. He and Grania went a good way westward with the stream, and came to land on the side of the province of Connacht.

And wherever they went, Diarmuid left unbroken bread behind him, as a sign to Finn that he had kept faith with him.

That is the rule of the bread. A whole loaf, left at every camp. It means: I have not touched her. It means: I am still your man. Finn would find every one of those loaves. You can decide for yourself what he thought, each time.

From there they went on to Doire-da-Bhoth, the Wood of the Two Huts. Diarmuid cut down the wood round about them, and made a fence with seven doors of woven twigs. And he set out a bed of soft rushes and the tops of the birch-tree for Grania in the very middle of the wood.

And now, Finn, son of Cumhal. I will tell his part of it.

Everyone in Teamhair rose early the next morning, and they found Diarmuid and Grania gone. A scorching jealousy came on Finn, and a weakness.

He sent his trackers out on the plain and told them to follow Diarmuid and Grania. They followed the track as far as the ford on the Sionnan, and Finn and the Fianna followed after them. But they could not carry the track across the ford. And Finn gave them his word that unless they found the track again without delay, he would hang them on either side of the ford.

That is Finn now. The man who never refused anyone. The judge who would give fair judgment between his enemy and his own son. He was going to hang his own trackers at a river because they had lost a trail.

Then the sons of Neamhuin went up against the stream and found a horse on each side of it. Then they went westward with the stream and found the track going along the side of the province of Connacht, and Finn and the Fianna of Ireland followed it on.

"I know well where we'll find Diarmuid and Grania now," said Finn. "It's in Doire-da-Bhoth they are."

Oisin and Osgar and Caoilte and Diorraing were listening when Finn said that.

"There's a danger they might be there," Oisin said to the others, "and it would be right for us to give them some warning. Look now, Osgar — where's Bran the hound? Finn himself is no dearer to her than Diarmuid is. Tell her to go now with a warning to him."

So Osgar told Bran, and Bran understood him well. She went to the rear of the whole troop so that Finn would not see her, and followed the track of Diarmuid and Grania until she came to Doire-da-Bhoth. And she put her head into Diarmuid's bosom as he slept.

Diarmuid started up out of his sleep and woke Grania. "Here's Bran, Finn's hound," he said, "come with a warning to tell us that Finn himself is coming."

"Let's take that warning, then," said Grania, "and make your escape."

"I won't take it," said Diarmuid. "If I can't escape Finn, I'd as soon he took me now as any other time."

When Grania heard that, great fear came on her.

Bran went away from them. When Oisin saw her coming back, he said: "I'm afraid Bran found no chance to get to Diarmuid, and we should send him some other warning. Look — where's Fearghoin, Caoilte's serving-man?"

Every shout Fearghoin gave could be heard in the three nearest hundreds. So they made him give three shouts, so that Diarmuid would hear him.

Diarmuid heard him. "I hear Caoilte's serving-man," he said to Grania. "He's with Caoilte, and Caoilte is with Finn. Those shouts were sent as a warning to me."

"Take that warning," said Grania.

"I won't take it," said Diarmuid. "Finn and the Fianna will come up with us before we leave the wood."

Fear and great dread came on Grania when she heard him say that.

As for Finn, he did not leave off following the track until he came to Doire-da-Bhoth. He sent the sons of Neamhuin to search through the wood, and they saw Diarmuid, and the woman with him. They came back to Finn, and he asked them whether Diarmuid and Grania were in the wood.

"Diarmuid's in it," they said, "and there's some woman with him. We know Diarmuid, but we don't know Grania."

"May no good come to the friends of Diarmuid for his sake," said Finn. "He won't leave that wood until he's given me satisfaction for everything he's done to me."

"It's jealousy has put you astray, Finn," said Oisin, "to think Diarmuid would stay here on the plain of Maen Mhagh, with no close place in it but Doire-da-Bhoth, and you following after him."

"Saying that will do you no good," said Finn. "I knew well when I heard the three shouts Caoilte's serving-man gave that it was you sent them to Diarmuid as a warning. And another thing: it was you sent my own hound Bran to him. But none of those things you've done will serve you. He won't leave Doire-da-Bhoth until he gives me satisfaction for everything he's done to me, and every disgrace he's put on me."

"It's great foolishness for you, Finn," said Osgar, "to think Diarmuid would stay in the middle of this plain with you waiting here to strike the head off him."

"Who but himself cut the wood this way," said Finn, "and made this close, sheltered place, with seven woven narrow doors to it? O Diarmuid," he called out, "which of us is telling the truth, myself or Oisin?"

"You never failed in your good judgment, Finn," said Diarmuid. "Indeed, Grania and I are here."

He would not lie to Finn. Even now. Especially now.

Then Finn called on his men to surround Diarmuid and Grania and take them.

At that time it was shown to Angus Og at Brugh na Boinne what great danger Diarmuid was in — his pupil once, and his dear foster-son. He set out on the clear cold wind and did not stop anywhere until he came to Doire-da-Bhoth. He went, unknown to Finn or the Fianna, into the place where Diarmuid and Grania were, and he spoke kind words to Diarmuid.

"What is this thing you've done, grandson of Duibhne?"

"The daughter of the King of Ireland has made her escape with me from her father and from Finn," said Diarmuid. "And it's not by my will she came."

"Let each of you come under an edge of my cloak, then," said Angus, "and I'll bring you out of here without the knowledge of Finn or his people."

"Take Grania with you," said Diarmuid. "But I'll never go with you. If I'm alive, I'll follow you before long. And if I'm not, give Grania to her father, and let him do well or badly by her."

With that Angus put Grania under the edge of his cloak and brought her out, unknown to Finn or the Fianna. No news is told of them until they came to Ros-da-Shoileach, the Headland of the Two Sallows.

As for Diarmuid, when Angus and Grania had gone, he stood up as straight as a pillar and put on his armour and took up his weapons. Then he went to one of the seven doors he had made, and asked who was at it.

"There's no enemy to you here," they said. "Oisin and Osgar are here, and the best men of the sons of Baiscne with us. Come out to us now, and nobody will dare do you any harm or hurt."

"I won't go out to you," said Diarmuid, "until I see at which door Finn himself is."

He went to another of the seven doors and asked who was at it.

"Caoilte, son of Ronan, and the rest of the sons of Ronan with him. Come out to us now, and we'll give ourselves for your sake."

"I won't go out to you," said Diarmuid. "I won't put you under Finn's anger for any good you do me."

He went on to another door and asked who was at it.

"Conan, son of Morna, is here, and the rest of the sons of Morna with him. We're enemies to Finn, and you're a great deal more to us than he is. Come out, and nobody will dare lay a hand on you."

"I won't indeed," said Diarmuid. "Finn would be better pleased to see the death of every one of you than to let me escape."

He went to another door and asked who was at it.

"A friend and a comrade of your own: Fionn, son of Cuadan, head of the Fianna of Munster, and his men with him. We're of the one country and the one soil, and we'll give our bodies and our lives for your sake."

"I won't go out to you," said Diarmuid. "I wouldn't like Finn to have a grudge against you for any good you did me."

He went to another door and asked who was at it.

"Fionn, son of Glor, head of the Fianna of Ulster, and his men with him. Come out to us now, and nobody will dare hurt or harm you."

"I won't go out to you," said Diarmuid. "You're a friend to me, and your father with you, and I wouldn't like Finn's unfriendliness to be put on you for my sake."

He went to another door and asked who was at it.

"There's no friend of yours here," they said. "Here are Aodh Beag the Little from Eamhuin, and Aodh Fada the Long from Eamhuin, and Caol Crodha the Fierce, and Goineach the Wounder, and Gothan the White-Fingered, and Aoife his daughter, and Cuadan the Tracker from Eamhuin. We're unfriendly people to you. If you come out to us we won't spare you at all, but we'll make an end of you."

"It's a bad troop that's in it," said Diarmuid, "you of the lies, and of the tracking, and of the one shoe. It's not fear of your hands that's on me. But because I'm your enemy, I won't go out."

He went to the last of the seven doors and asked who was at it.

"No friend of yours," they said. "It's Finn, son of Cumhal, and four hundred paid fighting men with him. If you come out to us we'll make opened marrow of you."

"I give you my word, Finn," said Diarmuid, "that the door you're at yourself is the first door I'll pass out of."

Seven doors. At six of them, his friends and his enemies. He would not go out through a friend's door, because it would cost the friend. He would not go out through an enemy's door, because it would look like fear. So there was only one door left, and it was Finn's.

When Finn heard that, he warned his battalions, on pain of lasting death, not to let Diarmuid past them without their knowing. But when Diarmuid heard him, he rose on the shafts of his spears and went with a very high, light leap far beyond Finn and his people, without their knowledge.

He looked back at them and called out that he had gone past them. Then he put his shield on his back and went straight on towards the west, and before long he was out of sight of Finn and the Fianna.

When he saw nobody coming after him, he turned back to where he had seen Angus and Grania leaving the wood, and he followed their track until he came to Ros-da-Shoileach.

He found Angus and Grania there in a sheltered, well-lighted cabin, with a great blazing fire kindled in it, and half a wild boar on spits. Diarmuid greeted them, and the life nearly went out of Grania with joy at the sight of him.

Diarmuid told them his news from beginning to end. They ate their share that night and slept until the coming of the day and the full light the next morning.

Angus got up early and said to Diarmuid: "I'm going from you now, grandson of Duibhne. And I leave you this advice.

"Don't go into a tree with one trunk when you're fleeing from Finn.

"Don't go into a cave of the earth that has only one door.

"Don't go to an island of the sea that has only one harbour.

"And wherever you cook your food, don't eat it there. And wherever you eat it, don't lie down there. And wherever you lie down, don't get up there in the morning."

That is the law of the hunted, and Angus gave it to him whole. It is how you live when the greatest man in Ireland wants you dead. You never sleep where you eat. You never wake where you sleep.

He said farewell to them after that, and went his way.

Then Diarmuid and Grania went westward along the right bank of the Sionnan until they came to Garbh-abha-na-Fiann, the Rough River of the Fianna. Diarmuid killed a salmon on the brink of the river and put it to the fire on a spit. Then he and Grania crossed the stream to eat it, as Angus had told them. And then they went on westward to sleep.

They rose early the next morning and travelled straight west until they came to the marsh of Finnliath.

On the marsh they met a young man of good shape and appearance, but without fitting clothes or weapons. Diarmuid greeted the young man and asked him for his news.

"I'm a fighting lad looking for a master," he said, "and Muadhan is my name."

"What would you do for me, young man?" said Diarmuid.

"I'd be a servant to you in the day, and watch for you in the night," he said.

"I tell you to keep that young man," said Grania. "You can't be always without people."

So they made an agreement with him and bound one another, and went on together westward until they reached the Carrthach river. Then Muadhan told Diarmuid and Grania to get up on his back until he carried them over the stream.

"That would be a big load for you," said Grania.

But he put them on his back and carried them over. Then they went on until they came to the Beith, and Muadhan brought them over on his back the same way.

They went into a cave at the side of Currach Cinn Adhmuid, the Woody Headland of the Bog, above Tonn Toime. Muadhan made ready beds of soft rushes and birch-tops for them at the far end of the cave. Then he went into the scrub near by and took a long straight rod of a quicken-tree. He put a hair and a hook on the rod, and a holly berry on the hook, and went up the stream, and took a salmon with the first cast. He put on a second berry and killed another fish, and a third berry and killed the third fish. Then he put the hook and the hair under his belt, and struck the rod into the earth, and brought the three salmon to where Diarmuid and Grania were, and put them on spits.

When they were done, Muadhan said: "I give the dividing of the fish to you, Diarmuid."

"I'd sooner you divided it than me," said Diarmuid.

"Then I'll give the dividing of the fish to you, Grania," said he.

"I'm better satisfied for you to divide it," said Grania.

"If it was you divided the fish, Diarmuid," said Muadhan, "you'd have given the best share to Grania. And if it was Grania divided it, she'd have given you the best share. And since it's I who am dividing it, you have the biggest fish, Diarmuid, and let Grania have the second biggest, and I'll have the smallest."

Three fish on a hook of holly. And a servant who could see into both their hearts and set the table accordingly.

They spent the night there. Diarmuid and Grania slept at the far end of the cave, and Muadhan kept watch for them until the rising of the day and the full light of the next morning.

Diarmuid rose early and told Grania to keep watch for Muadhan while he went and took a walk around the country. He went out and up a hill that was near, and looked about him, east and west, north and south.

He had not been there long when he saw a great fleet of ships coming from the west, straight towards the bottom of the hill where he stood. When they came to land, nine times nine of the chief men of the ships came ashore. Diarmuid went down and greeted them, and asked them for news, and what country they belonged to.

"We are three kings of the Green Champions of Muir-na-locht," they said. "Finn, son of Cumhal, sent for us because of a thief of the woods, an enemy of his, who has gone into hiding from him. It's to stop him we've come. We are twenty hundred good fighting men, and every one of us a match for a hundred. And besides that, we have three deadly hounds with us. Fire won't burn them, and water won't drown them, and weapons won't redden on them. We'll lay them on his track, and it won't be long before we have news of him. Tell us who you are, and have you any word of the grandson of Duibhne?"

That is the rule of the hounds. Fire, water, weapons: nothing ordinary. Remember it. Diarmuid did.

"I saw him yesterday," said Diarmuid. "And as for me, I'm only a fighting man, walking the world by the strength of my hand and the hardness of my sword. And by my word, you'll know Diarmuid's hand when you meet it."

"Well, we've found nobody up to now," they said.

"What are your own names?" said Diarmuid.

"Dubh-chosach, the Black-footed; Fionn-chosach, the Fair-footed; and Treun-chosach, the Strong-footed," they said.

"Is there wine in your ships?" said Diarmuid.

"There is," they said.

"If you have a mind to bring out a tun of wine," said Diarmuid, "I'll do a trick for you."

They sent men to get the tun. When it came, Diarmuid took it between his two hands and drank a drink out of it, and the others drank what was left. Then Diarmuid took the tun up to the top of the hill, and got up on it himself, and let it roll down the steep of the hill to the bottom. Then he brought it up the hill again, riding it coming and going, and he did that trick three times in front of the strangers.

But they said that a man who called that a trick had never seen a good trick. One of them got up on the tun. But Diarmuid gave a push of his foot at it, and the young man fell off before it began to move, and it rolled over him and crushed him, so that he died. Another man got on it, and another after him, until fifty of them had been killed trying to do Diarmuid's trick. And as many as were not killed went back to their ships that night.

Diarmuid went back to where he had left Grania. Muadhan put the hair and the hook on the rod until he had killed three salmon, and they ate their meal that night, and he kept watch for them the same way as before.

Diarmuid went out to the hill again early the next day. It was not long before he saw the three strangers coming towards him, and he asked them whether they would like to see any more tricks. They said they would sooner have news of the grandson of Duibhne.

"I saw a man who saw him yesterday," said Diarmuid.

With that he took off his weapons and his clothes, all but the shirt next his skin, and he struck the Crann Buidhe, the spear of Manannan, into the earth with the point upwards. Then he rose with a leap and landed on the point of the spear, as light as a bird, and came down off it again without a wound on him.

"It's a man who's never seen feats who'd call that a feat," said a young man of the Green Champions. He took off his clothes and made a leap, and he came down heavily on the point of the spear, and it went through his heart, and he fell to the ground.

The next day Diarmuid came again. He brought two forked poles out of the wood and stood them upright on the hill, and put the sword of Angus Og, the Mor-alltach, the Big Fierce One, between the two forks, on its edge. Then he rose lightly over it and walked on the sword three times, from the hilt to the point, and came down and asked whether there was a man of them could do that feat.

"That's a foolish question," said one of them. "There was never any feat done in Ireland but a man of our own would do it."

And with that he rose up to walk on the sword. This is what happened: he came down heavily on it, and he was cut into two halves.

The rest of the champions told him to take his sword away then, before any more of their people fell by it, and asked him whether he had any word of the grandson of Duibhne.

"I saw a man who saw him today," said Diarmuid, "and I'll go and ask him for news tonight."

Every day, a truth, and they never heard it.

He went back to where Grania was, and Muadhan killed three salmon for their supper and kept watch for them through the night.

Diarmuid rose at the early break of day. He put on his battle-clothes, that no weapon could go through. He took the sword of Angus, which left no leavings after it, at his left side, and his two thick-handled spears, the Gae Buidhe and the Gae Dearg, the Yellow and the Red, which gave wounds there was no healing for. Then he woke Grania and told her to keep watch for Muadhan, and said he would go out and take a look around.

When Grania saw him looking so brave, dressed in his clothes of anger and of battle, great fear took hold of her, and she asked him what he was going to do.

"It's for fear of meeting my enemies I'm like this," he said.

That quieted Grania. Then Diarmuid went out to meet the Green Champions.

They came to land and asked whether he had news of the grandson of Duibhne.

"I saw him not long ago," said Diarmuid.

"If that's so, tell us where he is," they said, "so we can bring his head to Finn, son of Cumhal."

"I'd be keeping bad watch for him if I did that," said Diarmuid. "His life and his body are under the protection of my valour, and because of that I'll do no treachery on him."

"Is that true?" they said.

"It's true indeed," said Diarmuid.

"Then leave this place yourself," they said, "or we'll bring your head to Finn, since you're an enemy of his."

"I'd be in bonds," said Diarmuid, "the day I'd leave my head with you."

With that he drew his sword, the Mor-alltach, out of its sheath and made a fierce blow at the head nearest him that put it in two halves. Then he attacked the whole host of the Green Champions and began to destroy them, cutting through the beautiful shining armour of the men of Muir-na-locht, until there was hardly a man of them who did not get the shortening of his life and the sorrow of death, or who could go back to give news of the fight — only the three kings and a few of their people, who escaped back to their ships.

Diarmuid turned back then, without wound or hurt on him, and went to where Grania and Muadhan were. They welcomed him, and Grania asked him whether he had heard any news of Finn and the Fianna of Ireland. He said he had not. And they ate their food and spent the night there.

He rose again with the early light of the next morning and went back to the hill, and when he got there he struck a great blow on his shield that set the strand shaking with the sound.

Dubh-chosach heard it, and said he himself would go and fight Diarmuid, and he came ashore there and then.

He and Diarmuid threw the weapons out of their hands and rushed at each other like wrestlers, straining their arms and their sinews, knotting their hands on each other's backs, fighting like bulls in madness, or like two daring hawks on the edge of a cliff. But at last Diarmuid raised Dubh-chosach up on his shoulder and threw him to the ground, and bound him fast and firm on the spot.

Then Fionn-chosach and Treun-chosach came one after the other to fight him, and he put the same binding on them.

He said he would strike their heads off, except that he thought it a worse punishment to leave them in those bonds. "For there's no one can free you," he said.

And he left them there, worn out and sorrowful.

That is the rule of Diarmuid's binding. No man in Ireland can loosen it but four. Keep that in mind as well.

The next morning Diarmuid told Grania the whole story of the strangers from beginning to end, and all he had done to them, and how on the fifth day he had put their kings in bonds.

"And they have three fierce hounds on a chain, ready to hunt me," he said.

"Did you take the heads off those three kings?" said Grania.

"I didn't," said Diarmuid. "There's no man of the heroes of Ireland can loosen those bonds but four only: Oisin, son of Finn; and Osgar, son of Oisin; and Lugaidh's Son of the Strong Hand; and Conan, son of Morna. And I know well none of those four will do it. But all the same, it won't be long before Finn gets news of them, and it's best for us to leave this cave, or Finn and the three hounds might come on us."

So they left the cave and went on until they came to the bog of Finnliath. Grania began to fall behind them, and Muadhan put her on his back and carried her until they came to great Slieve Luachra.

Then Diarmuid sat down on the brink of the stream that flows through the heart of the mountain. Grania was washing her hands, and she asked him for his knife to cut her nails with.

As for the strangers, as many of them as were still alive came to the hill where their three leaders were bound, and tried to loose them. But the way those bonds were, all their meddling only drew them tighter.

They had not been there long when they saw a woman coming towards them with the quickness of a swallow, or a weasel, or a blast of wind over bare mountain-tops. She asked them who had done that great slaughter on them.

"Who are you that's asking?" they said.

"I'm the Woman of the Black Mountain, the woman-messenger of Finn, son of Cumhal," she said. "It's looking for you Finn sent me."

"Indeed, we don't know who did this slaughter," they said. "But we'll tell you what he looked like. He was a young man with dark curling hair and ruddy cheeks. And it's worse again to us that our three leaders are bound like this, and we can't loose them."

"Which way did that young man go from you?" said the woman.

"It was late last night he left us," they said, "and we don't know where he's gone."

"I give you my word," she said, "it was Diarmuid himself. Take your hounds now and lay them on his track, and I'll send Finn and the Fianna of Ireland to you."

They left a woman-Druid attending on the three champions who were bound. They brought their three hounds out of the ship and laid them on Diarmuid's track, and followed them until they came to the mouth of the cave. They went into the far end of it and found the beds where Diarmuid and Grania had slept. Then they went on westward until they came to the Carrthach river, and to the bog of Finnliath, and so on to great Slieve Luachra.

Diarmuid did not know they were after him until he saw them coming, with their banners of soft silk, and their three wicked hounds at the front of the troop, and three strong champions holding them on chains. When he saw them coming like that, a great hatred of them filled him.

One of them, in a well-coloured green cloak, came out far ahead of the others.

Grania gave the knife back to Diarmuid.

"I think you haven't much love for that young man in the green cloak, Grania," said Diarmuid.

"I haven't indeed," said Grania. "And it would be better if I'd never given love to any man at all to this day."

It is the only time in the whole long story that she says it. She is tired, and hunted, and cutting her nails by a stream in the mountains, and she says it once.

Diarmuid put the knife in its sheath and went on. Muadhan put Grania on his back and carried her on into the mountain.

It was not long before one of the three hounds was loosed after Diarmuid.

Muadhan told him to go after Grania, and said he himself would check the hound. Then Muadhan turned back. He took a whelp out of his belt and put it on the flat of his hand. When the whelp saw the hound rushing towards it with its jaws open, it rose up and leapt from Muadhan's hand into the throat of the hound, and came out through its side, bringing the heart with it. Then it leapt back into Muadhan's hand, and left the hound dead behind it.

Fire would not burn those hounds, nor water drown them, nor weapons redden on them. Nobody had said anything about a whelp.

Muadhan went on after Diarmuid and Grania, and he took Grania up again and carried her a bit of the way into the mountain.

Then another hound was loosed after them.

"I've often heard," Diarmuid said to Muadhan, "that nothing can stand against weapons of Druid wounding, and the throat of no beast can be made safe from them. Will you stand now, while I put the Gae Dearg, the Red Spear, through that hound?"

Muadhan and Grania stopped to watch the cast. Diarmuid threw at the hound, and the spear went through its body and brought out its bowels. He took up the spear again, and they went on.

It was not long after that the third hound was loosed.

"This is the fiercest of them," said Grania, "and there's great fear on me. Mind yourself now, Diarmuid."

It was not long before the hound overtook them. The place it overtook them was Lic Dhubhain, the Flagstone of Dubhan, on Slieve Luachra. It rose with a light leap over Diarmuid, as if it meant to seize Grania. But Diarmuid took it by the two hind legs and struck its carcase against the side of the nearest rock, until he had let out its brains through the openings of its head and its ears.

Then Diarmuid took up his weapons and his battle-clothes, and put his narrow-topped finger into the silken string of the Gae Dearg, and made a good cast at the young man in the green cloak at the head of the troop, and killed him. Then he made another cast at the second man and killed him, and the third man the same way. And since it is not the custom to stand when the leaders have fallen, the strangers, when they saw what had happened, took to flight.

Diarmuid followed them, killing and scattering, so that unless some man of them got away over the forests, or into the green earth, or under the waters, there was not a man or a messenger of them left to tell the news — except the Woman-Messenger of the Black Mountain, who kept moving round about while Diarmuid was putting down the strangers.

It was not long before Finn saw her coming towards him where he was, her legs failing, her tongue muttering, her eyes drooping, and he asked her for news.

"It's very bad news I have to tell you," she said. "And it's my opinion I'm a person without a lord now."

Then she told Finn the whole story from beginning to end: of the destruction Diarmuid had done, and how the three deadly hounds had fallen by him.

"And it was hardly I got away myself," she said.

"Where did the grandson of Duibhne go?" said Finn.

"I don't know that," she said.

When Finn heard of the Kings of the Green Champions that Diarmuid had bound, he called his men to him, and they went by every short way and every straight path until they reached the hill. It was a torment to Finn's heart to see the state they were in.

"Oisin," he said, "loosen those three kings for me."

"I won't loosen them," said Oisin. "Diarmuid put bonds on me not to loosen any man he'd bind."

"Loosen them, Osgar," said Finn.

"I give my word," said Osgar, "I'd sooner put more bonds on them than loosen them."

Neither would Conan help them, nor Lugaidh's Son.

Four men in Ireland could have loosed them. Finn's son, and Finn's grandson, and his old enemy, and his own kinsman. Not one of them would lift a finger. That is how Finn learned where the Fianna's hearts were.

And in any case, they had not been talking about it long before the three kings died under the hardness of the bonds that were on them.

Then Finn made three wide-sodded graves for them. A flagstone was put over them, and another stone raised over that again, and their names were written in branching Ogham. And Finn was tired and heavy-hearted after that. He and his people went back to Almhuin of Leinster.

As for Diarmuid and Grania and Muadhan, they went on through Ui Chonaill Gabhra, and by left-hand ways to Ros-da-Shoileach. Diarmuid killed a wild deer that night, and they had their fill of meat and of pure water, and slept until the next morning.

Muadhan rose early and spoke to Diarmuid. He said he was going away.

"It's not right for you to do that," said Diarmuid. "Everything I promised you, I fulfilled without any dispute."

But he could not stop him. Muadhan said farewell to them and left them there and then. And Diarmuid and Grania were sorrowful and downhearted after him.

He had come from nowhere, and carried them over rivers, and fed them from a hook of holly, and killed a hound with a whelp from his belt. And he left. The story never tells us who he was. Some things that help you are not meant to be understood.

After that they travelled straight north to Slieve Echtge, and from there to the hundred of Ui Fiachrach. When they got there Grania was tired out, but she took courage and went on walking beside Diarmuid until they came to the wood of Dubhros.

There was a wonderful quicken-tree in that wood, and this is how it came to be there.

A dispute rose once between two women of the Tuatha de Danaan, Aine and Aoife, daughters of Manannan, son of Lir. Aoife had given her love to Lugaidh's Son, and Aine had given her love to a man of her own race, and each said her own man was the better hurler. Out of that dispute came a great hurling-match, set between the Men of Dea and the Fianna of Ireland, and the place it was to be played was a beautiful plain near Loch Lein.

They all came together there. The highest and most daring men of the Tuatha de Danaan were there: the three Garbhs of Slieve Mis, and the three Mases of Slieve Luachra, and the three yellow-haired Murchadhs, and the three Eochaidhs of Aine, and the three Fionns of the White House, and the three Sgals of Brugh na Boinne, and the three Ronans of Ath na Riogh, and the Suirgheach Suairc, the Pleasant Wooer from Lionan, and the Man of Sweet Speech from the Boinn, and Ilbrec the Many-Coloured, son of Manannan, and Neamhanach, son of Angus Og, and Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, and Manannan, son of Lir.

They and the Fianna played the match for three days and three nights, from Leamhain to the valley of the Fleisg, which is called the Crooked Valley of the Fianna, and neither side scored a goal. When the Tuatha de Danaan watching the game on either side of Leamhain saw how hard it was for their hurlers to win a goal against the Fianna, they thought it just as well to go away again without playing the game out.

The provisions the Men of Dea had brought with them from the Land of Promise were crimson nuts, and apples, and sweet-smelling rowan-berries. As they were passing through the district of Ui Fiachrach by the Muaidh, one of the rowan-berries fell from them, and a tree grew up from it.

There was virtue in its berries. No sickness or disease would ever come on anyone who ate them. Those who ate them would feel the liveliness of wine and the satisfaction of mead in them. Any old person of a hundred years who ate them would go back to being young again. And any young girl who ate them would grow into a flower of beauty.

After the tree had grown, it happened that some messengers of the Tuatha de Danaan were going through the wood of Dubhros. They heard a great noise of birds and bees, and went to where the noise was, and saw the beautiful Druid tree. They went back and told what they had seen. When all the chief men of the Tuatha de Danaan heard it, they knew the tree must have grown from a berry of the Land of the Ever-Living Living Ones. They asked among all their people until they found it was a young man of theirs, a musician, who had dropped the berry.

They agreed to send him in search of a man of Lochlann who would guard the tree by day and sleep in it by night. The women of the Sidhe were very downhearted to see him going from them, for there was no harper who could play half as sweetly on his harp as he could play on an ivy leaf.

He went on until he came to Lochlann. He sat down on a bank and sleep came on him, and he slept until sunrise the next day. When he woke, he saw a very big man coming towards him, who asked him who he was.

"I'm a messenger from the Men of Dea," he said. "I've come looking for some very strong man who'd be willing to guard a Druid tree in the wood of Dubhros. And here are some of the berries he'll be eating from morning to night."

When the big man had tasted the berries, he said: "I'll go and guard all the trees of the wood to get those berries."

His name was the Searbhan Lochlannach, the Surly One of Lochlann. He was very black and ugly, with crooked teeth and only one eye, in the middle of his forehead. He had a thick collar of iron around his body. And it was in the prophecy that he would never die until three strokes of his own iron club were struck upon him.

That is the rule of the Surly One. Nothing kills him but his own club. Three strokes of it. No fewer.

He slept in the tree by night and stayed near it in the daytime, and he made a wilderness of the whole district around him, and none of the Fianna dared go hunting there, for dread of him.

But when Diarmuid came to the wood of Dubhros, he went into it to where the Surly One was, and made a bond of agreement with him, and got leave from him to hunt in the wood, as long as he did not touch the berries of the tree. Then he made a cabin in the wood for himself and for Grania.

As for Finn and his people, they had not been long at Almhuin when they saw fifty armed men coming towards them, with two at the front who were taller and handsomer than the rest. Finn asked whether any of his people knew them.

"We don't know them," they said, "but maybe you know them yourself, Finn."

"I don't," he said. "But it seems to me they're enemies of mine."

The troop of armed men came up and greeted him, and Finn asked them for news, and what country they came from.

"I'm Aonghus, son of Art Og, of the children of Morna," said one of them, "and this is Aodh, son of Andela. We're enemies of yours. Our fathers were at the killing of your father, and they died themselves for that deed. It's to ask for peace we've come to you now."

"Where were you when my father was killed?" said Finn.

"In our mothers' wombs," they said. "And our mothers were two women of the Tuatha de Danaan. It's time for us now to get our fathers' place among the Fianna."

"I'll give you that," said Finn, "but I must put a fine on you first, in satisfaction for my father's death."

"We have neither gold nor silver nor goods nor cattle to give you, Finn," they said.

"Don't put a fine on them, Finn," said Oisin, "beyond the death of their fathers for your father."

"It's my opinion," said Finn, "that if anyone killed me, Oisin, it would be easy to pay the fine you'd ask. No one comes among the Fianna without giving what I ask in satisfaction for my father's death."

"What is it you're asking of us?" said Aonghus, son of Art Og.

"I'm asking only the head of a champion," said Finn, "or the full of a fist of the berries of the quicken-tree at Dubhros."

Once, Lugh asked a fine that sounded small, of men who had killed his father. You remember how that went. Finn remembered too. He had Lugh's blood in him.

"I'll give you good advice, children of Morna," said Oisin. "Go back to the place you were reared, and don't ask Finn for peace for the length of your lives. It's no easy thing Finn is asking of you. Do you know whose head he's asking you to bring him?"

"We don't," they said.

"The head of Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, is the head he's asking of you. And if you were twenty hundred men in your full strength, Diarmuid wouldn't let you take that head."

"And what are the berries Finn is asking of us?" they said.

"There's nothing harder for you to get than those berries," said Oisin.

Then he told them the whole story of the tree, and of the Searbhan, the Surly One of Lochlann, who had been set to mind it by the Tuatha de Danaan.

But Aodh, son of Andela, said he would sooner get his death looking for those berries than go home again to his mother's country. He asked Oisin to look after his people until he came back, and if anything should happen to him and his brother on their journey, to send them back to the Land of Promise.

The two of them said farewell to Oisin and to the chief men of the Fianna, and went on until they reached Dubhros. They went along the wood until they found a track, and followed it to the door of the hunting-cabin where Diarmuid and Grania were.

Diarmuid heard them coming, and put his hand on his weapons and asked who was at the door.

"We're of the children of Morna," they said. "Aodh, son of Andela, and Aonghus, son of Art Og."

"What brings you to this wood?" said Diarmuid.

"Finn, son of Cumhal, has set us looking for your head, if you're Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne," they said.

"I am indeed," said Diarmuid.

"If that's so," they said, "Finn will take nothing from us but your head, or a fistful of the berries of the quicken-tree of Dubhros, as satisfaction for the death of his father."

"It's not easy for you to get either of those things," said Diarmuid. "And it's a pity for anyone to be under that man's power. Besides, I know it was he himself made an end of your fathers, and that was satisfaction enough for him to get. And if you do bring him what he asks, it's likely he won't make peace with you in the end."

"Isn't it enough for you," said Aodh, "to have taken his wife away from Finn, without speaking ill of him?"

"It's not for the sake of speaking ill of him I said that," said Diarmuid, "but to save you from the danger he's sent you into."

"What are those berries Finn is asking for," said Grania, "that they can't be got for him?"

Diarmuid told her the whole story of the berry the Tuatha de Danaan had lost, and the tree that had sprung up from it, and the man of Lochlann who was keeping the tree.

"When Finn sent me hiding here and became my enemy," he said, "I got leave from the Surly One to hunt. But he told me never to meddle with the berries. And now, sons of Morna, there's your choice: to fight me for my head, or to go and ask the Surly One for the berries."

"I swear by the blood of my people," said each of them, "I'll fight you first."

With that the two young men made ready for the fight. They chose to fight with the strength of their hands alone. And Diarmuid put them down and bound the two of them there and then.

"That's a good fight you made," said Grania. "But by my word, though the children of Morna don't go looking for those berries, I won't lie in a bed ever again until I get a share of them. And I won't live if I don't get them."

She had never asked him for anything, in all that long hunt. This was the one thing. It was the one thing he could not give without breaking his word.

"Don't make me break my peace with the Surly One," said Diarmuid. "He won't let me take them."

"Loose these bindings off us," said the two young men, "and we'll go with you, and give ourselves for your sake."

"You mustn't come with me," said Diarmuid. "If you got the full of your eyes of that terrible one, you'd be more likely to die than to live."

"Well, do us this kindness, then," they said. "Loosen these bonds on us, and let us go by ourselves and see the fight, before you strike off our heads."

So Diarmuid did that for them.

Then Diarmuid went to the Surly One. He happened to be asleep. Diarmuid gave him a push with his foot, so that he lifted his head and looked up at him.

"Have you a mind to break our peace, Grandson of Duibhne?" he said.

"That's not what I want," said Diarmuid. "But Grania, daughter of the High King, has a desire to taste those berries, and it's to ask a handful of them I've come."

"I give my word," said the Surly One, "if she's to die for it, she'll never taste a berry of those berries."

"I wouldn't do treachery on you," said Diarmuid. "So I'm telling you: willing or unwilling, I'll take those berries from you."

Even here. He warned him first. He would not take so much as a berry by surprise.

When the Surly One heard that he got up on his feet, and lifted his club, and struck three great blows on Diarmuid that gave him some small hurt in spite of his shield. But when Diarmuid saw him not minding himself, he threw down his own weapons and made a great leap and took hold of the club with his two hands. And when he had hold of the club, he struck the Surly One three great blows with it that put his brains out through his head.

Three strokes of his own club. The prophecy was kept.

The two young men of the sons of Morna had watched the whole fight, and when they saw the Surly One was killed, they came out.

Diarmuid sat down, for he was spent with the force of the fight. He told the young men to bury the body under the thickets of the wood, so that Grania would not see it. "And after that," he said, "go back to her and bring her here."

So they dragged the body away and buried it, and then went for Grania and brought her to Diarmuid.

"There are the berries you were asking for, Grania," he said. "You may take what you like of them now."

"I give my word," said Grania, "I won't taste a berry of those berries except the one your own hand plucks, Diarmuid."

Diarmuid got up and plucked the berries for Grania, and for the children of Morna, and they ate their fill.

"Take all you can of these berries," he said to the young men, "and bring them with you to Finn, and tell him it was you made an end of the Surly One of Lochlann."

"We give you our word," they said, "we begrudge giving any of them to Finn."

But Diarmuid plucked a load of the berries for them, and they thanked him greatly for all he had done, and went back to where Finn was with the Fianna.

Diarmuid and Grania went up into the top of the tree, where the Surly One's bed was. The berries below were only bitter berries beside the ones above, in the tree.

When the two young men came to Finn, he asked them for their news.

"We've killed the Surly One of Lochlann," they said, "and we've brought you berries from the quicken-tree of Dubhros in satisfaction for your father, so that we may get peace from you."

They gave the berries into Finn's hand. He knew them.

"I give you my word," he said to the young men, "it was Diarmuid himself plucked those berries, for I know the smell of his hand on them. I know well it was he killed the Surly One. I'll go now and see whether he himself is alive at the quicken-tree."

He knew the smell of Diarmuid's hand. That is how close they had been. That is what makes the rest of this so hard.

After that he called for the seven battalions of the Fianna, and set out and went forward to Dubhros. They followed Diarmuid's track to the foot of the quicken-tree, and found the berries without anyone to guard them, and ate their fill of them.

The great heat of the day came on them, and Finn said they would stay where they were until the heat was past. "For I know well," he said, "that Diarmuid is up in the quicken-tree."

"It's a great sign of jealousy in you, Finn," said Oisin, "to think Diarmuid would stay up there in the quicken-tree when he knows you want to kill him."

Finn asked for a chessboard after that. "I'll play a game with you now on this," he said to Oisin.

They sat down, Oisin and Osgar and Lugaidh's Son and Diorraing on one side of the board, and Finn on the other.

They played that game with great skill and knowledge. Finn pressed Oisin so hard that he had no move left but one.

"There's one move would win the game for you, Oisin," said Finn, "and I defy all who are with you to show you that move."

Then Diarmuid said, up in the tree where he was, so that no one heard him but Grania: "It's a pity you're in straits, and me not there to show you that move."

"You're worse off yourself," said Grania, "in the bed of the Surly One of Lochlann at the top of the quicken-tree, with the seven battalions of the Fianna all round it to take your life."

But Diarmuid took a berry from the tree, and aimed it at the chessman that ought to be moved. Oisin moved it, and turned the game against Finn with that move.

It was not long before the game was going against Oisin a second time. When Diarmuid saw that he threw another berry at the chessman it was right to move, and Oisin moved it and turned the game against Finn the same way.

The third time Finn was getting the game from Oisin, Diarmuid threw the third berry on the man that would give Oisin the game. And the Fianna gave a great shout when the game was won.

He could not help himself. It was his friend, losing, and he knew the move.

Then Finn spoke. "It's no wonder you win the game, Oisin," he said, "with the help of Osgar, and the watchfulness of Diorraing, and the skill of Lugaidh's Son, and the teaching of the grandson of Duibhne with you."

"That's a great sign of jealousy in you, Finn," said Osgar, "to think Diarmuid would stay in this tree with you so near him."

"Which of us has the truth, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne," Finn called out, "myself or Osgar?"

"You never lost your good judgment, Finn," said Diarmuid. "Grania and I are here, in the bed of the Surly One of Lochlann."

Then Diarmuid stood up and gave Grania three kisses, in the sight of Finn and the Fianna.

A scorching jealousy and a weakness came on Finn when he saw it.

"It was worse to me, Diarmuid," he said, "that the seven battalions of the Fianna saw what you did at Teamhair, taking Grania away the night you were yourself my guard. But for all that, you'll give your head for the sake of those three kisses."

With that Finn called on the four hundred paid fighting men he had with him to make an end of Diarmuid. He put their hands into one another's hands in a ring around that quicken-tree, and told them that if they wanted to keep their lives, they must not let Diarmuid pass out through them. And he said that to whatever man took Diarmuid he would give his weapons and his armour, and a place among the Fianna of Ireland.

Then one of the Fianna, Garbh of Slieve Cua, said it was Diarmuid had killed his own father, and he would avenge him now. And he went up the quicken-tree to make an end of him.

About that time it was made known to Angus Og in Brugh na Boinne what danger Diarmuid was in, and he came to his help, unknown to the Fianna.
