When Garbh of Slieve Cua was coming up the tree, Diarmuid gave him a kick of his foot, and he fell down among the hired men. And they struck his head off, for Angus Og had put the appearance of Diarmuid on him. After he was killed his own shape came back on him, and the Fianna knew it was Garbh who had been killed.

Then Garbh of Slieve Crot said it was Diarmuid who had killed his father, and he went up to avenge him, and the same thing happened. And in the end all nine Garbhs — of Slieve Cua, and Slieve Crot, and Slieve Guaire, and Slieve Muice, and Slieve Mor, and Slieve Lugha, and Ath Fraoch, and Slieve Mis, and Drom-mor — went up trying to take Diarmuid's life, and lost their own. Every one of them had the shape and appearance of Diarmuid when he died.

Nine times, Finn watched Diarmuid die. Nine times, it was someone else.

Finn was very sorry and discouraged when he saw that these nine men had come to their death.

Then Angus said he would take Grania away with him.

"Do," said Diarmuid. "And if I'm living at evening, I'll follow you."

Angus said farewell to Diarmuid, and put his Druid cloak about Grania and about himself, and they went away in the safety of the cloak, unknown to Finn and the Fianna, until they came to Brugh na Boinne.

Then Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, spoke.

"I'll come down to you, Finn, and to the Fianna," he said. "And I'll do death and destruction on you and on your people. I'm certain your mind is made up to give me no rest, but to bring me to my death in some place. And I have nowhere to go from this danger. I have no friend or comrade under whose protection I could go, in any far part of the great world, for I've often fought against the men of the great world for love of you. There never came battle or fight, danger or trouble on you, but I'd go into it for your sake and the sake of the Fianna. And not only that, but I'd fight in front of you and behind you. And I give my word, Finn, you'll pay hard for me. You won't get me as a free gift."

"It's the truth Diarmuid is speaking," said Osgar. "Give him forgiveness now, and peace."

"I won't do that," said Finn, "to the end of life and time. He'll never get peace or rest until I get satisfaction from him for every reproach he's put on me."

"It's a great shame and a great sign of jealousy for you to say that," said Osgar. "And I give the word of a true champion: unless the skies come down on me, or the earth opens under my feet, I won't let you or any one of the Fianna of Ireland give him cut or wound. I take his body and his life under the protection of my valour, and I'll keep him safe against all the men of Ireland."

Osgar, who would rather die than be helped, putting his whole life between his friend and his grandfather.

"Those are big words you have, Osgar," said Goll, "to say you'd bring a man away in spite of all the men of Ireland."

"It's not you will raise them up against me, Goll," said Osgar. "None of them would mind what you'd say."

"If that's what you're saying, you champion of great fights," said Goll, "let's see now what you can do."

"You'll have to go through with the fight you've taken on yourself," said Corrioll, son of Goll, in a loud voice.

And Osgar answered him fiercely: "If I do, I'll shorten your bones, and your father's bones along with them. Come down now, Diarmuid, since Finn has no mind to leave you in peace, and I promise on my body and my life no harm will be done to you today."

Then Diarmuid stood up on a high bough of the tree, and rose with a light leap by the shaft of his spear, and landed on the grass far beyond Finn and the Fianna. He and Osgar went towards each other, in spite of the Fianna who came between them. Diarmuid struck down those who were in his way. As for Osgar, the throwing of his spears as he scattered the Fianna was like the sound of the wind going through a valley, or water falling over flagstones.

And Conan, who was always bitter, said: "Let the sons of Baiscne go on killing one another."

But when Finn saw that Diarmuid was gone from him, he told them to put up their weapons and turn back again to Almhuin.

He sent those of his men who could be healed to places of healing. The nine Garbhs, and the others of his men who had been killed, he put into wide-sodded graves. He was tired and downhearted and sorrowful after that. And he swore an oath that he would take no great rest until he had avenged on Diarmuid everything he had done.

As for Osgar and Diarmuid, they went on, without cut or wound on them, to where Angus and Grania were at Brugh na Boinne. There was a good welcome for them, and Diarmuid told them the whole story from beginning to end. It was a wonder Grania did not die there and then, hearing all he had gone through.

Then she and Diarmuid set out again, and they went and stayed a while in a cave near the sea.

One night while they were there a great storm came on, so that they went into the far part of the cave. Bad as the night was, a man of the Fomor came over the western ocean in a currach with two oars, and drew it into the cave for shelter. Ciach, the Fierce One, was his name.

Diarmuid made him welcome, and they sat down to play chess together. Ciach got the best of the game. What he asked for his winnings was Grania, to be his wife. And he put his arms around her, as if to carry her away.

"I've been this long time going with the third best man of the Fianna," said Grania, "and he never came as near to me as that."

She said it in front of both of them. It was not a thing that could be taken back.

Diarmuid took his sword to kill Ciach. There was anger on Grania when she saw that. She had a knife in her hand, and she struck it into Diarmuid's thigh.

Diarmuid made an end of the Fomor. He said no word to Grania, but ran out and away through the storm.

Grania went after him, calling to him. But there was great anger on him, and he would not answer her.

At last, at the break of day, she caught up with him. After a while they heard the cry of a heron, and she asked him what had made the heron cry out.

"Tell me that," she said, "Grandson of Duibhne, to whom I gave my love."

"O Grania, daughter of the High King," said Diarmuid, "woman who never took a step right: it's because she was frozen to the rocks she gave that cry."

Grania was asking his forgiveness, and he was reproaching her, and this is what he said:

"O Grania of the beautiful hair, though you are more beautiful than the green tree in blossom, your love passes away as quickly as the cold cloud at break of day. You are asking a hard thing of me now. And it is a pity, what you said to me, Grania, for it was you brought me away from the house of my lord, so that I am banished from it to this day; and now I am troubled through the night, fretting after its delight in every place.

"I am like a wild deer, or a beast gone astray, going ever and always through the long valleys; there is great longing on me to see one of my kindred from the host.

"I left my own people, who were brighter than lime or snow. Their heart was full of generosity to me, like the sun that is high above us. But now they follow me angrily, to every harbour and every strand.

"I lost my people by you, and my lord, and my large bright ships on every sea. I lost my treasure and my gold. It is hunger you gave me, through your love.

"I lost my country and my kindred, my men who used to serve me. I lost quietness and affection. I lost the men of Ireland and the Fianna entirely.

"I lost delight and music. I lost my own right-doing and my honour. I lost the Fianna of Ireland, my great kinsmen, for the sake of the love you gave me.

"O Grania, white as snow, it would have been a better choice for you to have given hatred to me, or gentleness to the Head of the Fianna."

It is all true. Every word of it. And she did not choose the love-spot any more than he did.

And Grania said:

"O Diarmuid of the face like snow, or like the down of the mountains, the sound of your voice was dearer to me than all the riches of the leader of the Fianna.

"Your blue eye is dearer to me than his strength, and his gold and his great hall. The love-spot on your forehead is better to me than honey in streams. The time I first looked on it, it was more to me than the whole host of the King of Ireland.

"My heart fell down there and then before your high beauty. When you came beside me, it was like the whole of life in one day.

"O Diarmuid of the beautiful hands, take me now the same as before. It was with me the fault was, entirely. Give me your promise not to leave me."

But Diarmuid said:

"How can I take you again? You are a woman too fond of words. One day you give up the Head of the Fianna, and the next day me — and no lie in it.

"It is you parted me from Finn, so that I fell under sorrow and grief. And then you left me yourself, when I was full of affection."

And Grania said: "Don't leave me this way now, with my love for you ever growing, like the fresh branches of the tree in the kind long heat of the day."

But Diarmuid would not give in to her. "You're a woman full of words," he said, "and it's you have put me under sorrow. I took you with me, and you struck at me for the sake of the man of the Fomor."

They came then to a place where there was a cave, with water running by it, and they stopped to rest.

"Have you a mind to eat bread and meat now, Diarmuid?" said Grania.

"I'd eat it indeed if I had it," said Diarmuid.

"Give me a knife, then," she said, "so I can cut it."

"Look for the knife in the sheath where you put it yourself," said Diarmuid.

Then she saw that the knife was still in his thigh, where she had struck it. He would not draw it out himself.

All night, running through a storm with her knife in him. And he would not pull it out, so that she would have to.

So she drew it out. And that was the greatest shame that ever came on her.

They stayed then in the cave.

And the next day, when they went on again, Diarmuid did not leave unbroken bread behind him, as he had left every other day as a sign to Finn that he had kept faith with him.

It was broken bread he left behind him.

Somewhere behind them, Finn found it, and knew.

They went on wandering after that all through Ireland, hiding from Finn in every place, sleeping under the cromlechs, or with no shelter at all. There was no place they dared stay long in.

Wherever they went, Finn followed them, for he knew by his divination where they went. But once he made out that they were on a mountain, for he saw them with heather under them. In fact they were beside the sea, asleep on heather that Diarmuid had brought down from the hills for their bed. So Finn went searching the hills, and did not find them.

That is why, in Ireland, the old stones are called the Beds of Diarmuid and Grania. There are a great many of them. They moved a great deal.

Grania would watch over Diarmuid while he slept, and she would make a sleepy song for him. This is what she would say:

"Sleep a little, a little little, for there is nothing at all to fear, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne. Sleep here soundly, soundly, Diarmuid, to whom I have given my love.

"It is I will keep watch for you, grandchild of shapely Duibhne. Sleep a little, a blessing on you, beside the well of the strong field; my lamb from above the lake, from the banks of the strong streams.

"Let your sleep be like the sleep in the South of Dedidach of the high poets, the time he took away old Morann's daughter, for all Conall could do against him.

"Let your sleep be like the sleep in the North of fair, comely Fionnchadh of Ess Ruadh, the time he took Slaine with bravery, as we think, in spite of Failbhe of the Hard Head.

"Let your sleep be like the sleep in the West of Aine, daughter of Gailian, the time she went on a journey in the night with Dubhthach from Doirinis, by the light of torches.

"Let your sleep be like the sleep in the East of Deaghadh the proud, the brave fighter, the time he took Coincheann, daughter of Binn, in spite of fierce Decheall of Duibhreann.

"O heart of the valour of the lands to the west of Greece, my heart will go near to breaking if I do not see you every day. The parting of us two will be the parting of two children of the one house; it will be the parting of life from the body, Diarmuid, hero of the bright lake of Carman."

Then, to rouse him, she would make another song, and this is what she would say:

"Caoinche will be loosed on your track; it is not slow the running of Caoilte will be. Do not let death reach you; do not give yourself to sleep for ever.

"The stag to the east is not asleep; he does not stop from bellowing. Though he is in the woods of the blackbirds, sleep is not in his mind. The hornless doe is not asleep, crying after her speckled fawn; she is going over the bushes; she does not sleep in her home.

"The cuckoo is not asleep; the thrush is not asleep; the tops of the trees are a noisy place. The duck is not asleep; she is made ready for good swimming. The bog lark is not asleep tonight on the high stormy bogs; the sound of her clear voice is sweet; she is not sleeping between the streams."

Two songs. One to put him to sleep, and one to wake him. She was the one who kept the watch. She was the one who knew what it cost to sleep.

Once they were in a cave of Beinn Edair, and there was an old woman befriending them, helping them keep watch. One day she happened to go up to the top of Beinn Edair, and she saw an armed man coming towards her. She did not know he was Finn. When he came near, she asked what he was looking for.

"I've come looking for a woman," he said, "and for a woman's love. Will you do everything I ask you?"

"I'll do that," she said. For she thought it was her own love he was asking for.

"Tell me, then," he said, "where is Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne?"

So she told him where he was hiding. And he told her to keep Diarmuid in the cave until he came back with his men.

It was a cruel trick, and it was Finn who played it. He had become a man who would play it.

The old woman went back. This is what she did: she dipped her cloak in the sea-water before she went into the cave.

Diarmuid asked her why her cloak was so wet.

"Because I never saw or heard of the like of this day for cold and for storms," she said. "There's frost on every hillside. There isn't a smooth plain in all Elga without a long rushing river between every two ridges. There isn't a deer or a crow in the whole of Ireland that can find shelter anywhere."

She was shaking the wet off her cloak and complaining of the cold, and this is what she said:

"Cold, cold, cold tonight is the wide plain of Lurg; the snow is higher than the mountains; the deer cannot get at their share of food.

"Cold for ever; the storm is spread over all. Every furrow on the hillside is a river, every ford is a full pool, every full loch is a great sea, every pool is a full loch. Horses cannot go through the ford of Ross, any more than a man on his two feet.

"The fishes of Inisfail are going astray; there is no strand and no pen against the waves; there are no dwellings in the country; there is no bell heard; no crane is calling.

"The hounds of the wood of Cuan find no rest and no sleep in their dwelling-place; the little wren cannot find shelter in her nest on the slope of Lon.

"A sharp wind and cold ice have come on the little company of birds; the blackbird cannot get a ridge to her liking, or shelter for her side, in the woods of Cuan.

"Steady our great pot hangs from its hook; broken is the cabin on the slope of Lon; the snow has made the woods smooth; it is hard to climb to the ridge of Bennait Bo.

"The ancient bird of Glen Ride gets grief from the bitter wind; great is her misery and her pain; the ice will be in her mouth.

"Mind well not to rise up from coverings and from down. Mind this well; there would be no good sense in it. Ice is heaped up in every ford. It is for that I am saying, and ever saying, 'Cold.'"

It was a beautiful poem. Treachery often is.

The old woman went out after that. When she was gone, Grania took hold of the cloak she had left behind and put her tongue to it, and found the taste of salt water on it.

"My grief, Diarmuid," she said. "The old woman has betrayed us. Get up now and put on your fighting-suit."

Grania. Again. She is the one who notices.

So Diarmuid did that, and went out, and Grania with him. No sooner were they outside than they saw Finn and the Fianna of Ireland coming towards them.

Diarmuid looked about him and saw a little boat close by, in the shelter of the harbour, and he and Grania got into it. There was a man in the boat ahead of them, with beautiful clothes on him, and a wide, embroidered, golden-yellow cloak over his shoulders behind. They knew it was Angus, who had come again to help them escape from Finn.

They went back with him for a while to Brugh na Boinne. And Osgar came to them there.

After a while Finn told his people to make his ship ready and put a store of food and drink in it. They did that, and he and a thousand of his men went into the ship. They were nine days, between sailing and rowing, before they came to harbour in the north of Alban.

They tied the ship to the posts of the harbour, and Finn and five of his people went to the dun of the King of Alban. Finn struck a blow with the hand-wood on the door. The door-keeper asked who was there, and they told him it was Finn, son of Cumhal.

"Let him in," said the king.

Finn and his people went in, and the king made them welcome and told Finn to sit in his own place, and they were given strong, pleasant drinks. And the king sent for the rest of Finn's people and made them welcome to the dun.

Then Finn told what had brought him there: that he had come to ask for help and advice against the grandson of Duibhne.

"And you have a right to give me your help," he said, "for it was he killed your father and your two brothers, and many of your best men along with them."

"That's true," said the king. "I'll give you my own two sons, and a thousand men with each of them."

Finn was glad to hear that. He and his men took their leave of the king and his household, and left wishes for life and health with them, and the king did the same by them.

It was near Brugh na Boinne that Finn and his people came to land. Finn sent messengers to the house of Angus to give out a challenge of battle against Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne.

"What should I do about this, Osgar?" said Diarmuid.

"We'll both go out and make a stand against them," said Osgar, "and we won't let a serving-man of them escape. We'll make an end of them all."

So they rose the next morning and put their battle-suits on their comely bodies. It would be a pity for anyone, many or few, who met those two men with their anger on them. They bound the rims of their shields together, so that they would not be parted from each other in the fight.

The sons of the King of Alban said they and their people would go first to meet them. They came ashore and made a rush at Diarmuid and Osgar. But the two fought so well that they beat them back and scattered them, and made a great slaughter, and put great terror on them, until at last there was not a man left to stand against them.

Two men, with their shields tied together. Two thousand, and the king's two sons. It was not close.

After that Finn went out on the sea again with his people, and there is no word of them until they came to the Land of Promise, where Finn's nurse was.

When she saw Finn coming she was very joyful. Finn told her the whole story from beginning to end, and the cause of his quarrel with Diarmuid. He said he had come to ask her advice, and that it was not possible to put Diarmuid down by the strength of any army, unless enchantment put him down.

"I'll go with you," said the old woman, "and I'll do enchantment on him."

Finn was very glad to hear that. He stayed there that night, and they set out for Ireland in the morning.

When they came to Brugh na Boinne, the nurse put a Druid mist around Finn and the Fianna, so that nobody would know they were there.

The day before, Osgar had parted from Diarmuid, and Diarmuid was out hunting by himself. That was shown to the hag. She took a water-lily leaf with a hole in it, like the eye of a millstone, and rose up on it by her enchantments on a blast of Druid wind, above Diarmuid. And she began to aim deadly spears at him through the hole, until she had done him great harm, for all his weapons and his armour. He could not get away, he was so hard pressed. Every danger he had ever been in was small beside that danger.

And he thought: unless I can strike the old woman through the hole in that leaf, she'll give me my death here and now.

He lay down on his back with the Gae Dearg, the Red Spear, in his hand, and made a great cast of the spear. It went through the hole, and the hag fell dead on the spot.

A hole the size of a millstone's eye, in a leaf, on the wind. That is a cast to remember.

He struck off her head and brought it back with him to Angus Og.

Early the next morning Angus got up and went to where Finn was, and asked him whether he would make peace with Diarmuid, and Finn said he would. Then Angus went to the King of Ireland to ask peace for Diarmuid, and the king said he would agree to it.

Then he went back to where Diarmuid and Grania were, and asked Diarmuid whether he would make peace with the High King and with Finn.

"I'm willing," said Diarmuid, "if they'll give the conditions I ask."

"What conditions are those?" said Angus.

"The district my father had," said Diarmuid, "that is, the district of Ui Duibhne, without right of hunting to Finn, and without rent or tribute to the King of Ireland. And with that, the district of Dumhais in Leinster, for they're the best in Ireland. And the district of Ceis Corainn from the King of Ireland, as a marriage-portion with his daughter. Those are the conditions on which I'll make peace with them."

"Would you be peaceable if you got those conditions?" said Angus.

"It would go easier with me to make peace if I got them," said Diarmuid.

Angus went with that news to where the King of Ireland was with Finn. They gave him every one of those conditions. And they forgave him all he had done through the whole time he had been in hiding, which was sixteen years.

Sixteen years. Think of it. Sixteen years of never sleeping where you ate.

The place Diarmuid and Grania settled in was Rath Grania, in the district of Ceis Corainn, far away from Finn and from Teamhair. Grania bore him children there, four sons and one daughter. They lived there in peace. And people used to say there was not a man living in his time who was richer in gold and silver, in cattle and in sheep, than Diarmuid.

It was a good peace, and it lasted a long time. It was not the end of the story. But for a while it was allowed to feel like one.

But at last, one day, Grania spoke to Diarmuid.

She said it was a shame on them, with all the people and the household they had, and all their riches, that the two best men in Ireland had never come to their house: the High King, her father, and Finn, son of Cumhal.

"Why do you say that, Grania," said Diarmuid, "when they're enemies of mine?"

"What I'd wish," said Grania, "is to give them a feast, so that you'd get their affection."

"I give leave for that," said Diarmuid.

She wanted her father at her table. She wanted Finn at peace. She wanted, perhaps, to be forgiven. There is nothing wrong in any of that. It is how the end began.

So Grania spent the length of a year making ready a great feast. Messengers were sent for the High King of Ireland, and for Finn and the seven battalions of the Fianna, and they came, and they were at the feast from day to day for the length of a year.

On the last night of the year Diarmuid was asleep at Rath Grania. In the night, through his sleep, he heard the voice of hounds. He started up. Grania caught him and put her two arms around him and asked what had startled him.

"It was the voice of a hound I heard," he said. "And it's a wonder to me to hear that in the night."

"Safe keeping on you," said Grania. "It's the Tuatha de Danaan doing that to you, on account of Angus of Brugh na Boinn. Lie down on the bed again."

But for all that, no sleep came to him. He heard the voice of the hound again, and started up a second time to go after it. Grania caught hold of him the second time and told him to lie down, and said it was no fitting thing to go after the voice of a hound in the night.

So he lay down again and fell asleep. But the voice of the hound woke him a third time. The day had come with its full light by then.

"I'll go after the voice of the hound now," he said, "since the day is here."

"If that's so," said Grania, "bring the Mor-alltach, the Great Fierce One, the sword of Manannan, with you, and the Gae Dearg."

"I won't," he said. "I'll take the Beag-alltach, the Little Fierce One, and the Gae Buidhe in one hand, and the hound Mac an Chuill, the Son of the Hazel, in the other."

Remember what she told him to take. Remember what he took instead.

Then Diarmuid went out of Rath Grania and made no delay until he came to the top of Beinn Gulbain. He found Finn there before him, with nobody at all in his company.

Diarmuid gave him no greeting, but asked him whether it was he who was making that hunt.

Finn said it was not a hunt he was making. He and some of the Fianna had gone out after midnight. "And one of our hounds that was loose beside us came on the track of a wild boar," he said, "and they haven't been able to bring him back yet. There's no use following that boar he's after. The Fianna have hunted him many a time, and he's got away from them every time until now, and he's killed thirty of them this morning. He's coming up the mountain towards us. Let's leave this hill to him now."

"I won't leave the hill for fear of him," said Diarmuid.

"It would be best for you, Diarmuid," said Finn. "It's the earless Green Boar of Beinn Gulbain that's in it. It's by him you'll come to your death. And Angus knew that well when he put bonds on you not to go hunting pigs."

"I never knew of those bonds," said Diarmuid. "But however it is, I won't leave here for fear of him. And leave Bran with me now, along with Mac an Chuill."

"I won't," said Finn. "She's often met this boar before, and could do nothing against him."

He went away then, and left Diarmuid alone on the top of the hill.

"I give my word," said Diarmuid, "you made this hunt for my death, Finn. And if it's here I'm to find my death, there's no use in my going aside from it now."

The earless boar. The Steward's son. His own half-brother, with a bond on him to kill Diarmuid, and a life no longer than Diarmuid's life. It had been waiting since before Diarmuid could walk.

The boar came up the face of the mountain then, with the Fianna after him.

Diarmuid loosed Mac an Chuill from his leash. That did not serve him. The hound did not wait for the boar, but ran from him.

"It's a pity not to follow the advice of a good woman," said Diarmuid. "Grania told me this morning to bring the Mor-alltach and the Gae Dearg with me."

Then he put his finger into the silken string of the Gae Buidhe, and took a straight aim at the boar, and hit him full in the face. The spear did not give him so much as a scratch.

Diarmuid was discouraged by that. But he drew the Beag-alltach and made a full stroke at the boar's back. That did not wound him either. It broke the sword in two.

The Yellow Spear, and the Little Fierce One. The lesser weapons. The Red Spear and the Great Fierce One were hanging on the wall at Rath Grania.

Then the boar made a brave charge at Diarmuid that cut the sod from under his feet and brought him down. But Diarmuid caught hold of the boar as he rose, and held on to him, with a leg on each side of him and his face to the boar's hindquarters. The boar went headlong down the hill, but could not rid himself of Diarmuid. He went on to Ess Ruadh, and when he came to the red stream he gave three high leaps over it, backwards and forwards, but he could not put Diarmuid off his back. And he went back by the same path until he was up on the height of the mountain again.

At last, on the top of the mountain, he freed himself, and Diarmuid fell on the ground. Then the boar made a rush at him and ripped him open, so that his bowels came out about his feet.

But Diarmuid, with the hilt of the broken sword still in his hand, made a cast at him that dashed out his brains, so that he fell dead there and then.

And Rath na h-Amhrann, the Rath of the Sword-Hilt, is the name of that place to this day.

Two brothers, on a mountain, dying of each other.

It was not long before Finn and the Fianna of Ireland came to the place, and the pains of death were coming on Diarmuid.

"I'm well pleased to see you that way, Diarmuid," said Finn. "And it's a pity all the women of Ireland aren't looking at you now. For your great beauty is turned to ugliness, and your comely shape to uncomeliness."

"For all that, you have the power to heal me, Finn," said Diarmuid, "if you had a mind to."

"How could I heal you?" said Finn.

"Easily enough," said Diarmuid. "When you were given the great gift of knowledge at the Boinn, you got this gift with it: that anyone you gave a drink to out of the palms of your hands would be young and well again from any sickness after it."

That is the rule of Finn's hands. Water carried in them heals. It is the one power in this whole story that could have ended it well.

"You don't deserve that drink from me," said Finn.

"That's not true," said Diarmuid. "It's well I deserve it from you. The time you went to the house of Dearc, son of Donnarthadh, with your chief men, for a feast, your enemies came round the house and gave three great shouts against you, and threw fire and firebrands into it. You got up and would have gone out. But I told you to stay there at your drinking and pleasure, for I'd go out myself and put them down. And I went out, and put out the flames, and made three red rushes round the house, and killed fifty in every rush, and came in again without a wound. And you were glad and merry and in good courage that night, Finn. If it was that night I'd asked you for a drink, you'd have given it. And it would be right for you to give it to me now."

"That's not so," said Finn. "It's badly you've earned a drink or any good thing from me. The night you went to Teamhair with me, you took Grania away from me in the presence of all the men of Ireland, and you my own guard over her that night."

"Don't blame me for that, Finn," said Diarmuid. "What did I ever do against you, east or west, but that one thing? And you know well Grania put bonds on me, and I wouldn't fail in my bonds for the gold of the whole world.

"And you'll know I've well earned a drink from you, if you bring to mind the night the feast was made in the House of the Quicken Tree, and how you and all your men were bound there until I heard of it, and came fighting and joyful, and loosed you with my own blood and with the blood of the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods. If I'd asked you for a drink that night, Finn, you wouldn't have refused it.

"And I was with you at the smiting of Lon, son of Liobhan. You're the man who should not forsake me beyond any other man. Many is the strait that has overtaken you and the Fianna of Ireland since I came among you, and I was ready every time to put my body and my life in danger for your sake. You ought not to do this unkindness on me now.

"And besides that, many a good champion has fallen through the things you yourself have done, and there's no end of them yet. Great misfortunes will soon come on the Fianna, and few of their seed will be left after them. And it's not for you I'm fretting, Finn, but for Oisin and Osgar and the rest of my dear comrades. And as for you, Oisin, you'll be left lamenting after the Fianna.

"You'll feel the want of me greatly yet, Finn. And if the women of the Fianna knew I was lying in my wounds on this ridge, their faces would be sorrowful at this time."

Then Osgar said: "Though I'm nearer in blood to you, Finn, than to Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, I won't let you refuse him this drink. And by my word, if any prince in the world did the same unkindness to Diarmuid that you've done, it's only whichever of us had the strongest hand would come away alive. Give him a drink now, without delay."

"I don't know of any well at all on this mountain," said Finn.

"That's not so," said Diarmuid. "There's not nine footsteps from you the well with the best fresh water that can be found in the world."

Then Finn went to the well and took the full of his two hands of the water.

But when he was no more than halfway back, the thought of Grania came on him, and he let the water slip through his hands. And he said he was not able to bring it.

"I give my word," said Diarmuid, "it was of your own will you let it go."

Then Finn went back a second time for the water. But coming back, at the thought of Grania, he let it through his hands again.

Diarmuid gave a pitiful sigh of anguish when he saw that.

"I swear by my sword and by my spear," said Osgar, "if you don't bring the water without any more delay, Finn, there won't leave this hill but you or me."

Finn went back a third time to the well, after what Osgar said, and brought the water to Diarmuid.

As he reached him, the life went out of Diarmuid's body.

Nine footsteps. Three times. He could have walked it in the time it takes to say so. And he walked it, in the end. And he was late.

Then the whole company of the Fianna who were there gave three great, heavy shouts, keening for Diarmuid.

Osgar looked very fiercely at Finn, and said it was a greater pity that Diarmuid was dead than if he himself had died, and that the Fianna of Ireland had lost their yoke of battle by him.

"Let's leave this hill," said Finn, "before Angus and the Tuatha de Danaan come on us. Though we have no share in the death of Diarmuid, he wouldn't believe the truth from us."

"I give my word," said Osgar, "if I'd thought it was against Diarmuid you made the hunt of Beinn Gulbain, you'd never have made it."

Then Finn and the Fianna went away from the hill, with Finn leading Diarmuid's hound, Mac an Chuill. But Oisin and Osgar and Caoilte and Lugaidh's Son turned back again and put their four cloaks over Diarmuid. Then they went after the rest of the Fianna.

When they came to the Rath, Grania was out on the wall looking for news of Diarmuid, and she saw Finn and the Fianna of Ireland coming towards her.

"If Diarmuid were living," she said, "it's not led by Finn that Mac an Chuill would be coming home."

She was heavy with child at that time. Her strength went from her, and she fell down from the wall.

When Oisin saw the state she was in, he told Finn and the others to go on and leave her. But she lifted up her head and asked Finn to leave Mac an Chuill with her. Finn said he would not. He said he did not think it too much, to inherit that from Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne.

When Oisin heard that, he snatched the hound out of Finn's hand and gave it to Grania. Then he followed after his people.

When Grania was certain of Diarmuid's death she gave a long, very pitiful cry that was heard through the whole place. Her women and her people came to her and asked what ailed her, to give a cry like that. She told them how Diarmuid had come to his death by the Boar of Beinn Gulbain in the hunt Finn had made.

"And there's grief in my very heart," she said, "that I can't fight Finn myself. I wouldn't have let him leave this place safe."

When her people heard of Diarmuid's death they gave three great heavy cries in the same way, that were heard in the clouds and the waste places of the sky. Then Grania told the five hundred she had for her household to go to Beinn Gulbain for Diarmuid's body.

When they were bringing it back, she went out to meet them. They put down the body of Diarmuid, and this is what she said:

"I am your wife, beautiful Diarmuid, the man I would do no hurt to. It is sorrowful I am after you tonight.

"I am looking at the hawk and the hound my secret love used to hunt with. She that loved the three, let her be put in the grave with Diarmuid.

"Let us be glad tonight; let us make all welcome tonight; let us be open-handed tonight, since we are sitting by the body of a king.

"And O Diarmuid, it is a hard bed Finn has given you, lying on the stones and wet with the rain. Ochone! your blue eyes to be without sight, you who were friendly and generous and pursuing. O love! O Diarmuid! it is a pity he sent you to your death.

"You were a champion of the men of Ireland, their prop in the middle of the fight; you were the head of every battle; your ways were glad and pleasant.

"It is sorrowful I am, without mirth, without light, only sadness and grief and long dying. Your harp used to be sweet to me; it wakened my heart to gladness. Now my courage is fallen down, not to hear you, but to be always remembering your ways. Och! my grief is going through me.

"A thousand curses on the day when Grania gave you her love, that put Finn of the princes out of his wits. It is a sorrowful story your death is today.

"Many heroes were great and strong about me in the beautiful plain; their hands were good at wrestling and at battle. Ochone! that I did not follow them.

"You were the best man of the Fianna, beautiful Diarmuid, whom women loved. Dark is your dwelling-place under the sod; mournful and cold is your bed. Pleasant was your laugh today. You were my happiness, Diarmuid."

Then she went back into the Rath, and told her people to bring the body to her there.

Just then it was shown to Angus at Brugh na Boinne that Diarmuid was dead on Beinn Gulbain. For he had kept no watch over him the night before.

One night. In all those years, one night he did not watch.

He went on the cold wind towards Beinn Gulbain, and his people with him. On the way they met Grania's people, bringing the body to the Rath. When they saw him they held out the wrong sides of their shields as a sign of peace, and Angus knew them. And he and his people gave three great, terrible cries over the body of Diarmuid.

Then Angus spoke, and this is what he said:

"I was never one night, since the time I brought you to Brugh na Boinne when you were nine months old, without keeping watch and protection over you — until last night, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne. And now your blood has been shed, and you've been cut off sharply, and the Boar of Beinn Gulbain has put you down, Diarmuid of the bright face and the bright sword. And it's a pity Finn has done this treachery, and you at peace with him.

"Lift up his body now and bring it to the Brugh, in the lasting rocks. And if I can't bring him back to life, I'll put life into him so that he can be talking with me every day."

Then they put his body on a golden bier, with his spears over it, pointed upwards, and went on until they came to Brugh na Boinne.

A god can do that much. Not life. Talk. Every day, in the hill, for ever, a voice. It is not the same thing, and Angus knew it was not the same thing.

Grania's people went to her and told her that Angus would not let them bring the body into the Rath, but had carried it away himself to Brugh na Boinne. And Grania said she had no power over him.

Then she sent for her four sons, who were being reared in the district of Corca Ui Duibhne. When they came she gave them a loving welcome, and they came into the Rath and sat down there according to their age. Grania spoke to them in a very loud, clear voice.

"My dear children," she said, "your father has been killed by Finn, son of Cumhal, against his own bond and agreement of peace. Avenge it well on him. And here's your share of your father's inheritance: his weapons and his armour, and his feats of valour and of power. I'll share these weapons among you myself, and may they bring you victory in every battle.

"Here's the sword for Donnchadh, the best son Diarmuid had. And the Gae Dearg for Eochaidh. And here's the armour for Ollann, for it will keep the body it's put on in safety. And the shield for Connla. And make no delay now, but go and learn every kind of skill in fighting, until you come to your full strength to avenge your father."

So they took leave of her then, and of their household.

Some of their people said, "What must we do now, since our lords are going into danger against Finn and the Fianna of Ireland?"

Donnchadh, son of Diarmuid, told them to stay in their own places. "If we make peace with Finn," he said, "there need be no fear on you. And if not, you can make your choice between us and him."

And with that they set out on their journey.

But after a while Finn went, secretly and without the Fianna knowing, to the place where Grania was. He got to see her, in spite of all her high talk, and he spoke gently to her.

She would not listen to him. She told him to get out of her sight, and whatever hard thing her tongue could say, she said it.

But all the same, he went on giving her gentle talk and loving words. Until, in the end, he brought her round to his will.

This is the hardest part of the story to tell, and it is told plainly, so it will be told plainly here.

No news is told of them until they came to where the seven battalions of the Fianna were waiting for Finn. When the Fianna saw him coming, and Grania with him, like any new wife with her husband, they gave a great shout of laughter and of mockery. And Grania bowed down her head with shame.

"By my word, Finn," said Oisin, "you'll keep a good watch on Grania from now on."

Some said the change had come on her because the mind of a woman changes like the water of a running stream. And some said it was Finn who had put enchantment on her.

Nobody asked her. Nobody ever did, in this whole story, except once — her father, in the sunny house, at the very beginning. And she had told him the truth then, and nobody had listened.

As for the sons of Diarmuid, they came back at the end of seven years, after learning all that was to be learned of valour in the far countries of the world. When they came back to Rath Grania they were told their mother had gone away with Finn, son of Cumhal, without leaving any word for them or for the King of Ireland.

They said that if that was so, there was nothing for them to do. But after that they said they would attack Finn. They went forward to Almhuin, and would take no offers, but made a great slaughter of every troop that came out against them.

But at last Grania made an agreement of peace between them and Finn, and they got their father's place among the Fianna. It did them little good. They lost their lives with the rest in the battle of Gabhra.

As for Finn and Grania, they stayed with one another to the end.

The Fianna were all gathered together once, doing feats and casting stones.

After a while the Druid of Teamhair, who was with them, said: "I'm afraid, Finn of the Fianna, that there's some trouble close at hand. Look at those dark clouds of blood threatening us, side by side, overhead. There's fear on me that some destruction is coming on the Fianna."

Finn looked up and saw the great cloud of blood, and he called Osgar to look at it.

"That needn't knock a start out of you," said Osgar, "with all the strength there is in your arms, and in the men who are with you."

Then all the Fianna looked up at the cloud. Some of them were glad and cheerful, and some were downhearted.

The Druid told Finn to call all his battalions together and divide them into two halves, so that they could be watching for the coming of the enemy.

So Finn sounded the Dord Fiann, and they answered with a shout, every man hurrying to be first. Finn told Osgar and Goll and Faolan to keep watch through the night. And he told Conan the Bald to stay in the darkness of the cave of Liath Ard. "For it's you can shout loudest," he said, "to warn us if you see the enemy coming."

"May I be pierced through the middle of my body," said Conan, "if I'll go watching for troubles or for armies alone, without some more of the Fianna with me."

"It's not fitting for you to refuse Finn," said Lugaidh's Son. "And it's you can shout loudest, if the enemies come near the height."

"Don't talk to me any more," said Conan. "I won't go there alone, for the length of my days, for Finn and the whole of the Fianna."

"Go, then, Conan," said Osgar, "and Aodh Beag will go with you, and you can bring dogs with you — Bran and Sceolan and Fuaim and Fearagan. Go now, and don't begrudge it."

So Conan went to Liath Ard, and Aodh Beag with him, and Finn's hounds.

As for Finn, he lay down to sleep. It was not long before he saw, through his sleep, Aodh Beag his son without his head. And after that he saw Goll fighting with a very strong man. He woke from his sleep and called the Druid of the Fianna to him and asked him the meaning of what he had seen.

"I'm afraid there's some destruction coming on the Fianna," said the Druid. "But Aodh Beag won't be wounded in the fight, nor Goll."

Dreams show you what you are afraid of. They are not always right about what will happen. The Druid knew the difference.

It was not long before Finn heard a great shout. He sounded the Dord Fiann, and then he saw Conan running, and the hounds after him. Finn sounded the Dord Fiann again before Conan came up. When he came, Osgar asked him where Aodh Beag was.

"He was at the door of the cave when I left it," said Conan, "but I haven't looked behind me since. It wasn't Aodh Beag was troubling me."

"What was troubling you, then?" said Osgar.

"Nothing troubles me but myself," said Conan. "Though I'm well pleased at any good that comes to you."

That may be the truest thing Conan ever said.

Osgar went running hard until he came to the cave. There he found Aodh Beag with no fear or trouble on him at all, staying there until he should hear the noise of the shields. Osgar brought him back to where the Fianna were. And they saw a great army coming, as if it were searching for them.

A beautiful woman in a crimson cloak came to them over the plain, and spoke to Finn, and her voice was as sweet as music. Finn asked her who she was and whom she had come looking for.

"I'm the daughter of Garraidh, son of Dolar Dian, the Fierce," she said. "And my curse on the King of Greece, who bound me to the man who's following me, the man I'm fleeing from: Tailc, son of Treon."

"Tell me why you're shunning him," said Finn, "and I'll protect you in spite of him."

"It's not without reason I hate him," she said. "He has no good look about him. His skin is the colour of coal, and he has the head and the tail of a cat. I've walked the world three times, and I haven't left a king or a great man without asking help of him, and I never got it yet."

Three times round the world, asking. That is a long way to walk to find one man who will say yes.

"I'll give you protection," said Finn, "or the seven battalions of the Fianna will fall for your sake."

With that they saw the big strange man, Tailc, son of Treon, coming towards them. He said no word of greeting to Finn, but called for battle on account of his wife.

So a thousand of the Fianna went out to meet him and his men. They all fell, and not one of them came back.

Then another thousand of the best men of the Fianna, with blue and green shields, went out under Caoilte, son of Ronan. And they were worsted by Tailc and his people.

Then Osgar asked Finn's leave to go out and fight the big man.

"I'll give you leave," said Finn, "though I'm sure you'll fall by him."

So Osgar went out. He and Tailc, son of Treon, fought for the length of five days and five nights, without food or drink or sleep. And at the end of that time Osgar made an end of Tailc, and struck his head off.

When the Fianna saw that, they gave one shout of lamentation for those of the Fianna they had lost, and two shouts of joy for the death of Tailc.

As for the young woman, when she saw all the slaughter that had been done on her account, shame reddened her face, and she fell dead there and then.

To see her die like that, after all she had gone through, preyed on the Fianna more than any other thing.

She had got what she walked the world for. It was too much. Two thousand men had died for her in one day, and she had never asked for any of them by name.

While the Fianna were still gathered on the hill where Tailc, son of Treon, had been put down, they saw a very great champion coming towards them, with an army behind him. He took no more notice of one man than another, but asked in a very rough voice where Finn, the Head of the Fianna, was.

Aodh Beag, who had a quiet heart, asked him who he was and what he had come for.

"I'll tell you nothing at all, child," said the big man. "Your years are short, and I'll tell nothing to anyone but Finn."

So Aodh Beag brought him to where Finn was, and Finn asked him his name.

"Meargach of the Green Spears is my name," he said. "Weapons were never reddened on my body yet, and no one ever boasted of driving me backwards. Was it you, Finn, who put down Tailc, son of Treon?"

"It wasn't by me he fell," said Finn, "but by Osgar of the Strong Hand."

"Wasn't it a great shame for you, Finn," said Meargach, "to let the queen-woman who had such a great name come to her death by the Fianna?"

"It wasn't by me or by any of the Fianna she got her death," said Finn. "It was seeing the army lost that brought her to her death. But if it's satisfaction for her death or for the death of Tailc you want, you can get it from a man of the Fianna. Or you can go quietly from this place."

Meargach said he would fight any man they brought against him, to avenge Tailc, son of Treon.

It was Osgar who stood up against him, and they fought a very hard fight for three days. At one point the Fianna thought Osgar was beaten, and they gave a great sorrowful shout. But in the end Osgar put Meargach down and struck his head off. At that the seven battalions of the Fianna gave a shout of victory, and the army of Meargach keened him very sorrowfully.

After that the two sons of Meargach, Ciardan the Swift and Liagan the Nimble, came up and asked who would come against them hand to hand, so that they could get satisfaction for their father.

It was Goll who stood up against Ciardan, and it was not long before he put him down.

Conan came out against Liagan. Liagan mocked him. "It's foolishness, your coming, bald man!"

But Conan made a quick blow and struck his head off before the fight had even begun.

"That was a shameful thing to do," said Faolan, "not to stand your ground and make a fair fight."

"If I could make an end of the whole army with one blow," said Conan, "I'd do it, and I wouldn't be ashamed, and the whole of the Fianna couldn't shelter them from me."

So much for fair fights. Conan never pretended to believe in them.

Then the two armies came towards each other and made ready for the attack. And they saw a beautiful golden-haired woman coming towards them, crying and crying. The battle was put off on both sides while they waited for her to come. The army of Meargach knew it was their queen, Ailne of the Bright Face, and they raised a great cry of grief. And the Fianna watched her, and said no word.

She asked where her husband was, and where her two sons were.

"High Queen," said Finn, "for all they were so complete and quick and strong, the three you're asking for fell in the fight."

When the queen-woman heard that she cried out aloud. She went to the place where her husband and her two sons were lying and stood over their bodies, with her golden hair hanging, and keened them there. Her own people raised a sharp lamentation, listening to her, and the Fianna themselves were in grief.

This is what she said:

"O Meargach of the sharp green spears, many a fight and many a heavy battle your hard hand fought, in the gathering of the armies or alone.

"I never knew any wound to be on your body after them; and I am full sure it was not strength but treachery got the upper hand of you now.

"Long was your journey from far off, from your own kind country to Inisfail, to come to Finn and the Fianna, who put my three to death through treachery.

"My grief! to have lost my husband, my head, by the treachery of the Fianna; my two sons, my two men that were rough in the fight.

"My grief! my food and my drink; my grief! my teaching everywhere; my grief! my journey from far off, and I to have lost my high heroes.

"My grief! my house thrown down; my grief! my shelter and my shield; my grief! Meargach and Ciardan; my grief! Liagan of the wide chest.

"My grief! my protection and my shelter; my grief! my strength and my power; my grief! there is darkness come from this thing; my grief tonight that you are in your weakness.

"My grief! my gladness and my pleasure; my grief! my desire in every place; my grief! my courage is gone and my strength; my grief from this night out for ever.

"My grief! my guide and my going; my grief! my desire to the day of my death; my grief! my store and my sway; my grief! my heroes that were open-handed.

"My grief! my bed and my sleep; my grief! my journey and my coming; my grief! my teacher and my share; my sorrowful grief! my three men.

"My grief! my beauty and my ornaments; my grief! my jewels and my riches; my grief! my treasures and my goods; my grief! my three Candles of Valour.

"My grief! my friends and my kindred; my grief! my people and my friends; my grief! my father and my mother; my grief and my trouble, that you are dead.

"My grief! my portion and my welcome; my grief! my health at every time; my grief! my increase and my light; my sore trouble, that you are without strength.

"My grief! your spear and your sword; my grief! your gentleness and your love; my grief! your country and your home; my grief! that you are parted from my reach.

"My grief! my coasts and my harbours; my grief! my wealth and my prosperity; my grief! my greatness and my kingdom; my grief and my crying are until death.

"My grief! my luck altogether; my grief for you in time of battle; my grief! my gathering of armies; my grief! my three proud lions.

"My grief! my games and my drinking; my grief! my music and my delight; my grief! my sunny house and my women; my crying grief, that you are under defeat.

"My grief! my lands and my hunting; my grief! my three sure fighters; och, my grief! they are my sorrow, to fall far off by the Fianna.

"I knew by the great host of the Sidhe that were fighting over the dun, giving battle to one another in the valleys of the air, that destruction would put down my three.

"I knew by the noise of the voices of the Sidhe coming into my ears that a story of new sorrow was not far from me. It was your death it was foretelling.

"I knew at the beginning of the day when my three good men went from me, when I saw tears of blood on their cheeks, that they would not come back to me as winners.

"I knew by the voice of the battle-crow over your dun every evening, since you went from me comely and terrible, that misfortune and grief were at hand.

"Well I remember, my three strong ones, how often I told you that if you went to Ireland, I would not see the joy of victory on your faces.

"I knew by the voice of the raven every morning since you went from me that your fall was sure and certain; that you would never come back to your own country.

"I knew, my three great ones, by your forgetting the thongs of your hounds, that you would not win the day, or escape from the treachery of the Fianna.

"I knew, Candles of Valour, by the stream near the dun turning to blood when you set out, that there would be treachery in Finn.

"I knew by the eagle coming every evening over the dun that it would not be long till I heard a story of bad news of my three.

"I knew by the withering of the tree before the dun that you would never come back as conquerors from the treachery of Finn, son of Cumhal."

She had known. Every sign. She had told them. They had gone anyway, the way men in stories always go.

When Grania heard what the woman was saying, there was anger on her.

"Don't speak against Finn or the Fianna, Queen," she said. "It wasn't by any treachery or any deceit your three men were brought to their end."

Grania. Defending Finn. You may make of that whatever you like; the story does not help you.

But Ailne made her no answer and paid her no heed, but went on with her lament, crying and crying.

"I knew, looking after you the day you went out from the dun, by the flight of the raven before you, there was no good sign of your coming back again.

"I knew by Ciardan's hounds, howling mournfully every evening, that it would not be long till I had bad news of you.

"I knew by my sleep that went from me, by my tears through every lasting night, that there was no luck ahead of you.

"I knew by the sorrowful vision that showed me myself in danger, my head and my hands cut off, that it was you who were without power.

"I knew by the voice of Uaithnin, the hound that is dearest to Liagan, howling early every morning, that death was certain for my three.

"I knew when I saw in a vision a lake of blood in the place of the dun, that my three were put down by the deceit that was always with Finn."

"Don't be faulting Finn," said Grania, "however vexed your heart is. Leave off speaking against the Fianna and against him. If your men had stayed in their own country without coming to avenge the son of Treon, no harm would have happened to them."

"I wouldn't put any reproach on the Fianna, Grania," said Ailne, "if my three men had been put down in fair battle. But they're not living to bear witness to me. And it's likely they were put under Druid spells first, or they'd never have given in."

"If they were living, Queen," said Grania, "they wouldn't be running down the Fianna. They'd tell you it was by bravery and the strong hand they fell."

"I don't believe you or the Fianna when you say that," said Ailne. "No one who came to meet them ever got the better of them by right of the sword."

"If you don't believe what I'm saying, beautiful Ailne," said Grania, "I tell you more of your great army will fall by the Fianna, and not by treachery."

"That's not so," said Ailne. "I have good hopes my own army will do destruction on the Fianna, for the sake of the men who are dead."

"Well, Ailne," said Grania, "I know it's a far journey you've come. Come now and eat and drink with me and with the Fianna."

Two women, both widowed by the Fianna, one way or another. One of them was offering the other supper.

But Ailne would not do it. She said it would not be fitting for her to take food from people who did such deeds, and what she wanted was satisfaction for the death of her husband and her two sons.

First it was settled that two men from each side should go out against each other. Then Ailne said there should be thirty men on each side. Then she said she would not be satisfied to go back to her own country until she brought Finn's head with her, or until the last of his men had fallen.

In the end a great battle was fought, and the Fianna seldom fought so hard a battle as that.

It would take too long to tell, and it would tire the hearers, how many good men were killed on each side. But in the end Ailne of the Bright Face was beaten. She went back with those of her men who were left to their own country, and nobody knew where they went.

And the hill in the west where those battles were fought got the name of Cnoc-an-Air, the Hill of Slaughter.

One day Finn and his people were hunting on Slieve Fuad. A stag stood against them for a while and fought them with his great rough horns, and then he turned and ran, and the Fianna followed him until they came to the green hill of Liadhas, and from there to rocky Cairgin. They lost him there for a while, until Sceolan started him again, and he went back towards Slieve Fuad with the Fianna after him.

But Finn and Daire of the Songs, who were together, went astray and lost the rest of their people. They did not know whether they were going east or west.

Finn sounded the Dord Fiann, and Daire played some sorrowful music to let their people know where they were. But when the Fianna heard the music, it seemed a long way off. Sometimes they thought it was in the north, and sometimes in the east, and then it moved to the west, so that they did not know where in the wide world it was coming from.

As for Finn and Daire, a Druid mist came around them, and they did not know which way they were going.

After a while they met a young woman, comely and pleasant, and asked her who she was and what had brought her there.

"Glanluadh is my name," she said, "and my husband is Lobharan. We were travelling over the plain together a while ago, and we heard the cry of hounds, and he left me and went after the hunt. I don't know where he is, or which way he went."

"Come on with us, then," said Finn, "and we'll take care of you. We don't know ourselves which way the hunt has gone, east or west."

So they went on, and before long they came to a hill, and heard sleepy music of the Sidhe beside them. After that there came shouts and noises, and then the music began again, and a heavy sleep came on Finn and Daire.

When they woke from their sleep they saw a very large lighted house in front of them, with a stormy blue sea all around it. Then they saw a very big grey man coming through the waves. He took hold of Finn and of Daire, and all their strength went out of them. He carried them across the waves and into the house, and shut the door of the house with iron hooks.

"My welcome to you, Finn of the great name," he said, in a very harsh voice. "We've been waiting here a long time for you."

They sat down on the hard side of a bed. The woman of the house came to them, and they knew her. It was Ailne, the wife of Meargach.

"I've been looking for you a long time, Finn," she said, "to get satisfaction for the treachery you did on Meargach and on my two comely young sons, and on Tailc, son of Treon, and all his people. Do you remember that, Finn?"

"I remember well," said Finn, "that they fell by the swords of the Fianna. Not by treachery, but in fighting."

"It was by treachery they fell," said the Grey Man. "And our witness to it is pleasant Ailne being the way she is, and many a strong army in grief on her account."

"What is Ailne to you, man of the rough voice?" said Finn.

"I'm her own brother," said the man.

With that he put bonds on the three of them, Finn and Daire and Glanluadh, and put them down in some deep, shut place.

They were very sorrowful then. They stayed there five days and five nights, without food, without drink, without music.

Without music. For Daire, that was the worst of it.

Then Ailne went to see them.

"O Ailne," said Finn, "remember the time you came to Cnoc-an-Air, and the way the Fianna treated you with generosity. It isn't fitting for you to keep us now in shame and weakness and in danger of death."

"I know well I got kind treatment from Grania," said Ailne, in a sorrowful voice. "But for all that, Finn, if all the Fianna were in that prison with you under hard bonds, it would please me well, and I wouldn't pity them."

Then she said to Glanluadh: "And what set you following after Finn? That's not a fitting thing for you to do, and his own kind wife still living."

Then Glanluadh told her the whole story: how she had been walking the plain with Lobharan her husband, and he had followed the hunt, and the mist had come around her so that she did not know east from west, and how she had met Finn then, whom she had never seen before.

"If that's so," said Ailne, "it isn't right for you to be under punishment without cause."

She called her brother the Grey Man and told him to take the spells off Glanluadh. When Glanluadh was set free, she was sorry to leave Daire and Finn in bonds. When she had said goodbye to them she went out with Ailne. Food was brought to her, but a cloud of weakness came on her suddenly, so that it was a pity to see the state she was in.

When Ailne saw that, she brought out an enchanted cup of the Sidhe and gave her a drink from it. No sooner had Glanluadh drunk from the cup than her strength and her own looks came back to her. But all the same, she was fretting after Finn and Daire in their bonds.

"It seems to me, Glanluadh, you're fretting after those two men," said Ailne.

"I'm sorry indeed," said Glanluadh, "that the like of those men should be shut up without food or drink."

"If it pleases you to give them food, you may give it," said Ailne. "I won't make an end of them until I see whether I can get the rest of the Fianna into bonds along with them."

So the two women brought food and drink to Finn and to Daire. Glanluadh gave Finn her blessing, and she cried when she saw the way he was. But as for Ailne, she had no pity at all for the King of the Fianna.

As for the Grey Man, he heard them talking about the Fianna, and saying that Daire had a great name for the sweetness of his music.

"I have a mind to hear that sweet music," he said.

So he went to the place where they were, and told Daire to let him hear what kind of music he could make.

"My music pleased the Fianna well," said Daire. "But I think it likely it wouldn't please you."

"Play it for me now," said the Grey Man, "so I'll know whether the report I heard of you is true."

"Indeed, I have no mind for music," said Daire, "weak and downhearted as I am through your spells that have put down my courage."

"I'll take my spells off you for as long as you play for me," said the Grey Man.

"I could never make music seeing Finn in bonds the way he is," said Daire. "It's worse to me that he's in trouble than that I am."

"I'll take the power of my spells off Finn while you play for me," said the Grey Man.

That is Daire. A harper who will not play while his lord is bound. Remember him when you think of what loyalty sounds like.

So the Grey Man weakened the spells and gave them food and drink. It pleased him greatly, the way Daire played, and he called Glanluadh and Ailne to come and listen to the sweetness of it. They were well pleased with it. And Glanluadh was glad to see the two of them not as discouraged as they had been.

As for the Fianna, they were searching for Finn and Daire in every place they had ever stayed. When they came to this place they could hear Daire's sweet music. At first they were glad when they heard it. Then, when they knew the state he and Finn were in, they attacked Ailne's dun to free them.

But the Grey Man heard their shouts, and he put the full power of his spells on Finn and Daire again. The Fianna heard the music begin to stammer, and then they heard a great noise like the loud roaring of waves. And when they heard that, there was not one of them who did not fall into sleep and the clouds of death, under those sorrowful spells.

Then the Grey Man and Ailne came out quietly from where they were, and brought all the men of the Fianna who were there into the dun. They put hard bonds on them and put them where Finn and Daire were. There was great grief on Finn and Daire when they saw them. And they were all left there together for a while.

Then Glanluadh said to the Grey Man: "If Daire's music pleases you, let him play it to us now."

"If you have a mind for music," said the Grey Man, "Daire must play it for us, and for Finn and his army as well."

So they went to where the prisoners were and told Daire to play.

"I could never play sweet music," said Daire, "at a time when the Fianna are in any trouble. For when they're in trouble I'm in trouble myself, and I couldn't sound any sweet string while there's trouble on any man of them."

The Grey Man weakened the spells on them all then. Daire played first the strings of sweetness, and of the noise of shouting; and then he sang his own grief and the grief of all the Fianna. At that the Grey Man said it would not be long before he put the whole of the Fianna to death. Then Daire played a tune of heavy shouts of lamentation. And then, at Finn's bidding, he played the music of sweet strings for the Fianna.

They were kept a long time in that prison, and got very hard treatment. Sometimes Ailne's brother would come in and strike the heads off some of them, for none of them could rise from the seats they were sitting on, through his enchantments.

But once, when he was going to strike off Conan's bald head, Conan made a great leap from the seat. And he left strips of his skin stuck to it, so that his back was left bare.

Then he came round the Grey Man with pitiful words.

"Stop your hand now," he said, "for that's enough for this time. Don't send me to my death yet awhile. Heal me of my wounds first, before you make an end of me."

The reason he said that was that he knew Ailne had an enchanted cup in the dun, the one that had cured Glanluadh.

Conan the bald, Conan the bitter, Conan who never said a good word of any man. He was the one who was thinking.

The Grey Man took pity on him, and brought him out and told Ailne to bring the cup and cure his wounds.

"I won't bring it," said Ailne. "It would be best to give no time at all to him or to the Fianna, but to make an end of them."

"It's not to be saved from death I'm asking, bright-faced Ailne," said Conan, "but only not to go to my death stripped bare the way I am."

When Ailne heard that, she brought a sheepskin and put it on Conan's back. It fitted, and grew to him, and covered his wounds.

"I won't put you to death, Conan," said the Grey Man then. "You can stay with me to the end of your life."

"You'll never be without grief and danger and fear of treachery if you keep him with you," said Ailne. "There's treachery in his heart, the same as in the rest of them."

"There's no fear of that," said her brother. "Or if there is, I'll make no delay in putting the whole of the Fianna to death."

With that he brought Conan to where the enchanted cup was, and put it in his hand.

Just at that moment they heard Daire playing very sweet, sorrowful music, and the Grey Man went to listen to it, very quick and proud. Conan followed him there. After a while the Grey Man asked him what he had done with the enchanted cup.

"I left it where I found it, full of power," said Conan.

The Grey Man hurried back to the place where the treasures of the dun were kept. No sooner was he gone than Conan took out the cup, which he had hidden, and gave a drink from it to Finn and to Osgar and to the rest of the Fianna. And they, who had been withered and shaking, without strength and without courage, got back their own looks and their strength that same moment.

When the Grey Man came back from looking for the cup and saw what had happened, he took his sword and struck at Conan. But Conan called on Osgar to defend him. Osgar attacked the Grey Man, and it was not long before he made him acquainted with death.

When Ailne saw that, with the grief and the dread that came on her, she fell dead there and then.

She had lost a husband, and two sons, and now a brother, all to the Fianna. The story calls it her revenge. It was mostly more grief.

Then all the Fianna made a feast of the food and drink they found, and they were very joyful and merry. But when they got up in the morning there was no trace or tidings of the dun. They were lying on the bare grass.

As for Conan, the sheepskin never came off him. And the wool used to grow on it every year, the same as on any other sheep.

Once, when the Fianna had gone off here and there hunting, Black Garraidh and Caoilte were sitting beside Finn, and they were talking about the battle in which Finn's father was killed.

"Tell me now," Finn said to Garraidh, "since you were there yourself: how was it you brought my father Cumhal to his death?"

"I'll tell you that, since you ask me," said Garraidh. "It was my own hand, and the hands of the rest of the sons of Morna, that made an end of him."

"That's cold friendship from my followers the sons of Morna," said Finn.

"If it's cold friendship," said Garraidh, "put away the liking you pretend to have for us, and show us the hatred you have for us all the while."

For forty years they had all known it. Nobody had said it out loud. Now somebody had.

"If I were to lift my hand against you now, sons of Morna," said Finn, "I'd be well able for you all without any man's help."

"It was by his arts Cumhal got the upper hand of us," said Garraidh. "And when he had power over us, he banished us to every far country. A share of us he sent to Alban, and a share to dark Lochlann, and a share to bright Greece, parting us from one another. For sixteen years we were away from Ireland, and it was no small thing to us to go all that time without seeing one another.

"And the first day we came back to Ireland we killed sixteen hundred men — and no lie in it — and not a man of them but would be keened by a hundred. We took their duns after that, and went on until we were all around one house in Munster with red walls. So great was the bravery of the man in that house, your father, that it was easier to find him than to kill him. We killed everyone of his race out on the hill, and then we made a quick rush at the house where Cumhal was, and every man of us made a wound on his body with his spear. I was there myself. It was I gave him the first wound.

"Avenge it on me now, Finn, if you have a mind to."

Finn did not. Not that day.

* * * * *

It was not long after that that Finn gave a feast at Almhuin for all his chief men. Two sons of the King of Alban came to it, and sons of the kings of the great world. When they were all sitting at the feast, the serving-men rose and took drinking-horns worked by skilled men, with shining stones in them, and poured out strong drink for the champions. Then mirth rose in their young men, and courage in their fighting men, and kindness and gentleness in their women, and knowledge and foreknowledge in their poets.

Then a crier rose and shook a rough iron chain to silence the clowns and the common lads and the idlers. Then he shook a chain of old silver to silence the high lords and the chief men of the Fianna, and the learned men. And they all listened and were silent.

Fergus of the True Lips rose and sang before Finn the songs and the good poems of his forefathers, and Finn and Oisin and Lugaidh's Son rewarded him with every good thing. Then he went on to Goll, son of Morna, and told the fights and the destructions and the cattle-drivings and the courtings of his fathers. And the sons of Morna were well pleased and high-minded, listening to that.

Then Goll said: "Where's my woman-messenger?"

"I'm here, King of the Fianna," she said.

King of the Fianna. She called Goll that, in Finn's own hall.

"Have you brought me my hand-tribute from the men of Lochlann?"

"I've brought it surely," she said.

With that she rose up and laid on the floor of the hall in front of Goll a load of pure gold the size of a good pig, that would be a heavy load for a strong man. Goll loosened the covering that was about it, and gave Fergus a good reward out of it, as he always did. For there never was a wise, sharp-worded poet, or a sweet harp-player, or any learned man of Ireland or of Alban, but Goll would give him gold or silver or some good thing.

When Finn saw that, he said: "How long, Goll, have you had this rent on the men of Lochlann — and my own rent on them always along with it, and one of my own men, Ciaran, son of Latharne, and ten hundred men of his household, guarding it and guarding my right of hunting?"

Goll saw there was anger on Finn.

"It's a long time, Finn, I've had that rent on the men of Lochlann," he said. "From the time your father put war and quarrels on me, and the King of Ireland joined him, and I was made to leave Ireland by them. I went into Britain, and took the country, and killed the king himself and did destruction on his people. But Cumhal put me out of it. From there I went to Fionnlochlann, and the king fell by me, and his household. And Cumhal put me out of it. From there I went to the country of the Saxons, and the king and his household fell by me. And Cumhal put me out of it.

"But then I came back to Ireland, and fought a battle against your father, and he fell by me there. It was at that time I put this rent on the men of Lochlann.

"And, Finn, it's not a rent of the strong hand you've put on them, but a tribute for having the protection of the Fianna of Ireland, and I don't lessen that. And you needn't begrudge me that tribute. If I had more than that again, it's to you and to the men of Ireland I'd give it."

Great anger came on Finn.

"You tell me yourself, Goll, by your own story," he said, "that you came from the city of Beirbhe to fight against my father, and that you killed him in the battle. It's a bold thing for you to tell that to me."

"By your own hand," said Goll, "if you gave me the same treatment your father gave me, I'd pay you back the same way as I paid him."

"It would be hard for you to do that," said Finn. "There are a hundred men in my household for every man in yours."

"That was the same with your father," said Goll. "And I avenged my disgrace on him. And I'd do the same on you, if you earned it."

Then Cairell of the White Skin, son of Finn, said: "It's many a man of Finn's household you've put down, Goll!"

When Bald Conan heard that, he said: "I swear by my weapons, Goll was never without a hundred men in his household, every one of them able to get the better of you."

"And is it to them you belong, crooked-speaking, bare-headed Conan?" said Cairell.

"It's to them I belong, you black, feeble, nail-scratching, rough-skinned Cairell. And I'll make you know it was Finn was in the wrong," said Conan.

With that Cairell got up and gave Conan a furious blow of his fist. Conan took it with no great patience, but gave him back a blow in the teeth. From that they went on to worse blows. The two sons of Goll got up to help Conan, and Osgar went to the help of Cairell. It was not long before many of the chief men of the Fianna were fighting on one side or the other, on the side of Finn or on the side of the sons of Morna.

Then Fergus of the True Lips rose, and the rest of the poets of the Fianna with him, and they sang their songs and their poems to check them and quiet them. At the sound of the poets' songs the men left off their fighting and let their weapons fall on the floor. The poets gathered the weapons up and made peace between the fighters. And they put bonds on Finn and on Goll to keep the peace for a while, until they could ask for a judgment from the High King of Ireland.

That was the end, for that time, of the little quarrel at Almhuin.

It is called little. It was the beginning of the end of everything.

But it broke out again. Once there was a falling-out between Finn and Goll over the dividing of a pig of the pigs of Manannan. At Daire Tardha, the Oak Wood of Bulls, in the province of Connacht, there was a great fight between Finn's men and the sons of Morna. The sons of Morna were worsted, and fifteen of their men were killed. And they made up their minds that from that time on they would set themselves against any friends of Finn or of his people. It was Conan the Bald who gave them that advice, for he was always bitter, and a maker of quarrels and mischief in every place.

They kept their word, and spared no one.

There was a yellow-haired queen Finn loved. Berach Brec was her name. She was wise and comely and worthy of any good man. Her house was full of treasures, and she never refused anyone who asked.
