Anyone who came to her house at Samhain could stay until Beltaine, and have his choice then to go or to stay.

The sons of Morna had fostered her. They went to her and told her to give up Finn, and then she need have no fear of them. She said she would not give up her kind lover to please them. She was going away from them to her ship, and Art, son of Morna, threw his spear, and it went through her body, and she died. Her people carried her up from the strand and buried her.

Their own foster-child. That is how far it had gone.

As for Goll, he took a little hound that Finn thought a great deal of — Conbeg was its name — and drowned it in the sea. A wave brought its body up on shore afterwards, and the Fianna buried it under a little green hill. Caoilte made a lament over it. He said how swift the little hound had been after deer or wild pigs, and how good at killing them, and that it was a pity it had died out on the cold green waves.

Goll. Who was kind and gentle and open-handed. Who drowned a little dog.

About that time nine women of the Tuatha de Danaan came to meet nine men of the Fianna, and the sons of Morna saw them coming and made an end of them.

When Caoilte met Goll, he threw his spear at him, and it struck the golden helmet off his head and a piece of his flesh with it. But Goll took it very proudly. He put the helmet on again, and took up his weapons, and called out to his brothers that he was in no way ashamed.

Finn went looking for the sons of Morna everywhere, to take vengeance on them. Once they were doing robbery and destruction on Slieve Echtge, which got its name from Echtge, daughter of Nuada of the Silver Hand. Finn and the Fianna were to the west, at Slieve Cairn in the district of Corcomruadh. Finn was not sure whether the sons of Morna had gone south into Munster or north into Connacht. So he sent Aedan and Cahal, two sons of the King of Ulster, with two hundred fighting men, into the beautiful, pleasant province of Connacht, and every day they went looking for the sons of Morna from place to place.

After a while the three battalions of the Fianna who were in Corcomruadh saw the track of a troop of men, and thought it was the track of the sons of Morna. They closed round them at night and made an end of them all.

When the full light came the next morning, they knew them. It was their own people, who had been with the King of Ulster's sons.

They gave three great heavy cries, keening the friends they had killed by mistake.

Caoilte and Oisin went to Rath Medba and brought a great stone and put it over the king's sons, and it was called Lia an Imracail, the Stone of the Mistake.

And the place where Goll took his men when he parted from Finn in anger got the name of Druimscarha, the Parting Hill of Heroes.

When the Fianna began killing each other in the dark, it was not a quarrel any longer. It was an ending.

At last it happened that Goll and Cairell, son of Finn, met each other and said sharp words. They fought in the sea near the strand, and Cairell got his death by Goll.

There was great anger and great grief on Finn, seeing his son, who had been so strong and comely, lying dead and grey, like a blighted branch.

Goll had killed the father. Now he had killed the son.

As for Goll, he went away to a cave on a point of land stretching out into the sea. He meant to stay there until Finn's anger had passed.

Osgar knew where he was, and went to see him, who had been his comrade in so many battles. But Goll thought he was coming as an enemy, and threw his spear at him. Osgar got no wound from it, but it struck his shield and crushed it.

Finn noticed the state of the shield. And when he knew that Goll had thrown at Osgar, his anger grew greater again. He sent out his men and told them to watch every path and every gap that led to the cave where Goll was, so that they could make an end of him.

When Goll knew that Finn was watching for his life like that, he made no attempt to escape. He stayed where he was, without food, without drink, blinded by the sand that was blowing into his eyes.

His wife came to a rock where she could speak with him, and called to him to come to her.

"Come over to me," she said. "It's a pity for you to be blinded where you are, on the rocks of the waste sea, with no drink but the salt water — a man who was first in every fight. Come now and sleep beside me. Instead of the hard sea-water I'll nourish you from my own breast, and it's I will do your healing. The gold of your hair is my desire for ever. Don't stay there withering like an herb in the wintertime, and my heart black with grief inside me."

But Goll would not leave the spot where he was, for all she could say.

"It's best as it is," he said. "I never took the advice of a woman, east or west, and I never will. And O sweet-voiced queen, what ails you to be fretting after me? Remember your silver and your gold, and your silks and stuffs. Remember the seven hounds I gave you at Cruadh Ceirrge, and not one of them slack until he's killed the deer. And don't be crying tears after me, queen of the white hands. Remember your constant lover, Aodh, the son of the best woman in the world, who came out of Spain asking for you, and whom I fought at Corcar-an-Deirg. Go to him now. It's bad when a woman is in want of a good man."

He was dying of hunger on a rock, blind, and he was arranging for her to be looked after. That is the whole of Goll, in one speech.

He lay down on the rocks, and at the end of twelve days he died.

His wife keened him there, and made a great lamentation for her husband who had such a great name, who was the second best of the Fianna of Ireland.

When Conan heard of the death of Goll his brother, great anger came on him. He went to Garraidh and asked him to go with him to Finn, to demand satisfaction for Goll.

"I'm not willing to go," said Garraidh, "since we could get no satisfaction for the great son of Morna."

"Whether you've a mind to go or not, I'll go," said Conan. "And I'll make an end of every man I meet, for the sake of yellow-haired Goll. I'll have the life of Oisin, Finn's great son, and of Osgar and of Caoilte and of Daire of the Songs. I'll have no forgiveness for them. We must show no respect for Finn, though we may die in the fight, with no help from Goll. Let's take that work in hand and make no delay. For if Finn is there, his strength will be there, until we put him under his flagstone."

But it is not likely Garraidh went with him, after he had spoken such foolish words.

What happened to Conan in the end is not known.

But there is a cairn of stones on a hill of Burren, near Corcomruadh, and the people of Connacht say it is there he is buried. And they say a stone was found there once with these words on it in the old writing: "Conan the swift-footed, the bare-footed."

But the Munster people say it is on their own side of Burren he is buried.

Nobody could agree about Conan while he lived. It is fitting that they cannot agree about him now.

With one thing and another, the High King of Ireland had grown somehow bitter against Finn and the Fianna.

Once, when he was holding a gathering of his people, he spoke out to them. He told them to remember all the harm that had been done them through the Fianna, and all their pride, and the tribute they asked.

"And as for me," he said, "I'd sooner die fighting the Fianna, if I could bring them down along with me, than live with Ireland under them the way it is now."

All his people were of the same mind. They said they would make no delay, but attack the Fianna and make an end of them. "And we'll have good days of joy and feasting," they said, "once Almhuin is clear of them."

The High King began to make plans against Finn, and sent to all the men of Ireland to come and help him. When everything was ready, he sent for Osgar to come to a feast he was making at Teamhair.

Osgar, who was never afraid before any enemy, set out for Teamhair with three hundred of his men.

On the way they saw a woman of the Sidhe washing clothes at a river, and there was the colour of blood on the water where she washed them.

"There's red on the clothes you're washing," Osgar said to her, "and it's for the dead you're washing them."

And the woman answered him. "It won't be long," she said, "until the ravens are croaking over your own head after the battle."

That is what she does, the Washer at the Ford. She washes the clothes of the ones who are about to die. You do not get to see her twice.

"Is there any weakness in our eyes," said Osgar, "that a little story like that would set us crying? Do another foretelling for us now. Tell us, will any man of our enemies fall by us before we ourselves are made an end of?"

"Nine hundred will fall by you yourself," she said. "And the High King himself will get his death-wound from you."

Osgar and his men went on to the king's house at Teamhair. They were well treated, and the feast was made ready, and they were three days at pleasure and drinking.

On the last day of the drinking the High King called out in a loud voice and asked Osgar whether he would exchange spears with him.

"Why do you ask for that exchange," said Osgar, "when I and my spear were often with you in time of battle? You wouldn't ask it of me if Finn and the Fianna were with me now."

"I'd ask it of any fighting man among you," said the king, "and rent and tribute along with it."

"Any gold or any treasure you might ask of us, we'd give you," said Osgar. "But it isn't right for you to ask for my spear."

There were very high words between them then, and they threatened one another. At last the High King said: "I'll put my spear of the seven spells out through your body."

"And I give you my word against that," said Osgar. "I'll put my spear of the nine spells between the meeting of your hair and your beard."

Two promises, made across a feasting-table. Both of them would be kept.

With that Osgar and his men got up and left Teamhair. They stopped to rest beside a river, and there they heard the sound of a very sorrowful tune, like keening, played on a harp. A great anger came on Osgar when he heard it. He got up and took his weapons and roused his people, and they went on again to where Finn was.

A messenger came after them from the High King. The message he brought was this: that the king would never pay tribute to the Fianna, or put up with them at all, from that time on.

When Finn heard that, he sent a challenge of battle, and gathered together all the Fianna he had left. But as for the sons of Morna, it was to the High King of Ireland they gathered.

It was at the hill of Gabhra that the two armies met. There were twenty men with the King of Ireland for every man with Finn.

It was a very hard battle that was fought that day, and there were great deeds done on both sides. There never was a greater battle fought in Ireland than that one.

As for Osgar, it would be hard to tell all he killed that day: five score of the Sons of the Gael, and five score fighting men from the Country of Snow, and seven score of the Men of Green Swords, who never took a step backward, and four hundred from the Country of the Lion, and five score of the sons of kings. And the shame of it was on the King of Ireland.

But as for Osgar himself, who began the day so swift and so strong, at the last he was like leaves on a strong wind, or like an aspen-tree that is falling.

Then he saw the High King near him, and he made for him like a wave breaking on the strand. The king saw him coming, and shook his greedy spear, and threw it. It went through Osgar's body and brought him down on his right knee. And that was the first grief of the Fianna.

The spear of the seven spells, out through his body. As promised.

But Osgar was in no way daunted. He threw his spear of the nine spells, and it went into the High King at the meeting of the hair and the beard, and gave him his death.

As promised.

When the men nearest the High King saw that, they put the king's helmet up on a pillar, so that his people would think he was still living. But Osgar saw it. He lifted a thin bit of slab-stone that was lying on the ground beside him and threw it, and it broke the helmet where it stood.

And then he fell himself, like a king.

The seven sons of Caoilte fell in that battle, and the son of the King of Lochlann who had come to help them. It would be hard to count the number of the Fianna who fell in that battle.

When it was over, those who were left went looking for their dead. Caoilte stooped over his seven brave sons, and every living man of the Fianna stooped over his own dear friends. It was a lasting grief to see all those who were stretched in that place. But the Fianna would not have taken it to heart the way they did, except that they were what they had become: a beaten race.

They had never lost before. That was the thing. Men die in every battle. It is losing that you do not recover from.

As for Oisin, he went looking for Osgar. This is how he found him: lying stretched out, resting on his left arm, with his broken shield beside him, and his sword still in his hand, and his blood around him on every side.

Osgar put out his hand to Oisin. Oisin took it, and gave out a very hard cry.

"I'm glad to see you safe, my father," said Osgar.

Oisin had no answer to give him.

Just then Caoilte came to where they were, and looked at Osgar.

"How are you now, my darling?" he said.

"The way you'd like me to be," said Osgar.

Then Caoilte searched the wound. When he saw how the spear had torn its way through to the back, he cried out, and a cloud came over him, and his strength failed him.

"O Osgar," he said, "you're parted from the Fianna. And they must be parted from battle from now on, and pay their tribute to the King of Ireland."

Then Caoilte and Oisin lifted Osgar on their shields and carried him to a smooth green hill, to take his clothes off him. There was not a hand's-breadth of his white body without a wound.

When the rest of the Fianna saw the state Osgar was in, there was not a man of them who keened his own son or his brother. Every one of them came keening Osgar.

After a while, at noon, they saw Finn coming towards them, with what was left of the Sun-banner raised on a spear-shaft. They all greeted Finn, but he made no answer. He came up to the hill where Osgar was.

When Osgar saw him coming he greeted him. "I've got my desire in death, Finn of the sharp arms," he said.

"You were in a worse way, my son," said Finn, "on the day of the battle at Beinn Edair, when the wild geese could have swum on your breast, and it was my hand gave you healing."

His hands. The water in his hands. The healing he could give, and had given once, to this boy.

"No healing can be done for me now, for ever," said Osgar, "since the King of Ireland put the spear of seven spells through my body."

"It's a pity it wasn't I myself who fell in sunny, scarce Gabhra," said Finn, "and you going east and west at the head of the Fianna."

"And if it was you who fell in the battle," said Osgar, "you wouldn't hear me keening after you. For no man ever knew any heart in me but a heart of twisted horn, covered with iron. But the howling of the dogs beside me, and the keening of the old fighting men, and the crying of the women one after another — those are the things that are vexing me."

He was dying, and what troubled him was the noise of everyone else's grief.

"Child of my child," said Finn, "calf of my calf, white and slender, it's a pity the way you are. My heart is starting like a deer, and I'm weak after you and after the Fianna of Ireland. Misfortune has followed us. Farewell now to battles and to a great name, and farewell to taking tributes. For every good thing I ever had is gone from me now."

When Osgar heard those words he stretched out his hands, and his eyelids closed.

And Finn turned away from the rest, and cried.

He never shed a tear in the whole length of his life except for Osgar, and for Bran.

All who were left of the Fianna gave three sorrowful cries after Osgar. For there was not one of the Fianna beyond him, unless it was Finn or Oisin.

Many of the Fianna were left dead at Gabhra, and graves were made for them. As for Lugaidh's Son, who was so tall a man and so good a fighter, they made a very wide grave for him, as was fitting for a king. And the whole length of the rath at Gabhra, from end to end, was the grave of Osgar, son of Oisin, son of Finn.

As for Finn himself, he never had peace or pleasure again from that day.

One day Finn was hunting, and Bran went after a fawn.

They were coming towards Finn, and the fawn called out.

"If I go into the sea below," it said, "I'll never come back again. And if I go up into the air above me, it won't save me from Bran."

For Bran could overtake the wild geese, she was that swift.

"Go out between my legs," said Finn.

So the fawn did that, and Bran followed her. And as Bran went under him, Finn squeezed his two knees together on her, so that she died that moment.

That is how Donn killed the Steward's son, long ago, at Brugh na Boinne. Between his two knees. Finn had seen it done. He had judged it.

There was great grief on him after that, and he cried the same as he did when Osgar died.

Some said it was Finn's mother the fawn was, and that it was to save his mother he killed Bran. But that is not likely. His mother was beautiful Muirne, daughter of Tadg, son of Nuada of the Tuatha de Danaan, and it was never heard that she was changed into a fawn.

It is more likely it was Oisin's mother. Sadbh, who was taken from the gate of Almhuin while Finn was away at the wars, and whom he looked for seven years and never found.

If it was her, then after all that time she had come back to him, running. And he had had to choose between her and Bran. And he chose.

But some say Bran and Sceolan are still seen at night, starting out of the thicket on the hill of Almhuin.

One misty morning, those who were left of the Fianna gathered together to Finn. They were sorrowful and downhearted after the loss of so many of their comrades.

They went hunting near the borders of Loch Lein, where the bushes were in blossom and the birds were singing, and they were waking up the deer, who were as joyful as the leaves of a tree in summertime.

It was not long before they saw, coming towards them from the west, a beautiful young woman riding a very fast, slender white horse.

She had a queen's crown on her head, and a dark cloak of silk down to the ground, with stars of red gold on it. Her eyes were blue, and as clear as the dew on the grass. A gold ring hung down from every golden lock of her hair. Her cheeks were redder than the rose, and her skin whiter than the swan on the wave, and her lips as sweet as honey mixed through red wine.

In her hand she held a bridle with a golden bit, and there was a saddle worked with red gold under her. As for the horse, he had a wide smooth cloak over him, and a silver crown on the back of his head, and he was shod with shining gold.

She came to where Finn was and spoke in a very kind, gentle voice.

"It was a long journey I had, King of the Fianna."

Finn asked her who she was, and what her country was, and why she had come.

"Niamh of the Golden Head is my name," she said. "And I have a name beyond all the women of the world, for I'm the daughter of the King of the Country of the Young."

"What brought you to us from over the sea, Queen?" said Finn. "Is it that your husband has gone from you, or what trouble is on you?"

"My husband hasn't gone from me," she said, "for I've never yet gone to any man. But O King of the Fianna, I've given my love and my affection to your own son, Oisin of the strong hands."

"Why did you give your love to him beyond all the troops of high princes under the sun?" said Finn.

"It was because of his great name," she said, "and the report I heard of his bravery and his comeliness. Many a king's son and high prince has given me his love, but I never consented to any of them until I set my love on Oisin."

When Oisin heard what she was saying, there was not a limb of his body that was not in love with beautiful Niamh. He took her hand in his.

"A true welcome to you in this country, young queen," he said. "It's you are the shining one. It's you are the nicest and the comeliest. It's you are better to me than any other woman. It's you are my star and my choice beyond the women of the entire world."

"I put on you the bonds of a true hero," said Niamh, "to come away with me now to the Country of the Young."

Bonds again. They were all of them bound, from the beginning to the end, by the same few words.

And this is what she said:

"It is the most delightful country of all that are under the sun; the trees are stooping down with fruit and with leaves and with blossom.

"Honey and wine are plentiful there, and everything the eye has ever seen. No wasting will come on you with the wasting away of time; you will never see death or lessening.

"You will get feasts, playing and drinking; you will get sweet music on the strings; you will get silver and gold and many jewels.

"You will get — and no lie in it — a hundred swords; a hundred cloaks of the costliest silk; a hundred horses, the quickest in battle; a hundred willing hounds.

"You will get the royal crown of the King of the Young, that he never gave to anyone under the sun. It will be a shelter to you night and day, in every rough fight and every battle.

"You will get a right suit of armour; a sword, gold-hilted, apt for striking; no one that ever saw it got away from it alive.

"A hundred coats of armour, and shirts of satin; a hundred cows and a hundred calves; a hundred sheep with golden fleeces; a hundred jewels that are not of this world.

"A hundred glad young girls shining like the sun, their voices sweeter than the music of birds; a hundred armed men, strong in battle, apt at feats, waiting on you, if you will come with me to the Country of the Young.

"You will get everything I have said to you, and delights beyond them that I have no leave to tell. You will get beauty, strength, and power. And I myself will be with you as a wife."

The Red Woman had offered Finn the Country of the Young once, a long time ago. He had said that he would not give up his own country for the whole world as an estate, and the Country of the Young along with it.

But that was when Finn was young, and the Fianna were whole. Osgar was under the rath at Gabhra now. Diarmuid was in the hill with Angus. Goll had died on a rock. And Oisin was standing on a hillside above Loch Lein with a woman made of gold holding his hand.

"O pleasant golden-haired queen," said Oisin, "you're my choice beyond the women of the world. I'll go with you willingly."

With that he kissed Finn his father and said farewell to him, and said farewell to the rest of the Fianna, and got up on the horse with Niamh.

The horse set out gladly. When he came to the strand he shook himself, and neighed three times, and then he made for the sea.

When Finn and the Fianna saw Oisin facing the wide sea, they gave three great sorrowful shouts.

"It's my grief to see you going from me," said Finn. "And I'm without a hope of ever seeing you coming back to me again."

He was right. He would not see it.

That was the last time Finn and Oisin and the rest of the Fianna of Ireland were gathered together, for hunting, for battle, for chess-playing, for drinking or for music. They all wore away after that, one after another.

As for Caoilte, who was old and had lost his sons, he used to fret and be lonesome after the old times. One day, when there was very heavy snow on the ground, he made this lament:

"Cold is the winter; the wind has risen; the fierce, high-couraged stag rises up. Cold is the whole mountain tonight, yet the fierce stag is calling. The deer of Slievecarn of the gatherings does not lay his side to the ground; he, no less than the stag on the top of cold Echtge, hears the music of the wolves.

"I, Caoilte, and brown-haired Diarmuid, and pleasant light-footed Osgar, we used to listen to the music of the wolves through the end of the cold night. Well the brown deer sleeps with its hide to the hollow, hidden as if in the earth, through the end of the cold night.

"Today I am in my age, and I know only a few men. I used to shake my spear bravely in the ice-cold morning. Often I put silence on a great army that is very cold tonight."

He had drunk the drink of remembrance, in the hill at Ess Ruadh. He forgot nothing. Every one of them was still there in his head, in the cold, listening to the wolves.

After a while he went into a hill of the Sidhe to be healed of his old wounds. Whether he came back from there or not is not known. Some say he used to talk with Patrick of the Bells at the same time as Oisin was with him. But that is not likely, or Oisin would not have complained of his loneliness the way he did.

But a long time after that, a king of Ireland was making a journey. He and his people lost their way, and when night came on they were in a dark wood, with no path in front of them.

A very tall man came to them, shining like a burning flame. He took hold of the bridle of the king's horse and led him through the wood until they came to the right road.

The King of Ireland asked him who he was.

First he said, "I am your candlestick."

Then he said, "I was with Finn one time."

And the king knew it was Caoilte, son of Ronan.

Once, in Teamhair, a king had said that the two eyes of Caoilte were in his candlestick. And Finn had said that Caoilte would never stand serving with a candle for all the gold in the world. But that was a long time ago, and there was nobody left to serve.

Three times nine of the rest of the Fianna came out of the west once to Teamhair. They saw that now, when they had lost their full strength and their great name, nobody took any notice of them or came to speak with them at all. When they saw that, they lay down on the side of the hill at Teamhair, and put their lips to the earth, and died.

And for three days and a month and a year from the time of the destruction of the Fianna of Ireland, Loch Dearg was under mists.

* * * * *

As for Finn, some say he died by the hand of a fisherman. It is likely that is not true, for that would be no death for so great a man as Finn, son of Cumhal. And some say he never died, but is alive in some place still.

Once a smith made his way into a cave he had found. It had a door, and he made a key that opened it. When he went in he saw a very wide place, and very big men lying on the floor. One bigger than the rest was lying in the middle, with the Dord Fiann beside him. And the smith knew it was Finn and the Fianna.

He took hold of the Dord Fiann. He could hardly lift it to his mouth. He blew a very strong blast on it, and the sound it made was so great that it was a wonder the rocks did not come down on him. At the sound, the big men lying on the ground shook from head to foot.

He gave another blast, and they all turned over on their elbows.

Great dread came on him when he saw that. He threw down the Dord Fiann and ran from the cave, and locked the door after him, and threw the key into the lake.

And he heard them crying after him: "You left us worse than you found us."

The cave has not been found since.

That is the rule of the horn. Three blasts. The smith gave two. It is a small and terrible thing, to stop one short.

But some say the day will come when the Dord Fiann will be sounded three times, and at the sound of it the Fianna will rise up as strong and as well as ever they were.

And some say Finn, son of Cumhal, has been on the earth now and again since the old times, in the shape of one of the heroes of Ireland.

As for the great things he and his men did when they were together, it is well they have been kept in mind by the poets of Ireland and of Alban.

One night two men were minding sheep in a valley, and they were saying the poems of the Fianna to each other while they were there. And they saw two very tall shapes on the two hills on either side of the valley. And one of the tall shapes said to the other:

"Do you hear that man down below? I was the second doorpost of battle at Gabhra. And that man knows all about it better than I do."

The dead are listening. They always have been. That is one reason to tell the stories right.

And so we come to the last of it: Oisin, and Patrick.

As for Oisin, it was a long time after Niamh took him away that he came back to Ireland. Some say he was hundreds of years in the Country of the Young, and some say thousands. Whatever time it was, it seemed short to him.

And whatever happened to him in the time he was away, it was a withered old man they found when he came back to Ireland, with his white horse going away from him, and he lying on the ground.

It was Saint Patrick who had power at that time, and it was to him Oisin was brought. Patrick kept him in his house, and used to teach him and question him. Oisin was in no way pleased with the way Ireland was then. He used to talk about the old times, and fret after the Fianna.

Patrick asked him to tell what had happened to him when he left Finn and the Fianna and went away with Niamh. And this is the story Oisin told.

"When I went away with golden-haired Niamh, we turned our backs to the land and our faces westward. The sea was going away in front of us, and filling up in waves behind us. We saw wonderful things on our journey: cities and courts and duns and lime-white houses, and shining sunny-houses and palaces.

"Once we saw beside us a hornless deer running hard, and an eager white hound with red ears following after it. Another time we saw a young girl on a horse, with a golden apple in her right hand, going over the tops of the waves. And there was a young man following after her on a white horse, with a crimson cloak and a gold-hilted sword in his right hand."

"Follow on with your story, pleasant Oisin," said Patrick, "for you haven't told us yet what country it was you went to."

"The Country of the Young, the Country of Victory, it was," said Oisin. "And O Patrick, there's no lie in that name. And if there are grandeurs in your Heaven the same as there are there, I'd give my friendship to God.

"We turned our backs to the dun then, and the horse under us was quicker than the spring wind on the backs of the mountains. It wasn't long before the sky darkened, and the wind rose in every part, and the sea was as if it were on fire, and there was nothing to be seen of the sun.

"But after we'd been looking at the clouds and the stars a while, the wind went down, and the storm, and the sun brightened. And we saw ahead of us a very delightful country in full blossom, with smooth plains in it, and a king's dun that was very grand and had every colour in it, and sunny-houses beside it, and palaces of shining stones made by skilled men.

"We saw three fifties of armed men coming out to meet us, very lively and handsome. I asked Niamh whether this was the Country of the Young, and she said it was.

"'And indeed, Oisin,' she said, 'I told you no lie about it. You'll see everything I promised you in front of you for ever.'

"After that a hundred beautiful young girls came out, in cloaks of silk worked with gold, and gave me a welcome to their own country. Then came a great shining army, and with it a strong, beautiful king, in a shirt of yellow silk with a golden cloak over it, and a very bright crown on his head. And there was a young queen following after him, with fifty young girls.

"When everyone had come to the one spot, the king took me by the hand and said out before them all: 'A hundred thousand welcomes to you, Oisin, son of Finn. As for this country you've come to, I'll give you news of it without a lie. Long and lasting your life will be in it, and you yourself will be young for ever. And there's no delight the heart ever thought of but it's here, waiting for your coming. You can believe my words, Oisin, for I myself am the King of the Country of the Young, and this is its comely queen, and it was golden-headed Niamh, our daughter, who went over the sea looking for you, to be her husband for ever.'

"I thanked him then, and I bowed myself down before the queen, and we went forward to the royal house. All the high nobles came out to meet us, men and women both, and a great feast was made there that lasted ten days and ten nights.

"And that's how I married Niamh of the Golden Hair, and that's how I went to the Country of the Young — though it's sorrowful to me to tell it now, O Patrick from Rome."

"Follow on with your story, Oisin of the destroying arms," said Patrick, "and tell me how you left the Country of the Young, for I'm longing to hear that. And tell us, had you any children by Niamh, and was it long you were in that place?"

"Two beautiful children I had by Niamh," said Oisin, "two young sons, and a comely daughter. Niamh gave the two sons the names of Finn and of Osgar. And the name I gave the daughter was The Flower."

He named his sons for his father and his son. Of course he did. Even in the Country of the Young, he was carrying them.

"And I didn't feel the time passing, and it was a long time I stayed there," he said, "until the desire came on me to see Finn and my comrades again. I asked the king and Niamh for leave to go back to Ireland.

"'You'll get leave from me,' said Niamh. 'But for all that, it's bad news you're giving me. I'm afraid you'll never come back here again, for the length of your days.'

"But I told her not to fear, since the white horse would bring me safe back from Ireland.

"'Bear this in mind, Oisin,' she said. 'If you once get off the horse while you're away, if you once put your foot to the ground, you'll never come back here again.

"'And O Oisin, I tell it to you now for the third time: if you once get down from the horse, you'll be an old man, blind and withered, without liveliness, without mirth, without running, without leaping.

"'And it's a grief to me, Oisin, that you should ever go back to green Ireland. It isn't now as it used to be. You won't see Finn and his people, for there's nothing now in the whole of Ireland but a Father of Orders and armies of saints. Here's my kiss for you, pleasant Oisin, for you'll never come back any more to the Country of the Young.'"

That is the rule of the horse. Do not get down. She said it three times. She knew.

"That's my story, Patrick," said Oisin, "and I've told you no lie in it. And O Patrick, if I was the same the day I came here as I was that day, I'd have made an end of all your clerks, and there wouldn't be a head left on a neck after me."

"Go on with your story," said Patrick, "and you'll get the same good treatment from me that you got from Finn. For the sound of your voice is pleasing to me."

So Oisin went on with his story. And this is what he said:

"I have nothing to tell of my journey until I came back into green Ireland. I looked about me on all sides, but there was no news to be got of Finn.

"It wasn't long before I saw a great troop of riders, men and women, coming towards me from the west. When they came near they wished me good health. And they all wondered when they looked at me, seeing me so unlike themselves, and so big and so tall.

"I asked them whether they'd heard if Finn was still living, or any other of the Fianna, or what had happened to them.

"'We've often heard of Finn, who lived long ago,' they said, 'and that there never was his equal for strength or bravery or a great name. There's many a book written down by the sweet poets of the Gael about his doings and the doings of the Fianna, and it would be hard for us to tell you all of them. And we heard Finn had a son,' they said, 'who was beautiful and shining, and a young girl came looking for him, and he went away with her to the Country of the Young.'

"When I knew by their talk that Finn was not living, nor any of the Fianna, I was downhearted, and tired, and very sorrowful after them. I made no delay, but turned my face and went on to Almhuin of Leinster. And there was great wonder on me when I got there, to see no sign at all of Finn's great dun, and his great hall, and nothing in the place where it had been but weeds and nettles."

Like Fionnuala, coming home after nine hundred years to Sidhe Fionnachaidh, and finding green hillocks and thickets of nettles. Every one of them, in the end, comes home to nettles.

And there was grief on Oisin, and he said: "Och, Patrick! Och, ochone, my grief! That was a bad journey for me. To be without news of Finn or the Fianna has left me in pain all my life."

"Leave off fretting, Oisin," said Patrick, "and shed your tears to the God of grace. Finn and the Fianna are slack enough now, and they'll get no help for ever."

"It would be a great pity," said Oisin, "for Finn to be in pain for ever. And who was it got the victory over him, when his own hand had made an end of so many a hard fighter?"

"It was God got the victory over Finn," said Patrick, "and not the strong hand of an enemy. And as for the Fianna, they're condemned to hell along with him, and tormented for ever."

"O Patrick," said Oisin, "show me the place where Finn and his people are, and there's not a hell or a heaven there but I'll put it down. And if Osgar, my own son, is there — the hero who was bravest in heavy battles — there's not a troop in hell or in the Heaven of God so great that he couldn't destroy it."

"Let's leave off quarrelling on each side now," said Patrick. "Go on, Oisin, with your story. What happened to you after you knew the Fianna had come to an end?"

"I'll tell you that, Patrick," said Oisin.

"I was turning to go away, and I saw the stone trough the Fianna used to put their hands in, and it was full of water. When I saw it I had such a longing for it, and such a feeling for it, that I forgot what I'd been told. And I got down off the horse.

"And in that minute all the years came on me. I was lying on the ground. The horse took fright and went away and left me there — an old man, weak and spent, without sight, without shape, without comeliness, without strength or understanding, without respect.

"There's my story for you now, Patrick, and no lie in it, of all that happened to me going away and coming back again from the Country of the Young."

A stone trough full of water. That was all. He wanted to put his hands where their hands had been.

Oisin stayed on with Saint Patrick. But he was not very well content with the way he was treated.

"They say I'm getting food," he said once, "but God knows I'm not, or drink. And I, Oisin, son of Finn, under a yoke, drawing stones."

"It's my opinion you're getting enough," said Saint Patrick, "and you getting a quarter of beef and a churn of butter and a griddle of bread every day."

"I've often seen a quarter of a blackbird bigger than your quarter of beef," said Oisin, "and a rowan-berry as big as your churn of butter, and an ivy leaf as big as your griddle of bread."

Saint Patrick was vexed when he heard that, and he told Oisin he had told a lie.

You can say many things to a man of the Fianna. That is not one of them.

A great anger came on Oisin. He went to where there was a litter of pups, and told a serving-boy to nail the hide of a freshly killed bullock up on the wall, and to throw the pups against it one by one. Every one he threw fell down off the hide, until it came to the last. That one held on with its teeth and its nails.

"Rear that one," said Oisin, "and drown all the rest."

Then he told the boy to keep the pup in a dark place and look after it well, and never let it taste blood or see the daylight. At the end of a year Oisin was so well pleased with the pup that he gave it the name of Bran Og, Young Bran.

One day he called the serving-boy to come on a journey with him, and to bring the pup on a chain. They set out and passed by Slieve-nam-ban, where the witches of the Sidhe sit spinning at their spinning-wheels. Then they turned eastward into Gleann-na-Smol.

Oisin raised a rock that was there, and told the lad to take three things out from under it: a great sounding horn of the Fianna, and an iron ball they used for throwing, and a very sharp sword.

When Oisin saw those things, he took them in his hands.

"My thousand farewells to the day when you were put here," he said.

Someone had hidden them, a long time ago, for a day that never came. He was the only one left who knew where.

He told the lad to clean them well. When he had done that, he told him to sound a blast on the horn. The boy did it, and Oisin asked whether he saw anything strange.

"I don't," said the boy.

"Sound it again, as loud as you can," said Oisin.

"That's as hard as I can sound it," said the boy, when he had done it, "and I can't see anything yet."

Then Oisin took the horn himself and put it to his mouth, and blew three great blasts on it.

Three. Not two. He knew the rule of the horn.

"What do you see now?" he said.

"I see three great clouds coming," said the boy, "and they're settling down in the valley. The first cloud is a flight of very big birds, and the second cloud is a flight of birds that are bigger again, and the third flight is of the biggest and the blackest birds the world ever saw."

"What's the dog doing?" said Oisin.

"The eyes are starting out of his head, and there isn't a hair on him but is standing up."

"Let him loose now," said Oisin.

The dog rushed down to the valley and attacked one of the birds, the biggest of them all, whose shadow was like a cloud. They fought a very fierce fight. But at last Bran Og made an end of the big bird, and lapped its blood.

And when he did, madness came on him. He came rushing back towards Oisin, with his jaws open and his eyes like fire.

"There's dread on me, Oisin," said the boy. "The dog is making for us, mad and raging."

"Take this iron ball and throw it at him when he comes near," said Oisin.

"I'm afraid to do that," said the boy.

"Put it in my hand, and turn it towards him," said Oisin.

The boy did that. And Oisin — blind, and old, and withered — threw the ball. It went into the dog's mouth and down his throat and choked him, and he fell down the slope, twisting and foaming.

That is the rule of the Fianna's dogs. Never let them taste blood until the day they are needed. And once they have tasted it, there is no getting it back.

Then they went to where the great bird lay dead. Oisin told the lad to cut a quarter off it with the sword, and he did. Then he told him to cut open the body. And in it they found a rowan-berry, the biggest he had ever seen, and an ivy leaf bigger than the biggest griddle.

So Oisin turned back and went to where Saint Patrick was, and showed him the quarter of the bird, which was bigger than any quarter of a bullock, and the rowan-berry, which was bigger than a churning of butter, and the leaf.

"And you know now, Patrick of the Bells," he said, "that I told no lie. This is what kept us all through our lifetime: truth that was in our hearts, and strength in our arms, and fulfilment in our tongues."

"You told no lie indeed," said Patrick.

Once, Grania was asked what was whiter than snow, and she said: the truth. It was the Fianna's whole religion. It was the thing Oisin had left.

When Oisin had no sight left at all, he used to put one of the serving-men up on his shoulders every night and carry him out to see how the cattle were doing.

One night the servants had no mind to go, and they agreed among themselves to tell him it was a very bad night.

This is what the first of them said: "Outside there's a heavy sound, with the heavy water dropping from the tops of the trees. The sound of the waves can't be heard for the loud splashing of the rain."

Then the next said: "The trees of the wood are shivering, and the birch is turning black. The snow is killing the birds. That's the story outside."

And the third said: "It's to the east they've turned their faces, the white snow and the dark rain. What's making the plain so cold is the snow that's dripping and getting hard."

But there was a serving-girl in the house, and she said: "Get up, Oisin, and go out to the white-headed cows, since the cold wind is plucking the trees off the hills."

So Oisin went out with the serving-man on his shoulders. But this is what the serving-man did: he brought a vessel of water and a birch broom with him, and kept dashing water in Oisin's face, so that he would think it was rain.

But when they came to the pen where the cattle were, Oisin found the night was quiet.

And after that he asked the servants for no more news of the weather.

He did not shout. He did not strike anyone. He was old and blind and the last of the Fianna, and he had learned what they were. He simply stopped asking.

Saint Patrick undertook to convert Oisin and bring him to baptism. It was no easy work. Whatever Patrick said, Oisin had an answer for it.

This is how they used to talk and argue with one another, as the poets of Ireland wrote it down afterwards.

PATRICK: "Oisin, your sleep is long. Get up and listen to the Psalm. Your strength and your readiness are gone from you, though you used to go into rough fights and battles."

OISIN: "My readiness and my strength are gone from me since Finn has no armies living. I have no liking for clerks. Their music isn't sweet to me after his."

PATRICK: "You never heard music so good from the beginning of the world to this day. A fine one you'd be to serve an army on a hill — you, old and silly and grey."

OISIN: "I used to serve an army on a hill, Patrick of the closed-up mind. It's a pity you should be faulting me. No shame was ever put on me until now.

"I've heard music sweeter than your music, however much you praise your clerks: the song of the blackbird in Leiter Laoi, and the sound of the Dord Fiann; the very sweet thrush of the Valley of the Shadow, or the sound of the boats striking the strand. The cry of the hounds was better to me than the noise of your schools, Patrick.

"Little Nut, little Nut of my heart, the little dwarf that was with Finn: when he made tunes and songs, he'd put us all into deep sleep.

"The twelve hounds that belonged to Finn, when they were let loose, facing out from the Siuir — their cry was sweeter than harps and pipes.

"I have a little story about Finn. We were only fifteen men. We took the King of the Saxons of the feats, and we won a battle against the King of Greece.

"We fought nine battles in Spain, and nine times twenty battles in Ireland. From Lochlann and from the eastern world there was a share of gold coming to Finn.

"My grief, that I'm staying on after him, without delight in games or in music, withering away after my comrades. My grief it is to be living. I and the clerks of the Mass-books are two that can never agree.

"If Finn and the Fianna were living, I'd leave the clerks and the bells. I'd follow the deer through the valleys. I'd like to be close on his track.

"Ask Heaven of God, Patrick, for Finn of the Fianna and his race. Make prayers for the great man. You never heard of his like."

PATRICK: "I won't ask Heaven for Finn, man of good wit that my anger is rising against, since his delight was to be living in valleys with the noise of hunts."

OISIN: "If you'd been in the company of the Fianna, Patrick of the joyless clerks and the bells, you wouldn't be attending on schools, or giving heed to God."

PATRICK: "I wouldn't part from the Son of God for all who have lived, east or west. O Oisin, O shaking poet, harm will come on you in satisfaction for the priests."

OISIN: "It was a delight to Finn, the cry of his hounds on the mountains, the wild dogs leaving their harbours, the pride of his armies. Those were his delights."

PATRICK: "There was many a thing Finn took delight in, and there's not much heed given to it after him. Finn and his hounds aren't living now. And you won't always be living, Oisin."

OISIN: "There's a greater story of Finn than of us, or of any who've lived in our time. Of all that are gone and all that are living, Finn was better at giving out gold than any of them."

PATRICK: "All the gold you and Finn used to give out, it does little for you now. He's in Hell, in bonds, because he did treachery and oppression."

This is the only time in the whole long story that anyone says it plainly. Treachery and oppression. A boar on Beinn Gulbain. Water let slip through the hands, three times. Patrick was not wrong. That is what makes this so hard to read.

OISIN: "I believe little of your truth, man from Rome with the white books: Finn, the open-handed Head of the Fianna, to be in the hands of devils or demons."

PATRICK: "Finn is in bonds in Hell, the pleasant man who gave out gold. In satisfaction for his disrespect to God, he's under grief in the house of pain."

OISIN: "If the sons of Morna were in there, or the strong men of the sons of Baiscne, they'd take Finn out of it, or they'd have the house for themselves."

PATRICK: "If the five provinces of Ireland were in there, or the strong seven battalions of the Fianna, they wouldn't be able to bring Finn out of it, however great their strength."

OISIN: "If Faolan and Goll were living, and brown-haired Diarmuid, and brave Osgar, Finn of the Fianna couldn't be held in any house that was made by God or devils."

PATRICK: "If Faolan and Goll were living, and all the Fianna that ever were, they couldn't bring Finn out of the house where he's in pain."

OISIN: "What did Finn ever do against God, but attend on schools and on armies? Giving gold for a great part of his time, and for another while trying his hounds."

PATRICK: "In payment for thinking of his hounds, and for serving the schools of the poets, and because he gave no heed to God, Finn of the Fianna is held down."

OISIN: "You say, Patrick of the Psalms, that the Fianna couldn't take Finn out, nor the five provinces of Ireland along with them.

"I have a little story about Finn. We were only fifteen men when we took the King of Britain of the feasts, by the strength of our spears and our own strength.

"We took Magnus the Great, the son of the King of Lochlann of the speckled ships. We came back in no way sorry or tired. We put our rent on far places.

"O Patrick, it's a pitiful story, the King of the Fianna to be under locks: a heart without envy, without hatred, a heart hard in earning victory.

"It's an injustice for God to be unwilling to give food and riches. Finn never refused strong or poor, though cold Hell is his dwelling-place now.

"This is what Finn had a mind for: to listen to the sound of Druim Dearg; to sleep at the stream of Ess Ruadh; to hunt the deer of Gallimh of the bays.

"The cries of the blackbird of Leiter Laoi; the wave of Rudraighe beating on the strand; the bellowing of the ox of Magh Maoin; the lowing of the calf of Gleann da Mhail.

"The noise of the hunt on Slieve Crot; the sound of the fawns round Slieve Cua; the scream of the sea-gulls out there on Iorrus; the screech of the crows over the battle.

"The waves vexing the breasts of the boats; the howling of the hounds at Druim Lis; the voice of Bran on Cnoc-an-Air; the outcry of the streams about Slieve Mis.

"The call of Osgar going to the hunt; the voice of the hounds on the road of the Fianna; to be listening to them and to the poets — that was always his desire.

"One desire of the desires of Osgar was to listen to the striking of shields; to be hacking at bones in a battle — that's what he always had a mind for.

"We went westward once to hunt at Formaid of the Fianna, to see the first running of our hounds.

"It was Finn who was holding Bran, and it was with me Sceolan was. Diarmuid of the Women had Fearan, and Osgar had lucky Adhnuall.

"Conan the Bald had Searc. Caoilte, son of Ronan, had Daol. Lugaidh's Son and Goll were holding Fuaim and Fothran.

"That was the first day we loosed out a share of our hounds to a hunt. And och, Patrick, of all who were in it, there isn't one left living but me.

"O Patrick, it's a pity, the way I am now: a spent old man without power, without quickness, without strength, going to Mass at the altar.

"Without the great deer of Slieve Luchra; without the hares of Slieve Cuilinn; without going into fights with Finn; without listening to the poets.

"Without battles, without taking spoils; without playing at nimble feats; without going courting or hunting, two trades that were my delight."

He names every hound. He names who held each one. It was one morning, a lifetime ago — several lifetimes ago — and he remembers exactly who was holding which leash.

PATRICK: "Leave off, old man. Leave your foolishness. Let what you've done be enough for you from now on. Think of the pains that are in front of you. The Fianna are gone, and you'll be going yourself."

OISIN: "If I go, may you not be left after me, Patrick of the hindering heart. If Conan, the least of the Fianna, were living, your buzzing wouldn't be left to you long.

"Or if this were the day I gave ten hundred cows to the headless woman who came to the Valley of the Two Oxen. The birds of the air carried off the ring I gave her. I never knew where she went herself from me."

PATRICK: "That's little to trouble you, Oisin. It was only for a while she was with you. It's better for you to be as you are than to be among them again."

OISIN: "O Son of Calphurn of the friendly talk, it's a pity for anyone who gives respect to clerks and bells. Caoilte my friend and I, we weren't poor when we were together.

"The music that put Finn to sleep was the cackling of the ducks from the lake of the Three Narrows; the scolding talk of the blackbird of Doire an Cairn; the bellowing of the ox from the Valley of the Berries.

"The whistle of the eagle from the Valley of Victories, or from the rough branches of the ridge by the stream; the grouse of the heather of Cruachan; the call of the otter of Druim-re-Coir.

"The song of the blackbird of Doire an Cairn — indeed I never heard sweeter music, if I could be under its nest.

"My grief that I ever took baptism. It's little credit I got by it, being without food, without drink, doing fasting and praying."

PATRICK: "In my opinion it did you no harm, old man. You'll get nine score cakes of bread, and wine and meat to put a taste on it. It's bad talk you're giving."

OISIN: "May this mouth that's talking with you never confess to a priest, if I wouldn't sooner have the leavings of Finn's house than a share of your own meals."

PATRICK: "He got only what he gathered off the banks, or whatever he could kill on the rough hills. He got hell in the end, because of his unbelief."

OISIN: "That wasn't the way with us at all, but our fill of wine and meat; justice, and a right beginning at the feasts; sweet drinks, and everyone drinking them.

"It's fretting after Diarmuid and Goll I am, and after Fergus of the True Lips, when you won't let me speak of them, O new Patrick from Rome."

PATRICK: "We'd give you leave to speak of them. But first you should give heed to God. Since you're at the end of your days now, leave your foolishness, weak old man."

OISIN: "O Patrick, tell me as a secret, since it's you have the best knowledge: will my dog or my hound be let in with me to the court of the King of Grace?"

Of all the questions a man might ask at the end of the world, this is the one he asks.

PATRICK: "Old man, in your foolishness that I can't put any bounds to: your dog or your hound won't be let in with you to the court of the King of Power."

OISIN: "If I had acquaintance with God, and my hound at hand, I'd make whoever gave food to me give a share to my hound as well.

"One strong champion who was with the Fianna of Ireland would be better than the Lord of Piety, and than you yourself, Patrick."

PATRICK: "O Oisin of the sharp blades, it's mad words you're saying. God is better for one day than the whole of the Fianna of Ireland."

OISIN: "Though I'm without power now, and my life is spent to the end, don't put abuse, Patrick, on the great men of the sons of Baiscne.

"If I had Conan with me, the man who used to run down the Fianna, it's he would break your head in among your clerks and your priests."

Conan. He is calling for Conan now. There is nobody else left to call for.

PATRICK: "It's a silly thing, old man, to be always talking of the Fianna. Remember your end has come, and take the Son of God to help you."

OISIN: "I used to sleep out on the mountain under the grey dew. I was never used to going to bed without food, while there was a deer on the hill over there."

PATRICK: "You're astray at the end of your life between the straight way and the crooked. Keep out of the crooked path of pains, and the angels of God will come beneath your head."

OISIN: "If I and open-handed Fergus and Diarmuid were together now on this spot, we'd go down every path we ever went down, and ask no leave of the priests."

PATRICK: "Leave off, Oisin. Don't speak against the priests who are telling the word of God in every place. Unless you leave off your daring talk, it's great pain you'll have in the end."

OISIN: "When the leader of the Fianna and I were looking for a boar in a valley, it was worse to me not to see it than for all your clerks to be without their heads."

PATRICK: "It's pitiful, seeing you without sense. That's worse for you than your blindness. If you got sight inside you, great would be your desire for Heaven."

OISIN: "It would be little good to me to be sitting in that city, without Caoilte, without Osgar, without my father being with me.

"The leap of the buck would be better to me, or the sight of badgers between two valleys, than all your mouth is promising me, and all the delights I could get in Heaven."

He had already had a paradise. He had lived in the Country of the Young, for longer than anyone knows. He had left it, for a stone trough of water. He knew exactly what he was turning down.

PATRICK: "Your thoughts are foolish. They'll come to nothing. Your pleasure and your mirth are gone. Unless you take my advice tonight, you won't get leave on this side or that."

OISIN: "If the Fianna and I were on the top of a hill today, drawing our spear-heads, we'd have our choice of being here or there, in spite of books and priests and bells."

PATRICK: "You were like the smoke of a wisp, or a stream in a valley, or a whirling wind on the top of a hill, every tribe of you that ever lived."

OISIN: "If I were in the company of the people of strong arms, the way I was at Bearna da Coill, I'd sooner be looking at them than at this troop of the crooked croziers.

"If I had Scolb Sceine with me, or Osgar, who was smart in battles, I wouldn't be without meat tonight at the sound of the bell of the seven tolls."

PATRICK: "Oisin, since your wits are gone from you, be glad at what I say. It's certain to me you'll leave the Fianna, and receive the God of the stars."

OISIN: "There's wonder on me at your hasty talk, priest who's travelled in every part, to say I'd part from the Fianna, a generous people, never niggardly."

PATRICK: "If you saw the people of God, the way they're settled at feasts — every good thing is more plentiful with them than with Finn's people, however great their name was.

"Finn and the Fianna are lying now, very sorrowful, on the flagstone of pain. Take the Son of God in their place. Make your repentance and don't lose Heaven."

OISIN: "I don't believe your talk now, O Patrick of the crooked staves — Finn and the Fianna to be in there, unless they find pleasure in being in it."

PATRICK: "Make right repentance now, before you know when your end is coming. God is better for one hour than the whole of the Fianna of Ireland."

OISIN: "That's a daring answer to make to me, Patrick of the crooked crozier. Your crozier would be in little bits if I had Osgar with me now.

"If my son Osgar and God were hand to hand on the Hill of the Fianna, if I saw my son put down, I'd say that God was a strong man.

"How could it be that God or his priests could be better men than Finn, the King of the Fianna, a generous man without crookedness?

"If there were a place above or below better than the Heaven of God, it's there Finn would go, and all his people with him.

"You say a generous man never goes to the hell of pain. There wasn't one among the Fianna who wasn't generous to all.

"Ask God, Patrick, whether He remembers when the Fianna were alive, or whether He's seen, east or west, any man better than they were in their fighting.

"The Fianna didn't use to speak treachery. We never had the name of telling lies. By truth and the strength of our hands we came safe out of every battle.

"There never sat a priest in a church — though you think it sweet to be singing psalms — who was better to his word than the Fianna, or more generous than Finn himself.

"If my comrades were living tonight, I'd take no pleasure in your crooning in the church. As they aren't living now, the rough voice of the bells has deafened me.

"Och, in the place of battles and heavy fights, where I used to have my place and take my pleasure — the crozier of Patrick being carried, and his clerks at their quarrelling.

"Och, slothful, cheerless Conan, it's great abuse I used to give you. Why don't you come to see me now? You'd get leave for making fun and reviling through the whole of the niggardly clerks.

"Och, where are the strong men gone, that they don't come together to help me? O Osgar of the sharp sword of victory, come and free your father from his bonds!

"Where is the strong son of Lugaidh? Och, Diarmuid of all the women! Och, Caoilte, son of Ronan, think of our love, and travel to me!"

Nobody came. There was nobody left to come.

PATRICK: "Stop your talk, you withered, witless old man. It's my King who made the Heavens. It's He who gives blossom to the trees. It's He made the moon and the sun, the fields and the grass."

OISIN: "It wasn't in shaping fields and grass my king took his delight, but in overthrowing fighting men, and defending countries, and carrying his name into every part.

"In courting, in playing, in hunting, in baring his banner at the start of a fight; in playing at chess, at swimming, in looking around him in the drinking-hall.

"O Patrick, where was your God when the two came over the sea who carried off the queen of Lochlann of the Ships? Where was He when Dearg came, the son of the King of Lochlann of the golden shields? Why didn't the King of Heaven protect them from the blows of the big man?

"Or when Tailc, son of Treon, came, the man who did great slaughter on the Fianna — it wasn't by God that champion fell, but by Osgar, in the sight of all.

"Many a battle and many a victory was won by the Fianna of Ireland. I never heard of any great deed done by the King of Saints, or that He ever reddened His hand.

"It would be a great shame for God not to take the locks of pain off Finn. If God Himself were in bonds, my king would fight for His sake.

"Finn left no one in pain or in danger without freeing him, by silver or by gold, or by fighting until he won the victory.

"For the strength of your love, Patrick, don't forsake the great men. Bring the Fianna in, without the King of Heaven knowing.

"It's a good claim I have on your God, to be among his clerks the way I am: without food, without clothing, without music, without giving rewards to poets.

"Without the cry of the hounds or the horns, without guarding coasts, without courting generous women. For all I've suffered by the want of food, I forgive the King of Heaven, in my will."

He forgives God. It is the last thing a man of the Fianna has to give, and he gives it, the way Finn would have: openly, and without being asked.

Then Oisin said: "My story is sorrowful. The sound of your voice isn't pleasant to me. I'll cry my fill — but not for God. Because Finn and the Fianna aren't living."

Oisin used to make laments. Sometimes he would make praises of the old times, and of Finn. These are some of them that are remembered still.

I saw the household of Finn. It was not the household of a soft race. I had a vision of that man yesterday.

I saw the household of the High King, he with the brown, sweet-voiced son. I never saw a better man.

I saw the household of Finn. No one saw it the way I saw it. I saw Finn with the sword, Mac an Luin. Och, it was sorrowful to see it.

I can't tell out every harm that is on my head. Free us from our trouble for ever. I have seen the household of Finn.

It is a week from yesterday I last saw Finn. I never saw a braver man. A king of heavy blows; my law, my adviser, my sense and my wisdom; prince and poet, braver than kings; King of the Fianna, brave in every country; golden salmon of the sea, clean hawk of the air; rightly taught, avoiding lies; strong in his doings, a right judge, ready in courage; a high messenger in bravery and in music.

A week from yesterday, he says. It had been hundreds of years. Some say thousands. To Oisin it was a week, and it always would be.

His skin was lime-white, his hair golden. Ready to work, gentle to women. His great green vessels were full of rough, sharp wine. Rich was the king, the head of his people.

Finn's house had seven sides, and seven score shields on every side. He had fifty fighting men about him in woollen cloaks; ten bright drinking-cups in his hall; ten blue vessels; ten golden horns.

It was a good household Finn had: without grudging, without lust, without vain boasting, without chattering, without any slur on any one of the Fianna.

Finn never refused any man. He never turned away anyone who came to his house. If the brown leaves falling in the woods were gold, if the white waves were silver, Finn would have given away the whole of it.

Blackbird of Doire an Chairn, your voice is sweet. I never heard, on any height of the world, music sweeter than your voice, and you at the foot of your nest.

It is the sweetest music in the world. It's a pity not to listen to it for a while, O son of Calphurn of the sweet bells. You'd catch up on your nones again afterwards.

If you knew the story of the bird the way I know it, you'd be crying lasting tears, and you'd give no heed to your God for a while.

In the country of Lochlann of the blue streams, Finn, son of Cumhal, of the red-gold cups, found that bird you hear now. I'll tell you its story truly.

Doire an Chairn, that wood there to the west, where the Fianna used to linger — it was there they put the blackbird, in the beauty of the pleasant trees.

The stag of the heather of quiet Cruachan; the sorrowful croak from the ridge of the Two Lakes; the voice of the eagle of the Valley of the Shapes; the voice of the cuckoo on the Hill of Brambles.

The voice of the hounds in the pleasant valley; the scream of the eagle on the edge of the wood; the early outcry of the hounds going over the Strand of the Red Stones.

In the time Finn lived, and the Fianna, it was sweet to them to listen to the whistle of the blackbird. The voice of the bells would not have been sweet to them.

It is still there, the blackbird. Or its children's children are. Finn brought it from Lochlann, and it outlived him, and it is singing somewhere in a wood to the west, and nobody listening knows who put it there.

There was no one of the Fianna without his fine silken shirt and his soft coat, without bright armour, without shining stones on his head, two spears in his hand, and a shield that brought victory.

If you searched the world you wouldn't find a harder man: best of blood, best in battle. No one got the upper hand of him. When he went out trying his white hound, which of us could be put beside Finn?

Once we went hunting on Slieve-nam-ban. The sun was beautiful overhead. The voice of the hounds went east and west, from hill to hill. Finn and Bran sat on the hill a while, and every man was eager for the hunt. We let out three thousand hounds from their golden chains, and every hound of them brought down two deer.

Patrick of the true crozier, did you ever see, east or west, a greater hunt than that hunt of Finn and the Fianna? O son of Calphurn of the bells, that day was better to me than listening to your lamentations in the church.

* * * * *

There's no strength in my hands tonight. There's no power in me. It's no wonder I'm sorrowful, thrown down in the sorrow of old age.

Everything is a grief to me beyond any other man on the face of the earth: to be dragging stones along to the church and the hill of the priests.

I have a little story of our people. Once Finn had a mind to make a dun on the bald hill of Cuailgne, and he put it on the Fianna of Ireland to bring stones for building it: a third on the sons of Morna, a third on me, and a third on the sons of Baiscne.

I gave Finn, son of Cumhal, an answer. I said I'd be under his rule no longer, and that I'd obey him no more.

When Finn heard that, he was silent a long time — the man without a lie, without fear. And then he said to me: "You yourself will be dragging stones before your death comes to you."

He had drunk from the salmon. He had drunk from the well of the moon. He knew. He always knew, and it never once saved anyone.

I got up then with anger on me, and a fourth of the brave battalions of the Fianna followed me. I gave my own judgments. There were many of the Fianna with me.

Now my strength is gone from me, I who was adviser to the Fianna. My whole body is tired tonight: my hands, my feet, and my head. Tired, tired, tired.

It's bad, the way I am, after Finn of the Fianna. Since he went away, every good thing is behind me.

Without great people, without mannerly ways. I'm sorrowful after our king who is gone.

I am a shaking tree with my leaves gone from me. An empty nut. A horse without a bridle. A people without a dwelling-place. I, Oisin, son of Finn.

* * * * *

Long are the clouds over me tonight. Long was last night. Though this day is long, yesterday was longer to me. Every day that comes is long to me.

That's not the way I used to be: without fighting, without battles, without learning feats, without young girls, without music, without harps, without bruising bones, without great deeds; without increase of learning, without generosity, without drinking at feasts, without courting, without hunting, the two trades I was used to; without going out to battle. Ochone, the want of them is sorrowful to me.

No hunting of deer or stag. It's not like this I'd wish to be. No leashes for our hounds. No hounds. Long are the clouds over me tonight.

Without rising up to do bravery as we used to; without playing as we had a mind to; without the swimming of our fighting men in the lake. Long are the clouds over me tonight.

There's no one at all in the world the way I am. It's a pity, the way I am: an old man dragging stones. Long are the clouds over me tonight.

I am the last of the Fianna, great Oisin, son of Finn, listening to the voice of bells. Long are the clouds over me tonight.

That is where the story ends. Not with a battle. Not with a god. With an old blind man who could have stayed young for ever, sitting in the rain that is not rain, carrying stones, and remembering the names of dogs.

The gods came to Ireland in a mist. The Fianna went out of it under clouds. Everything in between is what we have left, and it is enough. It will have to be.


NOTES

I. The Apology

Lady Gregory explained, at the end of her book, how she had made it.

The Irish text of most of these stories had already been published, and she worked from that text, making her own translation as far as her scholarship went, and, where it failed, taking the meaning given by better scholars. Where the Irish text had not been printed, she worked by comparing and piecing together various translations. She put in a connecting sentence of her own here and there. She fused different versions together, condensed many passages, and left out many — "the choice that is a perpetual refusing," as she put it — trying to get a clear outline of the doings of the heroes.

She said she found it more natural to tell the stories in the manner of the thatched houses, where she had heard so many legends of Finn and his friends, and Oisin and Patrick, and the Ever-Living Ones, and the Country of the Young, than in the manner of the slated houses, where she had never heard them told at all.

She told why she had done the work. Four years before, Dr Atkinson, a Professor of Trinity College, Dublin, giving evidence before the Commission of Intermediate Education, had said that the old literature of Ireland was untouched by the great literatures of the world; that it was "the untrained popular feeling," and almost intolerably low in tone; that where the Greek and Latin and French books each had something with an ideal ring about it, a lasting treasure a child might carry away, he could find nothing ideal in the Irish books, and very little imagination.

Dr Atkinson was an Englishman, she noted, but other professors at Trinity, and students there, had been influenced by his opinion that Irish literature was a thing to be despised. She did not quote him to draw attention to a battle still being fought, she said, but to explain her own purpose: to make part of Irish literature available to many, especially young Irish people, who had neither the chance to read the translations of the scholars, scattered through learned journals, nor the patience and time to untangle overlapping and contradictory versions — so that they could judge for themselves its "lowness" and its "want of imagination."

She believed that those who once learned to care for the story of Cuchulain of Muirthemne, and of Finn and Lugh and Etain, and to recognise the enduring belief in an invisible world and an immortal life behind the visible and the mortal, would not be content with her version, but would go first to the fuller versions of the best scholars, and then to the manuscripts themselves. She believed the forty students of Old Irish lately called together by Professor Kuno Meyer would not rest until they had explored the scores and scores of uncatalogued and untranslated manuscripts in Trinity College Library, and that the enthusiasm the Gaelic League had given birth to would lead to much fine scholarship.

She mentioned a letter from one of the best Greek scholars and translators in England, himself an Irishman, who said her Cuchulain had opened up to him a great world of beautiful legend he had never known, and that he was sending copies to Irish friends in Australia, expecting them to feel, as he had, something like pride in the beauty of the Irish mind. And she mentioned that President Roosevelt had written to her that, after reading Cuchulain of Muirthemne, he had sent for every other translation from the Irish he could get, to take with him on his journey to the Western States.

She gave those words, she said, not from vanity — for they were not for her, but for her material — to show the effect the old literature had on those who came fresh to it, and that such readers did not complain of its want of imagination. She was proud and glad to have helped make it known, and the task had been pleasant, though toilsome. On the sixth of October, writing that note, she was tired enough, she said, and thought with sympathy of the old Highland piper who complained that he was "withered with yelping the seven Fenian battalions."

II. The Age and Origin of the Stories of the Fianna

Lady Gregory drew on Mr Alfred Nutt's pamphlet, Ossian and the Ossianic Literature, number three in his series Popular Studies in Mythology, Romance, and Folklore.

Nutt set out that the body of Gaelic literature connected with the name of Ossian — Oisin — is very large and of respectable age. The oldest texts, mostly prose but some in verse, survive in Irish manuscripts of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and go back at least a hundred and fifty to two hundred and fifty years before that. Most of the Ossianic literature, in the form we have it, is later. A number of important prose texts survive in fourteenth-century manuscripts, probably shaped in the thirteenth and twelfth centuries. But by far the largest mass consists of narrative poems, usually dramatic in form, which have come down in manuscripts written in Scotland from the end of the fifteenth century to the middle of the seventeenth, and in Ireland from the sixteenth century down to the middle of the nineteenth. And the Gaelic-speaking country people of both Ireland and Scotland had preserved by word of mouth a large number of these ballads, and a great mass of prose tales about Ossian and his comrades.

If every Ossianic text in manuscripts older than the nineteenth century were printed, Nutt reckoned, they would fill eight to ten thousand pages. For five hundred years this body of romance had been the chief imaginative recreation of the Gaelic world, in Ireland and Scotland alike, and a peasantry that could not read or write had kept it almost whole.

On whether the stories were history, Nutt said the question hardly mattered. The romances take place in a world entirely romantic, full of divine and half-divine beings, monsters and giants, men and women changing shape with animals, heroes' lives stretched by miracle: a land of Faery. And the conditions they describe do not match anything known of the third century, when Finn was supposed to have lived. The Fianna are always guarding Ireland against over-sea raiders called Lochlannach, clearly thought of as Norsemen — but the Norse only came to Ireland at the end of the eighth century, their great period of invasion running roughly from 825 to 925, followed by a time of settlement in the tenth century, until the battle of Clontarf, fought by Brian, the great chieftain of the south, at the start of the eleventh century, broke up the separate Norse powers and absorbed them into Irish life. So if the stories ever reflected the third century, that reflection was later distorted, and a pseudo-history built on events of the ninth and tenth centuries was put in its place. What the historian looks for in legend, Nutt said, is a picture of the society in which it arose, more than a record of the events it claims to remember.

Nutt went on to ask whether third-century customs could be found in the stories; which parts first found their way into writing; and whether the Oisin and Patrick dialogues were written under the influence of real Pagan feeling surviving from Pagan times, or of a change in the feeling of the Gaelic world during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, when those dialogues began to be written in their present form. His conclusion was that "well-nigh the same stories that were told of Finn and his warrior braves by the Gael of the eleventh century are told in well-nigh the same way by his descendant to-day."

Nutt did not ask how long the stories were told before the first was written down. But Larminie — whose early death, Lady Gregory said, was the first great loss of the Irish intellectual movement — pushed them back into untold ages, in the introduction to his West Irish Folk Tales and Romances. He argued, carefully and in detail, that the Scottish Highlands and Ireland received their folklore from both "Aryan and non-Aryan sources," and that there is more non-Aryan influence and blood in the Highlands than in Ireland. Nothing, he said, is less likely than that all folk-tales are Aryan. They bear the stamp of more than one race: the pure, placid, often cold imagination of the Aryan in some; in others, the more picturesque fancy, the fierceness and sensuality, the finer sense of artistic elegance, of older peoples.
