And since the greatest art has often come from a blending of Aryan with other blood, he thought the same might be true in the humbler realm of the folk-tale.

Larminie divided the larger body of Irish legend into three cycles: the divine, the heroic, and the Fenian. The Fenian cycle was so well known by word of mouth in Scotland that people had argued over which country it belonged to — and in fact, he said, it belonged to both. But the divine cycle was, as far as he knew, wholly unknown in Scotland, and the heroic cycle comparatively unknown. Why? Professor Zimmer had not established his view that Finn was a late historical figure, and scholarly opinion had been moving towards seeing Finn as mythical. Mr O'Grady, seeing the difficulty while still believing Finn historical, had placed him before Cuchulain and his companions — but that could not stand once Finn was understood not to be historical at all.

There remained one explanation, Larminie said. The bodies of legend came into Ireland earlier or later with the different races they belonged to. The wider spread of the Finn saga showed it belonged to an early people who had lived in both Ireland and Scotland. Then came the Aryan Gael, who ruled the island, and whose own bards sang his own gods and heroes — a court poetry, an aristocratic literature. When the Gael conquered Scotland he brought his gods and heroes with him, but the bardic system never took hold there, so only faint echoes of the heroic cycle survived in the northern mountains. In Ireland itself the heroic cycle survived almost entirely through bardic writing; the people had all but forgotten it, if they ever knew it. But they had not forgotten the Fenian cycle. It was everywhere, still loved by the conquered peoples, holding its ground in Scotland and Ireland alike, and in Ireland forcing its way even into written literature, so gaining a double lease of life. The Fenian cycle, in a word, was non-Aryan folk-literature partly given Aryan treatment.

The whole problem, Lady Gregory said, is extremely complex, and others had written on it. Mr Borlase, for instance, had argued in his big book on the dolmens that the cromlechs — and so, presumably, the legend of Diarmuid and Grania — were connected with old religious rites of an erotic kind, coming down from a very primitive state of society.

She came to her own conclusion less by weight of argument than because she found it impossible to arrange the stories in any coherent form while she thought of them as history. She had tried to build on the Annalists and fit the Fianna into a definite historical period, but the whole story seemed trivial and incoherent until she began to think of them as almost contemporary with the battle of Magh Tuireadh, which even the Annalists put back into mythical ages. In this she followed some of the storytellers, who made the mother of Lugh of the Long Hand the grandmother of Finn, and gave Finn a shield soaked in the blood of Balor. She could not think of any of the stories as modern in origin, or believe that the century in which each was written down said anything about its age. "How Diarmuid got his Love-Spot," for instance, taken down only a few years before by Dr Hyde from an old man's recitation, might well be as old as "Finn and the Phantoms," which is in one of the earliest manuscripts. There was as good evidence, she said, for Finn being of the blood of the gods as for his being, as some of the people told her, "the son of an O'Shaughnessy who lived at Kiltartan Cross."

Dr Douglas Hyde, though he had placed the Fenian cycle after the Cuchulain cycle in his History of Irish Literature, allowed her to print his view: that while he believed the Fenians really existed, as a body of household troops who lived, ruled and hunted in King Cormac's time, it was equally certain that hundreds of stories, traits and legends far older and more primitive than anything they themselves could have given rise to had gathered around them. There was probably as much primitive mythology in the Finn legend as in that of the Red Branch. The story of the Fenians was a kind of nucleus to which a great deal of the flotsam and jetsam of a far older period had attached itself, and so been preserved.

Since she could not give the stories a historical date, Lady Gregory, without adding anything to support her theory, left out names such as Cormac and Art and other more or less historical figures, putting "the High King" in their place. In the Battle of the White Strand she left out the name of Caelur, Tadg's wife, because she had already followed another chronicler in giving him Ethlinn for a wife. And in the earlier part of the book she gave back to Angus Og the name of "the Disturber," which she believed had strayed from him to the saint of the same name.

III. The Authorities

Lady Gregory listed the authorities that had most helped her, in putting the stories together and in translating the texts. She said the list could not be quite exact, since she had sometimes moved a phrase, or a whole passage, from one story to another where it seemed to fit better, and sometimes, in the second part of the book, used stories preserved in Scottish Gaelic. She wrote her notes away from any library, and could not check them, but thought them fairly correct.

She said she had followed no fixed rule for spelling Irish names. She took her spellings from various good authorities, but they varied so much that complete accuracy was not easy, and she sometimes went by custom and convenience. She used "Slieve" for "Sliabh," for instance, because it came up so often and a mispronunciation would spoil so many names. She treated "Inbhir," a river-mouth, the same way, spelling it "Inver," and even adopting it as an English word, because it was so useful. The forty scholars of the new school of Old Irish, she said, would do good service if they worked at the spelling and pronunciation of the old names and settled them as far as possible.
